article_title: PAX Good Behavior Game — Reading
citation: Evidence for Learning. (2023). PAX Good Behavior Game (Evidence Rating). https://evidenceforlearning.org
title: Team-based group contingency for behavior management
description: The PAX Good Behavior Game organizes classroom behavior management around a group contingency: students are divided into two or more teams, and when a member violates class rules "discussed and agreed upon by the students themselves", the team receives a check mark. The team with the fewest checkmarks, or all teams meeting a set criterion, receives a small privilege such as lining up first for recess. This structure is "intended to create a situation in which students encourage and assist their peers to behave appropriately".
requirements: class rules discussed and agreed upon by the students themselves
teacher monitoring of student behavior
small privileges as reinforcers
target_learning_goals: self-regulation and appropriate classroom behavior
examples: Teams receive checkmarks on a whiteboard for rule violations; the winning team or all qualifying teams receive a small privilege such as lining up first for recess.
key_sources: Evidence for Learning. (2023). PAX Good Behavior Game (Evidence Rating). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/pax-good-behavior-game-reading/

article_title: Classworks Math
citation: Classworks Individualized Learning. (2022). Evidence summary. https://www.classworks.com
title: Teachers should actively monitor progress and reassign assignments to support mastery in individualized learning programs
description: The summary presents teacher monitoring as essential to realizing the program's benefit: "To ensure the optimal impact of Classworks Individualized Learning, it is essential for teachers to actively monitor student progress and reassign assignments as needed to support student mastery." Individualized paths only produce learning when adults track progress and adjust assignments rather than letting the software run unattended.
requirements: Teachers have access to student progress data and the ability to reassign instructional units
target_learners: Students using individualized online intervention units
target_learning_goals: Skill mastery in intervention contexts
examples: Classworks implementation guidance directs teachers to monitor progress and reassign assignments as needed during use of Individualized Learning Paths
key_sources: Classworks Individualized Learning. (2022). Evidence summary. https://www.classworks.com

article_title: PAX Good Behavior Game — Math
citation: PAX Good Behavior Game. (2021). Evidence Rating. https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/pax-good-behavior-game/
title: Team-based group contingency with checkmarks and small privileges to encourage peer support for appropriate behavior
description: The pattern divides students into two or more teams and applies a group contingency: when a team member violates class rules, the team receives a checkmark on the whiteboard, and the team with the fewest checkmarks, or all teams meeting a criterion, receives a small privilege such as lining up first for recess. The summary states "This group contingency is intended to create a situation in which students encourage and assist their peers to behave appropriately."
requirements: Class rules must be discussed and agreed upon by the students themselves
Teacher monitoring of student behavior during lessons
constraints: Privileges are small, such as the opportunity to line up first for recess
target_learning_goals: self- and peer-regulation of classroom behavior
examples: Teams receive checkmarks on the whiteboard for rule violations; the winning team or all teams meeting criterion line up first for recess.

article_title: Megastudies Improve the Impact of Applied Behavioural Science
citation: Kautz, T., Milkman, K. L., Gromet, D., et al. as printed in full author line. (2021). Megastudies Improve the Impact of Applied Behavioural Science. Nature, vol. 600. https://www.nature.com
title: Test many intervention ideas at once in a shared population and outcome to improve the evidentiary value of behavioural science
description: The article recommends running many interventions concurrently in the same population on the same objectively measured outcome for the same duration, because typical scattered studies lack comparability. Because "Forecasts by impartial judges failed to predict which interventions would be most effective," the authors argue this "underscor[es] the value of testing many ideas at once and, therefore, the potential for megastudies to improve the evidentiary value of behavioural science."
requirements: A large shared population, an objectively measured outcome held constant across arms, a fixed duration, and multiple independent teams designing interventions.
constraints: In the demonstrated megastudy, only 8% of interventions produced behaviour change significant and measurable after the four-week intervention, so parallel testing does not guarantee durable effects.
target_learners: Adults targeted by applied behavioural-science interventions, here fitness-chain members
target_learning_goals: Identifying which behaviour-change interventions work, e.g. increasing physical exercise
examples: 30 scientists from 15 different US universities worked in small independent teams to design 54 different four-week digital programmes encouraging exercise, all compared on the same gym-attendance outcome.
key_sources: Kautz, T., Milkman, K. L., Gromet, D., et al. as printed in full author line. (2021). Megastudies Improve the Impact of Applied Behavioural Science. Nature, vol. 600. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/megastudies-improve-the-impact-of-applied-behavioural-science

article_title: Technical Methods Report: The Estimation of Average Treatment Effects for Clustered RCTs of Education Interventions
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2009). Technical Methods Report: The Estimation of Average Treatment Effects for Clustered RCTs of Education Interventions. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Test the sensitivity of RCT impact findings using different estimation methods and cluster-level weighting schemes
description: Because standard errors from alternative estimators of treatment effects in clustered RCTs can differ, the report's key recommendation is that analysts "test the sensitivity of their impact findings using different estimation methods and cluster-level weighting schemes". This guards policy conclusions against dependence on a single estimator choice.
requirements: Access to data from the clustered RCT so impacts can be re-estimated under alternative estimators and weighting schemes
constraints: The recommendation is made in the context of two-stage clustered RCTs of education interventions
target_learners: students in education interventions evaluated through clustered RCTs
target_learning_goals: robust estimation and reporting of intervention effects
examples: The report's empirical analysis re-estimated impacts and standard errors for five large-scale clustered education RCTs using the considered estimators
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2009). Technical Methods Report: The Estimation of Average Treatment Effects for Clustered RCTs of Education Interventions. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: Classroom Composition Affects Teacher Performance Ratings
citation: Delgado, W., & Sartain, L. (2026). Classroom composition affects teacher performance ratings. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 48(2).
title: Interpret teacher performance ratings as partly reflecting classroom composition, since teachers working with more challenging students may be systematically undervalued
description: The article's central principle is that "Teacher performance ratings do not purely reflect teaching quality—they are also shaped by the students in the classroom." Evaluation systems should therefore account for classroom context when interpreting ratings, because teachers assigned more challenging students may be undervalued, with equity consequences for groups such as Black teachers.
requirements: Awareness of the classroom composition measures (prior achievement, attendance, behavior, demographics, class size) that influence ratings.
constraints: Effects were driven by academic and behavioral factors rather than demographics for observation ratings; the bias interpretation rests on the absence of corresponding effects in student growth measures.
target_learners: K-12 teachers in urban public school districts
target_learning_goals: Fair and accurate measurement of teaching quality for tenure, promotion, and dismissal decisions
examples: In Chicago Public Schools data, teachers received higher ratings when assigned students with higher prior achievement, more regular attendance, and fewer behavioral challenges.
key_sources: Delgado, W., & Sartain, L. (2026). Classroom composition affects teacher performance ratings. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 48(2). https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/classroom-composition-affects-teacher-performance-ratings

article_title: Do Classroom Environments Matter for Noncognitive Aspects of Student Performance and Students' Course Grades?
citation: Camille A. Farrington, Shanette Porter, Joshua Klugman. (2019). Do Classroom Environments Matter for Noncognitive Aspects of Student Performance and Students' Course Grades? University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Teachers have more influence over student motivation than they may often assume
description: Because within-student analyses showed a sizable relationship between classroom environment and students' self-reported motivation in a specific class (β=0.234), the article concludes that teacher practice shapes motivation rather than motivation being a fixed student trait. The article states: "This suggests that teachers have much more influence over student motivation than they may often assume." Classrooms with more teacher support, organization, goal clarity, relevance, meaningful work, and positive community were associated with higher student motivation in that class.
requirements: Teachers shape classroom environments through behaviors and instructional practices that students perceive, such as support, goal clarity, and relevance
constraints: The evidence is correlational within-student; the article calls for rigorous experimental or quasi-experimental designs to build causal knowledge
target_learning_goals: Supporting student motivation to work hard in class
examples: Students reported greater motivation to do well in classrooms their classmates rated more highly on teacher support, organization, goal clarity, relevance, and community than in their own lower-rated classrooms
key_sources: Camille A. Farrington, Shanette Porter, Joshua Klugman. (2019). Do Classroom Environments Matter for Noncognitive Aspects of Student Performance and Students' Course Grades? University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/do-classroom-environments-matter-for-noncognitive-aspects-of-student-performance-and-students-course-grades

article_title: How Did Chicago Connected Broadband Access Affect Remote Learning During COVID-19?
citation: Schachner, J.N., Marwell, N.P., de la Torre, M., Gwynne, J.A., & Allensworth, E.M. (2025). How did Chicago Connected broadband access eligibility and participation affect remote learning engagement and achievement during the COVID-19 pandemic? Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai25-1153
title: Treat expanded technology access as potentially a double-edged sword and identify which students need additional supports alongside access
description: The article's policy takeaway is that broadband expansion alone may not uniformly help students: "technology access may be a double-edged sword for student engagement and achievement." It recommends that as access expands, families, educators, and policymakers learn which students most need additional supports, and calls for mixed-methods research on how high-achieving students leverage digital technologies and why low-achieving students experience setbacks.
requirements: Programs expanding technology access should be paired with identification of students likely to need additional supports
constraints: Findings come from pandemic-era Chicago; the authors note effects may look different in non-pandemic contexts and other locations
target_learners: Grade 5-8 students in urban public school districts receiving expanded broadband access
target_learning_goals: Remote learning engagement
Academic achievement (GPA)
examples: The study examined Chicago Connected, which aimed to connect 100,000 students in 60,000 households to free broadband for up to four years starting summer 2020
key_sources: Schachner, J.N., Marwell, N.P., de la Torre, M., Gwynne, J.A., & Allensworth, E.M. (2025). How did Chicago Connected broadband access eligibility and participation affect remote learning engagement and achievement during the COVID-19 pandemic? Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai25-1153

article_title: The learning curve: Revisiting within-year linear growth assumptions
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2021). The learning curve: Revisiting within-year linear growth assumptions. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 14:1, 143-171.
title: Test the linearity of within-year growth assumptions before using growth estimates for policy decisions
description: This principle holds that research and policy uses of achievement growth should first verify the assumption of linear within-year growth, because related research has relied on a "mostly untested assumption: that growth in achievement is linear throughout the entire school year." The article tests this assumption directly with seasonal score data and finds it often unjustified, particularly in reading, so growth estimates for policy should not default to linearity.
requirements: Achievement data collected at multiple within-year time points (fall, winter, spring) to test seasonal growth patterns
constraints: The article reports the assumption is especially problematic in reading
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of annual learning for policy decisions such as school-year length
examples: The authors examined the assumption using math and reading test scores for over seven million students across three seasonal time points in 2016-17
key_sources: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2021). The learning curve: Revisiting within-year linear growth assumptions. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 14:1, 143-171. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/35099/

article_title: Practitioner-reported Needs for Enacting, Implementing, and Adopting OpenSciEd Curriculum Materials
citation: McElhaney, K., Urban, R., Kamdar, D., Baker, A., Tsai, K., and Roschelle, J. (2024). Practitioner-reported Needs for Enacting, Implementing, and Adopting OpenSciEd Curriculum Materials [White paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/215
title: District implementation of OpenSciEd should value teachers' assets and give teachers agency and voice in adoption and enactment decisions
description: The report's focus groups indicate that district adoption approaches promoting teacher agency support buy-in, particularly from experienced teachers accustomed to non-practice-based pedagogy. One leader described balancing non-negotiable core principles with "negotiable" elements such as lesson sequence and timing, so that teachers "felt like they had some say in what was going to be most important." The report concludes that such an approach "promotes teachers’ agency in the process" and that valuing teachers' assets could especially help create buy-in from experienced teachers.
requirements: District culture of enabling and supporting teachers, including time and space for peer collaboration and support for finding and accessing OpenSciEd resources
constraints: The authors note such adoption and implementation models could introduce new organizational tensions, such as with districts' accountability to state standards or allocation of time and resources for teacher PL
target_learners: middle and high school science teachers
district and school leaders implementing OpenSciEd
target_learning_goals: teacher buy-in and sustained implementation of phenomenon-based science instruction
examples: A district leader described designating some enactment elements as negotiable, such as lesson sequence and timing, while holding all teachers to shared core principles
key_sources: McElhaney, K., Urban, R., Kamdar, D., Baker, A., Tsai, K., and Roschelle, J. (2024). Practitioner-reported Needs for Enacting, Implementing, and Adopting OpenSciEd Curriculum Materials [White paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/215

article_title: ATS Field Note — Using AI in Prototyping
citation: McGurl, C. & Maisscotte, B. (2026). ATS Field Note: Using AI in Prototyping. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/298
title: Test designs in working prototype form rather than as polished concepts or wireframes
description: The article recommends using AI to move quickly from concepts such as wireframes to functional prototypes users can interact with and give feedback on. AI-generated wireflows looked logical and complete on paper, but once turned into a simple working prototype, problems became obvious: too many clicks, poor timing of key information, and recommendations that did not match teacher needs.
requirements: Small, testable prototypes updated more often, so educators can interact with the tool and give concrete feedback
constraints: Paper wireframes alone hid usability problems such as excessive clicks, poor information timing, and mismatched recommendations
target_learners: K-2 educators providing feedback on literacy tool prototypes
target_learning_goals: Early surfacing of usability issues and avoidance of costly rework
examples: Educators interacting with a working prototype gave feedback such as "I need this earlier," or "I wouldn't use this," which helped the team refine ideas early
key_sources: McGurl, C. & Maisscotte, B. (2026). ATS Field Note: Using AI in Prototyping. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/298

article_title: The Art and Science of Learning: How New Mexico School for the Arts Uses Research
citation: The Art and Science of Learning: How New Mexico School for the Arts Uses Research. (2016). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Adopt research-based practice school-wide by aligning professional development so each teacher selects, implements, monitors, and presents one research-based strategy per year
description: Starting in fall 2016 NMSA required each teacher to select one research-based strategy from the training, create an implementation plan, monitor modifications based on data, and present learnings to the school community in the spring. Leaders report that freedom to choose a strategy of interest "improves buy-in," and teachers discuss improvement ideas with colleagues.
requirements: Administrative support and time for teachers to carry out small research projects; the article quotes that what it takes is "support from the administration"
target_learners: high school teachers as adult learners
target_learning_goals: evidence-based instructional practice
teacher agency in applying learning sciences research
examples: Teachers share learnings informally throughout the year and in a formal spring presentation; Montoya reported improved state math assessment performance while focusing on learning rather than drill and kill
key_sources: The Art and Science of Learning: How New Mexico School for the Arts Uses Research. (2016). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/4e829bdc-764f-4f2e-85de-abc138e21bdd

article_title: Teaching Partner, Grading Assistant, Substitute Teacher: Three Ways Teachers Positioned an Artificial Intelligence Tool in Writing Instruction
citation: Hillary Greene Nolan, Ph.D, Merijke Coenraad, Ph.D, Viki Young, Ph.D. (2024). Teaching Partner, Grading Assistant, Substitute Teacher: Three Ways Teachers Positioned an Artificial Intelligence Tool in Writing Instruction. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Keep the teacher at the instructional helm when AI tools enter writing instruction
description: The article argues that AI tools should augment rather than replace the teacher's instructional role. Citing the US Department of Education's insistence that "teachers remain at the helm of major instructional decisions" and Warshauer Freedman et al.'s caution that "the role of the teacher must be augmented rather than diminished," the study treats the partner positioning, in which the teacher stays instructional leader and the AI is one tool among many, as the approach associated with richer instruction, learning-focused interactions, and student AI literacy.
requirements: Teachers need AI awareness of the tool's biases and limitations to partner with it effectively
Preparation and framing before platform use supported the partner approach in the study
constraints: The study is observational and qualitative; it describes associations between positioning and practice, not tested causal effects
target_learners: Students in writing classrooms adopting AI tools
target_learning_goals: Argumentative writing
AI literacy
Teacher professional judgment with automated feedback
examples: Partner teachers in the study wove Topeka into existing practice, conferenced with students, re-taught based on score data, and taught students how the AI works
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Ruiz, P., Lee, K., Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., Roschelle, J., & Weisgrau, J. (2024). AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/218
title: Teach AI literacy practices without AI tools, particularly in the early grades
description: The report recommends that AI literacy skill development begin offline: 'each of these practices can be learned and/or taught without the use of an AI tool.' The authors 'suggest that learners should explicitly engage in AI literacy skill development (such as analyzing and organizing datasets) without AI tools, particularly in the early grades,' so that foundational practices are built before learners apply them to AI tools.
requirements: Educators identify offline analogues for each AI literacy practice, such as analyzing and organizing datasets without AI tools
constraints: Recommended particularly for early grades
target_learning_goals: foundational AI literacy practices such as data analysis and algorithmic thinking
examples: The report suggests analyzing and organizing datasets as an offline AI literacy activity for young learners
key_sources: Mills, K., Ruiz, P., Lee, K., Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., Roschelle, J., & Weisgrau, J. (2024). AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/218

article_title: Challenge-Based Learning for Global Competence and Employability
citation: April Williamson. (2024). Challenge-Based Learning for Global Competence and Employability. Digital Promise, ISTELive Global Collaboration Playground. https://www.acteonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Career_Readiness_Paper_COLOR.pdf
title: Position teachers as designers and facilitators within challenge-based learning
description: The presentation states that CBL "Promotes teachers as designers and facilitators", assigning educators the role of designing challenge-based experiences and facilitating student investigation and action rather than delivering content directly. The Ciena Solutions Challenge supports this role with a Facilitation Guide and free online courses for educators.
requirements: Educator capacity-building supports such as facilitation guides and online courses
target_learning_goals: Designing and facilitating real-world challenge projects for students
examples: The Ciena Solutions Challenge provides a Facilitation Guide and Challenge Builder to help educators design and run CBL projects
key_sources: April Williamson. (2024). Challenge-Based Learning for Global Competence and Employability. Digital Promise, ISTELive Global Collaboration Playground. https://www.acteonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Career_Readiness_Paper_COLOR.pdf

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Build transdisciplinary teams that reflect served communities and balance power dynamics
description: Fresh perspectives, ideas from other sectors, and innovative partnerships — grounded in strong understanding of the education sector and problems of practice — are key to developing novel solutions to persistent challenges. Teams "should include representatives from research, industry, and education practice/policy" and "should reflect the communities they serve." Teams must also set up conditions for productive interdisciplinary participation and ensure that power dynamics do not favor one perspective over another.
requirements: Conditions for productive interdisciplinary participation; power dynamics balanced across perspectives
target_learning_goals: developing completely novel ideas for persistent education challenges
examples: The note lists research, industry, and education practice/policy as the three team constituencies
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

article_title: Designing Student Success Systems Intentionally: How Warwick Public Schools and Panorama Bridge the Gap with Co-Designed Technical Solutions
citation: Cocuzza, B., Noakes, S., Aso, C., Goldschmidt, L., and Bennett, K. (2026). Designing student success systems intentionally: How Warwick Public Schools and Panorama bridge the gap with co-designed technical solutions. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/303
title: Design AI-enabled tools around immediate teacher needs and preserve human oversight in AI workflows
description: The article recommends that AI in student success systems support routine tasks within larger workflows rather than open-ended deliverables, and that solutions be designed around immediate teacher needs rather than district priorities alone. It advises that "AI-embedded workflows should lessen administrative burden and produce consistent results," and that classroom, school, and district perspectives all be considered so solutions are needs-driven. Warwick's own shift after low uptake was from top-down to bottom-up AI development aligned with actual teacher pain points.
requirements: Involve teachers in co-design conversations from the outset
Ensure classroom, school, and district perspectives are considered in designing new functionalities
constraints: AI is suited to routine tasks where users know they need the task and have a clear perspective on the output; open-ended tasks requiring heavy scrutiny of prompting and product are not
target_learners: Solution providers building AI-enabled education tools
target_learning_goals: Successful adoption of AI-enabled student success tools
Human-centered AI implementation in schools
examples: Warwick leadership used usage data to shift development of the next custom tools toward user pain points rather than district priorities
key_sources: Cocuzza, B., Noakes, S., Aso, C., Goldschmidt, L., and Bennett, K. (2026). Designing student success systems intentionally: How Warwick Public Schools and Panorama bridge the gap with co-designed technical solutions. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/303

article_title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom
citation: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Teach and reinforce new skills to increase appropriate behavior and preserve a positive classroom climate
description: Just as explicit instruction can remediate academic skill deficits, it can teach students the social and behavioral skills they are expected to exhibit at school. Teachers should actively teach socially and behaviorally appropriate replacement skills to individual students and the whole class, so that "teachers help students with behavior problems learn how, when, and where to use these new skills", and should manage consequences so reinforcers follow appropriate behavior and are withheld for inappropriate behavior. This recommendation carries the panel's strong evidence rating.
requirements: Identify where the student needs explicit instruction for appropriate behavior
Teach skills by providing examples, practice, and feedback
Manage consequences so that reinforcers are provided for appropriate behavior and withheld for inappropriate behavior
constraints: Acquiring positive behaviors takes time; the guide notes challenging behaviors are learned over a long period and progress monitoring with celebration of small achievements helps sustain effort
target_learners: Elementary general education students (K-5) with behavior skill deficits
target_learning_goals: Socially and behaviorally appropriate replacement behaviors and adaptive skills
examples: The guide frames the parallel with academics: some students' failure to meet behavioral expectations reflects deficits in specific social or behavioral skills, addressed through explicit instruction and consistent positive reinforcement.
key_sources: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/4

article_title: Encouraging Girls in Math and Science
citation: Halpern, D., Aronson, J., Reimer, N., Simpkins, S., Star, J., and Wentzel, K. (2007). Encouraging Girls in Math and Science (NCER 2007-2003). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Research, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncer.ed.gov
title: Explicitly teach students that academic abilities are expandable and improvable through effort
description: Teachers should communicate that math and science abilities can be improved through consistent effort and learning, because students who view abilities as fixed experience decreased confidence and performance when facing setbacks. The guide's evidence summary states that "when students are taught that intelligence and abilities can be increased with hard work, their test scores and their grades improve." Teachers can discuss neuroscience showing brains grow new synaptic connections with practice and remind struggling students that understanding gets easier over time.
requirements: Teachers themselves must examine and modify preconceptions that intelligence and abilities are fixed at birth
Teachers remind students of malleability both when they struggle and when they make progress
constraints: Some adults favor natural-ability explanations for success, making it harder to convince students that effort matters
target_learners: K-12 students, especially girls in math and science
target_learning_goals: Accurate beliefs about the malleability of academic ability
Persistence in the face of difficult math and science material
examples: The panel rated this recommendation Moderate based on two small experimental studies with K-12 students, one experimental study with college students, and supporting correlational research.
key_sources: Halpern, D., Aronson, J., Reimer, N., Simpkins, S., Star, J., and Wentzel, K. (2007). Encouraging Girls in Math and Science (NCER 2007-2003). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Research, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/5

article_title: Teaching Math to Young Children
citation: Frye, D., Baroody, A. J., Burchinal, M., Carver, S. M., Jordan, N. C., & McDowell, J. (2013). Teaching math to young children: A practice guide (NCEE 2014-4005). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Teach number and operations using a developmental progression, starting with subitizing small collections
description: The guide's first recommendation establishes number and operations as the foundational early math content area and prescribes an ordered sequence: "First, provide opportunities for children to practice recognizing the total number of objects in small collections (one to three items) and labeling them with a number word without needing to count them." Teachers then promote one-to-one counting, counting-based comparison of quantities, labeling collections with number words and numerals, and finally solving basic problems, moving from small to progressively larger collections at each step.
requirements: Instruction must build on the knowledge children already possess and identify the next developmental step
Children should first work with small collections of one to three objects before moving to larger collections
constraints: The evidence supports number and operations instruction generally, not any particular developmental progression
target_learners: children ages 3 to 6 in preschool, prekindergarten, and kindergarten
target_learning_goals: subitizing
one-to-one counting and cardinality
comparing quantities
basic arithmetic problems
examples: The Basic Hiding game practices subitizing by covering one to three objects and asking children how many are hidden; snack-time and transition moments are used for quick "How many?" practice.
key_sources: Frye, D., Baroody, A. J., Burchinal, M., Carver, S. M., Jordan, N. C., & McDowell, J. (2013). Teaching math to young children: A practice guide (NCEE 2014-4005). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/18

article_title: Teaching Math to Young Children
citation: Frye, D., Baroody, A. J., Burchinal, M., Carver, S. M., Jordan, N. C., & McDowell, J. (2013). Teaching math to young children: A practice guide (NCEE 2014-4005). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Teach geometry, patterns, measurement, and data analysis using a developmental progression alongside number
description: The guide's second recommendation extends developmental-progression teaching beyond number to four other content areas. It advises: "Help children to recognize, name, and compare shapes, and then teach them to combine and separate shapes," and similarly to have children identify then extend, correct, and create patterns, make direct comparisons and use informal and formal measurement units, and collect, organize, and graphically represent information. The panel argues early experience in these areas prepares children for later subjects such as algebra and statistics.
requirements: Material in each content area must be organized according to a developmental progression
constraints: This recommendation received a minimal evidence rating; supporting studies combined it with other practices
target_learners: children ages 3 to 6 in preschool, prekindergarten, and kindergarten
target_learning_goals: shape recognition, combining and separating
pattern extension and creation
measurement with informal and formal units
collecting, organizing, and graphing data
examples: Examples include the Shapes game, creating and extending patterns, a favorites survey represented graphically, and vocabulary tables for types of measurement.

article_title: Teaching Strategies for Improving Algebra Knowledge in Middle and High School Students
citation: Star, J. R., Caronongan, P., Foegen, A., Furgeson, J., Keating, B., Larson, M. R., Lyskawa, J., McCallum, W. G., Porath, J., & Zbiek, R. M. (2015). description: This recommendation directs teachers to make the underlying mathematical features and relationships of expressions, equations, and graphs explicit through precise mathematical language, reflective questioning, and comparison of alternative representations. The guide states that "Paying attention to structure helps students make connections among problems, solution strategies, and representations that may initially appear different but are actually mathematically similar." Steps include promoting language that reflects mathematical structure, encouraging reflective questioning while solving, and teaching that different forms of the same equation convey different information.

Using precise mathematical language
Comparing multiple representations of the same relationship

A reflective-questioning poster lists questions such as asking what relationships exist between quantities in an expression

description: The guide recommends incorporating technologies that model and foster self-regulated learning strategies, such as interactive interfaces supporting strategy use, text-based reminders and prompts, individualized emails based on student goals and performance, and tools for students to monitor their own progress. description: One of the guide's four overarching themes, based on the panelists' judgment and experience, is that "Technology is best used to facilitate and enhance advising, not to replace advisors." article_title: Exploring Coaching for Powerful Technology Use in Education
citation: Tina Ehsanipour & Florencia Gomez Zaccarelli. (2017). Exploring Coaching for Powerful Technology Use in Education. Center to Support Excellence in Teaching - Stanford University. https://ce.stanford.edu
title: Keep technology in a supportive rather than starring role, and have technology experts coach the coaches so content stays central
description: Because "technology integration is not the ultimate goal; rather the goal is to engage students in authentic problem-solving," technology should support learning goals rather than drive them. The paper recommends a coach-the-coaches model in which content-specific instructional coaches receive technology training, or alternatively a collaboration between a technology-expert coach and teachers who are content experts, so content stays in the starring role.
requirements: Coaches need expertise in the teacher's specific content area in addition to technology expertise
constraints: This may pose a challenge in schools where there is at most one technology coach to begin with
target_learning_goals: Meaningful technology integration in service of content-area learning goals
examples: The paper describes Dinse de Salas and colleagues' (2016) alternative: a coach expert in technology collaborating with coached teachers who are the experts in their domains' content

article_title: Potholes on the Road to College
citation: Roderick, M., Coca, V., & Nagaoka, J. (2011). title: Teacher Assessment of College-going Climate measure
description: A new school-level measure developed by the authors to capture whether teachers express shared goals, behaviors, and obligations regarding college attendance. It is based on teachers' responses to five questions on the 2005 CCSR high school teacher survey, covering teacher expectations, help with college planning outside class, curriculum focus on college readiness, job responsibility for college preparation, and perceived student college plans. The measure was constructed using Rasch rating scale analysis and represents the average of teacher reports in the high school. Approximately 4,000 teachers in 87 high schools responded.

Four-year college enrollment
College match

title: Teaching is My Favorite Color: a three-district regional support ecosystem for teachers of color
description: Teaching is My Favorite Color was developed by Avonworth, Hampton Township, and South Fayette Township school districts as "an initiative to create a holistic ecosystem of support for teachers of color across the Southwest Pittsburgh region." It had four vital elements: empowerment and amplification of voices, building a sense of belonging, professional development opportunities, and attracting and retaining diverse teachers. Activities included a social hour with a guest speaker and a convening with breakout sessions such as "Having an Affirming Classroom for Students of Color."
requirements: Combined resources and insights across districts; emphasis on support for new and early-career teachers of color

target_learning_goals: Belonging, professional growth, recruitment and retention of teachers of color

article_title: The Center of Black Student Excellence: A Place without Barriers and the 10 Elements That Lay Its Foundation
citation: Powell, K. (2024). The center of black student excellence: A place without barriers and the 10 elements that lay its foundation. Long Beach Unified School District. https://www.wested.org
title: The 10 Elements of Black Excellence as an organizing design pattern
description: The brief organizes the Center's foundation around 10 Elements of Black Excellence: Empowering Genius, Overcoming Systemic Barriers, Embracing Black Identity, Liberating Greatness, Elevating Intergenerational Wisdom, Promoting Advocacy and Awareness, Centering Health and Well-Being, Uplifting the Community, Encouraging Authenticity, and Cultivating Beauty and Joy. Each element emerged from recurring themes in community listening sessions and is elaborated with community quotes, a collective definition, Center aims, and practical approaches. The brief notes "These elements were identified and named based on the expressed envisioning of representative voices of LBUSD's Black Community" and that no element is ordered above another.
requirements: Each element is discussed with direct community quotes, a collective definition, plausible Center aims, and practical approaches
constraints: Elements are not displayed in any particular order; each shares equal importance per the brief
target_learning_goals: Belonging, cultural pride, advocacy, well-being, and academic excellence
examples: Each element section pairs community quotes with Center strategies, such as mentorship programs, cultural programming, and wellness services

article_title: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment
citation: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment. (2024). WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Ten Aspects of Community framework for organizing youth-supporting community assets
description: The Ten Aspects of Community, developed by the Forum for Youth Investment (Pittman et al., 2003, based on Pittman & Irby, 1996), is a taxonomy of community features that directly affect youth. The report states it "defines Ten Aspects of Community": Basic Services; Cultural and Artistic; Economic; Civic and Political; Education and Information; Health and Human Services; Individual Development; Physical; Social and Associational; and Spiritual and Religious. The needs assessment used this framework to organize and categorize the county's community assets and services data by aspect and by Supervisorial District.
requirements: Community assets and services data must be classifiable into the ten aspects for the framework to organize the inventory
constraints: Applied in this report to Yolo County community assets and services for children, youth, and families, organized also by Supervisorial District
target_learners: Children, youth, and families in Yolo County
target_learning_goals: Healthy youth development through access to community assets and services, including education and information resources
examples: The team refined and categorized Yolo County community assets and services according to the Ten Aspects of Community, sourcing data from Concordia's asset mapping and 211 Yolo's databases

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work Beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities With Formative Assessment. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://www.wested.org/
title: Scaffolding is temporary, contingent support that is adjusted or removed as students grow in competence — not simplified content
description: The brief defines instructional scaffolding as "an intentionally designed and thoughtfully implemented system of temporary support that allows students to engage with content" they cannot yet accomplish independently. It explicitly warns against confusing scaffolding with doing the thinking for students or reducing access to grade-level content. Once students' independent capabilities expand, scaffolding is adjusted or removed, supporting emerging autonomy.
requirements: Support must be structured and contingent, provided by a teacher or peer for tasks students cannot yet do alone
Educators need ongoing professional learning to enact this work
constraints: Scaffolding should not be kept in place indefinitely
It must not mean simplifying content or reducing, postponing, or limiting access to grade-level content
target_learners: English learners at any level of English proficiency
target_learning_goals: Access to and participation in grade-level conceptual, analytic, and linguistic disciplinary practices
examples: The brief states students can engage in disciplinary practices such as using mathematical models or comparing character development in literature given appropriate support

article_title: AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle
citation: Ruiz, P., and Noakes, S. (2025). AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/272
title: Establish comprehensive support systems and teacher-involved planning to implement AI-enabled edtech
description: The article argues effective implementation requires comprehensive support systems including professional learning, clear usage guidelines, and usage tracking to prevent purchased tools going unused. It emphasizes that "Teachers must be directly involved in developing implementation strategies to ensure that AI tools are integrated meaningfully," and that vendor-district partnerships should co-design implementation plans with educators.

Vendor partnerships providing research-based recommendations and co-designed implementation plans
Attention to hardware requirements, scheduling constraints, and classroom logistics

article_title: From Childcare to Educare: Inspiring Change in Early Childhood Education for Rural Tennessee
citation: Jacobs, B., Babineau, K., Parker, D. (2024). From Childcare to Educare: Inspiring Change in Early Childhood Education for Rural Tennessee. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/222
title: TECTA: Tennessee Early Childhood Training Alliance
description: TECTA is 'a statewide program that provides free training and academic tuition support to childcare providers and administrators throughout the state of Tennessee.' It offers a free 30-hour orientation with instruction in five areas — center-based child care, infant/toddler care, family child care, school-age child care, and administrator training — after which participants become eligible for tuition assistance for coursework at any public higher education institution in Tennessee. Nine state and community colleges currently offer TECTA programs, which support workers pursuing the CDA, associate degree, and bachelor's degree, and provide CDA candidates with tuition assistance, textbooks, professional development, and application support.
requirements: Participation is open to any staff employed in a licensed child care facility in Tennessee; completing the free 30-hour orientation is the gateway to tuition assistance eligibility.
constraints: The program's stipend funds are limited and allocated on a first-come, first-served basis, creating financial barriers for those unable to secure funding promptly.
target_learners: childcare providers and administrators employed in licensed Tennessee child care facilities, including rural providers
target_learning_goals: early childhood education credentials (CDA, associate, bachelor's) and professional skills such as classroom management and professionalism
examples: Five focus groups with 80 service providers and one with 8 administrators were conducted between February and April 2024 to evaluate the program's benefits and barriers.

article_title: Using Data to Ensure That Teachers Are Learner Ready on Day One
citation: Data Quality Campaign. (2017). Using Data to Ensure That Teachers Are Learner Ready on Day One. https://www.dataqualitycampaign.org
title: Tennessee EPP report card combining public accountability with secure individual data access
description: Legislation passed in 2007 requires Tennessee's State Board of Education, Department of Education, and Higher Education Commission to produce a report card for all EPPs in the state. The report card includes quantitative data required by law (licensure pass rates, placement, retention, and teacher growth data) plus qualitative data such as principal observations, delivered through an online interactive tool and downloadable PDFs. The State Board also gives EPPs secure, non-public access to their graduates' individual teacher data, including value-add scores broken out by subject, for targeted program improvements.
requirements: Ongoing collaboration with EPPs so reports include data programs want and need
Investment in standardizing data collection and data cleaning to ensure reliable, correct information
Varying levels of access and specificity to balance stakeholder needs while protecting individual teacher data privacy
constraints: Graduates' individual teacher data, including value-add scores, is not available to the public
target_learning_goals: understanding graduates' performance to make targeted program improvements and informed enrollment and hiring decisions
examples: State leaders credit success to ongoing collaboration with EPPs, investment in high-quality accurate data, and emphasizing transparency while meeting the public's needs
key_sources: Data Quality Campaign. (2017). Using Data to Ensure That Teachers Are Learner Ready on Day One. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED586474

article_title: From the Brink of Closure: Key Factors in One Charter School's Successful Turnaround
citation: Evan, A. (2019). From the brink of closure: Key factors in one charter school's successful turnaround. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://dcpcsb.egnyte.com/dl/hdsUO9pDbh/
title: TenSquare's Data-Driven School Improvement Process
description: A continuous-improvement cycle in which a turnaround partner first conducts a comprehensive school performance audit covering academic, financial, and operational areas, then develops a multi-year redesign plan prioritized by intensity of focus, identifies evidence-based interventions, monitors implementation and impact toward goals, adjusts implementation, and provides ongoing feedback. At Perry Street the process began with an audit "to identify the areas in need of improvement — from academic to financial to operational" and its findings "served as the basis for the creation of a multifaceted five-year redesign plan."
requirements: A comprehensive baseline audit of performance, processes, and resources to set improvement goals
Ongoing progress-monitoring structures at board, leadership, and staff levels
constraints: The report presents this as one school's process; it states no framework should be a magic bullet and decisions should consider each school's needs and context
target_learners: Charter school leaders, board members, and authorizers pursuing school turnaround
target_learning_goals: School-wide organizational improvement and improved student achievement outcomes
examples: TenSquare's five-year engagement at Perry Street from May 2014 through 2018–19, moving from intense daily support to feedback-only consultation

article_title: Teacher Residency Programs in California: Financial Sustainability Challenges and Opportunities
citation: Hirschboeck, K., Eiler White, M., Brannegan, A., & Reade, F. (2022). Teacher residency programs in California: Financial sustainability challenges and opportunities. WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org
title: Teacher residency model: LEA–IHE partnership integrating coursework with a yearlong clinical placement under an expert mentor teacher
description: The teacher residency model is a pathway into teaching developed and operated by a partnership between an LEA and a state-approved preparation program at an IHE. The brief describes it as focusing on rigorous "clinical preparation" whereby "a resident's credentialing coursework is integrated with a yearlong placement in the classroom of an expert mentor teacher," with the resident gradually assuming increased responsibility. Financial supports such as living stipends or tuition reductions are central, lowering barriers for candidates from underrepresented or low-income backgrounds. In California, grants of $20,000 per resident funded 38 LEA–IHE partnerships targeting STEM, special education, and bilingual credential areas.
requirements: A partnership between an LEA and an IHE with a state-approved teacher preparation program
Financial supports (stipends or tuition reductions) so residents can complete a year of intensive clinical placement and coursework
An expert mentor teacher providing mentorship and regular observations and feedback
constraints: The brief notes California's grant funding was one-time, and authorizing legislation initially capped administrative funding at 5 percent, so sustainability depends on LEA and IHE cost sharing over time
target_learners: Teacher residency candidates, particularly those in STEM, special education, and bilingual credential areas, and candidates of color or from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Rigorous clinical preparation for credentialing, including planning, teaching, and connecting with students and staff
Gradual assumption of increased classroom responsibility under expert mentorship
examples: California's Teacher Residency Grant Program released grants of $20,000 per resident to 33 LEA grantees in March 2019, funding 38 LEA–IHE partnerships, with residents expected to teach in their residency LEA for at least 4 years

Over 90 percent of residents reported strong mentor working relationships, regular observations with high-quality feedback, and coursework relevant to their clinical placement, even after the shift to virtual learning
key_sources: Hirschboeck, K., Eiler White, M., Brannegan, A., & Reade, F. (2022). Teacher residency programs in California: Financial sustainability challenges and opportunities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED620723

article_title: Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools That Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees
citation: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD.
title: Orienting newcomers to be students through structured school-norms onboarding
description: The first promising practice is explicit orientation to schooling itself, since many newcomers lack practical classroom skills such as holding a pencil, writing on paper, and sitting at desks. Schools welcome students "into our family" by orienting them to attendance, transportation, grading, homework, behavior expectations, and emergency procedures, delivered by administrators, teachers, cultural liaisons, and classmates at year opening and on a rolling basis. Newcomer Academy runs a week-long structured orientation addressing practical matters and belonging; The Manhattan International High School embeds orientation in its Grade 9 foundations curriculum.
requirements: Combination of site administrators, teachers, cultural liaisons, and classmates to convey norms
rolling orientation as students enter any day of the year
constraints: Orientation content varies by school; for adolescent SLIFE the starting line is "wherever they're at" because they are unaccustomed to all aspects of school life
target_learners: Recently-arrived K-12 newcomers, including SLIFE with little or no formal schooling
target_learning_goals: School norms and practices
classroom survival skills
learning-to-learn skills
social connection with teachers and classmates
examples: Newcomer Academy's 'week of welcome' teaches students to use a binder, keyboard, locker, restorative circles, and to say their name, phone number, and address in English
key_sources: MAEC, Inc. (2019). Creating New Futures for Newcomers: Lessons from Five Schools that Serve K-12 Immigrants, Refugees, and Asylees. Bethesda, MD. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627813

article_title: Evaluation of "The Electric Company" Summer Learning Program
citation: McCarthy, B., Michel, L., Tiu, M., Atienza, S., Rice, J., Nakamoto, J., & Tafoya, A. (2011). Evaluation of The Electric Company Summer Learning Program. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: The Electric Company Summer Learning Program transmedia curriculum with Prankster Planet
description: The TEC Summer Learning Program is a 36-hour out-of-school-time transmedia curriculum for children ages 6 to 8 combining DVDs of 12 Electric Company episodes, scripted small- and large-group activities, and the Prankster Planet online game. The report describes it as "a transmedia curriculum that presents a narrative story to students that is presented across multiple forms of media, including television episodes and an online gaming experience." The curriculum is divided into 24 sessions with a repetitive structure of activity blocks (Watch and Learn, Stretch and Assess, Get Electric, Show Off Your Skills, Feel the Power), and Prankster Planet includes 12 missions centered on the vocabulary of each episode. The evaluation found it was well received and associated with pre-to-post skill gains.
requirements: Internet-ready computer access for students (sites were required to have at least one computer per two students)
teacher training via live or archived orientation webinars and a detailed curriculum guide with scripted facilitation
constraints: implemented in 5- to 6-week summer programs of 90 minutes a day; several shorter programs used a reduced 30-hour, 20-day model omitting two episodes
target_learners: students ages 6 to 8 between first and second grades, largely from low-income families and including English language learners
target_learning_goals: mathematics vocabulary
numeracy skills
literacy and phonics skills
motivation and confidence to engage in learning activities
examples: In the study, content was implemented in 5- to 6-week summer programs for 90 minutes a day for a total of 24 days by 16 teachers in 12 programs serving 152 students
key_sources: McCarthy, B., Michel, L., Tiu, M., Atienza, S., Rice, J., Nakamoto, J., & Tafoya, A. (2011). Evaluation of The Electric Company Summer Learning Program. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED533408

article_title: The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers
citation: Guha, R., Hyler, M.E., and Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-residency
title: Teacher residency model: district-university partnership grounding deep clinical training
description: A teacher residency is a certification pathway grounded in a full-year clinical apprenticeship alongside an expert mentor teacher, with tightly integrated coursework from a partner university leading to a credential and master's degree. The report defines it as "a mutually beneficial partnership between preparation providers and districts, one in which the integration of clinical experiences and coursework throughout the preparation program is co-designed". Residents receive financial support in exchange for a multi-year teaching commitment.
requirements: Strong district/university partnership with co-designed curriculum
Expert mentor teachers who co-teach with residents
Financial support exchanged for a three- to five-year teaching commitment
constraints: Attracting and developing a large pool of qualified mentors is a major challenge because monetary incentives are limited and time commitments considerable
target_learners: Prospective teachers in hard-to-staff urban and rural districts
target_learning_goals: Preparation for teaching in high-need schools and shortage subject areas
examples: The San Francisco Teacher Residency, founded in 2010 by SFUSD, University of San Francisco, Stanford, and the local teachers' union
key_sources: Guha, R., Hyler, M.E., and Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-residency

article_title: A Coming Crisis in Teaching? Teacher Supply, Demand, and Shortages in the U.S.
citation: Sutcher, L., Darling-Hammond, L., & Carver-Thomas, D. (2016). A coming crisis in teaching? Teacher supply, demand, and shortages in the U.S. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/coming-crisis-teaching
title: Supply-and-demand framework defining teacher shortage as inability to staff vacancies at prevailing wages with qualified individuals
description: The report adopts "a theoretical framework of supply and demand that defines a teacher shortage as an inadequate quantity of qualified individuals willing to offer their services under prevailing wages and conditions." This departs from a narrow definition counting only new-teacher production against retirements, incorporating turnover, program changes, pupil-teacher ratios, and the attractiveness of teaching. The framework supports modeling projections of hires demanded and supply available, and yields clearer policy implications because shortages can be addressed on both the supply and demand sides.
requirements: Data on new entrants, re-entrants, projected hires, and attrition rates to model supply and demand
constraints: Shortage estimates depend on modeling assumptions about entrant rates and re-entry rates, producing upper- and lower-bound supply estimates
target_learning_goals: Access to fully qualified teachers across all fields and school settings
examples: The report applies the framework using Schools and Staffing Survey, Teacher Follow-Up Survey, Baccalaureate and Beyond, and Title II data to project shortages by field, state, and school type
key_sources: Sutcher, L., Darling-Hammond, L., & Carver-Thomas, D. (2016). A coming crisis in teaching? Teacher supply, demand, and shortages in the U.S. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/coming-crisis-teaching

article_title: Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems
citation: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Involve practicing teachers as scorers of performance tasks to strengthen instruction
description: The paper recommends that practicing teachers serve as primary scorers of performance tasks in statewide assessments, as California, New Hampshire, and New York have required. It states that "Evidence shows that this involvement strengthens teachers' understanding of the standards and the assessments and informs classroom instruction", and that "Teachers learn significantly and can improve their practice from the scoring process". Allocating professional development days for scoring or including teacher scoring in test administration contracts can enhance teacher learning and reduce costs.
requirements: Reliable scoring requires training, moderation processes, and auditing; strong task design and careful rater training
constraints: Human scoring adds modest costs; the paper notes SBAC and PARCC developed systems for reliably scoring tasks for a few dollars per item per student
target_learners: K-12 students in states using performance tasks, and their teachers
target_learning_goals: teacher understanding of standards, curriculum, and assessment; classroom instruction aligned to higher-order skills
examples: New York teachers score extended writing tasks on professional development days set aside at the end of the school year, with a proportion of tests audited annually by the state education agency
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606777

article_title: Taking Deeper Learning to Scale
citation: Noguera, P. (2017). Taking deeper learning to scale. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/deeper-learning-to-scale
title: Make school improvement teacher-led rather than administration-driven
description: The report argues that school-improvement initiatives should be led by teachers rather than imposed top-down by administrations. In Brockton, a Restructuring Committee of veteran teachers framed the work, designed the literacy goals, and won over colleagues; the report states "the literacy initiative was teacher led, and this was undoubtedly a key factor responsible for the success that was achieved." It contrasts this with districts that expect compliance with central-office orders rather than building genuine buy-in.
requirements: Willingness of site and district leadership to accept a gradual approach rather than demand immediate widespread adoption
constraints: Initially the teachers' union objected and supported teachers who refused to participate; the strategy relied on working with the willing
target_learners: high school students in large urban schools
target_learning_goals: literacy across content areas
higher order thinking
examples: Teachers calling themselves the Restructuring Committee began by posting MCAS scores with the question: Is this the best we can be?
key_sources: Noguera, P. (2017). Taking deeper learning to scale. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/deeper-learning-to-scale

article_title: Restarting and Reinventing School: Learning in the Time of COVID and Beyond
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Schachner, A., & Edgerton, A. K. (with Badrinarayan, A., Cardichon, J., Cookson, P. W., Jr., Griffith, M., Klevan, S., Maier, A., Martinez, M., Melnick, H., Truong, N., Wojcikiewicz, S.). (2020). Restarting and reinventing school: Learning in the time of COVID and beyond. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/restarting-reinventing-school-covid
title: A ten-priority framework for restarting and reinventing school around equity, authentic learning, and stronger relationships
description: The report presents an overarching framework organizing research, state and local examples, and policy recommendations into ten priorities: closing the digital divide, strengthening distance and blended learning, assessing student needs, supporting SEL, redesigning for relationships, authentic culturally responsive learning, expanded learning time, community schools, educator preparation, and equitable funding. It states that the framework 'focuses on how policymakers as well as educators can support equitable, effective teaching and learning regardless of the medium through which that takes place.' The priorities are intended both for the 2020-21 restart and as a long-term vision for addressing educational quality and inequity.
requirements: Universal broadband and device access is described as 'the absolute minimum for ensuring that every child can continue learning'
constraints: The report does not replicate health and safety reopening guidance, focusing instead on equitable teaching and learning regardless of medium
target_learners: All k-12 students in the United States
target_learning_goals: Equitable, effective teaching and learning across in-person, online, and hybrid media
examples: Figure 1 diagrams the ten priorities as a framework for restarting and reinventing school
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L., Schachner, A., & Edgerton, A. K. (with Badrinarayan, A., Cardichon, J., Cookson, P.
