article_title: State Approaches to Developing Educational Leaders
citation: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572
title: Team-based professional learning engaging school and district leadership teams collaboratively
description: Ten states offer statewide opportunities for school- or district-based teams to learn collaboratively, acknowledging that "leadership within a school or district is distributed, rather than concentrated in singular roles." Team-based professional learning can enhance the quality and effectiveness of team interactions, broaden the stakeholders invested in new practices, and incorporate broader perspectives. Programs focus on general leadership development (5 states), a specific topic or skill (4 states), or team-identified problems of practice (3 states), and frequently tailor content through coaching or team goal-setting.
requirements: Teams composed of multiple role types (e.g., principal plus teacher leaders or district leaders)
Coaching or goal-setting structures that tailor content to the team's school or district context
constraints: The report notes this approach shows potential for broader shifts in culture and practice but does not report evaluated outcomes
target_learners: Vertical teams of central office and school-based staff
target_learning_goals: Distributed leadership
Collective improvement of instructional practices
Implementing policy frameworks
examples: North Carolina's Instructional Leadership Academy enrolled approximately 1,500 leaders in 2022–23 in 2-year team programs; South Carolina's Collective Leadership Initiative worked with teams from 27 schools over 2 years
key_sources: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572

article_title: Successful Teacher Residencies: What Matters and What Works
citation: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Successful teacher residencies: What matters and what works. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/480.783
title: Teacher residency model: LEA–EPP partnerships providing a full-year clinical placement with integrated coursework in exchange for a teaching commitment
description: The teacher residency model, "modeled after medical residencies," consists of "partnerships between local education agencies (LEAs) and educator preparation programs (EPPs)" in which "residents" spend "a full year in a clinical placement alongside an expert teacher while completing highly integrated coursework focused on skills for successful teaching." In paid programs, residents typically make a multiyear teaching commitment to the host LEA in exchange for financial support during preparation. The report uses this model as the organizing framework for its cross-case analysis of five California programs.
requirements: A partnership between an LEA and an educator preparation program
A full-year clinical placement alongside an expert mentor teacher
Integrated coursework aligned with clinical practice
constraints: Considerable variability exists between programs that are nominally referred to as teacher residencies, and non-grant-funded programs may lack important features required by the TRGP
target_learners: Teacher candidates (residents) preparing for high-need shortage areas
target_learning_goals: Pedagogical skill for successful teaching
Readiness to teach in high-need subject areas and LEA contexts
examples: Five case study programs: Alder Graduate School of Education, Claremont Graduate University, Kern Urban Teacher Residency and TRRE at CSU Bakersfield, and Tri-County Teacher Residency at CSU Monterey Bay
key_sources: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Successful teacher residencies: What matters and what works. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/480.783

article_title: Building a Positive School Climate.
citation: Knight, James A. (1985). Building a Positive School Climate. Paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the Midwestern Educational Research Association, Chicago, IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED265663
title: Ten strategies for building a positive school climate
description: The paper enumerates ten strategies said to rise out of a broad research base on achievement, discipline, teaching effectiveness, and business productivity: "make students feel important, (2) make students feel invited, (3) deal with needed changes in others from a positive point of view, (4) learn to make appropriate nonverbal cues, (5) get to know each student personally, (6) learn to empathize, (7) establish parameters, (8) use student-centered instruction, (9) learn to know and understand the difference between discipline and punishment, and (10) be enthusiastic about teaching." Each strategy is elaborated in the body of the paper.
requirements: Teachers, administrators, and staff must consistently apply the strategies in daily interactions with students
constraints: The strategies stem from the author's review of research rather than a direct test of the full set
target_learning_goals: positive school climate supporting achievement, discipline, and student self-concept
examples: The paper recommends that teachers wanting inviting classrooms visit lower elementary (K-3) classes to observe warmth, colors, evaluation practices, and voice tones
key_sources: Knight, James A. (1985). Building a Positive School Climate. Paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the Midwestern Educational Research Association, Chicago, IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED265663

article_title: The Road to High-Quality Early Learning: Lessons from the States
citation: Wechsler, M., Kirp, D., Tinubu Ali, T., Gardner, M., Maier, A., Melnick, H., & Shields, P. (2016). The road to high-quality early learning: Lessons from the states. Palo Alto: Learning Policy Institute. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/
title: Build early education quality on ten research-based building blocks, from whole-child assessment to quality rating and improvement systems
description: Drawing on its prior report The Building Blocks of High-Quality Early Childhood Education Programs, the report specifies "the key elements of quality" in programs with exemplary results. These include "Using early learning standards and curricula that address noncognitive as well as cognitive dimensions of children's experiences," assessing the whole child, preparing and coaching teachers, attending to varying needs including English language learners, engaging families, providing sufficient learning time, small classes and low ratios, program-level assessments, and a quality rating and improvement system used for improvement and accountability.
requirements: Programs must implement the blocks together: the report states "Quality is the key: If the potential of early education is to be realized, the program has to be of high quality."
target_learners: Preschool-aged children, including low-income children, English language learners, and children with special needs
target_learning_goals: Cognitive and noncognitive development, school readiness, and narrowed achievement gaps
examples: The four case study states mandate curricula grounded in child development principles such as play-based instruction, and favor "unobtrusive observation-based instruments over paper-and-pencil tests."
key_sources: Wechsler, M., Kirp, D., Tinubu Ali, T., Gardner, M., Maier, A., Melnick, H., & Shields, P. (2016). The road to high-quality early learning: Lessons from the states. Palo Alto: Learning Policy Institute. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/

article_title: Scaling California's Teacher Residency Grant Program: Findings and Implications from the Grant's First 4 Years
citation: Brannegan, A., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Scaling California's Teacher Residency Grant Program: Findings and implications from the grant's first 4 years. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/support/formative-evaluation-of-the-california-teacher-residency-grant-program
title: Teacher residency pathway: LEA-IHE partnership integrating credentialing coursework with a yearlong placement in an expert mentor teacher's classroom
description: A teacher residency is an intensive preparation pathway in which "a resident's credentialing coursework is integrated with a yearlong placement in the classroom of an expert mentor teacher." It is developed and operated by a partnership between a local educational agency and an institution of higher education with a state-approved preparation program, and residents typically receive financial support in exchange for a multi-year teaching commitment in the host LEA. The brief treats residencies as a route to well-prepared, retained 1st-year teachers responsive to local hiring needs.
requirements: A partnership between an LEA and an IHE with a state-approved teacher preparation program
Financial support for residents, typically tied to a several-year teaching commitment in the host LEA
constraints: The brief notes residency evidence is cited from prior studies (e.g., Guha et al., 2016; Silva et al., 2015) rather than tested in this brief
target_learners: teacher residency candidates in shortage fields such as special education, bilingual education, and STEM
target_learning_goals: rigorous clinical preparation for teaching
responsiveness to local LEA workforce needs
examples: TRGP residencies prepared 516 residents in special education, 366 in bilingual education, and 350 in STEM between 2019-20 and 2022-23
key_sources: Brannegan, A., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Scaling California's Teacher Residency Grant Program: Findings and implications from the grant's first 4 years. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/support/formative-evaluation-of-the-california-teacher-residency-grant-program

article_title: Taking the Long View: State Efforts to Solve Teacher Shortages by Strengthening the Profession
citation: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view
title: Teacher residency model with eight key characteristics of strong programs
description: A teacher residency is an accelerated certification pathway in which candidates "work as paid apprentices to skilled expert teachers while completing highly integrated coursework" during a full-year clinical placement in a high-need classroom, with tuition and living support repaid through a multi-year service commitment. The report lists eight characteristics of strong residencies drawn from a research review, including strong district-university partnerships, tightly integrated coursework, expert mentor co-teaching, cohorts in partnership teaching schools, and ongoing mentoring for graduates. States including California, Texas, Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Louisiana fund or mandate residency models.
requirements: Strong district and university partnerships
A full year of residency teaching alongside an expert mentor teacher
Financial support for residents in exchange for a 3- to 5-year post-residency teaching commitment
Expert mentor teachers who co-teach with residents
constraints: Programs are typically targeted to postbaccalaureate candidates and hard-to-staff positions in sponsoring districts
target_learners: Career changers and paraprofessionals entering teaching
target_learning_goals: Effective teaching in high-need fields and school districts
Retention of new teachers in hard-to-staff positions
examples: California invested $75 million in a Teacher Residency Grant Program for special education, STEM, and bilingual shortage areas, funding more than 3,500 new teachers with up to $20,000 per teacher matched by districts
Louisiana adopted regulations requiring a yearlong residency as a pathway to licensure, with $7.3 million in transitional funding for stipends and mentor training
key_sources: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view

article_title: California Teachers and COVID-19: How the Pandemic is Impacting the Teacher Workforce
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., Leung, M., & Burns, D. (2021). California teachers and COVID-19: How the pandemic is impacting the teacher workforce. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/california-covid-19-teacher-workforce
title: Teacher residency programs as district-preparation partnerships for high-need positions
description: Teacher residency programs are "partnerships between school districts and teacher preparation programs designed to recruit and prepare a diverse pool of candidates to teach in high-need positions." They are yearlong apprenticeships modeled on medical residencies, providing residents extensive clinical practice under an expert mentor teacher while completing tightly integrated coursework. Districts with residencies reported certainty about the number and quality of teachers they could expect to hire.
requirements: District-preparation partnership capacity; state or local investment to fund resident supports
constraints: The report notes many residents struggle financially and such programs can be out of reach for smaller districts with lean administrative teams
target_learners: Teacher candidates in high-need subjects and locations
target_learning_goals: Fully prepared, retained teachers for shortage fields
examples: Districts expanded residencies leveraging state investments; leaders valued predictable hiring from yearlong preservice cohorts

article_title: Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847
title: Teacher wage competitiveness index
description: An indicator defined as "the average public school teacher weekly wage as a percentage of the estimated weekly wage for other college-educated workers within each state". Weekly wages are used because they "adjust for any differences in the work year across occupations". The report transforms Economic Policy Institute weekly wage penalty data to a 0-100% scale and bands states from less competitive (below 75%) to more competitive (90% or above).
requirements: Population Survey data controlling for factors that typically influence wages
Weekly wage estimates for other college-educated workers in each state
constraints: State estimates are based on data from 2014 through 2019, and the national estimate is based on 2019 data
target_learning_goals: Assessing how competitively teacher pay compares with other college-educated occupations in a state
examples: The report reports state index values ranging from Wyoming at 98.0% down to Virginia at 67.3%, with a U.S. average of 80.8%.
key_sources: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847

article_title: Meeting Urban and Rural District Needs for Educators: California State University, Bakersfield's Teacher Residencies
citation: Fitz, J., & Yun, C. (2025). Meeting urban and rural district needs for educators: California State University, Bakersfield's teacher residencies. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/825.823
title: Teacher residency model with yearlong clinical apprenticeship, cohort coursework, stipend-for-commitment exchange, and LEA co-construction
description: The report describes a teacher residency preparation model in which candidates spend a full school year coteaching in a mentor teacher's classroom while taking residency-specific coursework in cohorts, receive a stipend in exchange for a multiyear teaching commitment in the partner district, and are prepared through university-LEA partnership. As printed, "All programs gave residents stipends to help cover their residency-year expenses, in exchange for a commitment to teach in the program's partner LEA(s) for 3 or 4 years following program completion." The model is organized around seven prioritized teaching practices aligned to California's Teacher Performance Expectations and the Danielson Framework for Teaching.
requirements: A partner LEA willing to co-construct programming, participate in admissions, and contribute funding
Mentor teachers with ongoing professional learning as clinical educators
A phase-in schedule pacing residents' progressive responsibility and focal Danielson Clusters
constraints: Residents commit to 3 or 4 years of teaching in partner LEAs after completion
Coordinators' heavily loaded combined role came at the expense of work-life balance and long-term retention in the role, per interviews
target_learners: Pre-service teacher credential candidates in urban and rural California districts
target_learning_goals: Preparation for preliminary teaching credentials with context-specific clinical competence
examples: Kern Urban paired residents with mentors and used a phase-in schedule breaking each semester into 2-week increments; TRRE placed residents in three rural districts via the Tulare County Office of Education
key_sources: Fitz, J., & Yun, C. (2025). Meeting urban and rural district needs for educators: California State University, Bakersfield's teacher residencies. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/825.823

article_title: Acceptance of AI-Gamified Adaptive Learning in EFL: Bifactor Evidence for Essential Unidimensionality and the Limits of Subscale Scoring
citation: Zhorabekova A, Duisenova M, Kurmasheva M and Yesnazar A (2026). Acceptance of AI-gamified adaptive learning in EFL: bifactor evidence for essential unidimensionality and the limits of subscale scoring. Front. Educ. 11:1929123. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1929123
title: Test discriminant validity and dimensionality before scoring multidimensional acceptance questionnaires with separate subscales
description: The article recommends that researchers who assemble multidimensional acceptance questionnaires verify that the assumed subdimensions are empirically distinct before interpreting subscale scores. It states that "Testing discriminant validity (HTMT) and dimensionality (ECV, ωh) before subscale scoring is therefore advisable", because closely related AI and gamification perceptions may not be empirically distinct even when each subscale is internally reliable. The recommendation generalizes beyond EFL to educational technology research where discriminant validity is rarely reported.
requirements: Access to item-level response data sufficient to estimate competing measurement models and HTMT ratios
constraints: The article's evidence is structural validity only, from a single-institution, predominantly female sample; criterion validity was not examined
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of learners' acceptance of AI-gamified adaptive learning tools
examples: For the 13-item measure, the authors conclude the evidence supports a general total score over separate subscale scores, with perceived gamification as an optional, interpretable facet
key_sources: Zhorabekova A, Duisenova M, Kurmasheva M and Yesnazar A (2026). Acceptance of AI-gamified adaptive learning in EFL: bifactor evidence for essential unidimensionality and the limits of subscale scoring. Front. Educ. 11:1929123. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1929123

article_title: Technical and pedagogical limitations of artificial intelligence in undergraduate EFL higher education: a systematic review
citation: Espinoza-Celi V and Vargas-Saritama A (2026) Technical and pedagogical limitations of artificial intelligence in undergraduate EFL higher education: a systematic review. Front. Educ. 11:1948091. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1948091
title: Higher-order analytical framework distinguishing technical from pedagogical limitations of AI in undergraduate EFL instruction
description: The review develops an inductively derived framework that separates system- and infrastructure-related constraints (technical limitations) from instructionally mediated constraints (pedagogical limitations), each grouped into higher-order categories. Technical limitations concern "constraints arising from AI system performance and technological infrastructure", while pedagogical limitations arise from how AI is selected, integrated, mediated, and interpreted in teaching. The categorization "emerged inductively from the synthesis of the included studies and was subsequently interpreted in relation to TPACK", which supplies a conceptual point of reference without serving as an a priori coding scheme.
requirements: Evidence extracted only from Results, Discussion, and Conclusions sections of empirical studies, with each study contributing one occurrence per category to prevent overrepresentation
constraints: The framework was derived from Scopus-indexed studies published 2021–2026 in undergraduate EFL contexts; reliance on a single database limits breadth of evidence retrieval
Technical and pedagogical limitations may co-occur within the same educational context, so the domains are not mutually exclusive
target_learners: Undergraduate EFL students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Identification and management of technical and pedagogical limitations in AI-supported language learning
examples: The framework organized seven technical limitations into two categories and eight pedagogical limitations into five categories across the 54 included studies
key_sources: Espinoza-Celi V and Vargas-Saritama A (2026) Technical and pedagogical limitations of artificial intelligence in undergraduate EFL higher education: a systematic review. Front. Educ. 11:1948091. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1948091

article_title: An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence
citation: Ismael I, Luo X and Li S (2026). An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853510. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853510
title: Trait Emotional Intelligence Questionnaire (TEIQue, 30 items, four factors) adopted under the trait EI perspective
description: The study measured emotional intelligence with the TEIQue: 'The questionnaire consists of 30 items covering 15 facets of trait emotional intelligence, grouped under four factors: Emotionality, Sociability, Well-Being, and Self-Control', rated on a 7-point Likert scale. The authors adopt the trait model rather than the ability model and add an explicit caveat: 'EI is treated here as a practically useful, self-reported indicator of emotional functioning relevant to teaching, not as a settled construct'.
requirements: Respondents complete the questionnaire before the practicum and again at the end of the intervention
constraints: Trait EI overlaps with established personality dimensions (e.g., low neuroticism), a debate the article acknowledges; findings from the trait model cannot be generalized to the ability model
target_learning_goals: measuring self-perceived emotional functioning relevant to teaching
examples: Both the TSES and TEIQue were administered in their original English form with no item modification
key_sources: Ismael I, Luo X and Li S (2026). An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853510. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853510

article_title: ANVIL: Analogies and Videos for Lecturers
citation: Noviello, Y., Birillo, A., Migut, G. (2026). ANVIL: Analogies and Videos for Lecturers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16295
title: Ground automated screening of generated instructional materials in teacher evaluation, then assign modality-specific automated roles
description: The article proposes evaluating generative educational tools by first grounding quality assessment in teacher judgment, then using those findings to design automated screening with modality-specific roles: an LLM-based evaluator for textual analogies, and an automated fidelity proxy for videos where subjective judgments are hard to automate. This "treats automated evaluation as a mechanism for pre-selection and auditing, rather than as a substitute for expert review". The approach balances pedagogical validity with scalability.
requirements: An initial human (teacher/expert) evaluation to establish how generated artifacts are perceived and where reliable automation is feasible
Controlled negative examples to validate a discriminative automated evaluator when positive examples dominate
constraints: Automated scoring of subjective video quality was deemed unreliable because experts disagree more on it and realistic negative videos are hard to define
LLM/VLM-based measures may reflect model biases and may not capture visual aesthetics or pedagogical effectiveness
target_learners: CS/SE educators and researchers deploying generative AI tools in teaching
target_learning_goals: Scalable quality assurance of AI-generated instructional analogies and animations
examples: The human evaluation's implications section derived the analogy-side discriminative evaluator and the video-side proxy-based audit from observed expert agreement patterns
key_sources: Noviello, Y., Birillo, A., Migut, G. (2026). ANVIL: Analogies and Videos for Lecturers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16295

article_title: AI-Integrated Learning Management System for Middle School: A Longitudinal Study of Learning Outcomes Through High
citation: Misan Paul Etchie, Olutosin Taiwo. (2026). AI-Integrated Learning Management System for Middle School: A Longitudinal Study of Learning Outcomes Through High School and Beyond. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07544
title: Teacher analytics and intervention dashboard translating learning traces into targeted classroom action
description: The article includes a teacher-facing dashboard that 'provides actionable summaries at the student and class levels', with views for concept-level mastery and growth, misconception trends clustering common wrong answers, engagement and persistence indicators, and intervention tools such as recommended review sets and flags for students needing follow-up. It closes the loop from detection to intervention: once a misconception is flagged, the teacher assigns a recommended practice set to affected students, and these actions are logged for fidelity analysis.
requirements: Logging of teacher mediation actions so analyses can distinguish direct student-facing effects from teacher-amplified effects
target_learners: Middle school teachers supporting grades 6-8 students
target_learning_goals: Timely instructional intervention on misconceptions and sustained struggle
examples: Misconception clustering view summarizing detected misconceptions, affected students, and representative wrong-answer patterns, followed by targeted intervention assignment
key_sources: Misan Paul Etchie, Olutosin Taiwo. (2026). AI-Integrated Learning Management System for Middle School: A Longitudinal Study of Learning Outcomes Through High School and Beyond. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07544

article_title: The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices
citation: Eimler, S.C., Erle, L., Flood, D., Haiman, A., Häckert, L., Helgert, A., McGinness, L., Yapici, B. (2026). The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11215
title: TerraFlops: open-source wrapper integrating hardware emissions data, PUE-equivalent values, and ML performance metrics
description: TerraFlops is an open-source proof-of-concept wrapper for tracking tools such as CodeCarbon that integrates raw hardware emissions data with facility-level PUE variables and ML performance metrics to generate a unified sustainability score. Its cloud mode applies fixed PUE values for providers such as AWS, GCP, or GENERIC to project data-centre deployment costs, while a local_auto mode calculates a dynamic PUE from real-time hardware load, assigning a PUE of 1.60 to workloads under 10% system capacity and scaling down to 1.08 at high utilisation.
requirements: An underlying tracking tool such as CodeCarbon; users may need to adjust the wrapper to reflect their specific hardware
constraints: The local PUE values may still be an under-estimate, as the energy efficiency of consumer-grade GPUs is significantly lower than cloud-based hardware
Refining these benchmarks remains an area for future work
target_learners: AIED researchers training or deploying ML models for educational applications
target_learning_goals: Reporting model accuracy alongside environmental and computational cost
examples: The authors used the TerraFlops wrapper when training a logistic regression model on the Iris and Breast Cancer datasets from the UCI machine learning repository, reporting the resulting sustainability statistics before their own introduction
key_sources: Eimler, S.C., Erle, L., Flood, D., Haiman, A., Häckert, L., Helgert, A., McGinness, L., Yapici, B. (2026). The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11215

article_title: AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education
citation: Alvaro Becerra, Alejandra Palma and Ruth Cobos. (2026). AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education. LASI Spain 26: Learning Analytics Summer Institute Spain 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-7793-2682
title: Keep teachers in the loop as mediators who curate AI-generated feedback before delivery
description: AICoFe positions teachers as active mediators of AI-generated content rather than passing model output directly to students. The Teacher Dashboard lets teachers "select individual sentences or entire paragraphs from the AI-generated feedback of each LLM and combine them to compose the final feedback" presented to the student. This selective composition reinforces the human-centered nature of the system and preserves pedagogical authority over the final feedback.
requirements: Requires a Teacher Dashboard exposing granular LLM outputs with sentence-level selection, plus draft management for curation across multiple sessions
target_learners: higher education teachers mediating AI-generated feedback
target_learning_goals: delivery of pedagogically appropriate, curated feedback to students
examples: Teachers compose final feedback by selecting sentences from the three LLM outputs and can save intermediate drafts before finalising

article_title: Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction
citation: Li Li, Yu Cao. (2025). Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction, A Case Study of the Compound Line Graph.
title: Scaling AI-integrated disciplinary lessons requires teacher competencies in disciplinary insight, discipline-centric positioning, and technical self-efficacy
description: The article argues that broader scaling of the three-stage trajectory "depend[s] significantly on three core teacher competencies": Disciplinary Insight (identifying structural correspondences such as trend estimation and machine prediction, with similar interfaces in probability models, cluster analysis, and statistical distributions), Pedagogical Positioning (maintaining discipline-centricity while using AI as a pedagogical scaffold), and Technical Self-Efficacy (proficiently operating LLMs with automated data visualization, though advanced programming is not required). This principle guides professional development for AI-integrated instruction.
requirements: Instructors must possess the capacity to identify structural correspondences between foundational disciplinary knowledge and AI principles
constraints: Activation of technological isomorphism awareness is strictly contingent upon robust internalization of the underlying mathematical concepts
target_learners: elementary mathematics teachers integrating AI education
target_learning_goals: designing discipline-anchored AI literacy instruction
examples: The article notes the trend-estimation/machine-prediction interface is merely one such interface among several in statistics
key_sources: Li Li, Yu Cao. (2025). Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction, A Case Study of the Compound Line Graph. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09598

article_title: Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of a Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education
citation: Angxuan Chen, Yuang Wei, Huixiao Le, Yan Zhang. (2024). Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15226
title: Prompt-based teachable ChatGPT agent structured by a five-stage help-seeking model
description: The teachable ChatGPT agent is a prompt-based configuration of gpt-4 that role-plays a help-seeking student learning the eight queens puzzle. The authors "employed a prompt-based design approach that could modify the role of ChatGPT", structuring its responses around Gall's five-stage help-seeking process model, and deliberately "used the original ChatGPT without other augmented techniques" so that its mistakes resemble a beginner and create opportunities for students to teach.
requirements: Learners first watch instructional videos covering the backtracking algorithm and the puzzle
An online judging platform that automatically evaluates whether the generated code solves the puzzle
Learners take an explicit teaching role, guiding the agent only in natural language
constraints: Accuracy of the agent's generated code was not controlled; the authors note ChatGPT may hallucinate wrong content without control
target_learners: university students with a computer-science background and self-reported fundamental C++ coding ability
target_learning_goals: knowledge of the backtracking algorithm and the eight queens puzzle
C++ programming skill for solving the eight queens puzzle
examples: Experimental-group participants helped the agent form correct code within a one-hour supervised session, sharing screens to prevent searching for solutions online
key_sources: Angxuan Chen, Yuang Wei, Huixiao Le, Yan Zhang. (2024). Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15226

article_title: TeachArena: Are Language Agents Ready for Realistic Teaching Work?
citation: Zixin Chen, Peng Liu, Rui Sheng, Haobo Li, Jianhong Tu, Xiaodong Deng, Kashun Shum, Dayiheng Liu, Huamin Qu. (2026). Are Agents Ready to Teach? A Multi-Stage Benchmark for Real-World Teaching Workflows. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14322
title: Teaching-system episode framework: knowing–teaching–acting across three capability surfaces
description: The article proposes that tutor-agent readiness requires three separable capability surfaces: Stage 1 pedagogical judgment (a bounded teacher decision from packaged evidence), Stage 2 situated tutoring (a history-dependent adaptive teaching policy over a multi-turn episode), and Stage 3 end-to-end LMS workflow execution (institutional action). It argues these "separate knowing what a teacher should do, teaching through an evolving interaction, and acting without losing the educational rationale across an institutional workflow." The framework defines an auditable teaching-system episode in which evidence supports a decision, the decision guides interaction or execution, and the learner or course consequence is observable, spanning six teacher-work capabilities: diagnosing, designing, creating, teaching, communicating, and evaluating.
requirements: Each task must link an educational target, supporting evidence, an observable response or environment transition, and a verifier matched to that trace
constraints: The three stages are complementary diagnostic surfaces rather than an ordered difficulty scale
target_learners: frontier language models evaluated as tutor agents
target_learning_goals: pedagogical judgment
adaptive multi-turn tutoring
end-to-end LMS teaching-workflow execution
examples: Stage 1 task EI-AFFECT-01 holds content, session, and score fixed while varying process evidence so identical 3/10 scores warrant opposite actions for two learners
key_sources: Zixin Chen, Peng Liu, Rui Sheng, Haobo Li, Jianhong Tu, Xiaodong Deng, Kashun Shum, Dayiheng Liu, Huamin Qu. (2026). Are Agents Ready to Teach? A Multi-Stage Benchmark for Real-World Teaching Workflows. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14322

article_title: TeachArena: Are Language Agents Ready for Realistic Teaching Work?
citation: Zixin Chen, Peng Liu, Rui Sheng, Haobo Li, Jianhong Tu, Xiaodong Deng, Kashun Shum, Dayiheng Liu, Huamin Qu. (2026). Are Agents Ready to Teach? A Multi-Stage Benchmark for Real-World Teaching Workflows. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14322
title: TEACHARENA benchmark: 354 audited source-grounded tasks with matched verifiers
description: TEACHARENA is a source-grounded benchmark of "354 audited tasks" spanning three stages and six teacher-work capabilities (diagnosing, designing, creating, teaching, communicating, evaluating). Tasks are built through a pedagogical-insight-driven pipeline: each specifies a target instructional insight, grounds it in transformed educational material, published pedagogy, or deterministic course state, and pairs it with a matched verifier over turn-level responses, tutoring trajectories, or persistent artifacts and environment states. Stage 1 has 117 tasks, Stage 2 has 100 tasks across 13 disciplines with six controlled learner profiles, and Stage 3 has 137 tasks in a deterministic synthetic Canvas-style LMS linking 126 learners, 432 course enrollments, 222 assignment records, 1,058 quiz attempts, and 13 editable presentations. Code and data are available on Hugging Face.
requirements: Each task is authored as an evidence-to-trace contract with a verifier matched to the evidence the task produces
constraints: Stage 2 uses simulated learners and Stage 3 a deterministic synthetic LMS; coverage remains weighted toward STEM
target_learners: frontier language models evaluated as tutor agents
target_learning_goals: evaluating tutor agents on pedagogical judgment, adaptive tutoring, and institutional workflow execution
examples: Stage 3 tasks span evidence-conditioned assessment and remediation, diagnosis-linked grading and feedback, privacy-sensitive outreach, construct-aligned material revision, and multi-artifact course updates
key_sources: Zixin Chen, Peng Liu, Rui Sheng, Haobo Li, Jianhong Tu, Xiaodong Deng, Kashun Shum, Dayiheng Liu, Huamin Qu. (2026). Are Agents Ready to Teach? A Multi-Stage Benchmark for Real-World Teaching Workflows. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14322

article_title: Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst
citation: Singh, M., Mansi, G., & Riedl, M. O. (2025). Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst. Georgia Institute of Technology. https://www.gatech.edu/
title: Keep the teacher in control of AI-generated scaffolds to preserve teacher agency
description: The article argues that LLM-based tools should support rather than replace teachers by keeping decision-making with the teacher and using the LLM only as a generator of suggestions. Concept Catalyst avoids the opacity of LLM-based decision making by keeping the decision making task entirely with the teacher: at every point the teacher can accept, reject, or modify any artifact the tool creates, preserving teacher agency while leveraging generative AI.
requirements: The interface must let teachers review, edit, accept, or reject every AI-generated artifact, including summaries, concepts, and questions
constraints: The article notes LLMs may not be reliable enough in a fully automated capacity, so oversight by teachers is required
target_learning_goals: Maintaining teacher agency and pedagogical judgment when using generative AI for lesson preparation
examples: Generated questions enter a question bank only after the teacher accepts or modifies them, and the final approved questions are printed or exported to PDF
key_sources: Singh, M., Mansi, G., & Riedl, M. O. (2025). Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst. Georgia Institute of Technology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20511

article_title: An Emancipatory Vision for Designing (Generative) AI for Learner Flourishing
citation: Luis P. Prieto, Yannis Dimitriadis. (2026). An emancipatory vision for designing (generative) AI for learner flourishing. International Workshop on Critical and More-than-human Perspectives on AI in Education (at EC-TEL 2026). https://luispprieto.com/
title: Ten tentative design principles for emancipatory AIED (tools not agents, appropriation, fading, exiting the screen, and more)
description: The paper offers an initial catalog of ten design principles for educational AI built on its alternative assumptions: design for multi-level agency (tools and services, not autonomous agents), appropriation and unfolding, fading scaffolding, exiting the screen, emotional detachment (avoiding attachment hacking), theoretical and value syncretism via modular plugin architectures, uncertainty (minimalist flexible designs), learner resourcefulness, metacognition, and socio-technical interoperability. The authors state these are tentative and later discussions and prototypes need to further exemplify them.
requirements: designs should support or be able to integrate with multiple theories of learning and pedagogy
constraints: principles are tentative and not yet exemplified in prototypes
target_learners: learners in classrooms and other educational settings using AIED systems
target_learning_goals: learner autonomy
metacognition
resilience and resourcefulness
social flourishing
examples: Principle 5 states AIED systems should avoid posing as people even while supporting the emotional aspects of learning, to prevent attachment hacking
key_sources: Luis P. Prieto, Yannis Dimitriadis. (2026). An emancipatory vision for designing (generative) AI for learner flourishing. International Workshop on Critical and More-than-human Perspectives on AI in Education (at EC-TEL 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07715

article_title: A Guiding Framework for K-12 Teachers in Creating AI-powered Learning Technologies through Vibe Coding
citation: Song, Y., Choi, S., Kim, J., Kim, Y., Weisberg, L., & Moon, J. (2026). A Guiding Framework for K-12 Teachers in Creating AI-powered Learning Technologies through Vibe Coding. https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383
title: Position teachers as primary designers of AI-powered learning technologies, supported by AI-enabled vibe coding
description: The article argues that prior co-design models positioned researchers or developers as primary drivers, with teachers contributing only domain expertise or partial participation. GAIDE instead "position[s] teachers as the primary designers, supported by AI-enabled vibe coding", which the authors say grants teachers greater agency and lets them shape technologies directly around their instructional goals. Vibe coding lowers the technical barrier so teachers can carry the full design process themselves.
requirements: AI-assisted vibe coding tools accessible to non-programmers
Structured guidance such as the GAIDE framework
constraints: The article notes the Presidential AI Challenge itself offers limited instructional scaffolding for educators with minimal prior AI design experience
target_learning_goals: Designing classroom-relevant AI-powered tools
Technology integration
examples: Three teachers collaboratively created the Math Mysteries platform themselves in Google AI Studio during the eight-week workshop
key_sources: Song, Y., Choi, S., Kim, J., Kim, Y., Weisberg, L., & Moon, J. (2026). A Guiding Framework for K-12 Teachers in Creating AI-powered Learning Technologies through Vibe Coding. https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383

article_title: A Guiding Framework for K-12 Teachers in Creating AI-powered Learning Technologies through Vibe Coding
citation: Song, Y., Choi, S., Kim, J., Kim, Y., Weisberg, L., & Moon, J. (2026). A Guiding Framework for K-12 Teachers in Creating AI-powered Learning Technologies through Vibe Coding. https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383
title: Teacher-friendly adaptation of INTERACT design components for educator-led AI design
description: Based on teacher feedback that INTERACT terminology was not intuitive, the authors revised the framework's component names: Motivation & Emotion became Motivation & Engagement, Mental Model became Knowledge mapping, Learner Variables became Learner Differentiation, and Cognitive Activities became Thinking Processes. Teachers said, for example, that "Knowledge mapping is a teacher-friendly language". Learning Environment was removed because such discussions were not observed, and Learning Objectives was added because teachers actively discussed objectives and standards before designing content.
requirements: Post-workshop review of framework terminology with teacher participants
constraints: Revisions reflect one workshop's three teachers; Learning Environment discussions were absent in this context
target_learning_goals: Designing pedagogically effective AI-mediated learning interactions
examples: Teacher B suggested replacing Mental Model with Knowledge mapping; Teacher C proposed Motivation & Engagement because engagement is easier to measure and observe than emotion
key_sources: Song, Y., Choi, S., Kim, J., Kim, Y., Weisberg, L., & Moon, J. (2026). A Guiding Framework for K-12 Teachers in Creating AI-powered Learning Technologies through Vibe Coding. https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383

article_title: Rethinking teachers’ diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis
citation: Hoppe T, Loibl K and Leuders T (2026). Rethinking teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis. Front. Educ. 11:1857661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1857661
title: Teacher dashboards visualizing AI-analyzed student learning data in real time
description: Teacher dashboards are a component of AI-supported diagnostic systems that visualize analyses of students' learning processes for teachers. The article states that 'Teacher dashboards visualize this information, providing up-to-date insights into individual learners' progress and task performance,' enabling teachers to keep track of many students at once, identify patterns across the class, and support micro- and macro-level adaptations of instruction. In the case example, a dashboard summary indicates which students show which error patterns, such as a possible place-value misconception.
requirements: Using dashboard information to inform instruction requires teachers to interpret AI-generated analyses in relation to their own classroom observations, contextual knowledge, and instructional goals.
constraints: Dashboard analyses capture the student's conceptual difficulty but, as the case example shows, may not capture emerging frustration or disengagement the teacher observes directly.
target_learning_goals: class-wide monitoring of learning processes
timely instructional adaptation
examples: In the AI-assisted case example, the integrated system analyses subtraction responses in real time, highlights recurring place-value errors, and suggests follow-up activities via a dashboard summary.
key_sources: Hoppe T, Loibl K and Leuders T (2026). Rethinking teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis. Front. Educ. 11:1857661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1857661

article_title: Harnessing Generative UI for Education: Tailored Learning Interactives
citation: Alisa Kovshov, Anisha Choudhury, Anna Iurchenko, Amy Keeling, Avinatan Hassidim, Ayelet Shasha Evron, Ayça Çakmakli, Diana Akrong, Femi Olanubi, Gal Elidan, Ian Li, Ido Lerer, Katherine Chou, Lidan Hackmon, Michal Gordon, Nir Kerem, Niv Efron, Preeti Singh, Rena Levitt, Rotem Yulzary, Shlomi Ben Shimon, Sophie Allweis, Tracey Lee-Joe, Tzvika Stein, Yaniv Carmel, Yael Haramaty, Yishay Mor, Yossi Matias and Yuri Lev. (2026). Harnessing Generative UI for Education: Tailored Learning Interactives. Google Research. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20738
title: Keep the teacher as orchestrator: teachers initiate requests, approve learning objectives, and select the best candidate simulation
description: The article holds that technology-enhanced learning tools are most effective when they support, rather than replace, classroom teachers. Its pipeline therefore positions educators as central orchestrators: "By allowing teachers to initiate requests, approve learning objectives, and select the best candidate simulations, we maintain their pedagogical intent while drastically reducing the time, cost, and technical barriers traditionally associated with creating custom simulations." Of K=5 generated candidates per idea, the best is selected before reaching the teacher.
requirements: Teacher review of generated learning objectives and selection among candidate simulations before classroom use
constraints: The framework preserves teacher agency but does not yet include alignment with learning standards, a need teachers raised in the usability study
target_learning_goals: Simulations aligned with the teacher's instructional intent and learning objectives
examples: In the usability study, the vast majority of AI-generated learning objectives were approved as is, and requested adjustments were inconsequential

(2026). Harnessing Generative UI for Education: Tailored Learning Interactives. Google Research. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20738

article_title: Ethical implications of prompt injection in AI-mediated grading: An adversarial red-team evaluation
citation: Niklas Humble. (2026). Ethical Implications of Prompt Injection in AI-mediated Grading: An Adversarial Red-Team Evaluation. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09758-9
title: Teach how AI models process prompts and how interactions can be exploited, to build cognitive resilience against manipulation
description: The article argues that integrating explicit instruction on how AI models process prompts, recognize system boundaries, and respond to linguistic cues serves a dual purpose in higher education: it builds technical proficiency and fosters "cognitive resilience against manipulation". By teaching both effective interaction and how interactions can be exploited, institutions can cultivate a more security-aware user base capable of identifying and resisting prompt injection attempts.
requirements: Curricula or professional development that cover both legitimate prompt engineering and adversarial exploitation of the same techniques
constraints: Grounded in one AI tool and one grading scenario; the article does not empirically test the educational intervention
target_learning_goals: understanding AI prompt processing and system boundaries
identifying and resisting direct and indirect prompt injection
examples: The article notes iterative refinement, personification, and example templates are effective for both ethical prompt design and adversarial injection, differing in intent
key_sources: Niklas Humble. (2026). Ethical Implications of Prompt Injection in AI-mediated Grading: An Adversarial Red-Team Evaluation. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09758-9

article_title: Hybrid E-Assessment in Higher Education: Semi-Automated Grading of Paper-Based Written Examinations
citation: Hartwig Grabowski, Michael Canz. (2026). Hybrid E-Assessment in Higher Education: Semi-Automated Grading of Paper-Based Written Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08855
title: In summative e-assessment, technology should support grading and post-processing without constraining the design of complex, stepwise problem-solving tasks
description: The principle holds that paper provides the design freedom for didactically rich examinations, and automation should enter at the standardized capture and evaluation of answers rather than at restriction of the task architecture. As the article states, "technology should support grading and post-processing without constraining the design of complex, stepwise problem-solving tasks". Existing paper examinations can be adapted to a structured answer-field or coding format with manageable effort while maintaining substantive and didactic freedom.
requirements: A structured answer-field or coding format that captures assessment-relevant intermediate results
constraints: Fully automated grading narrows the range of didactically meaningful task formats when closed formats cannot represent derivation, application, and transfer
target_learning_goals: summative assessment that both measures performance and supports reasoning and learning
examples: The article's free-fall physics task, where students derive the impact velocity by hand and the mass parameter cancels within the calculation, showing the examination acting as a learning opportunity
key_sources: Hartwig Grabowski, Michael Canz. (2026). Hybrid E-Assessment in Higher Education: Semi-Automated Grading of Paper-Based Written Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08855

article_title: Can LLMs Model Incorrect Student Reasoning? A Case Study on Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions
citation: Yanick Zengaffinen, Andreas Opedal, Donya Rooein, Kv Aditya Srivatsa, Shashank Sonkar, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). Can LLMs Model Incorrect Student Reasoning? A Case Study on Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15547
title: A ten-strategy taxonomy of distractor-generation strategies grounded in learning-science literature and observed LLM reasoning
description: The article introduces a taxonomy of ten distractor-generation strategies, "grounded in learning-science literature and empirical observations of LLMs’ reasoning traces", spanning task understanding (INTER, CORR), candidate construction (LINK, ERR_DESC, ERR_SIM, INST), quality control and selection (PLAUS, DISCR, CURATE), and cross-cutting reconsideration (RECON). It was built by merging expert-practice strategies from the literature with strategies extracted via manual open coding of LLM traces, and is applied to annotate 885 reasoning traces span by span.
requirements: Requires reasoning traces (CoT or reasoning prompting) that can be annotated with strategy tags; direct prompting produces no intermediate traces to analyze.
constraints: The article notes reasoning traces are not guaranteed to faithfully reflect the underlying decision process, so strategies are descriptions of externalized reasoning rather than mechanistic claims.
target_learners: AI-in-education researchers and assessment designers modeling student misconceptions
target_learning_goals: Generating plausible, misconception-aligned distractors for multiple-choice assessment items
examples: The article annotates a DEEPSEEK-V3.2 trace for the problem "Simplify the following if possible: (6+9m)/3", labeling spans for correct-answer reference, error description, error simulation, outcome instantiation, plausibility assessment, final set curation, and discriminability check.
key_sources: Yanick Zengaffinen, Andreas Opedal, Donya Rooein, Kv Aditya Srivatsa, Shashank Sonkar, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). Can LLMs Model Incorrect Student Reasoning? A Case Study on Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15547

article_title: Measuring Whether LLM Tutors Teach or Solve: A Diagnostic for Educational Impact
citation: Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, and Baichuan Li. (2026). Beyond Helpfulness: A Teaching-over-Solving Diagnostic for Measuring Educational Impact in LLM Tutors. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16206
title: Teaching-over-solving diagnostic: separating answer-production ability from learning-support behavior via solving and pedagogy composites and their gap
description: The article proposes a lightweight diagnostic that reaggregates public tutoring benchmark scores into two composites: a solving composite (problem solving, solution correctness, mistake location, mistake correction) and a pedagogy composite (socratic questioning, scaffolding win rate, pedagogy instruction-following win rate, hard scaffolding, hard pedagogy instruction-following). For each model it defines "Gap(m) = Teach(m)−Solve(m)", where positive values indicate models relatively stronger on pedagogy than on solving. It is intended for education-oriented NLP work that lacks private classroom data.
requirements: Requires public benchmark artifacts reporting task-level scores that can be grouped into solving-oriented and pedagogy-oriented composites, with no student-private data.
constraints: The article states its grouping is "intended as a transparent diagnostic rather than a definitive taxonomy" and that alternative task groupings could change the reported gaps.
target_learners: learners interacting with LLM tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: learning support and student-agency-preserving tutoring behavior in educational NLP evaluation
examples: Applied to the eight-model MathTutorBench leaderboard, the diagnostic yields gaps ranging from +0.077 for LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct to −0.452 for Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct.
key_sources: Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, and Baichuan Li. (2026). Beyond Helpfulness: A Teaching-over-Solving Diagnostic for Measuring Educational Impact in LLM Tutors. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16206

article_title: Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning
citation: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047
title: Temporal decoupling of metacognitive knowledge and regulation under experiential AI-assisted learning
description: The article proposes that components of metacognitive awareness are not only separable but "can be temporally decoupled under experiential AI-assisted learning": knowledge of cognition rises immediately while regulation of cognition develops later through reflection. Drawing on the experiential learning cycle, it suggests the immediate knowledge gain "may have functioned as the basis that students gradually converted into reflective regulation", making the two gains part of a single developmental process rather than independent outcomes. This account explains why a null immediate result for regulation may mask delayed experiential effects.
requirements: Assessment designs must include delayed follow-up measurements, since relying solely on post-test measurements risks misclassifying regulatory effects that only emerge over time.
constraints: The between-group regulation difference did not reach statistical significance, possibly due to a lack of power, so long-term regulatory advantage warrants future exploration.
target_learning_goals: development of metacognitive knowledge and regulation of cognition in AI-assisted learning
examples: In the study, the experiential group's MKC gain appeared at post-test while its MRC gain emerged only at the five-week follow-up.
key_sources: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047

article_title: The Policy Deficit in AI × Social-Emotional Learning Research
citation: Tran Van Cuong, Liu Yihan, Nguyen Van Tuong. (2026). The Policy Deficit in AI x Social-Emotional Learning Research.
title: The techno-solutionist trap: AI × SEL research foregrounds technical potential while leaving institutional conditions under-specified
description: The review characterizes the field as dominated by "techno-solutionism": the belief that AI applications will inherently solve SEL challenges without sufficient engagement with institutional or regulatory hurdles that prevent scaling. Policy, when mentioned, is treated as a "horizon" rather than practice-oriented tools, risking a "pilot-study paradox" where robust results fail to achieve real-world impact for lack of regulatory and resource-allocation frameworks. The authors propose reorienting from "implication-as-afterthought" to "implication-as-methodology", designing research with policy in mind from the start.
requirements: Researchers, reviewers, and editors must foreground policy considerations despite incentives prioritizing technical novelty
constraints: The authors note rapid technology lifecycles and rigid academic publication formats complicate integrating deep policy suggestions into short papers
target_learners: AI × SEL researchers, editors, reviewers, and policymakers
target_learning_goals: translating AI × SEL research findings into educational governance and implementation
examples: The review found some papers promise policy implications in impact statements yet ignore them in the main text
key_sources: Tran Van Cuong, Liu Yihan, Nguyen Van Tuong. (2026). The Policy Deficit in AI x Social-Emotional Learning Research. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29950

article_title: AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study
citation: Luiz Rodrigues, Guilherme Guerino, Thomaz Edson Silva, Luana Bianchini, Mariana Alves, Geiser Chalco Challco, Thales Vieira, Marcelo Marinho, Valmir Macario, Diego Dermeval, Ig Ibert Bittencourt, Seiji Isotani. (2026). AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00465-x
title: Teacher-mediated AI offers a preliminary practical strategy for improving educational opportunities in resource-constrained settings
description: The article's findings support positioning the teacher, rather than the student, as the operator of AI systems where student devices are unavailable. The authors conclude that "these findings provide preliminary evidence that teacher-mediated AI may offer a practical strategy for improving educational opportunities in resource-constrained settings, calling for replications to establish whether this potential holds in longer interventions and other educational settings". The mechanism runs through the teacher: the system reduced reported effort, which was negatively associated with learning gains.
requirements: Teachers must be properly trained, and studies must experimentally control for training, since training itself enhanced students' learning outcomes in this study
constraints: Evidence is preliminary: the intervention lasted two weeks, the system showed technical and usability issues that added to teachers' work, and the indirect effect was exploratory
target_learners: students in under-resourced schools lacking per-student devices and reliable connectivity
target_learning_goals: mathematics/numeracy learning in elementary education
examples: In the study, experimental-condition teachers used the app on their own smartphones under intermittent classroom connectivity while students worked with paper and pen

article_title: Artificial intelligence in educational leadership: a comprehensive taxonomy and future directions
citation: Martin Sposato. (2025). Artificial intelligence in educational leadership: a comprehensive taxonomy and future directions. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00517-1
title: Ten-domain taxonomy of AI applications in educational leadership
description: The article develops a taxonomy that synthesizes AI applications in higher education leadership into ten distinct domains: Administrative Efficiency, Personalized Learning, Enhancing Teaching Practices, Decision-Making and Policy Formulation, Student Support Services, Organizational Leadership and Strategic Planning, Governance and Compliance, Community Engagement and Communication, Ethical AI Leadership, and DEI Initiatives. It was built through a systematic literature review and inductive analysis, and the article states it "provides educational leaders with a structured framework for understanding, evaluating, and implementing AI solutions in their institutions." Table 1 lists each domain's key components and example applications.
requirements: Domains were validated through three rounds of review and refinement: initial categorization, validation against existing frameworks, and review for practical applicability in educational leadership contexts
constraints: The taxonomy was developed from published literature from 2017 to 2024 and English-language publications, which the authors note may not capture the most recent developments or other cultural contexts
The article states the taxonomy should be viewed as a living framework requiring ongoing validation and adjustment
target_learners: educational leaders in higher education institutions
target_learning_goals: understanding, evaluating, and implementing AI solutions in educational institutions
examples: Table 1 maps each domain to key components and examples, e.g., AI-optimized class schedules and room assignments under Administrative Efficiency and AI-driven equity audits under DEI Initiatives

article_title: TeachBench - Evaluating LLM Teaching Ability
citation: Zheng Li, Siyao Song, Jingyuan Ma, Rui Li, Ying Zeng, Minghao Li, Zhifang Sui. (2026). TeachBench: A Syllabus-Grounded Framework for Evaluating Teaching Ability in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21375
title: TeachBench: a syllabus-grounded framework measuring LLM teaching capability via post-instruction student performance improvement
description: TeachBench evaluates LLMs as teacher agents by having them conduct multi-turn instruction over structured knowledge points derived from an exam syllabus, with a fixed-capability student agent as a learner proxy. Teaching effectiveness is "assessed by the student's performance improvement after instruction", enabling controlled comparison across teacher agents. Restricting teachers to knowledge points and example problems "avoids information leakage and enables reuse of existing benchmarks". The workflow has three stages: knowledge structuring, a teaching loop, and evaluation.
requirements: A structured knowledge tree extracted from an exam syllabus, questions annotated with knowledge paths, and a fixed student agent with room for improvement
constraints: The student agent is an LLM proxy, which the authors state "may not fully reflect the diversity and complexity of human learning behaviors"; no human-teacher baseline is included
target_learners: LLM student agents proxying learners preparing for the Chinese National College Entrance Examination (Gaokao)
target_learning_goals: Mastery of syllabus-defined knowledge points across mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and politics
examples: Instantiated on Gaokao syllabi and C-Eval questions, with 1,089 tagged evaluation questions across seven subjects
key_sources: Zheng Li, Siyao Song, Jingyuan Ma, Rui Li, Ying Zeng, Minghao Li, Zhifang Sui. (2026). TeachBench: A Syllabus-Grounded Framework for Evaluating Teaching Ability in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21375

article_title: TeachBench - Evaluating LLM Teaching Ability
citation: Zheng Li, Siyao Song, Jingyuan Ma, Rui Li, Ying Zeng, Minghao Li, Zhifang Sui. (2026). TeachBench: A Syllabus-Grounded Framework for Evaluating Teaching Ability in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21375
title: TeachBench knowledge-structured benchmark: Gaokao knowledge tree, LLM tagger, and difficulty-graded question generator
description: The benchmark converts Gaokao syllabi into a knowledge structure tree (semi-automatically built with Gemini-3 and GPT-5, then manually inspected), tags each question with root-to-leaf knowledge paths via an LLM tagger using depth-first traversal, and generates example problems at three difficulty levels per knowledge point. The final dataset "contains 1,089 questions in total" across seven subjects, with Mathematics (166), Physics (143), Chemistry (140), Biology (165), History (125), Geography (175), and Politics (175). Generated items undergo second-pass verification for alignment, answer correctness, and difficulty appropriateness.
requirements: Manual inspection of the knowledge tree and verifier acceptance of generated items under knowledge-point alignment, answer correctness, and difficulty criteria
constraints: Level 3 items must not directly reuse official Gaokao items; questions failing tagging after up to six attempts are dropped
target_learners: LLM teacher and student agents evaluated on Gaokao-domain knowledge
target_learning_goals: Syllabus-defined knowledge points across seven Gaokao subjects
examples: The generator produces three problems per knowledge point: easy in-class exercises, medium unit-quiz-style practice, and hard Gaokao-level reasoning items

citation: Abigail Victoria Gurin Schleifer, Moriah Ariely, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Asaf Salman, Giora Alexandron. (2026). Quality-Conditioned Agreement in Automated Short Answer Scoring: Mid-Range Degradation and the Impact of Task-Specific Adaptation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07647v2
title: Ten-category analytic rubric for open-ended cellular-respiration explanation items
description: The study scores explanations to two open-ended cellular-respiration items with an analytic rubric that "decomposes a student’s scientific explanation into a collection of 10 binary categories, each representing an essential property that the student response should include". Both items share this rubric; responses were administered in Hebrew to about 800 high-school students across two data-collection cycles.
requirements: each rubric category scored 1 if addressed in the response text and 0 otherwise; items and rubric developed by a biology education expert
constraints: the two items are conceptually similar and share one rubric; the article notes they still constitute a limited sample of possible tasks
target_learning_goals: scientific explanation of how smoking and anemia impair exercise via cellular respiration
examples: training data came from 669 responses annotated by two raters (kappa 0.89-0.98 across categories on n=130), and test data from 304 responses in a second cycle

article_title: What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI
citation: Anna-Maria Velentza, Konstantina Nikou, Anne-Gwenn Bosser, Nikolaos Fachantidis. (2026). What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22What+Robots+Do+Matters+More+Than+What+They+Look+Like%22
title: Ten-item Greek-language trust questionnaire assembled from established HRI trust scales with Lawshe content validation
description: A 10-item questionnaire rated on a five-point Likert scale after each video, developed by a multidisciplinary group of psychologists, engineers, and teachers by combining items from established trust and perception questionnaires (including trust perception, Jian et al., Kohn et al., and Godspeed items). Items cover willingness, competence, explicit trust, relative performance, reliability, and communication clarity. Content validity was assessed with Lawshe's CVR by five experts: "The resulting CVR met the critical threshold for five experts (CVR = .883, two-tailed p = .05)". Internal consistency across robot–task conditions ranged from α = .853 to .948.
requirements: Items were adapted to Greek following the bilingual-speakers technique and reviewed by five subject-matter experts
constraints: Validated with a five-expert panel and used with Greek-speaking undergraduate education students
target_learning_goals: measuring trust in robots across educational interaction tasks
examples: The same 10 items followed each of the nine videos, with mandatory responses and Cronbach's α between .85 and .95 across conditions
