article_title: Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects
citation: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1
title: Teacher intervention in AI-based instruction operates as a cyclical four-phase process of monitoring, judgment, intervention, and orchestration
description: The review conceptualizes teacher intervention as an integrated framework connecting AI-generated information with classroom practice. Analysis of the 29 included studies showed that "teacher intervention operates as a cyclical process comprising monitoring, judgment, intervention, and orchestration." AI outputs do not constitute pedagogical intervention by themselves; they gain instructional meaning only when teachers interpret, judge, and translate them into situated classroom support, and each link in the cycle is not automatic.
requirements: Teachers must interpret and judge AI-generated information before it becomes pedagogical action; the framework presupposes teacher presence in AI-based instruction
constraints: Derived from a synthesis of 29 K-12 studies published 2016-2025, relatively concentrated in middle and high school mathematics and science contexts
target_learning_goals: Transforming AI-generated information into pedagogical action and classroom adjustment
examples: The review presents the framework in Fig. 2, organizing the synthesis of processes, strategies, and effects across the 29 studies
key_sources: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1

article_title: Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects
citation: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1
title: Teacher-facing AI tools should provide actionable information and preserve teachers' control over instructional decisions
description: Across design and co-design studies in the review, teachers perceived that AI tools supported orchestration when two conditions held: the tools "provided actionable information and preserved teachers' control." Relatedly, teachers preferred shared control in which they could accept, modify, reject, or override AI suggestions rather than fully automated decision-making. This principle guides the design of teacher-facing AI systems in K-12 classrooms.
requirements: AI tools must present interpretable, actionable information; systems must allow teachers to accept, modify, reject, or override AI suggestions
constraints: The degree of preferred control varied according to classroom context, trust in AI, and teachers' perceptions of the accuracy of AI recommendations
target_learning_goals: Classroom orchestration and teacher judgment in AI-based instruction
examples: In VanLehn et al. (2021), modifying the system so some questions went directly to students without passing through the teacher showed control could be redistributed between system and students
key_sources: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1

article_title: TeachingCoach: A Fine-Tuned Scaffolding Chatbot for Instructional Guidance to Instructors
citation: Isabel Molnar, Peiyu Li, Si Chen, Sugana Chawla, James Lang, Ronald Metoyer, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawla. (2026). TeachingCoach: A Fine-Tuned Scaffolding Chatbot for Instructional Guidance to Instructors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18189
title: TeachingCoach data-centric pipeline: rule extraction, synthetic dialogue generation, expert filtering, and fine-tuning
description: TeachingCoach is built through a pipeline in which experts extract pedagogical rules from authoritative education resources, GPT-4o generates teacher profiles, teaching challenges, and multi-turn synthetic dialogues, human experts filter the dialogues, and the curated data fine-tune a LLaMA-2-13B-Chat model. The article states that "experts extract 36 core instructional rules and encode them as structured system prompts," anchoring conversations in evidence-based practices. Dialogues progress through clarifying the challenge, exploring strategies, planning next steps, and reflecting.
requirements: Access to authoritative education resources from which experts extract and encode instructional rules as structured system prompts
Human expert review to remove conversations that are inconsistent, repetitive, or pedagogically unsound
constraints: The evaluation focused on instructors' perceptions and did not directly assess student learning outcomes
target_learning_goals: Instructional problem identification, diagnosis, and strategy development
Reflective teaching practice
examples: Each conversation starts from a validated teaching dilemma violating one of the 36 practices, paired with a synthetic instructor profile, and unfolds over 20-30 turns mirroring teaching-center consultations
key_sources: Isabel Molnar, Peiyu Li, Si Chen, Sugana Chawla, James Lang, Ronald Metoyer, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawla. (2026). TeachingCoach: A Fine-Tuned Scaffolding Chatbot for Instructional Guidance to Instructors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18189

article_title: TeachingCoach: A Fine-Tuned Scaffolding Chatbot for Instructional Guidance to Instructors
citation: Isabel Molnar, Peiyu Li, Si Chen, Sugana Chawla, James Lang, Ronald Metoyer, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawla. (2026). TeachingCoach: A Fine-Tuned Scaffolding Chatbot for Instructional Guidance to Instructors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18189
title: TeachingCoach synthetic dialogue dataset (406,183 training examples)
description: A fully synthetic dataset of multi-turn instructor-consultant dialogues generated by GPT-4o from extracted rules, teacher profiles, and teaching challenges, then filtered by human experts. The article reports that "After filtering, the dataset contains 406,183 training, 4,156 validation, and 4,143 test examples." Each dialogue includes a system message with phase-keyed teaching rules, a user message with profile and challenge, and assistant messages that first predict a step descriptor and then generate the response.
requirements: GPT-4o generation of profiles, challenges, and dialogues conditioned on the extracted rules
Expert filtering for quality before fine-tuning
constraints: Data are synthetic rather than human-collected teaching conversations
target_learning_goals: Pedagogically grounded instructional guidance
examples: Dialogues span 20-30 turns with assistant turns tagged Step 1: Identify the Problem, Step 2: Explore Reasons, Step 3: Develop Strategies

article_title: Teacher-Authored Prompts for Configuring Student-AI Dialogue: K-12 Classroom Implementation
citation: Alex Liu, Min Sun, Lief Esbenshade, Victor Tian, Zachary Zhang, and Kevin He. (2026). Teacher-Authored Prompts for Configuring StudentAI Dialogue: K12 Classroom Implementation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16738
title: Recurring teacher authoring schema for encoding instructional intent in AI prompts (role, discourse moves, constraints, evidence demands, finish line)
description: Across pilot configurations the authors observed a recurring schema of five schema elements for encoding instructional intent in teacher prompting layers: AI role, discourse moves, constraints, evidence and rigor demands, and finish line. Each element functions as a pre-specification that makes progress legible and intervention points predictable across many simultaneous conversations. The article reports that "we observed a recurring schema for encoding instructional intent that maps directly onto our prompt-coding dimensions and subsequent conversation outcomes," illustrated in Table 1 with paraphrased examples such as "Act as a coach; do not give final answers."
requirements: Teachers author the prompting layer before deployment so intent can be enacted consistently across simultaneous conversations
constraints: The article notes most teachers used scaffolding sparingly, which may indicate unfamiliarity with AI-powered tools leading to underutilization of available scaffolding mechanisms
target_learners: K-12 teachers authoring AI-mediated discussions for grades 6–12 students
target_learning_goals: Structuring student-AI dialogue to preserve instructional intent
managing concurrent AI conversations
scaffolding responsible use
examples: Table 1 schema elements include a finish line defined as "Stop after the student produces two evidence-backed discussion points" and constraints such as "Keep responses to 1–2 sentences"
key_sources: Alex Liu, Min Sun, Lief Esbenshade, Victor Tian, Zachary Zhang, and Kevin He. (2026). Teacher-Authored Prompts for Configuring StudentAI Dialogue: K12 Classroom Implementation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16738

article_title: Teachy Mini: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Knowledge-Based Generative Social Robot for Higher Education
citation: Stephan Vonschallen, Karim Kaufmann, Dominique Oberle, Friederike Eyssel, Theresa Schmiedel. (2026). Teachy Mini: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Knowledge-Based Generative Social Robot for Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22345
title: Teachy Mini: a knowledge-based generative social robot tutoring prototype on the Reachy Mini platform
description: Teachy Mini is a generative social robot tutoring prototype built on the open-source Reachy Mini desktop platform, supporting spoken dialogue and head/antenna social cues via the OpenAI Realtime API. The authors "usedthreemainmethodstoprovidetherobotwiththerequiredknowledge:Dynamic system prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, andstateful prompt orchestration". It personalizes through a seven-question onboarding profile, retrieves uploaded PDF lecture slides for grounded explanations, detects conversational states (frustration, confusion, requests for depth) via regex, and injects state-specific instructions such as rephrasing explanations with a concrete analogy. Implementation code is on GitHub and materials on researchbox.org (ID: #8129).
requirements: Requires an external knowledge source for RAG grounding, an onboarding conversation to build the learner profile, and predefined verbal patterns for state detection.
constraints: Designed as an experimental single-session implementation, not a fully deployable educational system; learning progress was only partly accounted for and only the study-buddy role profile was evaluated.
target_learners: university students and recent graduates in single-session tutoring interactions
target_learning_goals: learning lecture content (research methodologies) through slide-grounded explanation, Socratic questioning, and personalized scaffolding
examples: In the evaluation, KBD and control versions shared the same Reachy Mini hardware and language model, differing only in the structured KBD configuration.

citation: Lin, Yi-Cheng; Guo, Yu-Kai; Chen, Szu-Chi; Feng, Bo-Han; Hsu, Yun-Man; Hsieh, Hsiang; Lin, Yu-Jung; Wu, Yue-Ling; Dong, Jia-Kai; Cheng, An-Yu; Huang, Yu-Han; Ieong, Lok-Lam; Chen, Kuan-Yu; Tchouang, Ming-Douo; Sun, Shao-Hua; Lin, Che; Ding, Jian-Jiun; Lee, Hung-yi. title: Teaching Monster Challenge benchmark: single-shot instructional video generation conditioned on a learner persona, with a three-layer evaluation protocol
description: A benchmark in which each item gives a system a course_requirement and a learner_persona and requires one complete instructional video generated end-to-end with no human in the loop. Items span four AP-aligned secondary STEM subjects; matched pairs hold the requirement fixed and vary the persona so that "Differencing within a pair removes item-level confounds." Evaluation proceeds through an LLM-judge screen, crowdsourced pairwise comparison aggregated into Elo ratings, and an expert panel ranking. The items, rubric, scoring traces, and human judgments are released as a testbed.

constraints: Limited to AP-aligned secondary STEM subjects in English; evaluates single-shot generation rather than interactive tutoring.
target_learners: secondary-school STEM learners described by persona (grade level, prior knowledge, attention span)
target_learning_goals: persona-adapted explanation of AP-level STEM topics
examples: The first edition ran a Warm-up phase (46 teams, 1,696 videos), a Preliminary phase (77 teams, 1,612 videos), and a Final phase with 48 videos from three finalists judged by a ten-member expert panel.

title: Two-type validation framework: technical validation and physical validation of AI-generated simulations
description: The article names and describes two complementary validation types for LLM-generated simulations. "Technical validation tests the simulation's behavior under various conditions and assess its response to parameter changes", while "Physical validation compares simulation results to known analytical solutions and verify consistency with established physical laws". The framework is applied to each of the three demonstrated simulations and can be conducted through natural-language dialogue with the model.

strengthening physics understanding by checking results against established laws
examples: Pendulum physical tests checked period accuracy against T = 2π√(L/g); Ising tests checked the critical temperature Tc = 2.269 for J = 1, H = 0

description: The paper adopts Pleasants and colleagues' construct of technoskepticism as a disposition cultivated by community-based AI learning: "a disposition toward continuously examining the relationships communities want to have with technology, asking whose needs AI serves, and whether its presence produces more wellbeing or more harm." This evaluation may lead to conditional use shaped by community criteria, or to refusal when AI misrepresents or harms the people it claims to serve.

citation: Li, Y.; Yang, H.; Fang, Q. (2025). Towards Trustworthy and Explainable-by-Design Large Language Models for Automated Teacher Assessment. Information 2025, 16, 882. https://doi.org/10.3390/info16100882
title: TeacherEval-2023 dataset of 12,450 rubric-annotated classroom dialog transcripts
description: TeacherEval-2023 is a public corpus used as the primary evaluation dataset: it comprises "12,450 classroom dialog transcripts annotated with rubric-aligned teacher performance scores and expert explanations across eight pedagogical dimensions", covering mathematics, language arts, and science across multiple grade levels. The article splits it 70/15/15 into train/validation/test with stratification across subjects and grade levels, and projects all datasets onto a unified eight-dimension framework spanning learning objectives clarity through subject-specific practices.
requirements: Rubric-aligned scores and expert explanations for supervised training
constraints: The article notes such datasets cannot fully capture multilingual or culturally specific instructional practices
target_learners: Teachers across mathematics, language arts, and science, multiple grade levels
target_learning_goals: Rubric-aligned teacher performance scoring across eight pedagogical dimensions
examples: Used as the primary benchmark in Table 3 comparisons and the ablation study on the TeacherEval-2023 test set
key_sources: Li, Y.; Yang, H.; Fang, Q. (2025). Towards Trustworthy and Explainable-by-Design Large Language Models for Automated Teacher Assessment. Information 2025, 16, 882. https://doi.org/10.3390/info16100882

article_title: A Systematic Review of Emerging Technology Applications for Teaching English as a Foreign Language Across Different Educational Levels
citation: Mengjia Liu, Harwati Hashim, Nur Ainil Sulaiman. (2026). A systematic review of emerging technology applications for teaching English as a foreign language across different educational levels. Educational Research Review 52 (2026) 100795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100795
title: Five categories of implementation challenges for emerging technologies in TEFL: technical infrastructure, teacher preparation, time constraints, student adaptation, and resource limitations
description: The review's hybrid deductive–inductive analysis of RQ4 data yielded "Five categories of implementation challenges emerged from the analysis, each with level-specific manifestations and proposed solutions." Technical infrastructure problems (connectivity, device compatibility) were acute in primary and secondary settings in developing countries; teacher preparation gaps included technical operation, pedagogical strategies, assessment design, and troubleshooting; time constraints were sharpest in settings with rigid curricula and high-stakes examinations; student adaptation difficulties affected younger learners and those with limited prior technology exposure; and hardware/software costs constrained resource-limited contexts. The review concludes that "practical implementation barriers evolve more slowly and require sustained, systemic institutional and policy attention rather than one-time investments."
requirements: Sustained, systemic institutional and policy attention rather than one-time investments
constraints: Infrastructure challenges persisted across the review period (2015–2024), suggesting technological advancement alone does not resolve access inequities
target_learners: EFL learners and teachers at primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, particularly in developing-country contexts
target_learning_goals: Effective implementation of technology-enhanced English language instruction
examples: Recommended solutions included offline-capable application modes, BYOD policies, comprehensive TPACK-focused teacher training, gradual implementation strategies, peer mentoring, and open-source software alternatives
key_sources: Mengjia Liu, Harwati Hashim, Nur Ainil Sulaiman. (2026). A systematic review of emerging technology applications for teaching English as a foreign language across different educational levels. Educational Research Review 52 (2026) 100795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100795

article_title: The Effect of Teacher Coaching on Instruction and Achievement: A Meta-Analysis of the Causal Evidence
citation: Kraft, M.A., Blazar, D., Hogan, D. (2018). The effect of teaching coaching on instruction and achievement: A meta-analysis of the causal evidence. Review of Educational Research, 88(4), 547-588. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318759268
title: Theory of action for teacher coaching: individualized observation-and-feedback cycles translate teacher knowledge into classroom practice and student achievement
description: The article situates coaching within a PD theory of action (Figure 1) in which student achievement rises only through changes in teacher knowledge and classroom practice, with coaching as the key lever for translating knowledge into practice. Coaching is characterized by "an observation and feedback cycle in an ongoing instructional or clinical situation" and is defined as individualized, intensive, sustained, context-specific, and focused on deliberate practice of specific skills. The authors use this framework to define their working definition of coaching interventions and to motivate the instruction and achievement outcomes they meta-analyze.
requirements: Coaches are instructional experts who work one-on-one with teachers, interacting at least every couple of weeks over an extended period, within the teachers' own classrooms
constraints: The article excludes teacher preparation and induction programs and programs where coaches also provided direct services to students, since effects on achievement could not be attributed to improved instruction
target_learners: in-service early childhood through 12th grade teachers in the U.S. and other developed nations
target_learning_goals: improving teachers' classroom instructional practice
raising student achievement on standardized assessments
examples: The meta-analysis codes 60 causal studies against this framework, including complementary elements such as group trainings, instructional content, and video libraries
key_sources: Kraft, M.A., Blazar, D., Hogan, D. (2018). The effect of teaching coaching on instruction and achievement: A meta-analysis of the causal evidence. Review of Educational Research, 88(4), 547-588. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318759268

article_title: What Schools Need to Know About Fostering School Belonging: a Meta-analysis
citation: Allen, K., Kern, M.L., Vella-Brodrick, D., Hattie, J., & Waters, L. (2018). What Schools Need to Know About Fostering School Belonging: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 1–34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9389-8
title: Ten student-level themes influence school belonging during adolescence
description: The article organizes the fragmented school belonging literature into a taxonomy of ten student-level themes identified through systematic review: "academic motivation, emotional stability, personal characteristics, parent support, peer support, teacher support, gender, race and ethnicity, extracurricular activities and environmental/school safety". This taxonomy resolves inconsistency in terminology and structures the subsequent meta-analysis of each theme's association with belonging.
requirements: Themes were derived from a systematic review of research on school belonging at the student level during adolescence in educational settings
constraints: The taxonomy addresses the student level during adolescence; the article notes research on school belonging has been "fragmented and diluted by inconsistency in the use of terminology"
target_learning_goals: school belonging
psychological functioning
examples: The systematic review identified the ten themes, which were then each meta-analytically examined across 51 studies
key_sources: Allen, K., Kern, M.L., Vella-Brodrick, D., Hattie, J., & Waters, L. (2018). What Schools Need to Know About Fostering School Belonging: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 1–34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9389-8

article_title: The role of biomedical knowledge in diagnosis of difficult clinical cases
citation: Woods, N.N., Brooks, L.R. & Norman, G.R. (2007). The role of biomedical knowledge in diagnosis of difficult clinical cases. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 12, 417–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-006-9054-y
title: Teach causal mechanisms alongside clinical features to prepare novices for difficult diagnoses
description: The article's results support teaching underlying causal mechanisms, not just clinical feature lists, when preparing novices for difficult diagnostic challenges. Causal training improved performance on cases with irrelevant findings and unfamiliar terminology, and the unfamiliar-terminology advantage persisted one week after training. The authors conclude the studies "provide additional support for the critical role of biomedical knowledge in diagnosis of difficult clinical cases."
requirements: Learners must be taught the underlying causal mechanisms of the diseases, not only a list of clinical features.
constraints: Evidence comes from artificial diseases learned by novice diagnosticians in two experiments, not from routine clinical cases.
target_learning_goals: diagnostic accuracy on difficult clinical cases
examples: In Experiment 1, participants were taught artificial diseases using either knowledge of causal mechanisms or a list of clinical features, then tested on cases with irrelevant findings and unfamiliar terminology.
key_sources: Woods, N.N., Brooks, L.R. & Norman, G.R. (2007). The role of biomedical knowledge in diagnosis of difficult clinical cases. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 12, 417–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-006-9054-y

article_title: SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT
citation: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311
title: Meta-analytic corpus of 97 reports, 105 independent samples, and 216 effect sizes on L2 anxiety and achievement
description: The study assembled a meta-analytic dataset on L2 anxiety and achievement. Following a comprehensive search, "a sample of 97 reports were identified, contributing a total of 105 independent samples (N = 19,933) from 23 countries," yielding 216 effect sizes (correlations). The corpus underpins the aggregate estimate and moderator analyses. The study earned an Open Data badge, with materials available at the IRIS database.
requirements: Comprehensive search to identify eligible reports of the anxiety–achievement relationship
target_learners: second language learners across 23 countries and multiple educational levels
target_learning_goals: second language achievement
examples: 97 reports contributing 105 independent samples (N = 19,933) from 23 countries
key_sources: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311

article_title: SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT
citation: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311
title: Open materials and data for the L2 anxiety meta-analysis hosted in the IRIS database
description: The article's materials are openly available: "The experiment in this article earned an Open Data badge for transparent practices. The materials are available at www.iris-database.org/iris/app/home/detail?id=york%3a935928&ref=search." The page also lists Open Practices badges for open materials and open data, supporting replication and reuse of the meta-analytic coding.

examples: Open Data badge with materials at the IRIS repository

article_title: Kindergarten teachers develop phoneme awareness in low-income, inner-city classrooms
citation: Blachman, B.A., Ball, E.W., Black, R.S. & Tangel, D.M. (1994). Kindergarten teachers develop phoneme awareness in low-income, inner-city classrooms. Read Writ 6, 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01027275
title: Classroom teachers and teaching assistants — not only researchers — can deliver effective phoneme awareness instruction in kindergarten
description: The study's central design choice was to have phonological awareness instruction delivered "by kindergarten teachers and their teaching assistants" in ordinary low-income, inner-city classrooms, rather than by outside researchers. The significant post-intervention advantages on phoneme segmentation, letter knowledge, reading, and invented spelling indicate classroom staff can implement this instruction effectively. This supports embedding phoneme awareness training in regular kindergarten practice.
requirements: Kindergarten teachers and teaching assistants deliver the instruction in their own classrooms over an extended period (11 weeks in this study)
constraints: Evidence comes from low-income, inner-city kindergarten classrooms in an urban district in upstate New York
target_learners: Kindergarten children in low-income, inner-city schools
target_learning_goals: Phoneme awareness, letter name and letter sound knowledge, beginning reading, and invented spelling
examples: The intervention was provided in low-income, inner-city kindergarten classrooms by kindergarten teachers and their teaching assistants over 11 weeks
key_sources: Blachman, B.A., Ball, E.W., Black, R.S. & Tangel, D.M. (1994). Kindergarten teachers develop phoneme awareness in low-income, inner-city classrooms. Read Writ 6, 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01027275

article_title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
citation: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7
title: Teachers should be prioritized and involved in the co-design of AI literacy didactic proposals, supported by TPACK-based training
description: The review identifies teachers as key players for integrating AI literacy in K-12 and concludes didactic proposals must be co-designed and implemented by the teachers at the schools involved. It reports a shortage of teachers with AI training and proposes working with teachers in training or in schools as an effective solution. It highlights TPACK as the model for the knowledge teachers need: "teachers imparting AI to K-12 students require TPACK to build an environment and facilitate project-based classes that solve problems using AI technologies."
requirements: Teacher training following a framework of standard competencies
Identification of teachers' perceptions and knowledge about AI
constraints: Teachers can swing between total resistance and overconfidence; resistance could arise from inadequate, inappropriate, irrelevant, or outdated professional development
target_learning_goals: Teacher professional development in AI
Integration of AI into teaching-learning processes
examples: The review reports co-design of ML curricula between AI researchers and K-12 teachers as an important current issue
key_sources: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7

article_title: Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on teaching and learning in higher education
citation: Popenici, S. A. D., & Kerr, S. (2017). Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on teaching and learning in higher education. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 12:22. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41039-017-0062-8
title: Teacherbots: AI-based virtual teaching assistants for content delivery, feedback and supervision
description: Teacherbots are defined by the article as "any machine-based software or hardware that assumes the role traditionally performed by a teacher assistant in organizing information and providing fast answers to a wide set of predictable questions". They can facilitate, monitor, assess and manage student learning in online spaces, providing bespoke content, supervision and guidance. The article presents them as a disruptive alternative to traditional teaching assistants, exemplified by Jill Watson on IBM's Watson platform.
requirements: A platform such as IBM Watson capable of providing an automated teacher presence for the duration of a course
constraints: The article notes that in 2017 there is little exploration of what a teacherbot is and what its capabilities are now and in a predictable future
target_learners: Higher education students in blended or fully online courses, including massive enrolments
target_learning_goals: Content delivery, basic and administrative feedback, supervision, and personalized learning support at scale
examples: Professor Ashok Goel's knowledge-based artificial intelligence course in Georgia Tech's online Master in Computer Sciences program used the Jill Watson teaching assistant
key_sources: Popenici, S. A. D., & Kerr, S. (2017). Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on teaching and learning in higher education. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 12:22. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41039-017-0062-8

article_title: Young Children Can Learn Scientific Reasoning with Teachable Agents
citation: Doris B. Chin, Ilsa M. Dohmen, and Daniel L. Schwartz. (2013). Young Children Can Learn Scientific Reasoning with Teachable Agents. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1109/TLT.2013.24
title: Three design principles for teachable agents: visible thinking, independent performance with recursive feedback, and student responsibility for the agent
description: The article organizes teachable agent (TA) design around three principles drawn from the learning sciences: the TA "makes its thought processes visible"; it "exhibits independent performance to produce recursive feedback," grounded in Premack's recursive thought and the prote´ge´ effect; and it engenders social responsibility toward the agent (naming, customization, game rewards). The authors stress the main value is that the principles "bring these positive learning mechanisms together into a single learning technology," instantiated in Betty's Brain.
requirements: The teacher, curriculum specialist, or researcher must produce hidden expert maps so the system can generate questions and feedback
constraints: The principles are not intended to exclude other approaches to TA design; they reflect features that asserted themselves over 15 years of work
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning schemas such as hierarchical class-inclusion reasoning
science content understanding
examples: Taxonomy Betty traces its reasoning by progressively highlighting links and nodes; the Triple-A-Challenge game show uses a hidden expert map to evaluate the agent's answers
key_sources: Doris B. Chin, Ilsa M. Dohmen, and Daniel L. Schwartz. (2013). Young Children Can Learn Scientific Reasoning with Teachable Agents. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1109/TLT.2013.24

article_title: Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment
citation: Mayer, I. (2018). Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment. Simulation & Gaming, 49(6), 602-619. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878118770831
title: TEAMUP multiplayer 3D team training and assessment game
description: TEAMUP (© The Barn) is a commercial, multiplayer three-dimensional serious game built in the Unreal Development Kit engine in which "Four players need to self-organise, communicate, collaborate and arrange team communication, coordination and leadership in order to solve five levels of puzzles/team challenges". Players stranded on a deserted island must reach the other side to be rescued, with five puzzle levels (door, tile, maze, bridge, pillar) requiring alternating leadership. The game logs any kind of game data, communicates with a scoring, assessment and visualisation tool, and supports distributed play and video recording.
requirements: Four-player teams seated so each player sees only their own screen, communicating only by speech
constraints: Available for team training under a commercial license
target_learners: professionals such as police officers, auditors and consultants
undergraduate and postgraduate students in engineering, management and entrepreneurship
target_learning_goals: team communication, coordination and leadership
team self-organisation and collaboration
examples: Played in 3-4 hour workshop mode with 3-6 teams in parallel, followed by a 1-hour facilitated plenary discussion showing team scores on a central screen
key_sources: Mayer, I. (2018). Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment. Simulation & Gaming, 49(6), 602-619. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878118770831

article_title: University students’ self-regulated learning using digital technologies
citation: Carmen Yot-Domínguez and Carlos Marcelo. (2017). University students' self-regulated learning using digital technologies. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education 14:38. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-017-0076-8
title: University teachers should incorporate digital technologies and create environments that favour independent, self-regulated learning
description: The article recommends that university teachers incorporate digital technologies into learning activities and design environments offering opportunities to seek challenges, reflect on progress, and take responsibility for accomplishments. It argues students' non-use of technologies for learning stems partly from teachers who "neither require nor encourage their use", and that failing to incorporate technologies perpetuates the gap between the university world and the labour and social world.
requirements: Teachers must require or encourage the use of digital technologies in learning activities, since students currently do not adopt them for SRL on their own.
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in a survey of Andalusian university students; the authors note the sample's size and diversity should be expanded and teachers should also be studied.
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
independent learning with digital technologies
examples: The authors analysed learning activities designed by Andalusian university instructors and found teachers neither require nor encourage technology use for self-regulation; they cite emerging intervention programs and pedagogical frameworks using Web 2.0 and social software to promote SRL.
key_sources: Carmen Yot-Domínguez and Carlos Marcelo. (2017). University students' self-regulated learning using digital technologies. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education 14:38. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-017-0076-8

article_title: Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders
citation: Kim, Y.-S., Al Otaiba, S., Sidler Folsom, J., & Gruelich, L. (2013). Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 28(3), 461–469. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2013.01.001
title: Promote teacher responsiveness to students' inquiries and responses as a lever for improving beginning writing quality
description: The article concludes that 'teachers' interaction with students, and teachers' responsiveness in particular, may be an important factor to consider and promote in facilitating children's writing development.' Responsiveness was defined as the extent to which teachers selected and incorporated students' responses and experiences in their instruction, rated from classroom observation. This general instructional quality dimension predicted substantive quality of writing even after accounting for child-level skills and content-specific instructional quality.
requirements: Classroom observation or professional development focused on teachers' incorporation of student responses and experiences during literacy instruction
constraints: Instructional quality was based on a single winter observation; the authors caution that 'caution needs to be exercised for interpretation and future replication would be informative'
target_learning_goals: Substantive quality of written composition
examples: Teachers rated highly responsive (score of 3) were those effective at selecting and incorporating students' responses and experiences; those punitive toward children's inquiries received low scores
key_sources: Kim, Y.-S., Al Otaiba, S., Sidler Folsom, J., & Gruelich, L. (2013). Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 28(3), 461–469. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2013.01.001

article_title: The interplay between math anxiety and working memory on math performance: a longitudinal study
citation: Pellizzoni, S., Cargnelutti, E., Cuder, A., & Passolunghi, M.C. (2021). The interplay between math anxiety and working memory on math performance: a longitudinal study. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.14722
title: Teachers' ratings are a useful measure of young children's general anxiety when self-report is unreliable
description: The article argues that measuring general anxiety in young children via self-assessment is problematic and that teacher assessments are a better indicator. It notes "Teachers’ ratings can, therefore, be taken as a useful measure of children's anxiety," and in this study only teacher-rated GA related to math performance and WM, while children's self-ratings did not. Teachers' essential role in assessing the emotional complexities of learning is underscored.
requirements: Teachers who know the child well enough to rate anxiety reliably
constraints: The DAYS_T teacher-rated anxiety subscale showed modest reliability (0.66) in this sample; the authors call for replication with more reliable tools
target_learning_goals: identifying emotional factors affecting math achievement
examples: In the study, teacher-rated GA (DAYS_T) predicted math performance while children's self-rated GA (RCMAS) did not
key_sources: Pellizzoni, S., Cargnelutti, E., Cuder, A., & Passolunghi, M.C. (2021). The interplay between math anxiety and working memory on math performance: a longitudinal study. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.14722

article_title: Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students’ Math Achievement
citation: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052
title: Anxiety-to-practice-to-perceived-mindset account of how teacher math anxiety shapes student math achievement
description: The article proposes that math anxious teachers, through their "teaching comments, behaviors, and teaching practices," create classroom environments that devalue sense-making and effort in favor of memorization and innate ability. Students decode these cues and infer the teacher's beliefs, so that "students who perceive more ability-oriented (as opposed to process-oriented) teaching practices may infer how their potential is regarded by the teacher and the environment." This account bridges teacher math anxiety, organizational incremental theory, and teacher expectancy research, positioning student-perceived teacher mindset as the key mediating construct rather than teachers' knowledge.
requirements: Teachers' classroom actions and practices must be observable by students, who infer beliefs from witnessed behaviors
constraints: The article states the supporting evidence is correlational, which prevents inferring causality
target_learners: ninth-grade adolescent students in mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement (course grades)
students' beliefs about mathematical ability
examples: The study measured student-perceived teacher fixed mindset with three items and process-oriented practices with Tripod 7Cs Challenge items, then tested the mediation chain in a SEM framework.
key_sources: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052

article_title: Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents
citation: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/
title: Teacher nomination procedure for observer-reported emotion regulation
description: Observer reports were collected through teacher nominations in which teachers selected up to 5 students they considered at the high and low ends of emotion regulation ability from alphabetical lists of students they taught. Nominations of difficulty regulating emotions were assigned −1, nominations of being good at regulating emotions were assigned 1, and non-nominated students received 0. To account for unequal numbers of students taught by different teachers, nominations by each teacher were standardized and summed across all teachers. Teachers were instructed to base judgments on classroom observation rather than general reputation.
requirements: Teachers must have directly observed students in instructional contexts
Nomination lists must be standardized to account for unequal class sizes
constraints: Based on a single nomination question rather than multiple items, which the authors identify as a reliability limitation
Captures teacher-perceived regulation in classroom settings specifically
target_learning_goals: assessing enacted emotion regulation observable in classroom behavior
examples: Teachers were asked to identify students "good at regulating their emotions (e.g., able to get energized when necessary and calm down when needed)" and those with most difficulty regulating emotions
key_sources: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/

article_title: The effects of teamwork on critical thinking: A serial mediation analysis of the influence of work skills and educational motivation in secondary school students
citation: Clemente Rodríguez-Sabiote, Eva María Olmedo-Moreno and Jorge Expósito-López. (2022). The effects of teamwork on critical thinking: A serial mediation analysis of the influence of work skills and educational motivation in secondary school students. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2022.101063
title: Foster teamwork alongside educational motivation and future work skills to develop secondary students' critical thinking
description: The article's outcomes imply that formative systems should develop teamwork together with motivational processes and future work skills, because these serve as "basic elements that permit effective social and occupational integration". Greater teamwork and higher degrees of motivation were associated with increased critical thinking, and better conceptions of teamwork impacted upon better future work skills. The authors argue student motivation should be a concern for teachers at any educational stage.
requirements: Formative processes that address teamwork, educational motivation and future work skills together rather than in isolation
Instruments adapted to the secondary school context to measure these constructs
constraints: Evidence is ex post facto and cross-sectional with a single measurement, so the model shows associations rather than tested causal effects
The sequential route through work skills then motivation was less relevant than the two two-path routes
target_learners: Compulsory secondary education students, including baccalaureate and vocational training students
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking
Teamwork capacity
Educational motivation
Future work skills
examples: The authors tested whether greater teamwork, together with higher levels of educational motivation, increase critical thinking (Ind2) and accepted all three mediational hypotheses
key_sources: Clemente Rodríguez-Sabiote, Eva María Olmedo-Moreno and Jorge Expósito-López. (2022). The effects of teamwork on critical thinking: A serial mediation analysis of the influence of work skills and educational motivation in secondary school students. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2022.101063

article_title: Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School
citation: Capellini, S. A., Giaconi, C., & Germano, G. D. (2017). Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School. Psychology, 8, 258-270. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.82015
title: Teach visual-perception and motor-coordination strategies before and during early alphabetization, since students start writing instruction lacking these essential skills
description: Because most 1st-grade students in this study were classified with dysgraphia, the authors conclude that "the students start the alphabetization process without some essential skills, such as viso -perception and motor coord ination", and state this finding "brings an important impact to educational policy". They further suggest that the absence of clear skill progression across grades "might suggest a lack of teac h-ing of strategies in classroom". The principle is that handwriting instruction should be preceded and accompanied by explicit teaching of visual-perceptual and motor-coordination strategies.
requirements: Classroom instruction must include systematic teaching of visual-perception, motor-coordination and visual-motor integration strategies alongside literacy activities.
constraints: The article notes the Dysgraphia Scale estimates are based on a limited number of subjects and that no national scale or test existed in Brazil for these parameters.
target_learners: 1st- to 5th-grade elementary school students in public schools
target_learning_goals: handwriting quality and legibility
visual-motor integration, visual perception and motor coordination
examples: The study found 80% of 1st graders classified with dysgraphia and no clear grade progression in visual-motor skills, which the authors link to missing classroom strategy teaching.
key_sources: Capellini, S. A., Giaconi, C., & Germano, G. D. (2017). Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School. Psychology, 8, 258-270. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.82015

article_title: Fostering alphabet knowledge development: a comparison of two instructional approaches
citation: Piasta, S. B., Purpura, D. J., & Wagner, R. K. (2010). Fostering Alphabet Knowledge Development: A Comparison of Two Instructional Approaches. Reading and Writing, 23(6), 607-626. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9174-x
title: Teach letter names and sounds together rather than letter sounds alone when fostering preschool alphabet knowledge
description: The article's central design recommendation is that for U.S. preschoolers, referring to each letter by its name and linking it to its corresponding sound (e.g., "the letter C that makes the sound/k/") fosters letter sound acquisition better than sound-only labeling. The authors state that "combined letter name and sound instruction may be most beneficial for U.S. preschoolers alphabet learning", while noting the mechanism is not entirely clear and more research is needed.
requirements: Instruction delivered in small groups (3-5 children) through scripted lessons of approximately 10-15 minutes, as in the study's 34-lesson curriculum
constraints: The advantage was specific to alphabet knowledge outcomes and did not generalize to other emergent literacy skills
The authors note the finding may not apply to children for whom letter sounds are a common, natural label, such as some children in the deaf community or UK-style instruction
Based on a small-scale study with observed power substantially lower than the intended 80%
target_learners: preschool-aged children (3- and 4-year-olds) with below-average letter knowledge
target_learning_goals: letter name knowledge
letter sound knowledge
examples: In the study, LNLS lessons referred to each letter by name and linked it to its sound, while LS lessons designated letters only by sound; both taught 26 uppercase letters plus 8 weekly review lessons over 9 weeks
key_sources: Piasta, S. B., Purpura, D. J., & Wagner, R. K. (2010). Fostering Alphabet Knowledge Development: A Comparison of Two Instructional Approaches. Reading and Writing, 23(6), 607-626. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9174-x

article_title: Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality
citation: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026
title: One-to-one teacher/instructor paradigm with synchronous and asynchronous feedback in immersive simulation training
description: The 3B training pattern pairs an immersed trainee teacher with a non-immersed instructor who monitors performance and controls stimuli in real time. The instructor interface consists of five boards: instructions, virtual student control, environment viewport, camera control, and feedback. Synchronous feedback uses "Thumb-up"/"Thumb-down" buttons with positive or negative audio cues to guide the teacher during the lecture without interrupting the session, while asynchronous feedback is a detailed evaluation form summarizing the teacher's performance after the session. Both feedback types are automatically logged as performance indicators to measure teacher progress across sessions.
requirements: Instructors were repeatedly reminded to give feedback via an animated message with sound displayed thirty seconds after each new bad-behavior-activation instruction
constraints: An option permits the instructor to enable or disable the audio feedback cues, thereby muting the feedback
target_learners: Trainee teachers in classroom management seminars
target_learning_goals: Adjusting teaching behavior in response to guided feedback on handling disruptive behavior
examples: In the user study, instructors increased class agitation across five phases while giving synchronous audio feedback in one condition and none in the other
key_sources: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026

article_title: Making rounds: The routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers
citation: Christian Greiffenhagen. (2011). Making Rounds: the routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (forthcoming). https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Taxonomy of teacher intervention types during 'making rounds' in computer-based collaborative learning
description: The paper organizes its analysis into distinct types of teacher intervention during rounds: ratifying pupils' work, reminding pupils of neglected task aspects, making suggestions, maintaining classroom control, and making whole-class announcements. Through "a close analysis of different types of teacher interventions into pupils working in pairs with a storyboarding tool", each type is illustrated with transcribed video fragments. The taxonomy describes what teachers actually do, not what they are supposed to do.
requirements: Video or direct observation of teacher activity during pupil pair work at computers
constraints: Derived from one teacher's lessons with one storyboarding task in secondary English; the paper analyses naturally occurring discourse rather than evaluating effectiveness
target_learning_goals: Engaging with Shakespeare's Macbeth through visual storyboarding
examples: Fragments show the teacher ratifying work, pointing out missing punctuation and spelling, reminding pupils about the caption box, suggesting breaking a monologue into smaller pieces, and a wordless 'BOO' reproach
key_sources: Christian Greiffenhagen. (2011). Making Rounds: the routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (forthcoming). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9134-8

article_title: Making rounds: The routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers
citation: Christian Greiffenhagen. (2011). Making Rounds: the routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (forthcoming). https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Teacher rounds as the routine organization of monitoring during pair work at computers
description: Once pupils start working in pairs, the teacher does not sit back but 'makes rounds' through the classroom to monitor, evaluate, and control what pupils are doing. The pattern comprises brief visits in which the teacher looks at screens, ratifies or corrects work, reminds pupils of neglected aspects, and makes suggestions. As Sorensen's description quoted in the paper shows, the teacher "wanders around among children", bending down, looking at screens, and talking to pupils.
requirements: An open classroom layout allowing the teacher to approach and view pupil screens
constraints: Open-ended, less sequentially structured computer tasks make it harder for the teacher to see what pupils have done and anticipate what they will do next, per Sorensen's account quoted in the paper
target_learners: Secondary school pupils working in pairs at computers
target_learning_goals: Completing all aspects of a multi-step production task
Staying on task during self-directed pair work
examples: In the study the teacher checked previous frames for empty caption boxes and reminded both individuals and the whole class to write their reasons
key_sources: Christian Greiffenhagen. (2011). Making Rounds: the routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (forthcoming). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9134-8

article_title: Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions
citation: Fu, E. L. F., van Aalst, J., & Chan, C. K. K. (2016). Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 441-478. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9245-3
title: Co-investigation of students' online discourse with teachers deepens principle-based understanding of knowledge building and generates feedback for teaching improvement
description: In the Knowledge Building Teacher Network, teachers and researchers met weekly to design and improve teaching practices, and teachers were guided to co-investigate their students' online discourse through the three modes of discourse framework and knowledge-building principles. The authors report that BCo-investigation into the online discourse not only generated feedback for the teachers to improve their teaching practices, but also became a method for them to deepen their principle-based understanding of knowledge building. This addresses the problem of Blethal mutationBwhere learning principles are lost when designs are implemented.
requirements: Weekly teacher-researcher collaboration meetings
A framework of discourse modes and knowledge-building principles to structure the analysis
constraints: Developed in the context of a professional development project in Hong Kong; not tested as a controlled intervention in the text provided
target_learning_goals: Teachers' principle-based understanding of knowledge building and CSCL discourse
examples: Teachers referred to the principle of constructive use of authoritative sources when students shared factual knowledge, to scaffold students toward interpreting and explaining information rather than merely locating it
key_sources: Fu, E. L. F., van Aalst, J., & Chan, C. K. K. (2016). Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 441-478. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9245-3

article_title: Collaboration scripts and scaffolding
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rosé, & Gerry Stahl. (2016). Collaboration scripts and scaffolding. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 381–385. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9247-1
title: Treat the teacher as an interactional partner who scaffolds students' efforts to become more productive
description: Across the CSCL studies in this issue, the editors emphasize that "The teacher's role is important in CSCL studies as an interactional partner scaffolding students in their efforts to become more productive in their academic work." Design of computational support should therefore recognize classroom complexity and how teachers appropriate new tools into daily routines, and naturalistic studies should involve teachers as part of the activities.
requirements: Teachers must recognize the advantages of new computational tools and embed them in their daily routines
constraints: The teacher is a limited resource compared with automated support
target_learners: school and university students in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: more productive academic work through scaffolded collaboration
examples: The editors note teachers can increase the quality of talk through more subtle, varied, and contextualized forms of intervention than agent prompts
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rosé, & Gerry Stahl. (2016). Collaboration scripts and scaffolding. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 381–385. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9247-1

article_title: What information should CSCL teacher dashboards provide to help teachers interpret CSCL situations?
citation: van Leeuwen, A., Rummel, N., & van Gog, T. (2019). What information should CSCL teacher dashboards provide to help teachers interpret CSCL situations? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 14, 261–289. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09299-x
title: Teacher noticing framework: detection and interpretation of classroom situations
description: The article adopts the teacher noticing framework of Van Es and Sherin to model how teachers make sense of classroom and dashboard situations. It distinguishes two processes: "detection", deciding what deserves attention, and interpretation, reasoning about events and their broader principles. Characteristics include which students and behaviors teachers focus on, the specificity and evidence use of interpretations, and teachers' stance ranging from describing to interpreting. The framework supplies the study's coding scheme and its outcome measures.
requirements: Applied here to the situation where a teacher consults a dashboard rather than directly observing student behavior
constraints: Taking an interpretative stance is not something teachers automatically do or are always capable of, per Van Es and Sherin as cited
target_learning_goals: Teacher skill in detecting and interpreting student collaboration during CSCL
examples: The experimental study coded teachers' open comments for evidence use, stance (levels 1-4), and specificity based on this framework
key_sources: van Leeuwen, A., Rummel, N., & van Gog, T. (2019). What information should CSCL teacher dashboards provide to help teachers interpret CSCL situations? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 14, 261–289. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09299-x

article_title: Ethnomethodologically informed
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3
title: Base collaborative-technology design on EM findings from interaction analysis
description: Stahl argues the insights obtained from EM interaction analysis can inform CSCL technology and pedagogy design: findings about which moments in interaction cause breakdown, struggle, or confusion can be used to critique a system or lesson and to suggest redesign. This connects EM microanalysis of learner interaction directly to design-based research in CSCL.
requirements: Access to detailed interaction data showing how learners use a specific technology or pedagogy in concrete settings
constraints: Design implications arise from single, situated case studies rather than statistical generalizations
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning: designing artifacts and lessons that better mediate collaborative meaning making
examples: Stahl notes EM can contribute to the analysis phase of design-based research (citing the Design-Based Research Collective, 2003)
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3

article_title: Studying teacher withitness in the wild: comparing a mirroring and an alerting & guiding dashboard for collaborative learning
citation: Reet Kasepalu, Pankaj Chejara, Luis P. Prieto, Tobias Ley. (2023). Studying teacher withitness in the wild: comparing a mirroring and an alerting & guiding dashboard for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:575–606. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09414-z
title: Teacher withitness: two-dimensional framework of classroom situational awareness plus real-time interventions during collaborative learning
description: Withitness is "the skill of teachers to process and handle classroom situations along two dimensions: classroom awareness (i.e., what is going on in the classroom) and what the teacher is doing to maintain learning (i.e., her interventions)". The article positions it as "the part of orchestration that happens in real-time during the learning activities", narrower than the broad orchestration construct, and draws on Endsley's three levels of situational awareness (perception, comprehension, prediction) measured via adapted SAGAT statements. The study uses this framework to structure its hypotheses H1 and H3.
requirements: Teachers must first achieve situational awareness of classroom events before choosing interventions to sustain learning
constraints: The article focuses less on disciplining students and more on supporting students to learn to work together and coregulate
target_learning_goals: real-time monitoring and support of collaborative learning
key_sources: Reet Kasepalu, Pankaj Chejara, Luis P. Prieto, Tobias Ley. (2023). Studying teacher withitness in the wild: comparing a mirroring and an alerting & guiding dashboard for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:575–606. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09414-z

article_title: A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Tiina Törmänen. (2026). A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09464-5
title: Temporal network analysis: combining the relational and temporal dimensions of CSCL interaction modeling
description: Temporal networks are a method that models both the relational aspects (who interacts with whom) and the temporal aspects (order, duration, concurrency) of collaborative learning. The article presents it as bringing the "best of both worlds" — combining network analysis's relational dimension with sequence methods' temporal dimension. Each node and edge carries timestamps marking start and end of activity; connections are temporary, only past interactions relate to future ones, and time-respecting paths replace static path length.
requirements: A timestamp must be attached to the start and end of each node and edge for an interaction network to count as a temporal network
constraints: The article notes centrality, connectivity, and diffusion must be reformulated for temporal dependencies, and the approach is fundamentally different from static networks rather than a straightforward generalization
target_learning_goals: capturing longitudinal dynamics of collaborative learning interactions and regulation
examples: The study used temporal networks to trace tied duration of uptake among coded interaction types in PBL forum discussions
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Tiina Törmänen. (2026). A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09464-5

article_title: Fostering pre-service teachers’ theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases
citation: Baier, F., Maurer, C., Dignath, C., & Kunter, M. (2021). Fostering pre-service teachers' theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09560-7
title: Use text-based cases to connect scientific theory to real-world classroom situations in teacher education, but treat them as one option rather than a panacea against inert knowledge
description: The article recommends employing text-based cases in formal teacher education because they relate theoretical input to authentic classroom situations and are economical to construct, distribute and update. It found a small advantage for case-based learning on knowledge application and higher situational interest, yet stresses that "the pre-service teachers studying without cases also substantially gained in their knowledge" and that "case-based learning may not necessarily be the only panacea to avoid inert knowledge". Designers should therefore consider the several causes of inert knowledge when designing learning environments.
requirements: Cases must be complex real-world classroom situations that learners analyse by generating courses of action grounded in the studied theory.
constraints: The measured advantage over a comparable model-based intervention was small and may not be of practical relevance; the vignette measure was of reduced complexity compared to real-life classroom situations.
target_learners: pre-service teachers in initial teacher education
target_learning_goals: productive application of scientific classroom-management theory to authentic classroom situations
examples: Pre-service teachers read theoretical input on classroom management and generated possible courses of action for two real-world text-based cases per week, with sample solutions and additional theoretical input as instructional support.
key_sources: Baier, F., Maurer, C., Dignath, C., & Kunter, M. (2021). Fostering pre-service teachers' theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09560-7

article_title: Teachers’ subjectivities in responsive instruction: when ambitious practice encounters challenging teaching situations
citation: Ilana Seidel Horn, Yeliz Günal Aggül, Shuqin Li, Christine E. Hood. (2025). Teachers’ subjectivities in responsive instruction: when ambitious practice encounters challenging teaching situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09742-7
title: Situative framework of teachers' subjectivities: relational agency supports epistemic agency, which enables responsive practice
description: The article develops a conceptual framework in which teachers' subjectivities — their prior experiences, interpretations, agency, and emotions — are central to responsive teaching. It synthesizes two sociocultural forms of agency: epistemic agency, where teachers take responsibility for initiating and negotiating ideas to create knowledge, and relational agency, the collaborative work of expanding interpretations of problems with others. The framework holds that "in institutional environments that support practitioners' relational work in addressing challenging workplace problems, relational agency can support the development of epistemic agency," producing a virtuous cycle that sustains responsive instruction.
requirements: Institutional environments that support practitioners' relational work in addressing challenging workplace problems
constraints: The framework was built from two critical events with two teachers committed to responsive instruction in one professional development organization
target_learning_goals: sustaining responsive and culturally responsive instruction in the face of challenging teaching situations
examples: The framework was built through case analysis of two teachers, Veronica and Linda, each facing a student who challenged something core to their vision of teaching
key_sources: Ilana Seidel Horn, Yeliz Günal Aggül, Shuqin Li, Christine E. Hood. (2025). Teachers’ subjectivities in responsive instruction: when ambitious practice encounters challenging teaching situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09742-7

article_title: Teacher vision: expert and novice teachers’ perception of problematic classroom management scenes
citation: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Niek van den Bogert, Henny P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teacher vision: expert and novice teachers' perception of problematic classroom management scenes. Instr Sci 44:243-265. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9367-z
title: Professional vision of teaching: knowledge-driven perception of classroom events underpinning withitness
description: The article frames teachers' professional vision as the skilfulness at observing, searching for, and making sense of classroom scenes, developing over time as teachers learn their profession's visual practices (Goodwin 1994; Sherin 2001). It is underpinned by Kounin's withitness: "teachers direct attention to relevant information in the classroom and continually monitor the progression of events". The account predicts that experience-built event-structured knowledge guides focused, selective attention to informative cues, whereas novices lacking such knowledge search indiscriminately and are drawn to salient but uninformative image features.
requirements: Requires event-structured classroom knowledge built through substantial teaching experience; the article notes five to seven years as a reasonable estimate for developing high-level skill
constraints: The study examined only problematic classroom situations and sheds no light on expert-novice differences in non-problematic situations
Findings concern visual processing of video scenes, not live teaching
target_learning_goals: classroom management awareness
noticing and interpreting classroom cues and events
examples: Experts revisited AOIs showing students' trunks, shoulders, arms, hands and interactive regions between rows, while novices revisited areas void of discernible student activity such as walls and a window showing hallway activity
key_sources: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Niek van den Bogert, Henny P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teacher vision: expert and novice teachers' perception of problematic classroom management scenes. Instr Sci 44:243-265. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9367-z

article_title: Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity
citation: H. P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity. Instructional Science, 44, 311–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9377-x
title: Teaching a class as one big regulation problem with multiple coordinated goals
description: The article frames teaching as "one big regulation problem (Cronin and Gonzalez 2007): multiple goals have to be pursued, while disturbances have to be minimised using different kinds of steering instruments." Goals vary along dimensions such as academic goals (per lesson, course, curriculum) and conducive goals (safety, quiet environment, good working relations). The goals, their hierarchy, and the quality of available instruments determine the outcome of the regulation problem.
requirements: Clear goals and valid, timely information on results for regulation
constraints: Information on results is often not available in natural practice
target_learning_goals: classroom management
instructional regulation
key_sources: H. P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity. Instructional Science, 44, 311–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9377-x

article_title: Spaced recall reduces forgetting of fundamental mathematical concepts in a post high school precalculus course
citation: Lindquist, D. S., Sparrow, B. E., & Lindquist, J. M. (2024). Spaced recall reduces forgetting of fundamental mathematical concepts in a post high school precalculus course. Instructional Science, 52, 859-878. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09680-w
title: Testing effect and desired difficulty account for durable retention through effortful spaced retrieval
description: The article frames its intervention with the testing effect: quizzing produces more durable memory than re-study because effortful retrieval strengthens memory. It states that "Memory is made more durable when effort is needed to recall information" and that testing creates new retrieval routes that increase retrieval effort. The 'desired difficulty' concept holds that increased retrieval effort leads to deeper connections and longer-lasting learning, and spacing quizzes so retrieval remains effortful is essential to the effect.
requirements: Initial retrieval attempts must be effortful; quizzing too soon after learning diminishes the effect
Spacing must balance effort against the learner's ability to still recall
constraints: The article notes mixed results in comparisons of open response versus multiple choice quiz formats
target_learners: students in mathematics courses requiring retention of foundational knowledge
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and recall of previously learned concepts
examples: The USMAPS treatment staggered and spaced quiz topics every 28 days to preserve desired difficulty and prevent students sharing quiz content.
key_sources: Lindquist, D. S., Sparrow, B. E., & Lindquist, J. M. (2024). Spaced recall reduces forgetting of fundamental mathematical concepts in a post high school precalculus course. Instructional Science, 52, 859-878. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09680-w

article_title: Fostering university students’ online reading: effects of teacher-led strategy training embedded in a digital literacy course
citation: Macedo-Rouet, M.; Saux, G.; Potocki, A.; Dujardin, E.; Dyoniziak, Y.; Pylouster, J.; Rouet, J.F. (2024). Fostering university students' online reading: effects of teacher-led strategy training embedded in a digital literacy course. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09676-6
title: Teacher-led online reading strategy training program embedded in a digital literacy course
description: A training program implemented and tested as part of a digital literacy course, in which instructors delivered strategy training after "instructors received background information and instructional materials prior to the beginning of the term." One hundred sixty-seven university students were assigned to either a treatment or a control condition, and outcomes were measured with search and evaluation tasks representative of the target skills.
requirements: Instructors received background information and instructional materials prior to the beginning of the term.
target_learning_goals: online reading: assessing task requirements, accessing relevant contents, and evaluating relevance and reliability of information
examples: One hundred sixty-seven university students were assigned to either a treatment or a control condition.
