article_title: Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers
citation: Frerejean, J., van Geel, M., Keuning, T., Dolmans, D., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Visscher, A. J. (2021). Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09540-x
title: Ten Steps approach guiding instructional designers from task analysis to training blueprint
description: The Ten Steps (Van Merriënboer & Kirschner, 2018) is a design process accompanying 4C/ID that guides designers through analysis activities (cognitive task analysis, cognitive strategy and mental model analysis, cognitive rules and prerequisite knowledge) and design steps for the four blueprint components. The article notes "The Ten Steps approach by Van Merriënboer and Kirschner (2018) lists 10 design activities that result in an educational blueprint describing the program in terms of the four components." Its strength, per the authors, lies in a comprehensive systematic approach particularly when the task is unfamiliar and few ready-made materials exist.
requirements: Requires designers familiar with 4C/ID, the Ten Steps, and cognitive task analysis approaches; requires access to expert performers for analysis
constraints: Provides guidance only for analysis and design, not for learner or context analysis, material development, implementation, motivation, or evaluation
target_learning_goals: systematic design of training for complex skills
examples: Applied to design a teacher PD program for differentiation based on expert performance analysis
key_sources: Frerejean, J., van Geel, M., Keuning, T., Dolmans, D., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Visscher, A. J. (2021). Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09540-x

article_title: Team learning: building shared mental models
citation: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3
title: Team learning behavior framework: construction, co-construction, and constructive conflict building shared mental models
description: The article frames learning at team level as the development of shared cognitions, defined as "team members' overlapping mental representation of key elements of the team's task environment". Three interaction processes constitute team learning: construction of meaning (articulating personal meaning), co-construction (building meaning by refining or building on others' offers), and constructive conflict, defined as "dealing with differences in interpretation between team members by arguments and clariﬁcations". The framework hypothesizes these behaviors build shared mental models, which in turn drive team effectiveness.
requirements: Both mutual understanding and mutual agreement are necessary for shared mental model development
constraints: Divergence in opinion only benefits the team if it leads to deep-level processing of diverse viewpoints
target_learning_goals: developing shared cognition and common ground in collaborative problem solving
examples: The framework was tested with 27 three-person student teams playing the Steer the Economy business simulation game, with behaviors measured by a nine-item questionnaire
key_sources: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3

article_title: Team learning: building shared mental models
citation: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3
title: Text-based cognitive mapping method for measuring team shared mental models
description: The study measures shared mental models using Carley's (1997) automated text-based cognitive mapping: team members' open-ended answers are coded as concept networks via filtering (delete lists and a thesaurus) and windowing (relations within a range of eight concepts), and the team's shared model is the intersection of individual maps under a lossy rule (concepts or statements identical in at least two of three maps). The article reports that "She collected evidence on the reliability and validity of the method, which showed to be satisfactory."
requirements: Researcher decisions on filtering (delete list, thesaurus) and window size
Open-ended text eliciting both declarative and procedural knowledge
constraints: The automated windowing approach based on physical proximity can be prone to accidental relation
target_learning_goals: assessing shared cognition and knowledge convergence in collaborative teams
examples: Applied to answers of 81 students in 27 teams about which game variables matter and how they influence company success
key_sources: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3

article_title: Immediate and delayed effects of a modeling example on the application of principles of good feedback practice: a quasi-experimental study
citation: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Gabriela-Olivia Truțescu, Roeland M. van der Rijst, Nadira Saab. (2019). Immediate and delayed effects of a modeling example on the application of principles of good feedback practice: a quasi-experimental study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09482-5
title: Modeling example intervention: teacher demonstrates giving feed-back and feed-forward on good and bad presentation videos
description: In one lecture version, the teacher showed videos of a bad and a good presentation and, after each, demonstrated feed-back and feed-forward "first on the presentation and then on the presenter", spelled out in a script and based on the eight assessment criteria. In the comparison practice condition, students instead wrote their own feed-back and feed-forward on the same videos using a training form. Students were not instructed to give feed-back during the modeling demonstration.
requirements: A teacher script specifying the modeled feed-back and feed-forward based on the assessment criteria
Videos of a good and a bad presentation created for training purposes
constraints: Students observed the model but were not instructed to give feed-back and feed-forward at that moment
The effect on feedback skills did not persist one week later without reinforcement
target_learners: second-year bachelor students in pedagogical sciences
target_learning_goals: giving feedback on oral presentations
using assessment criteria in feedback
examples: Students observed a bad presentation (4:50 min) and a good presentation (6:59 min), after each of which the teacher presented feed-back and feed-forward from a script

Immediate and delayed effects of a modeling example on the application of principles of good feedback practice: a quasi-experimental study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09482-5

article_title: Analyzing multimodal data to understand medical trainees' regulation strategies and physiological responses in high- fidelity medical simulation scenarios
citation: Moreno, M., Patino Melo, L., Grewal, K., Matin, N., Azher, S., & Harley, J.M. (2024). Analyzing Multimodal Data to Understand Medical Trainees' Regulation Strategies and Physiological Responses in High-Fidelity Medical Simulation Scenarios. Metacognition and Learning, 19, 1161–1213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09403-z
title: A team regulation-based framework for high-fidelity medical simulation linking COPES phases, SSRL strategies and physiological activation across scenario segments
description: The article advances a team regulation-based framework in which the regulatory needs of individuals and teams change across the 'Beginning', 'Escalation' and 'Peak' segments of a CRM simulation, and rising physiological activation coincides with increased team-regulated learning strategies. The authors state that "the regulatory needs of individuals and teams change throughout different sections of a simulation to meet the contextual needs of simulated medical care", and that the COPES model (Winne & Hadwin, 1998) can be used with a coding scheme to describe team members' regulation strategies in theory-driven terms.
requirements: Multimodal data channels (behavioral, SRL/SSRL codes, and EDA) aligned to common time points so regulation strategies and physiological responses can be compared across segments
constraints: Findings come from ten CRM simulations with 29 residents at one North American university; simulations were 10–13 minutes long and ended at the 'Peak' without a resolution segment
target_learners: 1st to 3rd year medical residents in team-based simulation training
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning and socially-shared regulation of team-based clinical decision making and crisis resource management
examples: The authors map Execution codes to the COPES Performance phase and Facilitation codes to its monitoring and controlling facets within the coded simulation segments

article_title: Introduction to special issue mind the gap between research and practice in the area of teachers’ support of metacognition and SRL
citation: Charlotte Dignath, Zemira Mevarech. (2021). Introduction to special issue mind the gap between research and practice in the area of teachers' support of metacognition and SRL. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09285-5
title: A generic model of teacher competence applied to teachers' promotion of SRL (knowledge, beliefs, self-efficacy)
description: The editorial describes applying a generic model of teacher competence (Baumert & Kunter, 2013) to the context of teachers' promotion of SRL. In the first study, profiles of teacher competence regarding SRL were "based on teachers' knowledge, beliefs, and self-efficacy about supporting SRL in the classroom" and were associated with teachers' self-reported SRL practice; a second study evaluated a professional development training on teacher and student levels.
requirements: Assessment of teachers' knowledge, beliefs, and self-efficacy about supporting SRL to identify competence profiles
constraints: Profiles were associated with teachers' self-reported SRL practice; training effects were examined in a separate second study
target_learning_goals: supporting students' self-regulated learning in the classroom
examples: The editorial describes a two-study program: profile identification from teacher characteristics, then a professional development training evaluated on both teacher and student levels, with competence profiles moderating training effects.
key_sources: Charlotte Dignath, Zemira Mevarech. (2021). Introduction to special issue mind the gap between research and practice in the area of teachers' support of metacognition and SRL. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09285-5

article_title: Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model
citation: Tillema, M., van den Bergh, H., Rijlaarsdam, G., & Sanders, T. (2011). Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9072-x
title: Analyze writing process data temporally, taking the moments at which cognitive activities occur into account
description: The article advocates analyzing cognitive processing during writing as a function of the moment in task execution, for example by splitting protocols into equally long episodes and modelling activity occurrence per episode. As the authors put it, "analyses of cognitive processing during writing should take the moment(s) at which cognitive activities occur into account." In this study this temporal modelling is what allowed offline questionnaire scores to predict online behaviour at all.
requirements: Online process data (think-aloud protocols, keystroke logs) segmented into episodes so that start, middle and end of task execution are comparable across writers and tasks.
constraints: The article notes temporal analysis is not always needed, since frequential main effects were also found for some activities.
target_learners: researchers and designers analysing writing processes of secondary school students
target_learning_goals: understanding and predicting the temporal distribution of (meta)cognitive activities during writing
examples: Protocols were split into five equally long episodes and occurrence of each activity was modelled with multilevel polynomial regression, including score-by-episode interactions.
key_sources: Tillema, M., van den Bergh, H., Rijlaarsdam, G., & Sanders, T. (2011). Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9072-x

article_title: Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior
citation: Süleyman Avcı, Mustafa Özgenel, Akif Avcu. (2025). Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09431-3
title: Teachers should invest in homework quality, feedback, and autonomy support to foster students' homework self-regulation
description: The article concludes that teachers' homework practices — planning and preparing quality homework, giving frequent and high-quality feedback, and supporting autonomy — encourage students to deploy self-regulation strategies, which in turn supports homework completion. As the authors put it, "teachers' efforts in the dimensions of homework quality, feedback quality, feedback quantity and autonomy support encourage students to use self-regulation strategies". Autonomy support means giving students choices in selection, preparation and presentation of assignments rather than pressuring them.
requirements: Homework should be matched to students' interests, needs and ability level; the article notes overly challenging homework can cause students with learning difficulties to develop negative attitudes toward homework
constraints: Findings come from a Turkish, moderately collectivist context; the authors note the strong involvement–management relationship differs from low relationships found in Chinese samples, so cultural context influences the strength of these links
target_learning_goals: homework completion
use of self-regulation strategies during homework
examples: In the study, students' perceptions of homework quality, feedback quality, feedback quantity and autonomy support were measured with the THIS and TFFS scales and entered as indicators of teacher homework involvement in the SEM model
key_sources: Süleyman Avcı, Mustafa Özgenel, Akif Avcu. (2025). Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09431-3

article_title: For unto every one that hath shall be given: teachers’ competence profiles regarding the promotion of self-regulated learning moderate the effectiveness of short-term teacher training
citation: Charlotte Dignath. (2021). For unto every one that hath shall be given: teachers' competence profiles regarding the promotion of self-regulated learning moderate the effectiveness of short-term teacher training. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09271-x
title: Generic model of teacher competence applied to promoting SRL: professional knowledge, pedagogical beliefs, and motivational orientations (self-efficacy)
description: The article proposes applying a generic model of teacher competence to the specific context of promoting SRL. "teaching competence is considered a multidimensional construct that comprises both cognitive and motivational-affective aspects, which have been found to predict teaching practice", comprising teachers' (1) professional knowledge, (2) pedagogical beliefs, and (3) motivational orientations. The model serves as the basis for deriving latent competence profiles in study 1 and for evaluating competence growth in the training study. The article argues this application can inspire future research on indicators of teachers' SRL practice.
requirements: Assessment of all three competence aspects (knowledge, beliefs, self-efficacy) simultaneously, e.g., via latent profile analysis
constraints: Studies relating such characteristics of teacher competence in the context of SRL are described as scarce
target_learning_goals: Teachers' competence to promote students' self-regulated learning
examples: Study 1 measured the three aspects with a 59-item online survey and derived two latent profiles; study 2 used the model to evaluate training effects on competence growth
key_sources: Charlotte Dignath. (2021). For unto every one that hath shall be given: teachers' competence profiles regarding the promotion of self-regulated learning moderate the effectiveness of short-term teacher training. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09271-x

article_title: Teachers’ Humour Use in the Classroom: A Scoping Review
citation: Hannah Robinson, Sarah E. Rose, Jade M. Elliott, Romina A. Vivaldi. (2024). Teachers' Humour Use in the Classroom: A Scoping Review. https://osf.io
title: Taxonomy of seven teacher humour styles and three affiliative sub-styles in adolescent classrooms
description: The review organises teachers' classroom humour into seven styles drawn from the included literature: course-related, course-unrelated, affiliative, aggressive, self-enhancing, self-defeating, and festive humour. It defines each, e.g. course-related humour is "humour used to explain or display information related to the class", and notes styles overlap and can be positive or negative in nature. Şahin's (2021) three affiliative sub-styles (shy, passive, partial) are included, with classroom observations identifying students as the most common trigger for teachers' humour.
requirements: Humour styles are identified via teacher and student self-report surveys, interviews, and classroom observations; existing scales do not capture all seven styles
constraints: The styles outlined in prior scales focused on higher education classrooms, so it is not known if all apply to adolescent classrooms
Styles are not distinct and may overlap when used in the classroom
target_learning_goals: Understanding how teachers' humour use shapes classroom environment, learning processes, motivation and wellbeing
examples: Şeďová (2015) identified festive humour such as teachers playing April Fool's Day pranks by pretending to assign a surprise test
key_sources: Hannah Robinson, Sarah E. Rose, Jade M. Elliott, Romina A. Vivaldi. (2024). Teachers' Humour Use in the Classroom: A Scoping Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09913-x

article_title: Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model
citation: Elena Savina, Caroline Fulton, Christina Beaton. (2025). Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10018-2
title: Teacher emotional competence model of eight competencies in two groups (teacher-oriented and students-oriented)
description: The article proposes a conceptual model of teacher emotional competence organized into two groups of competencies: those related to teachers' own emotions and those related to students' emotions. As the abstract states, the eight competencies include "(1) understanding teachers' own emotions; (2) effective emotion regulation; (3) effective emotional communication; (4) maintaining teachers' emotional well-being; (5) understanding and responding to students' emotions; (6) utilizing emotions to promote learning; (7) utilizing emotions to foster positive relationships and emotional climate in the classroom; and (8) promoting students' social-emotional learning." Each competency is further delineated into discrete emotional skills, and the skills are described as building on and working in conjunction with each other, e.g., awareness of one's emotions supports regulation, which supports responding to students' emotions.
requirements: The model is grounded in integration of emotion, developmental, educational, and clinical research and in the identified emotional demands of the teaching profession
constraints: The model is a conceptual proposal intended as a springboard for training programs and assessment, not itself an empirically tested intervention
target_learning_goals: using emotions for instructional and relational purposes
managing teachers' own and students' emotions
preventing emotional burnout
examples: Table 1 organizes the eight competencies into teacher-oriented and students-oriented columns
key_sources: Elena Savina, Caroline Fulton, Christina Beaton. (2025). Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10018-2

article_title: Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model
citation: Elena Savina, Caroline Fulton, Christina Beaton. (2025). Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10018-2
title: Distinction between emotional demands of teaching and demands for emotional skills, with teacher emotional work as an others-oriented construct
description: The review differentiates the emotional demands of teaching (job aspects requiring sustained emotional effort, such as emotional labor, dealing with anger, and disturbing situations) from the demands for emotional skills, which reflect the need to use those skills to achieve instructional, relational, and behavioral goals. A unique feature is that teacher emotional skills "serve not only teachers but students as well." Drawing on Strazdins's construct of emotional work, the authors state: "We conceptualize teacher emotional work as an intentional use of emotions to facilitate students' learning, enact effective behavior management, and promote positive relationships in the classroom." This distinction grounds the model's two-group structure.
requirements: Conceptualizing teacher emotional skills must capture the transactional and contextual nature of emotions in the classroom, per the Ecological Dynamic Systems framework
constraints: The distinction is a conceptual proposal by the authors, adapted from the Job Demands-Resources model and Strazdins's family-interaction construct
target_learning_goals: understanding the emotional requirements of the teaching profession
examples: Emotional labor is discussed via Hochschild's definition as effort to conceal or fabricate emotions according to professional display rules
key_sources: Elena Savina, Caroline Fulton, Christina Beaton. (2025). Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10018-2

article_title: Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education
citation: Michael Noetel, Philip Parker, Theresa Dicke, Mark R. Beauchamp, Nikos Ntoumanis, Ryan M. Hulteen, et al. (2023). Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09786-6
title: Test predictive models on held-out data not used in training, checking them only once
description: The article recommends that educational psychologists evaluate predictive accuracy on data never used to build the model. It states that "the least biased assessment of predictive models involves testing those models on new data, not used to train the model", and warns that checking test data more than once means learning from it and overfitting again. Researchers may use cross-validation or AIC to choose among competing models, then check the chosen model on unseen data once.
requirements: Reserve a portion of the data (the article used a 70% training to 30% testing split) that is never used for model building or tuning
constraints: More data held out for testing means less data for building models, so models themselves may fit the general population more poorly
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of how well models generalise to new data
examples: In this study, elastic-net hyperparameters were tuned on training data and predictive validity was assessed once on the held-out 30%
key_sources: Michael Noetel, Philip Parker, Theresa Dicke, Mark R. Beauchamp, Nikos Ntoumanis, Ryan M. Hulteen, et al. (2023). Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09786-6

article_title: A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education
citation: Gardner-Vandy, K., Utley, J., Just, A., Hathcock, S., & Stansberry, S. (2025). A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251329570
title: Five-theme guideline set for incorporating Two-Eyed Seeing into P-20 classrooms
description: Twelve of the 13 reviewed articles suggested recommendations or guidelines for incorporating TES into the classroom, which the review compiled and organized into five themes, each divided into categories (Figure 7). "These included guidelines that dealt with philosophical framework, teacher supports, generation of curriculum, the teacher's role in the learning process, and the classroom environment." The philosophical framework theme includes inclusive science, holistic approaches, identity-building and self-reflection, and acknowledgment of settler-colonialism; the curriculum-generation theme includes experiential, inquiry-based, and land-based learning, interweaving knowledges, lesson planning, storytelling, and respectful inclusion of Indigenous knowledges.
requirements: Educators must develop relationships within the Indigenous community first, holding elders and knowledge holders as experts and trusted consultants and instructors
constraints: Guidelines were compiled from only 13 peer-reviewed articles, nearly all from Canada, and one article offered no specific guidelines
target_learners: P-20 educators and their students, including Indigenous students
target_learning_goals: Incorporating Two-Eyed Seeing into classroom curriculum and instruction
examples: Slightly more than half of the articles (n = 7) noted that educators and administrators must acknowledge that Indigenous knowledge and Western science are equally significant, valid, and complimentary
key_sources: Gardner-Vandy, K., Utley, J., Just, A., Hathcock, S., & Stansberry, S. (2025). A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251329570

article_title: Gaining Insight Into Human Nature: A Review of Literature Classroom Intervention Studies
citation: Schrijvers, M., Janssen, T., Fialho, O., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2019). Gaining insight into human nature: A review of literature classroom intervention studies. Review of Educational Research, 89(1), 3-45. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318812914
title: Select texts deliberately as part of designing literature education for insight into human nature
description: The review’s first derived design principle concerns "text selection": choosing literary texts is treated as a design decision that conditions whether literature education fosters insight into human nature. It was derived from the analysis of interventions with full or partial empirical support, alongside the writing and dialogue principles.
requirements: Text choices must be made deliberately in relation to the intended insight outcomes
target_learning_goals: insight into human nature
understanding of others
examples: The review names text selection as design principle (a) among the principles yielded by supported interventions
key_sources: Schrijvers, M., Janssen, T., Fialho, O., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2019). Gaining insight into human nature: A review of literature classroom intervention studies. Review of Educational Research, 89(1), 3-45. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318812914

article_title: The role of social capital for teacher professional learning and student achievement: A systematic literature review
citation: Demir, Ema Kristina. (2021). The Role of Social Capital for Teacher Professional Learning and Student Achievement: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2021.100391
title: Three-dimension framework of teacher social capital: bonding, bridging and linking
description: The review organises teacher social capital into named dimensions of bonding, bridging and linking, which it treats as distinct facets that school organisational structures may foster to different degrees. It states that "different organisational structures may foster different dimensions of social capital, such as bonding, bridging and linking." The framework underpins the review's call for research linking these dimensions to school structure and to desired teacher social capital outcomes.
requirements: Research is needed relating the dimensions to the organisational structure of schools, as the review states this relationship is under-studied.
target_learning_goals: teacher professional learning
educational equity
key_sources: Demir, Ema Kristina. (2021). The Role of Social Capital for Teacher Professional Learning and Student Achievement: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2021.100391

article_title: The Role of Teachers’ Emotions and Their Assessment in Professional Development Research: A Systematic Review
citation: Mareike Ehlert, Carola Grunschel, Friederike Koehler. (2025). The Role of Teachers' Emotions and Their Assessment in Professional Development Research: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10048-w
title: Adjusted framework integrating teacher emotions into Desimone's four-component PD process model
description: The review proposes an adjusted version of Desimone's (2009) PD framework in which emotions both influence and are influenced by each of the four PD components (core features, knowledge/attitude change, instructional change, student outcomes). The article states that "emotions can both influence and be influenced by each component of the PD process" and that emotions experienced in one component spill over into others, making emotions in PD context-sensitive and time-sensitive. It is offered as a conceptual map for future research and PD design.
requirements: Assessment must distinguish the PD component toward which an emotion is directed and the time point (prospective, current, retrospective) it refers to
constraints: The framework is presented as theoretical integration; the article notes existing ideas are largely theoretical or based on single case studies
target_learners: in-service and pre-service teachers participating in professional development
target_learning_goals: teachers' emotional engagement with and adoption of new instructional practices during PD
examples: The framework is illustrated with examples such as frustration during classroom-management implementation carrying over to emotions about student improvement
key_sources: Mareike Ehlert, Carola Grunschel, Friederike Koehler. (2025). The Role of Teachers' Emotions and Their Assessment in Professional Development Research: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10048-w

article_title: Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships
citation: Jantine L. Spilt, Helma M. Y. Koomen, & Jochem T. Thijs. (2011). Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9170-y
title: Hypothetical model: mental representations of teacher–student relationships affect teacher wellbeing through everyday emotional responses
description: The review proposes a hypothetical model, depicted in Fig. 1, in which teachers' mental representations of teacher–student relationships affect wellbeing "through their everyday emotional responses." Grounded in Lazarus's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, it holds that appraisal of stressors triggers discrete emotions whose prolonged experience changes wellbeing. Teachers are postulated to have a basic need for relatedness and to internalize relationship experiences into representational models at global, domain-specific, and relationship-specific levels, which may "mediate or moderate the well-studied effects of perceived student behavior on teacher wellbeing."
requirements: Teachers must have a need or desire for personal relationships with students for relationships to be harmful or beneficial to their wellbeing
constraints: The review states there is virtually no research that has directly tested the propositions of the conceptual model represented in Fig. 1
The model assumes causal effects, but wellbeing in turn most likely influences the ability to form personal relationships with children
target_learners: teachers in preschool, primary, and secondary education
target_learning_goals: teacher wellbeing
stress and burnout prevention
professional development and retention
key_sources: Jantine L. Spilt, Helma M. Y. Koomen, & Jochem T. Thijs. (2011). Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9170-y

article_title: Worth the Effort: the Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties (S2D2) Framework
citation: Anique B. H. de Bruin, Felicitas Biwer, Luotong Hui, Erdem Onan, Louise David, Wisnu Wiradhany. (2023). Worth the Effort: the Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties (S2D2) Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09766-w
title: Provide adequate teacher training on effective learning strategies before student training
description: Because strategy-level training programs depend on teachers or mentors, the article argues that student training on desirable difficulties must be preceded by teacher training. Teachers, like students, hold misbeliefs about effective learning, so programs delivered by untrained teachers risk transmitting those misbeliefs. The article states: "Providing adequate teacher training therefore should precede student training." This principle applies whenever educators deliver instruction about desirably difficult learning strategies.
requirements: Teachers and mentors must endorse the importance of and understand how to teach the use of desirable difficulties
constraints: The article notes teachers suffer from misbeliefs and lack adequate knowledge about effective learning strategy use, citing Morehead et al. (2016) and Surma et al. (2018)
target_learners: teachers and mentors delivering learning strategy training
target_learning_goals: accurate teacher knowledge of effective learning strategies to support student strategy training
examples: The article cites the Study Smart framework (Biwer & de Bruin, 2023) and the KBCP framework (McDaniel & Einstein, 2020) as starting points for such training programs
key_sources: Anique B. H. de Bruin, Felicitas Biwer, Luotong Hui, Erdem Onan, Louise David, Wisnu Wiradhany. (2023). Worth the Effort: the Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties (S2D2) Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09766-w

article_title: The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks
citation: Tamara van Gog & Vincent Hoogerheide & Milou van Harsel. (2020). The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09544-y
title: Teach students a simple task selection rule that combines self-assessed performance and invested mental effort when choosing the next problem-solving task
description: This principle holds that self-regulated learning with problem-solving tasks improves when students are explicitly taught, via video modeling examples, to select their next task by combining their self-assessed performance and self-reported invested mental effort on the prior task. The review concludes that "teaching students a relatively simple task selection rule based on a combination of their self-assessed performance and invested mental effort improves their self-regulated learning outcomes", a replicated finding rare among monitoring interventions. The rule must stay simple enough for students to understand, remember, and apply during self-study.
requirements: Video modeling examples demonstrating the full performance-assessment-selection cycle, and a task database ordered from simple to complex with support faded within complexity levels
constraints: Training did not transfer to a different problem domain (math posttest performance was not improved); any algorithm must be much simpler than adaptive-system algorithms, and effort ratings affected by extraneous variables will limit effectiveness
target_learners: secondary education students learning biology problem solving
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment
adaptive task selection
improved posttest performance on problem-solving tasks
examples: Kostons et al. (2012) and Raaijmakers et al. (2018b) trained students with video models using a selection table advising, e.g., high performance with low effort: select a task with much less support or more complexity
key_sources: Tamara van Gog & Vincent Hoogerheide & Milou van Harsel. (2020). The Role of Mental Effort in Fostering Self-Regulated Learning with Problem-Solving Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09544-y

article_title: Intervention Programs Targeting the Mental Health, Professional Burnout, and/or Wellbeing of School Teachers: Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses
citation: Joanne R. Beames, Samantha Spanos, Anna Roberts, Lauren McGillivray, Sophie Li, Jill M. Newby, Bridianne O'Dea, Aliza Werner-Seidler. (2023). Intervention Programs Targeting the Mental Health, Professional Burnout, and/or Wellbeing of School Teachers: Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09720-w
title: Design future teacher mental health program research with methodologically rigorous designs, co-design with teachers, and attention to implementation factors
description: The review's stated research priorities are "using methodologically rigorous designs, developing programs for teachers with teachers (i.e. co-design), and considering implementation factors to ensure feasibility, acceptability, and uptake." The authors also call for increased consistency in measurement using standardised, teacher-validated measures, more comprehensive follow-up evaluation, and measurement of program fidelity and adherence, which they argue must be a priority in future research.
requirements: Studies should use standardised measures with sound psychometric properties that are validated with teachers and the school context.
constraints: The review found an inadequate number of comparisons to perform sub-group analyses, meta-regression, or publication bias analyses.
target_learning_goals: Mental health
Professional burnout reduction
Wellbeing
examples: The review measured risk of bias with ROB-II for RCTs and ROBINS-I for nRCTs and found quality generally poor, particularly in non-randomised trials.
key_sources: Joanne R. Beames, Samantha Spanos, Anna Roberts, Lauren McGillivray, Sophie Li, Jill M. Newby, Bridianne O'Dea, Aliza Werner-Seidler. (2023). Intervention Programs Targeting the Mental Health, Professional Burnout, and/or Wellbeing of School Teachers: Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09720-w

article_title: Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review
citation: Alazne Fernández Ortube, Ernesto Panadero, Charlotte Dignath. (2024). Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09919-5
title: Teachers' dual role in SRL: self-regulated professional and promoter of students' SRL
description: The review frames teachers as occupying a dual role in SRL: they must "apply the SRL principles to their own learning" as self-regulated professionals, and they must be "promoters of their students' SRL". The professional role requires metacognitive knowledge and SRL content knowledge; the promoter role requires pedagogical content knowledge, awareness of students' strategy use, and SRL assessment. The review also cites a proposed third role, self-regulation for teaching actions, and codes interventions against four dual-role subcategories (SRL knowledge, SRL practice, teaching SRL, SRL diagnosis).
requirements: Pre-service teachers need SRL content knowledge and metacognitive knowledge to reflect on their own learning before mastering the pedagogical practice of teaching SRL
constraints: The review notes few studies exist on how teachers assess students' SRL, and that many teachers hold SRL conceptions inconsistent with SRL theory
target_learners: pre-service teachers in initial teacher education
target_learning_goals: regulating one's own learning
teaching and promoting students' SRL
assessing students' SRL strategy use
examples: The review coded 66 interventions against the four dual-role subcategories and found only three covered all of them
key_sources: Alazne Fernández Ortube, Ernesto Panadero, Charlotte Dignath. (2024). Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09919-5

article_title: Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models
citation: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2
title: Test the linearity assumption before reporting linear models for mental-effort relations
description: The article recommends that researchers check whether relations involving self-rated mental effort are linear before fitting and interpreting linear models, because "predictions based on linear models may be substantially biased for most of the range of mental effort". It demonstrates a pragmatic approach: fit competing models of increasing polynomial complexity (none, linear, quadratic, cubic, more complex) in two-level mixed-effects models and compare them on R2M, AIC and BIC. The response-time finding is presented as "a clear example of why testing the linearity assumption and reporting the core outcomes of that check is important".
requirements: Data with multiple measurements per participant on the variables of interest, or sufficiently large samples (the article mentions e.g. 200 students in a course) for single-measurement designs
constraints: With small samples, more flexible random-effects structures and multiple imputation are not to be trusted; the article used compound-symmetry random-intercept models and omitted a small percentage of missing covariate observations
target_learners: researchers and practitioners measuring cognitive load in learning or task-performance settings
target_learning_goals: valid interpretation of self-rated mental effort as a predictor of workload, time on task, or metacognitive variables
examples: The authors reanalysed data from four published studies, comparing Models 0–4 per study on R2M, AIC and BIC in Jamovi
key_sources: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2

article_title: Student Characteristics in the Eyes of Teachers: Differences Between Novice and Expert Teachers in Judgment Accuracy, Observed Behavioral Cues, and Gaze
citation: Seidel, T., Schnitzler, K., Kosel, C., Stürmer, K., & Holzberger, D. (2021). Student Characteristics in the Eyes of Teachers: Differences Between Novice and Expert Teachers in Judgment Accuracy, Observed Behavioral Cues, and Gaze. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09532-2
title: Teacher gaze as an additional operationalization of the noticing component of the cognitive model of teacher professional vision
description: The article works within a cognitive model of teachers' professional vision comprising perceptual noticing and knowledge-based reasoning (Lachner et al. 2016). It argues that gaze, measured with eye-movement methodology, "provides a suitable operationalization for noticing processes in the forefront of further processing and interpreting observed events." The study extends this model to diagnosing individual student characteristics, distinguishing bottom-up (stimulus-driven) and top-down (goal-driven) gaze drivers, and tentatively concludes that "adding teacher gaze to the model can enrich our understanding of the processes involved in knowledge-based reasoning."
requirements: Eye-tracking methodology with defined areas of interest on the observed students is needed to operationalize noticing through gaze.
constraints: The article notes the findings are limited in generalizability and replicability as a first study, and that marking students with visible letters might have forced bottom-up processing due to the letters' saliency.
target_learning_goals: teacher diagnostic competence in judging student characteristic profiles
teacher professional vision (noticing and reasoning about student engagement)
examples: In the study, teachers' eye movements were recorded while observing five marked students in whole-class instruction and seatwork scenes of an 11-min geometry video.
key_sources: Seidel, T., Schnitzler, K., Kosel, C., Stürmer, K., & Holzberger, D. (2021). Student Characteristics in the Eyes of Teachers: Differences Between Novice and Expert Teachers in Judgment Accuracy, Observed Behavioral Cues, and Gaze. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09532-2

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: TESSERA framework: repeated short-term personality states drive long-term trait development
description: The TESSERA framework (Wrzus & Roberts, 2017) elaborates how "repeated short-term, situational processes lead to long-term personality development" through recursive sequences of Triggering situations, Expectancy, States/State expressions, and Reactions. Momentary motivation in the form of expectancies influences which personality state emerges after a trigger, and reactions (internal reinforcement through positive emotions or external feedback) help sustain sequences. The article makes the framework educationally relevant by situating it in learning situations, e.g., a selective advanced mathematics program repeatedly prompting high state conscientiousness that feeds into trait development, and stresses effects are not one-way but likely reciprocal between motivation states and personality states.
requirements: Repeated experiences of personality states that differ from one's typical trait level, accompanied by reinforcing reactions, are needed for trait change over time
constraints: The article notes external expectations should lead to smaller personality changes than internal expectations, per the TESSERA framework's own reasoning
target_learners: students in selective programs, school groups, and everyday learning settings
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and personality development through learning situations
examples: A student in a school theatre group behaves more outgoing than usual due to context-specific expectations, and repeated higher-than-usual state extraversion may feed into trait development
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Promoting Temporal Investigations of Development in Context: a Systematic Review of Longitudinal Research Linking Childhood Circumstances and Learning-related Outcomes
citation: Molly Grant, Kane Meissel, Daniel Exeter. (2023). Promoting Temporal Investigations of Development in Context: a Systematic Review of Longitudinal Research Linking Childhood Circumstances and Learning-related Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09734-4
title: Temporality framework: duration, developmental timing, and mobility as longitudinal dimensions through which childhood context affects learning and development
description: The review organizes evidence on how childhood social and economic circumstances affect educational and cognitive outcomes through three temporal dimensions grounded in ecological systems theory (the chronosystem) and life course theory. As the review defines it, "temporality" refers to "the timing-related dynamics of the duration of exposure, developmental time points of exposure, and changes in exposure to contextual factors across time." The framework structures the review's four themes and identifies when children are particularly vulnerable to contextual effects.
requirements: Longitudinal data with circumstances assessed at least twice within childhood (pregnancy to age 12) to distinguish duration, timing, and mobility effects
constraints: The review restricts circumstances to family and neighborhood levels, excluding school and early childhood education factors
target_learning_goals: educational outcomes (academic performance, qualifications, school engagement)
cognitive outcomes (language, attention, memory, executive function, general cognitive composites)
examples: The four themes (duration effects, developmental timing effects, mobility effects, no temporal effects) were constructed via reflexive thematic analysis of 75 studies
key_sources: Molly Grant, Kane Meissel, Daniel Exeter. (2023). Promoting Temporal Investigations of Development in Context: a Systematic Review of Longitudinal Research Linking Childhood Circumstances and Learning-related Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09734-4

article_title: Relations between Teachers’ and Students’ Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis
citation: Nguyen, T.-A., Hidajat, T., Zhou, T., Ma, T., Hoang, A., Poed, S., & Edwards, E. J. (2026). Relations between Teachers' and Students' Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10218-4
title: Socialisation, co-regulation, and prosocial classroom mechanisms linking teacher SEC to student SEC
description: The review organises explanatory accounts of the teacher-student SEC link into three named frameworks. It states "Teachers are often viewed as socialisers of students' emotions (Denham et al., 2012), a process by which children learn culturally acceptable knowledge, values, and skills about social and emotional situations from a significant adult (Eisenberg et al., 1998)." The Co-regulation Framework holds that teachers guide students' social and emotional behaviours towards shared goals shaped by teachers' emotional schemas, while Jennings and Greenberg's prosocial classroom framework proposes reciprocal interaction through teachers' well-being, relationships, classroom management, SEL programs, and climate. The review notes less theoretical work has examined the reverse pathway from student SEC to teacher SEC.
requirements: Mechanisms operate through teachers modelling competencies, providing effective SEL, and responding supportively rather than dismissively to students' emotions
constraints: Empirical findings on the prosocial classroom mechanisms are mixed, with discrepancies partly attributable to common method bias of self-reports versus more objective tools
Less theoretical work has examined how student SEC may influence teacher SEC
target_learning_goals: Development of students' social-emotional competence through teacher modelling, co-regulation, and classroom climate
examples: A teacher with strong self- and social awareness who views emotions as teachable opportunities may respond to a heated group dispute by calmly labelling feelings and scaffolding problem-solving
key_sources: Nguyen, T.-A., Hidajat, T., Zhou, T., Ma, T., Hoang, A., Poed, S., & Edwards, E. J. (2026). Relations between Teachers' and Students' Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10218-4

article_title: Is Empathy the Key to Effective Teaching? A Systematic Review of Its Association with Teacher-Student Interactions and Student Outcomes
citation: Karen Aldrup · Bastian Carstensen · Uta Klusmann. (2022). Is Empathy the Key to Effective Teaching? A Systematic Review of Its Association with Teacher-Student Interactions and Student Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09649-y
title: Heuristic working model linking teacher empathy to interaction quality and student outcomes (based on the prosocial classroom model)
description: The review proposes a heuristic working model (Fig. 1), largely based on the prosocial classroom model (Jennings & Greenberg, 2009), in which teacher empathy — defined as including both "affective and cognitive components" — supports high-quality teacher-student interactions, especially emotional support, and thereby indirectly fosters student development. Cognitive empathy enables reading students' nonverbal signals and understanding their perspectives; affective empathy motivates sensitive responses. Expected associations are strongest for emotional support and weakest for student achievement.
requirements: Empathy must be measured in accordance with the review's dual-component (affective plus cognitive) definition; fantasy and personal distress subscales were excluded as not measuring empathy
constraints: The model is heuristic; the review found empirical support only for the empathy–bullying-intervention path, not consistently for emotional support, classroom management, instructional support, or student outcomes
target_learners: teachers from preschool to tertiary education
target_learning_goals: quality of teacher-student interactions (emotional support, classroom management, instructional support) and student cognitive and psychosocial development
key_sources: Karen Aldrup · Bastian Carstensen · Uta Klusmann. (2022). Is Empathy the Key to Effective Teaching? A Systematic Review of Its Association with Teacher-Student Interactions and Student Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09649-y

article_title: Congruence and friction between learning and teaching
citation: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753
title: Three teacher-regulation strategies: strong, shared and loose control of learning functions
description: The article places teaching methods on a dimension "ranging from very strongly teacher-regulated to very loosely teacher-regulated" and singles out three positions. Under strong control the teacher substitutes learning functions for students (e.g. presenting overviews, giving analogies); under shared control the teacher activates students to perform the functions themselves (e.g. asking for main points, letting students invent test questions); under loose control students perform all functions and the teacher mainly presents subject matter and tests outcomes. Teacher control includes regulation exerted by tasks, materials and other instructional agents, and every form of teaching can be characterized by a three-by-fifteen matrix of strategies by learning functions.
requirements: A task division between teachers and students in fulfilling learning functions always exists in practice
constraints: Complete teacher control or total absence of teacher control rarely occur; the three positions are a simplification of a continuum with many intermediate positions, including mixed control
target_learners: upper secondary and higher education students
target_learning_goals: regulation of students' learning and thinking activities during instruction
examples: Tables 2 and 3 give examples of teacher substitution and teacher activation of learning functions for each of the fifteen functions
key_sources: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753

article_title: Levels of comprehension of scientific prose: the role of text variables
citation: Vidal-Abarca, E., & Sanjosé, V. (1998). Levels of comprehension of scientific prose: The role of text variables. Learning and Instruction, 8(3), 215-233. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959475297000200
title: Textbase and situation model: two levels of comprehension that textual changes affect differently
description: The article adopts van Dijk and Kintsch's (1983) distinction between comprehension levels: the textbase, the semantic and rhetorical relationships encoded from the text, and the situation model, a deeper level where "theinformationprovidedbythetext iselaboratedfrompriorknowledgeandisintegratedintoit". The article uses this framework to predict that coherence changes mainly affect the textbase (main ideas, recall) while deep problem solving requires a situation model built by integrating text information with background knowledge, which the authors argue occurs only when readers first form good textbases.
requirements: Deep comprehension requires text information to be integrated with previously assimilated knowledge, so good textbase formation is described as a necessary prior stage
constraints: The article notes studies showing good situation models with poor textbases, but argues those used short, familiar paragraphs and recognition tasks unlike normal scientific text reading
target_learners: tenth-grade high school students reading unfamiliar scientific texts
target_learning_goals: deep comprehension of scientific prose enabling problem solving in novel contexts
examples: Four text versions manipulated coherence and linking changes separately and in tandem to test level-specific predictions
key_sources: Vidal-Abarca, E., & Sanjosé, V. (1998). Levels of comprehension of scientific prose: The role of text variables. Learning and Instruction, 8(3), 215-233. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959475297000200

article_title: Exploring paths of change: Analyzing teachers’ emotion regulation repertoire over time using multi-level latent profile analysis
citation: Hilger, K. J. E., Scheibe, S., Frenzel, A. C., Grund, S., & Keller, M. M. (2025). Exploring paths of change: Analyzing teachers’ emotion regulation repertoire over time using multi-level latent profile analysis. Learning and Instruction, 101, Article 102234. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102234
title: Person-level emotion regulation repertoire profiles as an organizing framework for teachers' combined strategy use
description: The article organizes teachers' emotion regulation not as isolated strategies but as person-level profiles combining multiple strategies. Daily-diary assessments covered 12 ER strategies, including "acceptance, positive reappraisal, social support, situation modification, situation selection, expressive suppression, experience suppression, distraction, acting-out, self-blame, rumination, substance use". Multilevel latent profile analysis identified profiles "at the person level", yielding five profiles whose members differ in the specific combination of strategies, which the article then links to job experience and occupational well-being.
requirements: Daily-diary measurement of multiple ER strategies at the daily level across at least two measurement bursts
Multilevel latent profile analysis applied to identify ER profiles at the person level
constraints: Profiles were identified in German primary and secondary school teachers across two bursts spaced six months apart
target_learning_goals: Regulation of negative emotions in teaching
Occupational well-being of teachers
examples: The study assessed 12 ER strategies daily in two bursts and derived five profiles, three common and two unique to the bursts
key_sources: Hilger, K. J. E., Scheibe, S., Frenzel, A. C., Grund, S., & Keller, M. M. (2025). Exploring paths of change: Analyzing teachers’ emotion regulation repertoire over time using multi-level latent profile analysis. Learning and Instruction, 101, Article 102234. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102234

article_title: Contrasting school dropout: The protective role of perceived teacher justice
citation: Grazia, V., Molinari, L., Mameli, C. (2024). Contrasting school dropout: The protective role of perceived teacher justice. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION, 89, 1-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101826
title: Treat students fairly to protect against early school leaving
description: The article argues that a feature of the proximal learning environment — students' perception of being treated fairly by teachers — can act as a protective factor against dropout. It reports that "perceptions of teacher justice had a negative association with the increase" in dropout intentions across the school year. Teachers' fair treatment is therefore positioned as a lever for dropout prevention.
requirements: Teachers must behave in ways students perceive as fair, since the measure is students' perception of teacher justice
constraints: The finding is an observational association from one three-wave study of 9th graders in Italy, not a tested intervention
target_learning_goals: Reducing students' intention to drop out of school
examples: 547 9th-grade students answered questionnaires on teacher justice and dropout intentions at the beginning, middle and end of the school year
key_sources: Grazia, V., Molinari, L., Mameli, C. (2024). Contrasting school dropout: The protective role of perceived teacher justice. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION, 89, 1-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101826

article_title: Contrasting school dropout: The protective role of perceived teacher justice
citation: Grazia, V., Molinari, L., Mameli, C. (2024). Contrasting school dropout: The protective role of perceived teacher justice. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION, 89, 1-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101826
title: Perceived teacher justice as a protective factor in the proximal learning environment
description: The article proposes that features of the proximal learning environment, notably students' perception of being treated fairly by teachers, function as protective factors against early school leaving. It notes that risk factors "related to the proximal learning environment have mostly been neglected" in dropout research, and positions teacher justice as a relevant protective factor within that environment. The framework links everyday classroom treatment to students' intention to persist in school.
requirements: Measurement of students' perceptions of teacher justice, typically via student questionnaires
constraints: Studied here as perceptions among 9th-grade students in Italian schools; generalization to other levels or systems is not tested
target_learning_goals: Understanding and reducing early school leaving
examples: The study measured perceived teacher justice three times across a school year alongside dropout intentions
key_sources: Grazia, V., Molinari, L., Mameli, C. (2024). Contrasting school dropout: The protective role of perceived teacher justice. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION, 89, 1-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101826

article_title: The role of rhythm in learning to read in children with and without reading difficulties: an intervention study
citation: Gutiérrez-Palma, N., Calet, N., Robles-Bello, M.A., & Valencia-Naranjo, N. (2026). The role of rhythm in learning to read in children with and without reading difficulties: an intervention study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102273
title: Temporal sampling theory of dyslexia (Goswami)
description: Temporal sampling theory, as described in this article, holds that phonological problems in dyslexia originate in a subtle deficit in detecting rise times, the acoustic correlate of rhythm. The article states that "this deficit would, in turn, be caused by a difficulty in sampling the speech signal at low frequencies, Delta (1–4 Hz) and Theta (4–10 Hz)", which correspond to stress and syllables. The study tests the theory's prediction that rhythm training facilitates attention to lower frequencies and improves phonological awareness, reporting partial support.
requirements: Rhythm perception is assumed to operate through sampling the speech signal at Delta (1–4 Hz) and Theta (4–10 Hz) frequencies corresponding to stress and syllables
constraints: The article reports only partial support: the combined training group was not the best on reading measures, contrary to the theory-based hypothesis H1
target_learners: children in the first year of primary education learning to read
target_learning_goals: phonological awareness
word reading
pseudoword reading
key_sources: Gutiérrez-Palma, N., Calet, N., Robles-Bello, M.A., & Valencia-Naranjo, N. (2026). The role of rhythm in learning to read in children with and without reading difficulties: an intervention study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102273

article_title: A change of scenery: Does the setting of an instructional video affect learning?
citation: Merkt, M., Lux, S., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Schwan, S. (2020). A Change of Scenery: Does the Setting of an Instructional Video Affect Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000414
title: Test-phase background screenshots reinstating the video setting as a contextual cue
description: In Experiment 2, the video's setting was reinstated during assessment: after watching the video, participants worked on the retention and application test "while a screenshot of the authentic or the neutral setting was presented as a background". This manipulation tested whether the setting could act as a contextual cue that further improves test performance, but the article reports no evidence for context effects.
requirements: Screenshots of the video's shooting setting must be presented as the background during the retention and application test.
constraints: The article found no evidence for context effects from this manipulation.
target_learners: adult participants completing retention and application tests in laboratory experiments
target_learning_goals: retention of video content
application of video content
key_sources: Merkt, M., Lux, S., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Schwan, S. (2020). A Change of Scenery: Does the Setting of an Instructional Video Affect Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000414

article_title: Teacher behavior and peer liking and disliking: The teacher as a social referent for peer status.
citation: Hendrickx, M. M. H. G., Mainhard, M. T., Oudman, V. S., Boor-Klip, H. J., & Brekelmans, J. M. G. (2017). Teacher Behavior and Peer Liking and Disliking: The Teacher as a Social Referent for Peer Status. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(4), 546-558. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000157
title: Social referencing theory applied to the teacher as a social referent for peer status
description: The article applies social referencing theory to classroom peer relations: according to this account, peers take cues from the teacher's positive and negative behavior toward a student, and these cues affect the student's peer liking and disliking status. The study extends the account with a mediation mechanism in which peers' perceptions of the teacher's liking and disliking for the student transmit the teacher's behavioral cues to peer status. As the article states, "According to social referencing theory, cues peers take from positive and negative teacher behavior toward a student affect the student's peer liking and disliking status."
requirements: Peers must observe teacher behavior directed toward individual students and form perceptions of the teacher's liking or disliking for that student.
constraints: In this study the referent function was supported only through negative teacher behavior and peer disliking, not positive behavior or liking.
target_learning_goals: Healthy peer relationships and peer status in the classroom
examples: The study tested the hypothesized mediation model longitudinally across three time points within one school year in 56 classes.
key_sources: Hendrickx, M. M. H. G., Mainhard, M. T., Oudman, V. S., Boor-Klip, H. J., & Brekelmans, J. M. G. (2017). Teacher Behavior and Peer Liking and Disliking: The Teacher as a Social Referent for Peer Status. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(4), 546-558. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000157

article_title: Pedagogical suggestions from memory tests.
citation: Patterson, T. L. (1909). Pedagogical Suggestions from Memory Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Teach educational subjects from the grapho-motor standpoint, alongside the other special senses, to approach maximal teaching efficiency
description: The article recommends that because the grapho-motor power exceeds the visual-motor power in acquiring knowledge through memory, "all educational subjects from the graded schools to the university, as far as possible and as far as time will permit, should be taught from the grapho-motor standpoint, as well as by the other special senses." It urges teachers to train the grapho-motor sense through drawing rather than relying only on receptive stimuli to the other senses.
requirements: The subject must lend itself to writing or drawing activity within available time, since the article qualifies the recommendation with as far as possible and as far as time will permit
constraints: The article states this cannot be applied to all subjects alike, singling out the biological sciences as a most satisfactory application and other subjects in varying degrees
target_learning_goals: memory for educational content
retention of subject-matter knowledge
examples: The author administered about 50 figure-reproduction tests at Anson Academy in 1909 using Meyerhardt's method before drawing the pedagogical recommendation.
key_sources: Patterson, T. L. (1909). Pedagogical Suggestions from Memory Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com

article_title: Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion.
citation: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Yanagida, T., Krannich, M., Roos, A.-L., Frenzel, A. C., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2023). Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/ftr4g/?view_only=beac4ca87987492294aeac4a1bb96c86
title: Test Boredom Scale (TBS-Trait and TBS-State)
description: The Test Boredom Scale is a multi-item self-report instrument constructed by modifying class- and learning-related boredom items from the Academic Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ). It comprises four sub-scales of three items each, representing the affective (e.g., "I'm bored during math exams"), cognitive, motivational, and physiological/expressive components of boredom, with parallel trait and state wordings on a 5-point response scale. Reliability "was α = .86 for the overall score comprising all four components" for the trait version, and coefficient α ranged from .83 to .94 across the five state assessments in Study 1.
requirements: Administration embedded in or alongside a test situation; the state version was administered five times before, during, and after the test
constraints: Developed and evaluated for mathematics tests with secondary-school students in the reported studies
target_learning_goals: measuring habitual and real-time boredom during tests
examples: Study 1 used the TBS-Trait one to three weeks before the test and the TBS-State within the test booklets
key_sources: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Yanagida, T., Krannich, M., Roos, A.-L., Frenzel, A. C., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2023). Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/ftr4g/?view_only=beac4ca87987492294aeac4a1bb96c86

article_title: Psychology in the schoolroom.
citation: J. D. Heilman. (1916). Psychology in the Schoolroom. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0073918
title: Select curriculum subjects for their content value and teach them for both content and formal values, avoiding radical views on mental discipline
description: The article argues that psychology shows both the older belief in formal mental training and the newer reaction against it were extreme. It recommends that "the safest procedure in practice is to select the subjects of the curriculum for their content value and to teach them for both their content and their formal values." The author adds that no one should hold radical views on mental discipline and predicts formal value will prove greater in the elementary school.
requirements: Curriculum decisions should draw on the psychological literature on formal training, which the article says presents problems by no means easy of solution
constraints: The article states the subject is not yet well understood and that valuable psychological contributions will continue to be made
target_learning_goals: curriculum content knowledge and transferable formal value of school subjects
examples: The article describes the shift from faculty psychology through the writings of James and Thorndike to an unwarranted disbelief in formal value
key_sources: J. D. Heilman. (1916). Psychology in the Schoolroom. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0073918

article_title: Experimental researches on learning to spell. Part I.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental researches on learning to spell. I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412810
title: Direct teacher attention during spelling practice, guiding learners letter by letter with combined sensory channels, benefits young children learning to spell
description: The article supports directing young learners' attention during spelling practice rather than leaving them to work independently. In the experiment, the teacher "spelt each word carefully, with slight pauses between the syllables" and boys spelt each word twice aloud while looking at each letter. This directed combined method outperformed undirected silent visual learning. The principle applies specifically to young children whose attention is not yet self-regulating for orthographic learning.
requirements: A teacher or experimenter must direct attention letter by letter during the spelling practice
constraints: Demonstrated only with young Standard II boys (average age 8 years 9 months) of relatively low ability in a poor London school; the author cautions results may not generalize to older or more able children
target_learners: young elementary school children (Standard II, average age 8 years 9 months)
target_learning_goals: correct spelling of common words
examples: The Head Master spelt each word on a black-board with slight pauses between syllables and clear pronunciation, and boys simultaneously spelt each word twice aloud looking at each letter
key_sources: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental researches on learning to spell. I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412810

article_title: Factors associated with children’s understanding of mathematical equivalence: An investigation across six countries.
citation: Şimşek, E., Xenidou-Dervou, I., Hunter, J., Gillon Dowens, M., Pang, J., Lee, Y., McNeil, N., Kirkland, P., & Jones, I. (2021). Factors Associated with Children's Understanding of Mathematical Equivalence: An Investigation across Six Countries. https://figshare.com/s/78625a6b0061200db6b7
title: Teacher instrument measuring knowledge of students' operational and relational strategies
description: A four-item teacher instrument asked teachers to identify possible correct and incorrect student answers and the strategies students might use when solving equivalence problems and defining the equals sign. Responses were coded with three codes per item: operational, sameness, and relational, using Hunter and Jones' (2016) scoring scheme. Composite scores for teachers' knowledge of students' operational and relational strategies were computed by averaging across items; Cronbach's α was .63 for the operational and relational codes together. A CFA confirmed a two-factor model with positively correlated factors (r = .406, p = .012).
requirements: Teachers must not have seen student assessments or asked students the instrument questions before completion
constraints: The definition item lacked variance in most countries (91% of teachers aware of both conceptions) and was excluded; sameness codes lacked variance and were not used in the analysis
target_learning_goals: knowledge of students' strategies for solving equivalence problems
key_sources: Şimşek, E., Xenidou-Dervou, I., Hunter, J., Gillon Dowens, M., Pang, J., Lee, Y., McNeil, N., Kirkland, P., & Jones, I. (2021). Factors Associated with Children's Understanding of Mathematical Equivalence: An Investigation across Six Countries. https://figshare.com/s/78625a6b0061200db6b7

article_title: Science as Subject-Matter and as Method.
citation: J. Dewey. (1910). Science as Subject-Mattcr and as Method. Science, 31: 787. https://www.science.org/journal/science
title: Teach science for its method-value — cultivating the scientific attitude through pupil inquiry — rather than primarily for informational subject-matter
description: The principle, drawn from Dewey's address as reported in the review, is that science instruction should constantly aim at the pupil's "scientific attitude and habit of mind" rather than placing informational subject-matter value uppermost.
