It works by leading pupils to take a hand in the making of knowledge, so that guess and opinion become belief authorized by inquiry. The review presents this as Dewey's remedy for the partial failure of school science.
requirements: Instruction must lead the pupil to participate in the making of knowledge rather than only receive information, per Dewey's stated condition that this is the only way to accomplish the aim.
constraints: The review notes some maintained this disciplinary attitude coincided with a relative falling off in science-registrations during the past ten years.
target_learning_goals: scientific attitude and habit of mind
inquiry-based belief formation
examples: The review reports Dewey's Boston address as the statement of this position, and notes secondary course organization and the spirit of instruction already seem to represent an attempt to realize this disciplinary value.
key_sources: J. Dewey. (1910). Science as Subject-Mattcr and as Method. Science, 31: 787. https://www.science.org/journal/science

article_title: Effects of a strategy-focused instructional program on the writing quality of upper elementary students in the Netherlands.
citation: Bouwer, R., Koster, M., & van den Bergh, H. (2018). Effects of a Strategy-Focused Instructional Program on the Writing Quality of Upper Elementary Students in the Netherlands. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(1), 58–71. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000206
title: Tekster: a comprehensive strategy-focused writing instruction program for Grades 4–6
description: Tekster is a program of 16 grade-level specific lessons in a student workbook with a teacher's manual, developed for fourth- through sixth-grade Dutch general education classrooms. "Tekster incorporates several different research-based practices to address both the focus and the mode of instruction." Its three design principles are writing strategies, text structures, and self-regulation skills, operationalized through observational learning (teacher and peer modeling, reader reaction), explicit instruction, and guided practice with scaffolding. Lessons use mnemonic acronyms (VOS, DODO, EKSTER) and authentic writing tasks across genres with specified communicative goals and audiences.
requirements: Teachers receive a 4-hour training session, a teacher's manual with 16 lesson plans, and a DVD with peer modeling video clips and examples of teacher modeling
constraints: In implementation, teachers taught an average of 10 of the intended 16 lessons, and 8% of students completed fewer than four lessons
target_learners: fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-grade students in general education classrooms in the Netherlands
target_learning_goals: writing quality across descriptive, narrative, and persuasive genres
use of a general writing strategy
self-regulation skills such as setting communicative goals and monitoring progress
examples: Grade 4 students learned the VOS (fox) strategy: Verzinnen, Ordenen, Schrijven; Grade 6 students learned EKSTER (magpie), which adds evaluating and revising steps
Writing tasks included personal advertisements, newspaper articles, emails nominating a TV program, recipes, and party invitations
key_sources: Bouwer, R., Koster, M., & van den Bergh, H. (2018). Effects of a Strategy-Focused Instructional Program on the Writing Quality of Upper Elementary Students in the Netherlands. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(1), 58–71. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000206

article_title: Effects of a strategy-focused instructional program on the writing quality of upper elementary students in the Netherlands.
citation: Bouwer, R., Koster, M., & van den Bergh, H. (2018). Effects of a Strategy-Focused Instructional Program on the Writing Quality of Upper Elementary Students in the Netherlands. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(1), 58–71. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000206
title: Tekster lesson format: mnemonic strategy steps taught through modeling, explicit instruction, and gradual release across a consistent lesson sequence
description: Tekster lessons follow a generally consistent format lasting 45–60 minutes, in which a mnemonic acronym (an animal name whose letters spell the strategy steps) anchors instruction. Each lesson explicitly states its goal, introduces text-type characteristics through modeling or explicit instruction, names the strategy acronym, and moves through generating content in keywords to writing, with "gradual release of responsibility from 1a to 1c, 3a to 3c" as printed in the lesson format table. Later phases have students read, evaluate, and revise texts based on feedback.
requirements: A student workbook and teacher's manual with detailed lesson plans
A DVD with peer modeling video clips and examples of teacher modeling
constraints: Phases 8a–10b (reading, evaluating, revising texts) apply only to Grades 5 and 6, with revision only in Grade 6
target_learners: fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-grade students in general education classrooms
target_learning_goals: applying the steps of a general writing strategy
setting and monitoring communicative goals
evaluating and revising texts on the basis of criteria
examples: Grade 4 students learned VOS (fox): Verzinnen (generate content), Ordenen (organize), Schrijven (write); Grade 6 students learned EKSTER (magpie), adding Teruglezen (reread), Evalueren (evaluate), and Reviseren (revise)
key_sources: Bouwer, R., Koster, M., & van den Bergh, H. (2018). Effects of a Strategy-Focused Instructional Program on the Writing Quality of Upper Elementary Students in the Netherlands. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(1), 58–71. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000206

article_title: Emotional transmission in the classroom: Exploring the relationship between teacher and student enjoyment.
citation: Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Lüdtke, O., Pekrun, R., & Sutton, R. E. (2009). Emotional Transmission in the Classroom: Exploring the Relationship Between Teacher and Student Enjoyment. Journal of Educational Psychology, 101(3), 705–716. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0014695
title: Teacher enjoyment scale developed for this study (5 class-referenced items)
description: Because no scales measuring teacher enjoyment existed, the authors developed a five-item scale referring to teaching a specific group of students, with items such as "I really enjoy teaching mathematics in this class" and "Teaching in this class gives me many reasons to be pleased," answered on a 5-point Likert scale. Internal consistency was high (Cronbach's α = .90). It was administered to the 71 Grade 8 mathematics teachers, whose mean rating was 3.69 (SD = 0.68).
requirements: Items refer to the specific class of students being taught, consistent with the study's context-specific, traitlike approach to emotions
target_learning_goals: assessment of teachers' enjoyment of teaching a particular class
examples: Observed range of the teacher enjoyment scale was 1.80 to 5.0, per Table 1
key_sources: Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Lüdtke, O., Pekrun, R., & Sutton, R. E. (2009). Emotional Transmission in the Classroom: Exploring the Relationship Between Teacher and Student Enjoyment. Journal of Educational Psychology, 101(3), 705–716. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0014695

article_title: Problems in the experimental pedagogy of geometry.
citation: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Teach general powers explicitly and across all subjects, never leaving them to accidental acquirement
description: The article recommends that powers such as concentration, accuracy, and honesty be made objects of instruction in themselves and be insisted upon in connection with every school subject, so that pupils apply them to everything they undertake. It argues that what is impressed from only one or two subjects "is not likely to be considered of much importance in others, and will not become a habit in all."
requirements: Teachers must explicitly point out the general value of the ability rather than limit it to the subject at hand
constraints: The article concedes there may be some truth to the objection that teaching accuracy in connection with everything dilutes subject-specific teaching
target_learning_goals: transferable habits such as concentration, accuracy, and honesty
examples: The article's analogy: a boy would hardly be expected to be honest if honesty were mentioned only in relation to his teacher
key_sources: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070947

article_title: Associations between teacher and student mathematics, science, and literacy anxiety in fourth grade.
citation: McLean, L., Janssen, J., Espinoza, P., Lindstrom Johnson, S., & Jimenez, M. (2023). Associations Between Teacher and Student Mathematics, Science, and Literacy Anxiety in Fourth Grade. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000790
title: Direct emotional transmission between teachers and students, framed by Sociocultural, Appraisal, and Control-Value Theories
description: The article organizes its inquiry around emotional transmission, defined via Frenzel et al. as a process "whereby an emotion expressed by one participant in an interaction is induced in their interaction partner(s), either directly or indirectly." Sociocultural Theory positions the teacher as the "more knowledgeable other" whose affective cues students observe; Appraisal Theory holds that individuals use others' emotional, behavioral, and affective cues to interpret and respond to their environment; Control-Value Theory describes how students' achievement emotions are shaped by appraisals of teacher-initiated social antecedents such as instruction, feedback, and classroom values. The article uses this framework to hypothesize that teachers' content-area anxiety transmits to students, potentially creating a "snowball effect" of anxiety, and to argue the teacher is the highest-leverage point for intervention even if relations are bi-directional.
requirements: Requires that students notice and appraise teachers' affective cues, as the framework posits students interpret and respond to emotional, behavioral, and affective cues from others in their environment.
constraints: The article notes teachers' and students' emotions likely influence each other bi-directionally and/or reciprocally, and the study's correlational design speaks only to associations, not directionality of effects.
target_learning_goals: Students' content-area anxiety in mathematics, science, and English language arts
examples: The article illustrates the mechanism with a teacher who experiences mathematics anxiety displaying rushed/nervous speech patterns, posturing that turns them away from students, and concerned/nervous facial expressions, which students may appraise as mathematics being threatening or intimidating.
key_sources: McLean, L., Janssen, J., Espinoza, P., Lindstrom Johnson, S., & Jimenez, M. (2023). Associations Between Teacher and Student Mathematics, Science, and Literacy Anxiety in Fourth Grade. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000790

article_title: A New Book for Teachers of History.
citation: Rugg, E. (1921). New Publications in Educational Psychology and Related Fields of Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Teachers should know that there are a number of ways of doing everyday classroom procedures
description: The reviewer endorses the preface's position that, while there are many ways of teaching history, it is fundamental to educational method "that the teacher know that there are a number of ways of doing the multitude of things connected with everyday procedure in that subject." He credits the reviewed book with telling history teachers about many of these ways and the procedures for managing them.
requirements: The teacher must be acquainted with multiple alternative procedures for everyday history-teaching tasks.
target_learners: junior and senior high school students
target_learning_goals: better history teaching through knowledge of alternative procedures
examples: The reviewer states the reviewed book tells teachers about many of these ways and points out the procedure in managing them.
key_sources: Rugg, E. (1921). New Publications in Educational Psychology and Related Fields of Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu

article_title: Alleged elements of waste in learning a motor problem by the "part" method.
citation: Pechstein, L. A. (1917). Alleged Elements of Waste in Learning a Motor Problem by the "Part" Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Withhold verdicts of whole-method superiority until modified part methods have been tested
description: Because modified part methods that progressively and distributively eliminate positional factors beat the whole method in maze learning, the article argues that its demonstrated advantages "lead the writer to question a thor- ough-going statement of the superiority of the whole method" in verbatim learning. Verdicts should wait "until the results of certain modified forms of part learning have been obtained and found inferior."
requirements: Modified part methods must provide a steady and progressive elimination of positional factors while the separate units are being mastered and connected
constraints: The article's remarks are meant to apply to that field of motor learning represented by the maze
target_learning_goals: efficient serial learning
motor skill acquisition
examples: The progressive part method: learn the first two units as units and proceed at once to the act of connection, then master Section III and join it to the established unity, then Section IV
key_sources: Pechstein, L. A. (1917). Alleged Elements of Waste in Learning a Motor Problem by the "Part" Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071944

article_title: Teacher personality and teacher effectiveness in secondary school: Personality predicts teacher support and student self-efficacy but not academic achievement.
citation: Kim, Lisa, Dar-Nimrod, Ilan and MacCann, Carolyn (2018) Teacher Personality and Teacher Effectiveness in Secondary School: Personality Predicts Teacher Support and Student Self-Efficacy but not Academic Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology. pp. 309-323. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000217
title: Emotional contagion and social modeling account for teacher neuroticism lowering student performance self-efficacy
description: The article proposes a mechanism account in which teachers high in neuroticism transmit negative emotions to students. Teachers act as social models: when a teacher "behaves anxiously and verbalizes their doubts and worries about their teaching and students' skills, students may model the teacher's low self-efficacy and nervous behaviors". Teachers' emotional expressions may also foster emotional contagion, in which students unconsciously synchronize their emotions with their teachers', raising student anxiety and self-doubt and diminishing the approach-oriented construct of performance self-efficacy. The study uses this account to motivate its hypothesis that teacher neuroticism negatively predicts PSE.
requirements: Requires observable teacher emotional expression in the classroom that students can perceive and model
constraints: The article presents this as a theoretical argument; it did not directly test the contagion or modeling mechanism
target_learners: Secondary school students in mathematics and English classes
target_learning_goals: Student performance self-efficacy and academic self-confidence
examples: The study's hypothesis H4c, that teacher neuroticism would negatively predict PSE, was derived from this account and received partial support in the multilevel regressions.
key_sources: Kim, Lisa, Dar-Nimrod, Ilan and MacCann, Carolyn (2018) Teacher Personality and Teacher Effectiveness in Secondary School: Personality Predicts Teacher Support and Student Self-Efficacy but not Academic Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology. pp. 309-323. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000217

article_title: Experimental researches on learning to spell. Part II.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental Researches on Learning to Spell, Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Teachers should improve instruction through controlled experiments with exact measurement, supported by educational psychologists rather than directives from superior persons
description: The article argues that teachers who try instructional issues for themselves are driven, by the logic of events, toward "controlled procedure with exact measurement," and that educational psychologists should be appointed to help teachers find out which methods work, not to tell them what to adopt. The subsidiary experiments in the article illustrate, in the author's words, "genetically the pathway to experimental pedagogy."
requirements: Teachers need guidance from educational psychologists to frame valid experiments; the article says teachers "cannot usually invent valid experiments, but they can carry them out."
constraints: The article notes the superior persons appointed to direct teachers "do not really know any more than the teachers do," so the principle excludes top-down prescription.
target_learners: elementary school children in poor urban neighbourhoods
target_learning_goals: spelling and orthography
examples: The Head Master's twelve-week home-copy method, the flash-card methods, and the head-to-head teaching contest each failed or proved inconclusive until the controlled First and Second Experiments were run.
key_sources: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental Researches on Learning to Spell, Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0076021

article_title: Physical training psychologized.
citation: New Publications in Educational Psychology and Related Fields of Education. (1922). https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Terry's photographic eye-movement apparatus for studying numeral reading
description: This element is the research setup described in Terry's monograph 'How Numerals are Read', a University of Chicago Supplementary Educational Monograph. Part I used introspective methods with graduate students in four preliminary studies; in Part II, "photographic apparatus was used to record the eye movements of six adult subjects". Subjects read simple arithmetical problems, isolated numerals of various lengths, and ordinary prose. The review presents it as an addition to the Chicago reading monographs and as introductory work on the eye habits involved in reading numerals.
requirements: Photographic apparatus to record eye movements, as used in Part II with six adult subjects
constraints: The review states the study is introductory to more elaborate detailed inquiry into the development of the specific eye habits involved
target_learners: adult subjects reading numerals and arithmetic problems
target_learning_goals: understanding eye-movement habits in reading numerals and arithmetic problems
examples: Part I used four preliminary introspective studies with graduate student subjects before the photographic eye-movement recordings
key_sources: New Publications in Educational Psychology and Related Fields of Education. (1922). https://eric.ed.gov/

article_title: Longitudinal relations among self-concept, intrinsic value, and attainment value across secondary school years in three academic domains.
citation: Arens, A. Katrin; Schmidt, Isabelle; Preckel, Franzis. (2019). Longitudinal relations among self-concept, intrinsic value, and attainment value across secondary school years in three academic domains. The Journal of educational psychology 111 (2019) 4, S. 663-684. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000313
title: Temporal reciprocal relations among motivation constructs in expectancy-value theory
description: The article applies expectancy-value theory's account of temporal relations among motivation constructs, examining how academic self-conpect, intrinsic value, and attainment value predict each other over time in cross-lagged panel models. It reports that "former academic self-concept was positively related to later intrinsic value and attainment value" in math and English, while in German "former intrinsic value and attainment value were positively related to later academic self-concept," with domain-specific patterns and stable relation sizes across Grades 5 to 9.
requirements: Requires longitudinal data with multiple annual measurement waves and cross-lagged panel modeling
Requires domain-specific measures of self-concept and separate value facets
constraints: Findings are domain-specific; directional patterns differ between math, English, and German
Based on German secondary school students in Grades 5 to 9
target_learners: German secondary school students in Grades 5 to 9
target_learning_goals: Academic self-concept and motivational value beliefs in math, German, and English
key_sources: Arens, A. Katrin; Schmidt, Isabelle; Preckel, Franzis. (2019). Longitudinal relations among self-concept, intrinsic value, and attainment value across secondary school years in three academic domains. The Journal of educational psychology 111 (2019) 4, S. 663-684. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000313

article_title: The Psychology of Drill in Arithmetic: The Amount of Practice.
citation: Thorndike, E. L. (1921). The psychology of drill in arithmetic: The amount of practice. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 12(4). https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/12/4
title: Know how much practice your instructional instrument actually gives before supplementing or omitting practice
description: Because textbooks may give far too little practice on certain bonds and may divide practice in apparently unjustifiable ways, the teacher needs to know how much practice the instrument actually provides. The article states "The teacher needs therefore to know how much practice it does give, where to supplement it, and what to omit." Omissions on grounds of apparent excess should be made only after careful consideration of the cases justifying over-learning.
requirements: Knowledge of the actual frequency counts of practice in the textbook or instrument of instruction
constraints: Omissions on grounds of apparent excess practice should be made only after careful consideration of the third principle described above
target_learners: Elementary school pupils in grades I to VI studying arithmetic
target_learning_goals: Mastery of elementary arithmetical facts in the four operations with integers
examples: Thorndike counted the occurrences of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division bonds in recent textbooks A and B through grade VI (Tables II–VII)
key_sources: Thorndike, E. L. (1921). The psychology of drill in arithmetic: The amount of practice. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 12(4). https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/12/4

article_title: Problems in the scientific study of the teaching of arithmetic.
citation: Stone, C. W. (1913). Problems in the Scientific Study of the Teaching of Arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IV(1). https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Teachers and special investigators should co-operate in scientific studies of teaching, with teachers following methods faithfully and results measured regardless of personal opinions
description: The article states that "The best conditions for scientific study are those in which teachers and special investigators co-operate." The investigator may be a superintendent, supervisor, principal or outsider, but must have the co-operation of class teachers, who must follow the methods definitely and accurately and submit results to measurement regardless of their personal opinions, while the investigator measures precisely and evaluates regardless of preconceived beliefs. Because larger numbers of measurements make results more conclusive, wide co-operation is desirable.
requirements: Class teachers must follow the methods definitely and accurately and submit results to measurement regardless of personal opinions
The investigator must measure precisely and adequately and evaluate results regardless of preconceived beliefs
constraints: The article notes that whatever is done in teaching or in the study of teaching depends in the last analysis on the teacher, since it is products rather than plans for products that must be measured
target_learners: classroom pupils in co-operating school systems
target_learning_goals: evaluating the relative value of conflicting methods of teaching arithmetic
examples: The article proposes that equally bright and capable teachers who differ fundamentally in their methods present exactly the material scientific study must evaluate, with measurement supplied by a trained investigator or by teachers themselves using standardized tests
key_sources: Stone, C. W. (1913). Problems in the Scientific Study of the Teaching of Arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IV(1). https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: Tests of applicants for admission to University of Minnesota Medical School.
citation: Haggerty, M. E. (1917). Tests of Applicants for Admission to University of Minnesota Medical School. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Mental test scores measure a complex mental state including non-intellectual functions, so correlations of .60-.80 may be the maximum expected
description: The article argues that test performance is not a purely intellectual product: association is "shot through with the very interests and emotions" discriminated from it in discussion, and a reading-scale product also indirectly tests "his interest, his endurance, persistence and other emotional and instinctive attitudes." On this account a correlation of .70 between test and marks means the test measures intellectual and non-intellectual factors all partially, and a test of purely intellectual functions could cap correlations near .60-.80, while a test capturing the complex state could conceivably approach a perfect relationship.
requirements: Interpreting a test correlation requires deciding whether the test measures purely intellectual functions or the complex mental state including interests, emotions and attitudes.
constraints: The article states the desirable amount of correlation between mental tests and academic achievement is difficult to fix.
target_learners: applicants to a university medical school
target_learning_goals: prognosis of success in a medical curriculum
examples: The author reasons that a time score recorded at the end of the association test is a measure of the complex mental state involving desire to succeed, speed, error avoidance, and affective states prompted by surprise, absurdity and complexity.
key_sources: Haggerty, M. E. (1917). Tests of Applicants for Admission to University of Minnesota Medical School. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071405

article_title: Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation
citation: Bihao Hu, Jiayi Zhu, Yiying Pei & Xiaoqing Gu. (2025). Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00300-x
title: Nine-category, nineteen-dimension teaching plan evaluation framework with expert rater panel
description: The article develops an evaluation framework of 9 categories and 19 indicators covering problem chains, teaching activities, knowledge content, teaching methods and strategies, teaching evaluation, interdisciplinarity, practical value, scope, and overall score, rated on an 8-point Likert scale. Three mathematics teachers with over five years of experience scored the 480 plans, aided by two expert teachers with over ten years of experience. The pre-evaluation consistency test "had an ICC (2, 3) value of 0.716, which exceedsthe 0.6 threshold, indicating a high degree of consistency in the teachers’evaluations."
requirements: Raters review each teaching plan for at least ten minutes and receive explanations and examples of each dimension; discrepancies are resolved by consultation with the two expert teachers
constraints: The framework omits assessment of instructional objectives and teaching priorities and challenges, which were retained from prior-generation output rather than re-evaluated
target_learners: high school mathematics teachers and pre-service teachers whose plans are evaluated
target_learning_goals: comprehensive assessment of teaching plan quality across pedagogical and content dimensions
examples: Raters pre-evaluated a mixed set of 15 plans from Datasets C and D before formal evaluation of the eight datasets
key_sources: Bihao Hu, Jiayi Zhu, Yiying Pei & Xiaoqing Gu. (2025). Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00300-x

article_title: Does pre-testing promote better retention than post-testing?
citation: Latimier, A., Riegert, A., Peyre, H., Ly, S. T., Casati, R. & Ramus, F. (2019). Does pre-testing promote better retention than post-testing? npj Science of Learning 4:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0053-1
title: Spend retrieval-practice time testing students after, not before, initial exposure to learning content
description: The article recommends that when a fixed amount of time is available for retrieval practice, quizzes should follow rather than precede the first exposure to content. Post-testing produced both larger retention gains and transfer to untrained questions, whereas pre-testing did not transfer. The authors state: "current evidence suggests that testing time dedicated to enhancing retention is better spent after than before the initial exposure to learning content."
requirements: Requires learning content that can be split into modules with associated quizzes and feedback, as in the Didask digital learning platform used in the experiment.
constraints: Conclusions are, per the authors, limited to scientific text material, an e-learning presentation mode, and adult workers doing a paid task rather than students; the effect of pre-testing on untested information may depend on content format (read vs. video).
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of scientific prose content
Transfer to related but untested questions
examples: In the experiment, participants in the reading-quiz condition studied each module's content before taking its quiz with elaborative feedback, while quiz-reading participants took the quiz first; the final test came 7 days later.
key_sources: Latimier, A., Riegert, A., Peyre, H., Ly, S. T., Casati, R. & Ramus, F. (2019). Does pre-testing promote better retention than post-testing? npj Science of Learning 4:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0053-1

article_title: A RCT for assessment of active human-centred learning finds teacher-centric non-human teaching of evolution optimal
citation: Buchan, L., Hejmadi, M., Abrahams, L. & Hurst, L. D. (2020). A RCT for assessment of active human-centred learning finds teacher-centric non-human teaching of evolution optimal. npj Science of Learning 5:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00078-0
title: Test lesson plans in series rather than in parallel, because serial designs expose interaction effects between teaching modes that parallel designs miss
description: The article argues that teaching happens in series while methodology tests are typically done in parallel, implicitly assuming no interaction effects. Its replicated 2×2 serial trial found a replicable interaction effect, leading the authors to state that "parallel modes of testing, even in an RCT format, might mislead and that lessons plans in series should be considered for fuller testing".
requirements: Requires large sample sizes, since detecting interaction effects between lessons in series demands more power, as with drug interaction trials
Requires adherence to prescribed lesson sequences, which the authors achieved through teacher training and recently-introduced curriculum topics
constraints: The 2×2 serial design used here excludes temporal effects because simultaneous delivery of the schemes was not feasible
The cause of the interaction effect could not be identified by the study
target_learning_goals: Understanding of evolution, including natural selection, variation, geological time and homology/common ancestry
examples: The study randomised whole classes to four four-lesson schemes in a 2×2 design modelled on drug interaction trials such as CHARIMMA, with pre, post and delayed retention testing in situ by trained classroom teachers
key_sources: Buchan, L., Hejmadi, M., Abrahams, L. & Hurst, L. D. (2020). A RCT for assessment of active human-centred learning finds teacher-centric non-human teaching of evolution optimal. npj Science of Learning 5:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00078-0

article_title: Prior text-based learning enhances the benefits of simulation-based learning on confidence and long-term recall
citation: Angélique Lebert & Óscar Vilarroya. (2025). Prior text-based learning enhances the benefits of simulation-based learning on confidence and long-term recall. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00380-9
title: Sequence structured text-based learning before immersive embodied simulation to scaffold later embodied encoding
description: The article reports that beginning with text-based learning improved subsequent simulation-based performance, while starting with simulation did not benefit later text learning. The authors suggest "initial symbolic structuring can scaffold later embodied encoding" and "underscores that sequencing effects are conditional." This principle recommends placing structured, low-to-high complexity text-based instruction before immersive embodied sessions, consistent with the authors' proposal of "a sequential, low-to-high complexity approach that progressively builds learners' long-term memory stores."
requirements: Applies when learning sessions are content-matched and temporally spaced, as in the study's "content-matched, temporally spaced sessions with distinct cases"
constraints: The authors note the order effect, while intriguing, requires further validation and may not generalize to other educational contexts
The mechanism (cognitive flexibility, engagement shifts, or proactive interference) remains speculative
target_learners: naïve adult learners acquiring novel structured knowledge
target_learning_goals: improving subsequent simulation-based learning accuracy through instructional sequencing
examples: In the study, participants who completed the text condition first showed enhanced subsequent performance in the simulation condition, whereas starting with simulation did not benefit the control condition

article_title: Mathematics interest, self-efficacy, and anxiety predict STEM career choice in emerging adulthood
citation: Ferdinand, R., Malanchini, M. & Rimfeld, K. (2024). Mathematics interest, self-efficacy, and anxiety predict STEM career choice in emerging adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00275-1
title: Twins Early Development Study (TEDS) longitudinal cohort and STEM career choice measure
description: TEDS is a UK longitudinal twin cohort born 1994–1996, representative of England and Wales in ethnicity and SES, with a 76.5% response rate by early adulthood. The study used waves at ~1.5 years, ~16, ~18–21 and ~21–24, randomly selecting one twin per pair. STEM career choice was self-reported degree/apprenticeship choices at age 21, classified via the HESA HECoS coding system and coded dichotomously.
requirements: Data available to researchers upon request under the TEDS data access policy; informed consent obtained at each wave.
constraints: Missingness showed MNAR patterns: missing data came from individuals with lower SES, with SES absence accounting for 43–44% of variance in maths achievement and STEM career choice missingness; career data limited to degree and apprenticeship decisions.
target_learners: UK adolescents and emerging adults (twins born 1994–1996)
target_learning_goals: Linking adolescent maths attitudes and achievement to adult STEM career participation
examples: 5.1% (117) of the 2254 participants with career data reported an apprenticeship choice and 29.4% (662) reported a STEM career choice.

article_title: A practical implementation science framework for education
citation: Allen, S. E., Bardach, L., Jirout, J., Mackey, A., McCoy, D., Pesando, L. M., & Kizilcec, R. F. (2026). A practical implementation science framework for education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00430-w
title: Teamwork & Communication: clear roles and shared decisions with students and teachers across all organizational levels
description: The second principle for success: "Successful projects have clear team member roles, make all important decisions in partnership with students and teachers, and openly share setbacks and successes." The article grounds this in Implementation Science consensus that any implementation project must consider both individual-level behavioral factors and systemic organizational factors, and that all levels of the organization have essential contributions to make. Budgets should actively build a team with clear lines of communication and formal roles for stakeholders, co-investigators, project staff, and leadership.
requirements: A budget allocated to actively build a team with clear lines of communication and formal stakeholder roles
constraints: The article notes many efforts fail by not engaging with stakeholders at all levels of the organization
target_learners: Students, teachers, administrators, and families as implementation stakeholders
target_learning_goals: Sustained adoption of evidence-based pedagogical practices through genuine stakeholder partnership
examples: In high-engagement postsecondary pedagogy implementations, the most common feature of successful projects was meaningful collaboration between instructors and departmental leadership, especially support amid early setbacks

article_title: Longitudinal changes in cortical responses to letter-speech sound stimuli in 8–11 year-old children
citation: Romanovska, L., Janssen, R. & Bonte, M. (2022). Longitudinal changes in cortical responses to letter-speech sound stimuli in 8–11 year-old children. npj Science of Learning 7:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00118-3
title: Text-based recalibration paradigm for probing letter-speech sound mappings
description: An audio-visual perceptual-learning paradigm in which "aba"/"ada" text is combined with an individually determined ambiguous /a?a/ speech sound during exposure blocks, shifting later auditory-only perception of the ambiguous sound toward the text. In this study children completed four runs with 24 exposure blocks and post-test trials on /a?a/ and its two flanking sounds, inside fMRI across three yearly sessions. The paradigm was "speci ﬁcally designed to investigate reading-induced changes in the left posterior STC" and avoided the working-memory demands of congruency paradigms.
requirements: Individual pre-test to identify each child's most ambiguous sound (response proportion closest to 0.5)
MR-compatible audio presentation in silent gaps between volume acquisitions
constraints: Behavioural recalibration did not reach significance in the MRI environment in this age range, likely due to scanner noise or altered visual attentional focus
The simple two-word text stimuli may not optimally engage the VWFA
target_learners: Children aged 8–11 learning to read in an orthographically transparent language (Dutch)
target_learning_goals: Short-term perceptual learning of letter-speech sound associations; probing automatisation of audio-visual letter-speech integration
examples: Eighteen children performed the task in yearly fMRI sessions with mock-scanner practice and motion training beforehand
key_sources: Romanovska, L., Janssen, R. & Bonte, M. (2022). Longitudinal changes in cortical responses to letter-speech sound stimuli in 8–11 year-old children. npj Science of Learning 7:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00118-3

article_title: Design of generative AI-powered pedagogy for virtual reality environments in higher education
citation: Ulla Hemminki-Reijonen, Noha M. A. M. Hassan, Minna Huotilainen, Jaana-Maija Koivisto & Benjamin Ultan Cowley. (2025). Design of generative AI-powered pedagogy for virtual reality environments in higher education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00326-1
title: Tero: a prompt-engineered GAI character acting as a realistic forest owner and interview source in IVR
description: Tero is a GAI character representing "a realistic-like representation of a forest owner" designed for Use case 1, in which students interview a local person to gather facts within participatory modelling's Fact Finding stage. Tero "was prompt-engineered based on research into forest ownership to accurately portray the responsibilities, decisions, and challenges faced by a forest owner," providing information about sustainability problems and intervention points in boreal forest. The character was developed as a text-based dialog in CurreChat (UH's GPT 4 interface) before 3D IVR deployment.
requirements: Prompt engineering informed by domain research (forest ownership research) with iterative refinement across LLM versions
constraints: Feedback indicated Tero presented a narrow perspective of forest ownership and the information was not completely up to date
target_learners: higher education students in sustainability education
target_learning_goals: systems-thinking competency: understanding intervention points for sustainability problems
examples: Domain experts tested Tero as text-based dialogs; after feedback that answers were too complete, prompt adjustments made later testers feel Tero portrayed a realistic forest owner

article_title: Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT
citation: Gilbert, S. B., Slavina, A., Dorneich, M. C., Sinatra, A. M., Bonner, D., Johnston, J., Holub, J., MacAllister, A., & Winer, E. (2017). Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0151-2
title: An object-oriented terminology ontology for describing team tutors
description: The article proposes a standardized vocabulary for team tutors, conceptualized "as an ontology, analogous to an object-oriented hierarchy in programming context." Terms include Team, Member, Role, Task, Team Task, Action, Skill, Skill Requirement, and Team Skill Requirement, plus a second set distinguishing action performance, performance state, task performance, and performance metric. The ontology lets authors map which skill requirements a team possesses through its members' roles and tasks, and is intended to ease planning and cross-platform comparison of team tutors.
requirements: Applied during initial tutor planning to map the tutor's purpose and functioning before authoring
constraints: Proposed terminology, adopted to ease internal communication; the article does not report validation with other teams
target_learners: teams of learners in team-training contexts
target_learning_goals: team skills such as communication and coordination
examples: In the Surveillance Scenario the ontology was instantiated as two members with roles whose tasks were Transfer, Acknowledge, and Identify, each with skill requirements
key_sources: Gilbert, S. B., Slavina, A., Dorneich, M. C., Sinatra, A. M., Bonner, D., Johnston, J., Holub, J., MacAllister, A., & Winer, E. (2017). Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0151-2

article_title: Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT
citation: Gilbert, S. B., Slavina, A., Dorneich, M. C., Sinatra, A. M., Bonner, D., Johnston, J., Holub, J., MacAllister, A., & Winer, E. (2017). Creating a Team Tutor Using GIFT. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0151-2
title: A seven-dimension design space of feedback choices for team tutoring testbeds
description: The article organizes feedback design as seven dimensions realizable in the Surveillance testbed: subject (individual vs. team), target (public vs. private), timing (immediate, after, omitted), type (proactive vs. reactive), specificity (generic vs. specific), tone (positive vs. negative), and style (collaborative vs. competitive). "Table 1 illustrates different dimensions of feedback that can be explored." The pattern lets researchers vary feedback systematically, since feedback at too high a frequency could be overwhelming and ignored, while immediate delivery has been reported effective under higher cognitive load.
requirements: A task testbed in which feedback can be delivered and varied along these dimensions without interrupting training
constraints: How much feedback is too much "may depend on the team members themselves"
target_learners: teams of two or more learners in real-time team tasks
target_learning_goals: team communication and task performance under feedback variation
examples: Specific feedback example from Table 1: 'You missed an OPFOR located at 7 o'clock'; collaborative style: 'Slow down scanning to help the team'

article_title: AIED—Coming of Age?
citation: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3
title: Teachers need AI literacy in both dimensions to support students and evaluate AIED tools
description: The author argues teachers in every discipline should develop AI literacy in both the human and technological dimensions of AI, for two reasons: 'so that they can best support their students' developing AI Literacy, and so that they are empowered to evaluate whether an AIED tool might be useful, effective, and ethical in their specific context.' Teachers should also be supported to teach about AI within their own discipline.
requirements: Support must extend to teachers from every discipline, not only computing teachers
target_learning_goals: Evaluating commercial AIED tools for usefulness, effectiveness and ethics; supporting students' AI literacy
examples: The author asks what the implications of generative AI are for literature and art, and how these technologies affect what it is to be human

citation: Andrew M. Olney, Stephen B. Gilbert, Kelly Rivers. (2021). Preface to the Special Issue on Creating and Improving Adaptive Learning: Smart Authoring Tools and Processes. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2022) 32:1–3. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00277-9
title: Teachable agent for cognitive task analysis and expert-model authoring in fraction arithmetic and equations (Matsuda)
description: One of the four accepted special-issue papers. Matsuda "describes using a teachable agent that learns a highly-accurate expert model for fraction arithmetic and equations to develop tutors and support cognitive task analyses". The editorial classifies this process, together with MacLellan and Koedinger's, as "adaptive authoring of adaptive content" — building adaptive tutors which are themselves adaptive.
requirements: A teachable agent that can learn a highly-accurate expert model of the target domain
constraints: Case study limited to fraction arithmetic and equations as the modeled domains
target_learners: teachers and trainers who are not programmers
target_learning_goals: developing tutors and supporting cognitive task analyses via expert-model authoring
examples: The teachable agent learned a highly-accurate expert model used for fraction arithmetic and equations

article_title: Guest Editorial: Special Issue on “Bridging Futures: The Convergence of Technology Enhanced Learning and Generative AI”
citation: Filippo Sciarrone, Pierpaolo Vittorini, Christothea Herodotou, Elvira Popescu, Nuno Palmero Otero, Chee-Kit Looi, Marcelo Milrad. (2025). Guest Editorial: Special Issue on “Bridging Futures: The Convergence of Technology Enhanced Learning and Generative AI”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00516-3
title: Responsible GAI integration framework: balancing innovation with pedagogical intent, ethics and human oversight
description: The editorial frames effective GAI integration in TEL as requiring a balance of innovation with responsibility. It states that "Effective implementation also requires a fundamental rethinking of educational frameworks, pedagogical strategies, and assessment methods to maximize GAI's benefits while minimizing potential drawbacks", and that ethical issues, data privacy and algorithmic bias must be addressed so systems remain "inclusive, equitable, and centered on human needs". The framework positions human oversight as essential to GAI's educational effectiveness.
requirements: Educational frameworks, pedagogical strategies and assessment methods must be rethought for GAI integration; ethical issues, data privacy and algorithmic bias must be addressed.
constraints: GAI's effectiveness hinges on thoughtful integration with human oversight; unchecked adoption risks perpetuating algorithmic bias.
target_learners: learners and educators across educational sectors
target_learning_goals: personalized learning, feedback, assessment, and equitable access to high-quality educational resources
examples: The editorial surveyed special-issue studies across architecture, literacy, computer science, data science, primary mathematics, biology assessment and teacher education as instances of this balancing act.

article_title: Preschoolers’ Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study
citation: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4
title: Learning-by-teaching with a teachable agent in three successive pedagogical modes
description: Magical Garden implements the learning-by-teaching pedagogy: the child instructs a digital tutee (the teachable agent) and learns by doing so. Each scenario is, in the article's words, "always repeated in three successive pedagogical modes": the child practices the task alone, then demonstrates it to the watching TA, then supervises the TA's attempt, accepting or correcting the TA's proposal with happy/unhappy smileys. The design yields two stated pedagogical gains: repeated, non-repetitive task practice, and the chance to evaluate someone else performing the task, which is more feasible for young children than reflecting on their own actions under cognitive load.
requirements: The child must be able to ascribe some knowledge to the TA that can differ from and be influenced by their own, and perceive the TA's behavior as goal-directed for meaningful instruction
constraints: Full benefit requires understanding that the TA has agency; the article questions whether preschoolers' less developed theory of mind supports this
target_learning_goals: early mathematics and number sense within the number range 1–9
examples: In mode three the TA proposes a button shown in a thought bubble and the child accepts or corrects it; after the three modes child and TA receive water droplets to grow the garden

article_title: Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research
citation: Robert A. Sottilare, Ryan S. Baker, Arthur C. Graesser, & James C. Lester. (2017). Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0149-9
title: Four-way typology of group-oriented tutoring: team taskwork, teamwork, collaborative learning, and collaborative problem solving
description: The article distinguishes four group-oriented tutoring capabilities that GIFT is being extended to support through intelligent, computer-guided instruction. Team taskwork tutoring develops proficiency in tasks requiring more than one member; teamwork tutoring enhances coordination, cooperation, and communication toward a shared goal; collaborative learning is defined as 'a situation in which two or more people learn or attempt to learn something together'; and collaborative problem solving involves agents pooling knowledge, skills, and efforts to reach a solution. The typology draws on Salas (2015), Dillenbourg (1999), and the PISA 2015 collaborative problem solving framework.
requirements: Validation of team models requires experimentation via the GIFT testbed across a variety of domains to generalize results
constraints: Team taskwork is domain-dependent, with learner models, team models, measures, and interventions potentially unique to each domain; teamwork tutoring is distinguished as targeting team processes rather than specific domains
target_learners: Teams and collaborative groups in military and civilian training
target_learning_goals: Team taskwork proficiency, teamwork processes (communication, coaching, conflict management, cooperation), collaborative learning, and collaborative problem solving
examples: Gilbert et al. (2017) extended the GIFT data structure to represent team taskwork domain knowledge in a simple surveillance mission involving two team members

article_title: The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations
citation: Michael J. Baker. (2015). The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0050-3
title: Tension-relaxation analysis of interpersonal relations in collaborative argumentation
description: Extending Bales' division of social interaction into a task zone and a socio-emotional zone, the author and Andriessen developed a formal analysis method aimed at studying "the 'interaction' between deepening of a conflict (extending down into an argument chain) and fluctuations in tension-relaxation". The expectation was that deepening conflicts raise tension up to a threshold supportable by the interpersonal relation. They also elaborated the notion of a collaborative working relation, which develops over time and acts as a buffer mediating the mutual regulation of tensions.
requirements: Analysis of both the depth of argumentative conflict and fluctuating tension levels in the same interaction data
constraints: Early results are described as preliminary; systematic analysis of interpersonal relations and affects in collaborative learning is described as very recent
target_learners: students in collaborative argumentation and problem-solving
target_learning_goals: sustaining productive argumentative collaboration while regulating interpersonal tension
examples: Early results showed a lag in tension lowering after a local conflict, which could raise tension levels for subsequent conflicts

article_title: Applying Large Language Models to Enhance Dialogue and Communication Analysis for Adaptive Team Training
citation: Spain, R., Min, W., Kumaran, V., Pande, V., Saville, J., & Lester, J. (2024). Applying Large Language Models to Enhance Dialogue and Communication Analysis for Adaptive Team Training. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4565500/v1
title: Team Communication Analysis Framework using transformer-based LLMs for dialogue act recognition with limited training data
description: The article presents a team communication analysis framework that leverages transformer-based LLMs, particularly GPT models, for dialogue act recognition in scenarios with limited training data. Speech uttered by team members is collected by the learning environment and converted into transcripts using automatic speech recognition; the framework then analyzes the transcripts to recognize dialogue acts, and these insights are passed to an adaptation engine that provides adaptive scaffolding to each team member. The framework is designed to support adaptive team training by enabling instructors and researchers to gain insights into team actions and processes that impact team coordination.
requirements: Speech uttered by team members is collected by the learning environment and converted into transcripts using automatic speech recognition
An adaptation engine component receives the analysis insights to provide adaptive scaffolding to team members
constraints: The article focuses on evaluating the Team Communication Analysis Framework component, specifically addressing dialogue act recognition in scenarios with limited training data
target_learners: team members in military squad training exercises
target_learning_goals: team communication behaviors
team coordination
dialogue act recognition for adaptive feedback
examples: The framework was evaluated with labeled transcripts from a U.S. Army training event where squads completed a 45-minute live training exercise involving observing and maintaining overwatch of a village

title: Technology adoption model as frame of reference for evaluating a writing instruction tool
description: The study uses "A technology adoption model served as a frame of reference for the research design." This organizes the evaluation around students' perceptions of the "use, usability, and usefulness of TW", studied through an online survey and focus groups in an explanatory sequential (mixed-methods) design. It frames how scaling of writing instruction through technology is assessed.
requirements: Evaluation should capture perceived use, usability, and usefulness of the tool
target_learning_goals: academic writing instruction
examples: Online survey and focus groups with 102 students assessing TW's use, usability, and usefulness

article_title: Designing for the co-Orchestration of Social Transitions between Individual, Small-Group and Whole-Class Learning in the Classroom
citation: Jennifer K. Olsen & Nikol Rummel & Vincent Aleven. (2021). Designing for the co-Orchestration of Social Transitions between Individual, Small-Group and Whole-Class Learning in the Classroom. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:24–56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00228-w
title: Divide orchestration control by planning phase: teachers design the lesson and may override; the system executes real-time transition decisions within that design
description: The article recommends splitting co-orchestration control around social transitions by phase. Teachers act as 'the instigators of the lesson-designing process', specifying when and how students transition between social levels, while 'the system is responsible for carrying out real-time orchestration decisions around social transitions within the confines of the teacher's lesson design'. This automation contrasts with systems that remain at the mirroring, alerting, or advising level, and frees teacher time for one-on-one support. Teachers retain the ability to make any real-time changes and override system decisions, which the authors say gives a sense of autonomy and control.
requirements: Teachers must specify the transition parameters (activity impact, group size direction, fluidity) during lesson design so the system can execute within them
The system's decisions must remain within the bounds of what the teacher has planned
constraints: If roles are not well distributed, the technology can lead to greater orchestration load rather than a reduction
target_learners: primary school students in technology-enhanced classrooms
target_learning_goals: managing transitions between social levels without consuming teacher time needed for student support
examples: In the design sessions teachers asked for an 'override button' to adjust to what is currently occurring in the classroom, and the desires were realized in a mid-fidelity prototype
key_sources: Jennifer K. Olsen & Nikol Rummel & Vincent Aleven. (2021). Designing for the co-Orchestration of Social Transitions between Individual, Small-Group and Whole-Class Learning in the Classroom. article_title: A Teachable Agent Game Engaging Primary School Children to Learn Arithmetic Concepts and Reasoning
citation: Pareto, L. (2014). A Teachable Agent Game Engaging Primary School Children to Learn Arithmetic Concepts and Reasoning. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0018-8
title: Teachable agent game environment combining learning-by-doing and learning-by-teaching for arithmetic
description: A digital learning game environment of 48 two-player card and board games where "the mathematical content is intrinsically interwoven with the game idea". Students play games based on a graphical model of arithmetic and can teach an agent to play via show-mode and try-mode. The agent asks situation-specific multiple-choice questions organized into five categories reflecting progression in mathematical thinking, from game idea to advanced strategic thinking. The design combines the motivational power of games with the reflective power of a teachable agent posing deep questions.
requirements: Students must be able to play the games and respond to the agent's multiple-choice questions during regular math classes
constraints: Question difficulty follows the agent's knowledge level; progression requires satisfactory answers
The agent looks ahead at most two steps to simulate human rather than optimal play
target_learners: students with difficulties in mathematics grades 7-8
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of the base-10 number system
arithmetic operations and their connections
causal and strategic mathematical reasoning
examples: In a Pack-Many game, adding 4 squares to 6 triggers a packing operation where 10 squares are packed into an orange square-box, mirroring carrying in the decimal system
key_sources: Pareto, L. (2014). A Teachable Agent Game Engaging Primary School Children to Learn Arithmetic Concepts and Reasoning. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0018-8

article_title: Measuring the Quality of Test-based Exercises Based on the Performance of Students
citation: Josu Arruarte, Mikel Larrañaga, Ana Arruarte & Jon A. Elorriaga. (2021). Measuring the Quality of Test-based Exercises Based on the Performance of Students. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 585–602. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00208-0
title: TEA – a Visual Learning Analytics tool for analyzing the quality of test-based exercises
description: TEA (test ariketen aztertzailea, "Test Exercises Examiner") is a teacher-oriented tool that uses Visual Learning Analytics to help instructors determine the appropriateness of test-based exercises. It analyzes performance at two granularity levels, each item and the whole test, using bar charts, circular charts and boxplots, and incorporates an alert mechanism highlighting suspicious tests or items. It can be used to supervise resource quality throughout a course or for retrospective analysis, and includes a guide describing each metric and plot for teachers who are not proficient in statistics.
requirements: For retrospective analysis, TEA requires additional information such as the final marks of the students, which could be considered their ground-truth knowledge level.
constraints: So far, TEA has only been used to evaluate manually created exercises.
Although TEA has been evaluated only on a single subject, giving satisfactory results.
target_learners: higher education students whose test performance data is analyzed
target_learning_goals: validity and quality of test-based assessment exercises measuring student knowledge
examples: Instructors of the Fundamentals of Computer Science module used TEA with Moodle-recorded answers and final grades to identify tests and items to improve or replace.
key_sources: Josu Arruarte, Mikel Larrañaga, Ana Arruarte & Jon A. Elorriaga. (2021). Measuring the Quality of Test-based Exercises Based on the Performance of Students. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 585–602. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00208-0

article_title: A Festschrift to Honour Jim Greer: Guest Editors’ Introduction
citation: Gord McCalla · Julita Vassileva. (2021). A Festschrift to Honour Jim Greer: Guest Editors’ Introduction — A Special Issue of the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2021) 31:337–356. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00273-z
title: TEA: a visual learning analytics tool for evaluating the quality of test-based exercises
description: TEA is a visual learning analytics tool introduced in the Festschrift paper by Arruarte, Larrañaga, Arruarte and Elorriaga from the University of the Basque Country. Per the introduction, "a visual learning analytics tool called TEA is introduced for evaluating the quality of test-based exercises, both at the item level and at the overall test level, to be used by teachers in determining the quality of their tests". The editors situate it among systems that inform actual teachers in real educational settings about important aspects of their interactions with students.

target_learners: Teachers evaluating their own test-based exercises
target_learning_goals: Assessing and improving the quality of test-based exercises at item and test level
examples: The tool evaluates exercise quality at the item level and at the overall test level

article_title: Instructing a Teachable Agent with Low or High Self-Efficacy – Does Similarity Attract?
citation: Betty Tärning, Annika Silvervarg, Agneta Gulz, Magnus Haake. (2019). Instructing a Teachable Agent with Low or High Self-Efficacy – Does Similarity Attract? International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0167-2
title: Design teachable agents to express low self-efficacy
description: The article proposes, as a preliminary conclusion from its experimental results, that teachable agents should preferably be designed to have low self-efficacy. Students teaching a low-SE digital tutee showed better in-game performance, and low-SE students matched with a low-SE tutee significantly increased their own self-efficacy. The principle directs designers of teachable-agent (digital tutee) software to give the tutee chat feedback expressing uncertainty and modesty about its knowledge and performance rather than confidence.
requirements: The agent must be a teachable agent/digital tutee where the student takes a teacher role, with a channel (here, chat feedback after each round) through which the tutee expresses its self-efficacy
constraints: The authors label this a preliminary conclusion on the basis of this single study with 10- to 11-year-olds in a place-value math game
the effect on high-SE students may be hidden behind a ceiling effect
target_learning_goals: place value and base-ten number system skills
math self-efficacy
examples: In the study, the tutee Lo's chat feedback was manipulated to express either high or low SE, e.g. upon losing: "We lost … But that might not be so strange, it feels like I don ’t remember anything of what you just taught me."

article_title: Empowering digital learning with open textbooks
citation: Ma, H. (2021). Empowering digital learning with open textbooks. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 393–396. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09916-9
title: Faculty adoption of high-quality open textbooks strengthens credibility and yields savings when teachers are willing to develop and use them
description: The commentary argues that open textbook use in higher education is credible and beneficial, but that its benefits are conditional on teacher engagement: "only if teachers are willing to develop and use open textbooks can millions be saved for students and higher performance be achieved by students." It therefore recommends encouraging faculty to utilize high-quality open textbooks, particularly in a post-pandemic world.
requirements: Teacher willingness to develop and use open textbooks
target_learning_goals: affordable access to learning materials
maintaining learning outcomes with open textbooks
examples: The commentary cites Hilton's synthesis of 16 studies as the evidentiary basis for encouraging faculty adoption of open textbooks.

article_title: Using mobile technologies for mathematics: effects on student attitudes and achievement
citation: Fabian, K., Topping, K. J., & Barron, I. G. (2018). Using mobile technologies for mathematics: effects on student attitudes and achievement. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-9580-3
title: Teachers, not just technology, drive successful mobile learning implementation
description: The article concludes that "it is the teacher not just the technology that drives the change in the classroom". Technical breakdowns, student characteristics and learning design are all seen as teacher responsibilities, and the authors argue it would be worthwhile addressing how teachers are trained to target those issues as well as being trained to use new technologies. The teacher in this study anticipated glitches, worked around a failed sharing facility, and adapted undifferentiated lesson plans to challenge advanced students and those who struggle.
requirements: Teacher training that covers troubleshooting technical breakdowns, managing student characteristics and learning design alongside device use
constraints: Technical breakdowns, student characteristics and learning design are all seen as teacher responsibilities
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
examples: The teacher connected tablets to a bigger display manually when Dropbox sharing failed and tweaked lesson plans to accommodate class differences

article_title: How do teachers engaging messages affect students? A sentiment analysis
citation: Samuel Falcon, Jaime Leon. (2023). How do teachers engaging messages affect students? A sentiment analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10230-3
title: Teachers' engaging messages conceptualised through Message Framing Theory and Self-Determination Theory
description: Teachers' engaging messages (TEM) are messages that push pupils to engage in school tasks, characterised by focusing on positive consequences and highlighting the benefits of engaging in a task or warning students if the task is not carried out. The article contextualises TEM with two theories: Message Framing Theory and Self-Determination Theory, the latter distinguishing extrinsic, introjected, identified and intrinsic forms of motivation the messages can appeal to. The study measures TEM with the introjected-benefits subscale of the Teachers' Engaging Messages Scale and tests whether TEM predict students' sentiment and motivation to learn.
requirements: Measured via student reports on the Teachers' Engaging Messages Scale, here the introjected messages focused on benefits subscale (McDonald's Omega 0.91)
constraints: The study analysed only the introjected-benefits subscale rather than all message types
target_learners: secondary school students (mean age 16.39) in mathematics classes
target_learning_goals: students' motivation to learn
students' sentiment about teacher communication
examples: Example TEM quoted in the article: 'If you work hard, you will feel fulfilled' and 'Unless you work hard, you will be disappointed with yourself'
key_sources: Samuel Falcon, Jaime Leon. (2023). How do teachers engaging messages affect students? A sentiment analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10230-3

article_title: Concept-guided development of technology in ‘traditional’ and ‘innovative’ schools: quantitative and qualitative differences in technology integration
citation: Sandra de Koster, Monique Volman, Els Kuiper. (2017). Concept-guided development of technology in 'traditional' and 'innovative' schools: quantitative and qualitative differences in technology integration. Education Tech Research Dev 65:1325–1344. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9527-0
title: Use a teacher-as-designer approach with voluntary participation to foster ownership and support implementation of technology-supported learning arrangements
description: The article's project had teachers at each school design, develop and realize learning arrangements of their own choosing, with limited time compensation and coaching from external educational counsellors. The authors state "The teacher-as-designer approach, with an active, voluntary role for the participating teachers, was expected to favourably affect the implementation and integration of the designed learning arrangements by installing a sense of ownership in the teachers". This principle operationalizes concept-guided development at the school-team level.

Coaching by educational counsellors who help teachers reflect on their school's educational concept
Time and support provision for design work
constraints: The researchers were not involved in the development of the learning arrangements, and the study could not attribute integration levels to this approach alone
target_learners: elementary school teachers designing technology-supported learning arrangements
target_learning_goals: successful implementation and integration of school-designed technology use

article_title: An exploratory study of a new concept macrostructure measure when learning history in middle school
citation: Chen, X., Wang, W., Peng, C., Guo, W., & Clariana, R. B. (2025). An exploratory study of a new concept macrostructure measure when learning history in middle school. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10536-4
title: Text knowledge structure at two grain sizes: microstructure and macrostructure
description: The article frames the knowledge structure (KS) of history lesson materials at two grain sizes: a microstructure of details, event sequences, and memorizable facts, and a macrostructure consisting of the structure of the text's macropropositions. Macropropositions are defined as "propositions that contain onlytop-level 'gist' information" and span across pages, so the topic structure must often be implicitly inferred while reading. The article argues many students cannot go beyond the microstructure, and that KS measures using only topic-level concepts provide a measure of macrostructure.
requirements: Elicitation tasks must use topic-level terms rather than sentence- or paragraph-level terms to capture macrostructure
constraints: Over time, text macrostructure is weighted more heavily than microstructure, so concurrent validity results may not generalize to macrostructure measured immediately after learning
target_learning_goals: organized conceptual understanding of history text content
examples: Study 1 used 43 topic-level key terms from an expert network of the Qin Dynasty lesson; Study 2 used 23 topics from the American Revolution text
key_sources: Chen, X., Wang, W., Peng, C., Guo, W., & Clariana, R. B. (2025). An exploratory study of a new concept macrostructure measure when learning history in middle school. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10536-4

article_title: Technology enhanced learner ownership and learner autonomy through creation
citation: Yu-Ju Lan. (2018). Technology enhanced learner ownership and learner autonomy through creation. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-9608-8
title: Introducing advanced technology alone cannot guarantee effective and autonomous learning; pedagogical theories, evaluation methods, and learning analytics must accompany it
description: The editorial argues that despite the potential of advanced technologies in learning, "simply by introducing advanced technologies to educational settings cannot guarantee effective and autonomous learning." It therefore recommends that "the corresponding pedagogical theories and approaches, as well as appropriate evaluation methods and learning analytical technique, should be involved" alongside any technology adoption aimed at fostering autonomy and ownership.
requirements: Appropriate pedagogical theories and approaches accompanying the technology
Appropriate evaluation methods and learning analytical techniques
target_learners: learners in technology-rich educational settings, from elementary students to college students
target_learning_goals: effective and autonomous learning supported by technology-enhanced environments
examples: The editorial cites the special issue's nine studies, which paired technologies such as 3D virtual worlds, mobile multimedia systems, and comic-drama creation systems with specific pedagogical approaches

citation: Buss, R. R., Lindsey, L., Foulger, T. S., Wetzel, K., & Pasquel, S. (2017). Assessing a technology infusion approach in a teacher preparation program. title: Technology infusion into methods courses as an alternative to a stand-alone technology course
description: When a stand-alone educational technology course was eliminated, the program replaced it by purposely infusing "technology-integration assignments, objectives, and lessons into methods courses," aligned to the ISTE-T standards. By fall 2015, 16 methods courses across five programs had been infused. The approach places responsibility for teaching technology integration on content-methods instructors rather than educational-technology experts, supported by specialist PD.

Standard syllabi with technology-infused objectives and assignments
