article_title: Multisite usability and safety trial of an immersive virtual reality implementation of a work organization system for autistic learners: implications for technology design
citation: Herrera, G., Vera, L., Pérez-Fuster, P., López-Fernández, A., López, Á., Savaş-Taşkesen, Ü., & Newbutt, N. (2024). Multisite usability and safety trial of an immersive virtual reality implementation of a work organization system for autistic learners: implications for technology design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10422-5
title: TEACCH Structured Teaching and the individual work system as a visually organized framework for independent practice
description: The TEACCH approach (Structured Teaching) organizes time, space and sequences of events to support autistic individuals in understanding and executing learning activities; it is a framework, not a curriculum. Its individual work system (IWS) is "a visually organized space where children practice acquired skills", a low-tech instructional technology using furniture, printed images and Velcro or magnets. A work system visually communicates four pieces of information: the tasks to do, how much work there is, how the student knows they are finished, and what to do when finished. The article implements this framework in immersive VR to promote independent learning.
requirements: Customization to each student's skills and needs, since one size does not fit all for autistic students
constraints: Effectiveness of comprehensive TEACCH programs is difficult to demonstrate because they comprise multiple components deployed in natural settings
target_learners: Autistic individuals, including those with intellectual disability
target_learning_goals: Independent learning, skill practice, generalization of skills across settings, and access to the curriculum
examples: The VR-IWS implements the four information elements virtually, with trays on an input shelf, completion at a work table, and storage on an output shelf

The lens frames the analysis of what universities in Zimbabwe required when online teaching became suddenly necessary during COVID-19, organising needs around readiness for technology-mediated teaching.

article_title: Introduction
citation: A Bibliography of Teaching Machines. (1960). Audiovisual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Bibliography+of+Teaching+Machines
title: Teaching machines defined by three functional criteria: visual presentation of units, a means of responding, and feedback on correctness
description: This theory contribution captures the bibliography's working definition of the teaching machine, the field's central artifact. The article states: "we have defined teaching machines as devices which" present information visually, provide a means of responding, and inform the student of correctness. Most machines also require correcting wrong responses before proceeding and organize subject matter step by step as a program.
requirements: A device must satisfy all three criteria: visual presentation of information units, a means of student response, and correctness feedback
constraints: The authors chose "to err in the direction of leniency," so some included training devices might not be classified as teaching machines by other specialists
target_learners: students using teaching machines across elementary, high school, college, and adult levels
target_learning_goals: subject-matter instruction delivered through automated, programmed presentation

article_title: Introduction
citation: A Bibliography of Teaching Machines. (1960). Audiovisual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Bibliography+of+Teaching+Machines
title: Catalogs of teaching-machine programs: Table 1 (older experimental programs) and Table 2 (programs in development, early 1960)

constraints: The authors state the tables are undoubtedly incomplete because programming effort is growing daily

target_learning_goals: subject-matter instruction across domains such as arithmetic, algebra, spelling, grammar, electronics, and foreign languages
examples: Table 1 lists programs by Pressey (1950), Gilbert (1955), Crowder (1958), Skinner (1958) and others with their institutions, subjects and levels

article_title: Introduction
citation: A Bibliography of Teaching Machines. (1960). Audiovisual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Bibliography+of+Teaching+Machines
title: Terminological distinction: a teaching-machine "program" is curriculum material, not computer instructions
description: The authors define the field's key term to prevent confusion: "When used by a teaching machine writer, a program refers to the curriculum material or subject matter that is placed in the machine." Such material "is usually carefully worked out and is composed of items on which the student can be successful a high percentage of the time." They note confusion arises because authors in electronic computing use "program" for instructions given to a computer. The note is signed with the initials J.W.R. in the text.
requirements: Readers new to the field need this distinction to interpret teaching-machine literature correctly, per the authors' stated purpose of the explanation
target_learners: new readers and researchers in the teaching-machine field

article_title: Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students’ perceived employability
citation: María-Jesús Martínez-Argüelles, Dolors Plana-Erta, Àngels Fitó-Bertran. (2023). Impact of using authentic online learning environments on students' perceived employability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10171-3
title: Use technology as a means of providing authenticity, not an end in itself
description: The article argues that communication, visualization, and simulation technologies can give online students opportunities to experience and solve real-world problems, but that tools alone do not create authenticity. As the authors put it, "Technological tools are a means of providing authenticity, not an end in themselves. The effectiveness of authentic learning scenarios depends on how the learning process is designed." The course redesign illustrates this: videos and the virtual classroom served a holistic, integrated design for cognitive authenticity rather than substituting for it.

constraints: Technologies are not sufficient to ensure the quality of authenticity on their own
target_learning_goals: cognitive authenticity connecting learning to real-world work practice
examples: The redesign used six embedded videos and the SABI database as supports within an integrated role-play scenario, not as standalone innovations.

article_title: What seams do we remove in mobile-assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature
citation: Lung-Hsiang Wong, Chee Kit Looi. (2011). What seams do we remove in mobile assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00696239
title: Ten-dimension framework characterizing mobile-assisted seamless learning

identifying research gaps in mobile-assisted seamless learning

article_title: Body in motion, attention in focus: A virtual reality study on teachers' movement patterns and noticing
citation: Yizhen Huang, Eric Richter, Thilo Kleickmann, Katharina Scheiter, Dirk Richter. (2023). Body in motion, attention in focus: A virtual reality study on teachers' movement patterns and noticing. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104912
title: Three-pattern taxonomy of preservice teacher movement in classrooms
description: The article proposes a three-category taxonomy of preservice teachers' classroom body movement patterns derived from K-means clustering of spatial point-pattern statistics. Immobile teachers "restricted their movement to the area behind the teacher's desk"; anchored teachers visited different locations but stayed mostly at the front; dynamic teachers dispersed their presence more evenly throughout the classroom, moving frequently to distant locations and spending less time in any one place. The taxonomy emerged from unsupervised clustering rather than being predefined.
requirements: Requires concurrent tracking of body and eye movements during teaching, which the article achieves with IVR technology
constraints: Identified within a standardized IVR classroom with a short teaching task and a small sample of preservice teachers
target_learning_goals: Teacher noticing of classroom events
Classroom management

article_title: Understanding validity criteria in technology-enhanced learning: A systematic literature review
citation: Haastrecht, M. A. N. van, Haas, M., Brinkhuis, M. J. S., & Spruit, M. R. (2024). Understanding validity criteria in technology-enhanced learning: a systematic literature review. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105128
title: Taxonomy of 27 validity criteria for technology-enhanced learning with synonyms
description: The review assembles a taxonomy of validity criteria considered in TEL research, including effectiveness, statistical validity, external validity, rigour, authenticity, fairness, trustworthiness, usability and usefulness, each paired with synonyms observed in the literature (e.g., generalisability for external validity). Rather than prescribing definitions, the authors "take author's claims of assessing particular criteria at face value" and pair each criterion with a quote from the relevant study to document implicit definitions. The taxonomy structures the review's data extraction and analysis.
requirements: studies must report at least one clearly defined validity criterion for inclusion
constraints: criteria reported under different terminology are mapped to the taxonomy where possible, rather than defined prescriptively
target_learners: learners and educators in TEL intervention studies
target_learning_goals: validity and evaluation of technology-enhanced learning interventions

increase perceived person-vocation fit

article_title: What is “technology integration” and how is it measured in K-12 education? A systematic review of survey instruments from 2010 to 2021
citation: Tessa Consoli, Juliette D´esiron, Alberto Cattaneo. (2023). What is “technology integration” and how is it measured in K-12 education? A systematic review of survey instruments from 2010 to 2021. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104742
title: Technology integration (TI) as a construct lacking a shared definition, encompassing views ranging from mere technology use to transformation of teaching and learning practices.
description: The article synthesizes existing definitions of technology integration, noting that some researchers use the term as a synonym for technology use while others refer to "a far more complex phenomenon, such as the transformation or enhancement of teaching and learning practices through the use of technology." The review adopts a definition emphasizing pedagogical quality over mere frequency of use, framing TI as the instructional use of digital technologies to support pedagogical goals. This construct serves as the organizing framework for the systematic review of survey instruments.
requirements: A shared understanding of TI as involving pedagogical quality rather than mere frequency of technology use
constraints: The term TI is used inconsistently across the field, with no single accepted definition
target_learning_goals: Integration of technology into teaching and learning practices

article_title: Teachers' emphasis on developing students' digital information and communication skills (TEDDICS): A new construct in 21st century education
citation: Siddiq F., Scherer R. & Tondeur J. (2015). Teachers’ Emphasis on Developing Students’ Digital Information and Communication Skills (TEDDICS): A New Construct in 21st Century Education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.10.006
title: TEDDICS scale — a multidimensional self-report instrument for teachers' emphasis on students' digital skills
description: The TEDDICS scale measures the degree to which teachers emphasize developing students' skills of accessing, evaluating, and sharing and communicating digital information, rated from "0 = no emphasis" to "3 = strong emphasis". It comprises 12 items across three subscales (3, 4, and 5 items) and showed very good reliability (ω = .92) with no ceiling or floor effects. The article proposes it as a qualitative component of ICT use in future research on technology acceptance and integration.
requirements: Teachers rate the degree to which they emphasize developing students' digital skills in their lessons on a 0–3 scale
constraints: Based on teacher self-reports, which may differ from actual classroom practice
target_learning_goals: developing students' digital information and communication skills
examples: Administered within the ICILS 2013 teacher questionnaire in Norwegian secondary schools
key_sources: Siddiq F., Scherer R. & Tondeur J. (2015). Teachers’ Emphasis on Developing Students’ Digital Information and Communication Skills (TEDDICS): A New Construct in 21st Century Education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.10.006

article_title: Teachers' emphasis on developing students' digital information and communication skills (TEDDICS): A new construct in 21st century education
citation: Siddiq F., Scherer R. & Tondeur J. (2015). Teachers’ Emphasis on Developing Students’ Digital Information and Communication Skills (TEDDICS): A New Construct in 21st Century Education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.10.006
title: TEDDICS construct — teachers' emphasis on developing students' digital information and communication skills as a qualitative facet of ICT use
description: TEDDICS is a goal-oriented construct describing "a qualitative rather than a quantitative facet of ICT use", combining curricular demands, teaching practice, and teachers' beliefs about which digital skills matter. It is conceptualized around three interwoven but distinct factors — accessing, evaluating, and sharing and communicating digital information — mirroring frameworks of students' digital competence. The construct differs from frequency-of-use reports and from beliefs such as self-efficacy and perceived usefulness, providing a link between classroom practice and students' digital skills.
requirements: Validation evidence via ESEM measurement modeling and invariance testing across groups
constraints: Self-report measure; no direct link to students' actual digital skills in ICILS 2013
target_learning_goals: fostering students' digital information and communication skills
key_sources: Siddiq F., Scherer R. & Tondeur J. (2015). Teachers’ Emphasis on Developing Students’ Digital Information and Communication Skills (TEDDICS): A New Construct in 21st Century Education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.10.006

article_title: A framework for teachers’ integration of ICT into their classroom practice
citation: Donnelly, D., McGarr, O. and O'Reilly, J. (2011). A Framework for Teachers' Integration of ICT Into Their Classroom Practice. Computers and Education;57(2), 1469-1483. https://hdl.handle.net/10344/2340
title: Teacher ICT Integration Model: four teacher types positioned on two intersecting conflict continuums
description: The article proposes a Teacher ICT Integration Model (Figure 2) that identifies four types of teachers in relation to ICT integration: a Contented Traditionalist, a Selective Adopter, an Inadvertent User and a Creative Adapter. These four types are positioned in terms of two main teacher conflict areas emerging from the research: empowerment versus fatalism and a learning focus versus an assessment focus. The two conflict areas are represented as two continuums intersecting, with assessment-focused teachers aligned with teacher-centred approaches and learning-focused teachers aligned with student-centred approaches. The model acknowledges different teacher stances on technology integration while highlighting significant boundaries between these stances.
requirements: The model is based on findings from initial interviews with teachers and stakeholders and a follow-on case study of five practising chemistry teachers using the VCL, combined with relevant literature.
constraints: The model is built on a small qualitative sample; the article notes it is difficult from this research to say exactly which teachers would fall into the Contented Traditionalist group.
target_learning_goals: effective integration of ICT resources such as virtual laboratories into classroom practice
examples: The model was developed from observations of five teachers using the Virtual Chemistry Laboratory and follow-up interviews, coded against Ertmer's first- and second-order barriers.
key_sources: Donnelly, D., McGarr, O. and O'Reilly, J. (2011). A Framework for Teachers' Integration of ICT Into Their Classroom Practice. Computers and Education;57(2), 1469-1483. https://hdl.handle.net/10344/2340

article_title: The impact of primary school teachers’ educational beliefs on the classroom use of computers
citation: Hermans, R., Tondeur, J., van Braak, J., & Valcke, M. (2008). The impact of primary school teachers’ educational beliefs on the classroom use of computers. Computers & Education, 51(4), 1499–1509. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.02.001
title: Teacher educational beliefs as antecedents of ICT adoption
description: The article frames teachers' educational beliefs — constructivist versus traditional orientations toward teaching and learning — as determinants of whether teachers adopt computers in the classroom, extending a literature that focused on technology-related variables. It argues "teachers’ classroom use of computers cannot be fully understood without taking their underlying educational beliefs into consideration". Beliefs are defined as "the individual conceptions about desirable ways of teaching and conceptions about how students come to learn", grounded in personal belief systems and relatively stable and resistant to change.
requirements: Measuring beliefs with validated scales (here the Constructivist and Traditional Beliefs scales of Woolley, Benjamin, and Woolley) alongside technology-related and demographic controls
constraints: Evidence concerns Flemish primary teachers; the article notes the interplay between school-level and teacher-level variables is not yet clear and calls for further research
target_learning_goals: classroom integration of computers to support teaching and learning
key_sources: Hermans, R., Tondeur, J., van Braak, J., & Valcke, M. (2008). The impact of primary school teachers’ educational beliefs on the classroom use of computers. Computers & Education, 51(4), 1499–1509. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.02.001

article_title: Variability of teachers’ technology integration in the classroom: A matter of utility!
citation: Backfisch, I., Lachner, A., Stürmer, K., & Scheiter, K. (2021). Variability of teachers’ technology integration in the classroom: A matter of utility!. Computers & Education, 166, 104159. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104159
title: Technology integration quality conceptualized on two dimensions: technology exploitation and teaching quality (task-specific and task-general)
description: The article conceptualizes the quality of technology integration on two dimensions: technology exploitation (teachers' capability to implement the distinct potential of educational technologies, drawing on hierarchical frameworks like SAMR and RAT) and teaching quality (comprising task-specific strategies of cognitive activation and individual learning support, and task-general strategies of classroom management). The authors operationalize these dimensions for coding lesson documentations, with subcategories scored 0-3 yielding a maximum of 12 points per dimension. This framework extends prior models that "only focus on the types of technology use and ignore the potential impact on learning processes".
requirements: Trained raters coding lesson documentations using the four subcategories per dimension
constraints: Relies on teachers' self-reported lesson documentations rather than direct observations
target_learning_goals: technology integration quality
teaching quality
key_sources: Backfisch, I., Lachner, A., Stürmer, K., & Scheiter, K. (2021). Variability of teachers’ technology integration in the classroom: A matter of utility!. Computers & Education, 166, 104159. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104159

article_title: A Systematic Review of Technology-Enhanced Project-Based Language Learning: Theoretical Frameworks, Project Types, and Implications for Future Research and Practice.
citation: Fikria Ainun; Setiawan Slamet; Munir Ahmad (2025). A Systematic Review of Technology-Enhanced Project-Based Language Learning: Theoretical Frameworks, Project Types, and Implications for Future Research and Practice. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.165491.1
title: TEPBLL is grounded in five conceptual frameworks: social constructivism, sociocultural theory, incidental vocabulary learning, communicative language learning, and self-determination theory
description: This systematic review of 31 SSCI articles on technology-enhanced project-based language learning (TEPBLL) identifies the theoretical foundations of the field. The authors report that "the study involved five major categories of theoretical frameworks or concepts, as outlined in Table 3, encompassing social constructivism, sociocultural theory, incidental vocabulary learning, communicative language learning, and self-determination theory." Social constructivism was the most cited framework, with learners acting as "developers of knowledge" through interaction, while sociocultural theory foregrounds social and cultural activities and scaffolding. The review uses these categories to organize the TEPBLL literature and to suggest that future work could combine frameworks for novelty.
requirements: Articles must report the theoretical or conceptual framework underpinning the TEPBLL intervention for this taxonomy to apply
constraints: Derived from 31 SSCI-indexed empirical articles published 2015-2024; non-SSCI and non-empirical work excluded
target_learning_goals: language skills and knowledge through project-based learning with technology
examples: Coding of frameworks was done bottom-up: researchers read articles one at a time, noted frameworks, combined similar concepts, and prepared a list of main frameworks
key_sources: Fikria Ainun; Setiawan Slamet; Munir Ahmad (2025). A Systematic Review of Technology-Enhanced Project-Based Language Learning: Theoretical Frameworks, Project Types, and Implications for Future Research and Practice. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.165491.1

article_title: A Systematic Review of Technology-Enhanced Project-Based Language Learning: Theoretical Frameworks, Project Types, and Implications for Future Research and Practice.
citation: Fikria Ainun; Setiawan Slamet; Munir Ahmad (2025). A Systematic Review of Technology-Enhanced Project-Based Language Learning: Theoretical Frameworks, Project Types, and Implications for Future Research and Practice. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.165491.1
title: Seven project types characterize TEPBLL: telecollaborative, digital storytelling, virtual reality, video making, mobile instant messaging-based, video conferencing, and audio-visual translation projects
description: The review classifies the technology-supported project types used in TEPBLL research. The authors state that "The 31 coded articles had identified seven big umbrellas of project-based language learning type, details exposed in Table 4." Each type is illustrated with named systems: telecollaborative projects use tools such as Canvas, Wikipedia, and WeChat; digital storytelling uses SlideShare and iMovie; virtual reality projects use SVVR, iVR, and Google Tour Creator; video making uses Movie Maker and YouTube; mobile instant messaging projects use WhatsApp and WeChat; video conferencing uses Skype; and audio-visual translation uses SubESPSKills and Moodle.
requirements: Projects must integrate technology into project-based language learning with a clear description of the technology used
constraints: Typology reflects only the 31 included SSCI empirical studies from 2015-2024
target_learners: second and foreign language learners in higher education and other contexts
target_learning_goals: speaking, listening, reading, writing, vocabulary, intercultural awareness, content knowledge, creative and critical thinking
examples: Telecollaborative projects were the most common, with eight papers applying that type
key_sources: Fikria Ainun; Setiawan Slamet; Munir Ahmad (2025). A Systematic Review of Technology-Enhanced Project-Based Language Learning: Theoretical Frameworks, Project Types, and Implications for Future Research and Practice. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.165491.1

article_title: Asynchronous e-learning with technology-enabled and enhanced training for continuing education of nurses: a scoping review.
citation: Kimura Rika, Matsunaga Mayumi, Barroga Edward, Hayashi Naoko. (2023). Asynchronous e-learning with technology-enabled and enhanced training for continuing education of nurses: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04477-w
title: TEET framework: classifying e-learning technologies into enabling and enhancing technological approaches
description: The technology-enabled and enhanced training (TEET) framework, adopted from Ngenzi et al. (2021), classifies the technological approaches of e-learning into two subcategories: enabling technologies (e.g., interactive online modules, videos, slides, online discussion forums, mobile devices, LMS) and enhancing technologies (e.g., computer simulation or virtual reality, resource access, scenario-based learning, gamification). The review states "The term technology-enabled and enhanced training (TEET) reflects the various contributions of technology to education" and uses it to map 60 studies of asynchronous e-learning for clinical nurses, alongside three delivery modes (face-to-face, blended, pure online).
requirements: Studies must describe whether the e-learning method is synchronous or asynchronous and which TEET option is used, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: TEET continues to evolve as it is closely aligned with technological advancements, per the article
target_learning_goals: continuing professional development knowledge and skills acquisition
examples: The review charted all 60 articles' modes of delivery and technological approaches using this classification in Tables 3 and 4

article_title: Learning about stress from building, drilling and flying: a scoping review on team performance and stress in non-medical fields.
citation: Dijkstra Femke S., Renden Peter G., Meeter Martijn, Schoonmade Linda J., Krage Ralf, van Schuppen Hans, de la Croix Anne. (2021). Learning about stress from building, drilling and flying: a scoping review on team performance and stress in non-medical fields. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-021-00865-7
title: The 'team brain': an umbrella concept uniting shared mental model, transactive memory and situational awareness as team cognition supporting performance under stress
description: The review introduces the 'team brain' as an umbrella term under which three overlapping cognitive themes come together: shared mental model, transactive memory and situational awareness. All three "revolve around the development of a common view of the situation, for which communication is important". The authors propose that developing a team brain could increase team performance in stressful situations and improve patient outcomes, and that simulation training might help develop these cognitive structures.
requirements: A clear, consistently used definition of the component concepts (shared mental model, situational awareness, transactive memory), which the review says is still lacking
constraints: The review states an integration of the three cognitive themes and team performance in stressful situations has not yet been specified; further research is needed before integrating the concept in training and education
target_learners: healthcare professionals in emergency and critical care teams
target_learning_goals: team performance in stressful situations
team communication
shared situational understanding
examples: The review cites medical simulation studies in which surgery residents developed shared mental models after a stressful scenario and emergency department professionals showed increased transactive memory after trauma simulation.

article_title: Evidence-based practice educational intervention studies: a systematic review of what is taught and how it is measured.
citation: Albarqouni Loai, Hoffmann Tammy, Glasziou Paul. (2018). Evidence-based practice educational intervention studies: a systematic review of what is taught and how it is measured. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1284-1
title: EBP curricula should cover all five EBP steps, with greater emphasis on applying evidence with patients
description: Because most evaluated interventions teach only some EBP steps and neglect apply and reflect, the review argues "greater emphasis should be placed on teaching learners how to apply and the evidence in collaboration with individual patients such as through shared decision making". It notes the international consensus statement of 68 core EBP competencies may help harmonise intervention content. Educational packages addressing all EBP steps are needed to improve EBP teaching.
requirements: Educational packages and instruments which address all EBP steps are needed
constraints: The review notes that if interventions remain mostly focused on locating and appraising evidence, research evidence may be poorly translated into clinical practice
target_learners: Health professionals, including undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing education learners
target_learning_goals: Applying research evidence in collaboration with patients, including shared decision making
examples: The review found only 10 of 85 controlled studies taught all five EBP steps, motivating the recommendation

article_title: Online technology use in physiotherapy teaching and learning: a systematic review of effectiveness and users' perceptions.
citation: Mącznik Aleksandra K., Ribeiro Daniel Cury, Baxter G. David. (2015). Online technology use in physiotherapy teaching and learning: a systematic review of effectiveness and users’ perceptions. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4587774/
title: Technology effectiveness varies by type: websites for practical skills, discussion boards for knowledge and reflective thinking
description: The review organizes its findings around a mapping between technology type and learning outcome. Websites containing web-based tutorials, videos and patient-therapist simulations support practical skills performance, while discussion boards support knowledge acquisition, critical thinking and reflective thinking. As the review states, "The effectiveness of interventions varied according to the technology used." This framework suggests educators should match technology choice to intended learning outcome rather than treating online technology as a uniform category.
requirements: Educators must identify the intended learning outcome before selecting a technology type
constraints: Based on heterogeneous study designs and outcome measures that precluded meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: practical skills performance
knowledge acquisition
critical and reflective thinking
examples: Websites with web-based tutorials and video repositories improved practical skills; discussion forums improved knowledge acquisition measured by final marks

article_title: Impact of Consciousness-Raising Activities on Young English Language Learners' Grammar Performance
citation: Hamidreza Fatemipour & Shiva Hemmati. (2015). Impact of Consciousness-Raising Activities on Young English Language Learners’ Grammar Performance. English Language Teaching, 8(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n9p1
title: In consciousness-raising activities the teacher confirms and summarises learner hypotheses rather than acting as the source of knowledge
description: The article recommends that during CR activities the teacher highlight correct learner assumptions, for example by writing them on the board, rather than delivering extended grammar explanations. It states that "the teacher is not necessarily the source of knowledge; he is the confirmer and summarizer of the knowledge posed by the students." The conclusion repeats that the teacher no longer needs to spend much time on grammar explanations.
requirements: Learners first form and present their own hypotheses about the grammar point
Correct assumptions are highlighted rather than wrong ones extensively corrected
constraints: The article warns that a ten-minute teacher grammar explanation at this stage defeats the purpose of consciousness-raising
target_learners: young EFL learners working in pairs or groups
target_learning_goals: grammar hypothesis formation and awareness of target structures
examples: In the study's confirmation step, the teacher confirmed learners' assumptions and highlighted correct ones on the board instead of correcting wrong assumptions at length

article_title: E-Classroom of the 21st Century: Information Gaps
citation: Oso Senny Oluwatumbi. (2015). E-Classroom of the 21st Century: Information Gaps. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.18. http://www.iiste.org
title: Teachers should employ a variety of technology-based techniques in their teaching repertoire to enhance academic achievement
description: Based on the finding that students exposed to the ICT package performed better than the control group, the article recommends that "teachers should employ varieties of techniques using technology resources in their teaching repertoire to enhance students academic achievement." It further recommends that e-classrooms be adopted in schools and that governments make technology resources available. The recommendation rests on a single quasi-experimental comparison.
requirements: Availability of technology resources such as computers, projectors, internet facilities and PowerPoint in schools
constraints: The supporting evidence is one quasi-experimental study of 80 purposively sampled students in Ekiti State
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
examples: The experimental group was taught with computers, projectors, internet facilities, PowerPoint presentations and online downloads for eight weeks

article_title: EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Development through MALL: Telegram Groups in Focus
citation: Naderi, S., & Akrami, A. (2018). EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Development through MALL: Telegram Groups in Focus. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 339-350. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11223a
title: Weekly supervised Telegram-group reading lesson sequence
description: A recurring lesson routine for teaching a reading passage through a messaging group: within a fixed two-and-a-half-hour online time span, the teacher first posts key vocabulary with synonyms, poses pre-reading questions for group discussion, gives time for silent reading and idea sharing, sends an audio file of the text, and closes with comprehension questions answered collaboratively under teacher supervision. The article used this sequence weekly for six passages with intermediate university EFL students.
requirements: All students must be online during the designated weekly time span
Students share questions, ideas and problems only in the group, not privately
A teacher supervises discussion and answers questions at the next session
constraints: Chat outside the designated time span receives no teacher feedback
The article applied the pattern only to intermediate-level university students
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
reading strategy use
examples: Once a week a two-and-a-half-hour span was set for each experimental group; the teacher "wrote some important and key vocabularies of the passage with their synonyms" before pre-reading questions and group discussion, then sent the audio file of the text.

article_title: Textbooks Thematic Based Character Education on Thematic Learning Primary School: An Influence
citation: Wuryani, M. T., Roemintoyo, & Yamtinah, S. (2018). Textbooks thematic based character education on thematic learning primary school: An influence. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 4(2), 75-81. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.4.2.75
title: Textbook thematic based character education for fourth-grade thematic learning
description: A teaching textbook developed for fourth-grade thematic learning that embeds character-education values in each theme and illustrates daily-life events, so that "there will be reciprocal between learning thematic with character education." It is intended as a supplement or supporting book that learners can use to study independently without teacher assistance, alongside existing teacher and student books. The article evaluated it against a conventional textbook in a quasi-experiment in two Surakarta state primary schools.
requirements: Themes must relate character-education elements to daily-life illustrations so learning is meaningful in contextual terms
constraints: The article notes some typing errors and lack of thematic learning as improvements to consider in the draft
target_learning_goals: thematic learning outcomes
character education (discipline, honesty, responsibility)
examples: Used as X1 in the experimental group of a matching-only pretest-posttest control group design in State Primary School Mangkubumen Kulon 83 Surakarta, with a 20-item test of reliability 0.856

article_title: Explanatory Modeling in Science through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach
citation: Susan R. Goldman, Cynthia Greenleaf, Mariya Yukhymenko-Lescroart, Willard Brown, Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Julia M. Emig, MariAnne George, Patricia Wallace, Dylan Blaum, & M. Anne Britt. (2019). Explanatory Modeling in Science Through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831219831041
title: Prepare teachers for deep instructional change by immersing them as learners in the intervention they will implement
description: Because the Project READI approach requires significant shifts in practice that scripted materials cannot deliver, the professional development pursued two focal goals: raising teachers' awareness of their own sense-making practices with challenging science materials, and immersing "the teachers-as-learners in the intervention they would subsequently implement with their students, a process similar to the educative curriculum approach." Immersion engaged teachers in constructing explanatory models of the course phenomena, providing a basis for discussing and reflecting on how to introduce and sustain the instructional routines and participation structures.

constraints: RCT design requirements (no prior intervention history, clearly defined intervention) made the inquiry-network PD model unfeasible for the efficacy study

target_learning_goals: understanding the deep structure of the instructional approach
enacting instructional routines and participation structures
examples: Intervention teachers began PD 9 months before the student intervention; control teachers received PD after all data collection concluded

article_title: The Effect of Instructional Methods (Lecture-Discussion versus Group Discussion) and Teaching Talent on Teacher Trainees Student Learning Outcomes
citation: Mutrofin, Degeng, I.N.S., Ardhana, I.W., & Setyosari, P. (2017). The Effect of Instructional Methods (Lecture-Discussion versus Group Discussion) and Teaching Talent on Teacher Trainees Student Learning Outcomes. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(9). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1143985
title: Teaching talent questionnaire based on Buckingham and Clifton (2001)
description: The teaching talent questionnaire is the instrument used to measure prospective teachers' teaching talent, defined as "the form of thoug hts, feelings, and naturally repetitive behaviors t hat can be applied as productive things". A total score of measurement results reflects strong or weak teaching talent, with indicators: (1) preferences to the teaching profession; (2) educational communication ability; (3) empathy for the child; and (4) learner human (adopted from The Gallup Organization). The questionnaire was designed based on Buckingham and Clifton (2001)'s model and used to split the 168 trainees into strong and weak talent groups.
requirements: Designed based on Buckingham and Clifton (2001)'s model
constraints: Measures prospective teachers' talent before they choose the teaching profession, tracked through answers to why he/she wanted to teach
target_learning_goals: identifying strong or weak teaching talent as a learner characteristic
examples: Used to collect data on teaching talents in the quasi-experiment, classifying 168 trainees into strong and weak talent dimensions

article_title: The Effect of Using Team Teaching on Jordanian EFL Eleventh Grade Students' Reading Comprehension and Their Attitudes towards This Strategy
citation: Ali Ibrahim Mohammad Migdadi; Abdallah Baniabdelrahman (2016). The Effect of Using Team Teaching on Jordanian EFL Eleventh Grade Students' Reading Comprehension and Their Attitudes Towards This Strategy. Journal of Education and e-Learning Research, 3(2): 38-50. https://doi.org/10.20448/journal.509/2016.3.2/509.2.38.50
title: Team teaching as two teachers collaboratively planning, instructing and assessing one class
description: The article treats team teaching as a strategy of instruction in which two qualified teachers share one classroom: "Both teachers planned for the lesson together and in advance divide their work. They share responsibilities and create an appropriate team teaching environment." The team teachers "deal with the same topic from different view", blend their experience, and cooperate in introducing content and developing structural goals. The article cites Bouck (2007) and Bauwens and Hourcade (1995) defining team teaching as two or more educators with distinct skills jointly teaching heterogeneous groups in an integrated setting.
requirements: Two qualified teachers who plan together in advance and divide their work
Support from school administration and compatibility between partners, as the literature review states
constraints: The article's evidence comes from one secondary school with eleventh-grade male EFL students in Jordan
target_learners: EFL eleventh-grade secondary students in heterogeneous, overcrowded classrooms
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension
examples: In the study, the team-teaching group was taught by two teachers who planned jointly, shared responsibilities, and presented the same reading topic from different viewpoints, while the control group had one teacher performing all lesson duties
key_sources: Ali Ibrahim Mohammad Migdadi; Abdallah Baniabdelrahman (2016). The Effect of Using Team Teaching on Jordanian EFL Eleventh Grade Students' Reading Comprehension and Their Attitudes Towards This Strategy. Journal of Education and e-Learning Research, 3(2): 38-50. https://doi.org/10.20448/journal.509/2016.3.2/509.2.38.50

article_title: TextNow Transition Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Maxwell, B., Connolly, P., Demack, S., O'Hare, L., Stevens, A., & Clague, L. (2014). TextNow Transition Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: TextNow Transition Programme: one-to-one volunteer reading coaching with the MyChoice! online book-choice resource
description: The TextNow Transition Programme, developed by the charity Unitas, is a reading-for-pleasure literacy programme in which pupils receive "20-minute one to one sessions with a volunteer coach each weekday for five weeks at the end of primary school and for a further 10 weeks at the start of secondary school". Pupils also access MyChoice!, an online resource with news, quizzes, competitions and a book store, and earn credits (worth 25p per attended day) to buy books and build a personal library. A school coordinator recruits and supports coaches, monitors progress and maintains quality assurance. The direct cost is estimated at £112 per pupil, excluding coordinators and volunteer coach time.
requirements: Each school must appoint a coordinator to recruit and manage volunteer coaches, manage delivery, and undertake quality assurance and reporting
Coaches are expected to undertake four online training modules prior to working with their young person
Volunteer coach time of 20 minutes per pupil per day for 75 days, plus training, preparation and record-keeping
constraints: The process evaluation found significant fidelity issues: some pupils did not receive the full dosage, some peer coaching was reported as poor quality, and some pupils had no or limited access to MyChoice!
Fidelity was most problematic where schools lacked commitment to the programme; some primary schools perceived no benefit because the intervention ran after SATs
target_learners: Year 6 pupils unlikely to achieve Level 4a in reading by the end of Key Stage 2, transitioning to secondary school
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Enjoyment of reading and motivation to read for pleasure
examples: In the trial, 501 pupils in 96 schools across England were randomised at the individual pupil level, blocked within schools; control pupils received business as usual and were given MyChoice! credits after the post-test
key_sources: Maxwell, B., Connolly, P., Demack, S., O'Hare, L., Stevens, A., & Clague, L. (2014). TextNow Transition Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581131

article_title: Effect of the Problem-Solving Approach on Academic Achievement of Students in Mathematics at the Secondary Level
citation: Kousar Perveen. (2010). Effect Of The Problem-Solving Approach On Academic Achievement Of Students In Mathematics At The Secondary Level. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, 3(3).
title: Develop a program of teaching mathematics through problem-solving at the secondary level
description: The article argues that because "the art of problem-solving is the heart and essence of mathematics", problem-solving "can serve as a vehicle for learning new mathematical ideas and skills", and that it is therefore necessary to develop a program of teaching mathematics by problem-solving. It supports this with its experiment showing significantly better post-test achievement for the problem-solving group.
requirements: Teachers need training in the problem-solving approach; the article recommends at least one month's duration
constraints: Students with weak foundational concepts may need preliminary clarification of basic concepts, postulates, formulas and geometry knowledge before heuristic instruction
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
problem-solving ability
examples: The six-week experiment in which the experimental group's problem-solving lessons produced significantly higher post-test scores than expository teaching
key_sources: Kousar Perveen. (2010). Effect Of The Problem-Solving Approach On Academic Achievement Of Students In Mathematics At The Secondary Level. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, 3(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1072552

article_title: Language Learners' Feelings about Pragmatics in Action
citation: Üstünbaş, Ü. (2017). Language Learners' Feelings about Pragmatics in Action. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 11(2), 155-168. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/novitasroyal
title: Teach pragmatic routines explicitly in EFL programs where learners lack exposure to real target-language use
description: Because EFL learners have few chances to interact with native speakers, the article suggests pragmatic routines be taught as part of language programs so learners at least notice target language they are deprived of in daily life. The study's own data support this: explicit teaching produced significant post-test gains over control and over implicit teaching, while learners themselves ranked pragmatic routines as their top speaking sub-skill need.
requirements: Target routines selected to match learners' proficiency level, here CEFR A2 descriptors
Instructional materials and lesson plans designed around the target routines
constraints: The study was carried out with only A2-level learners in a particular setting, which the authors say makes it difficult to generalize the findings
The number of participants decreased because they did not show up in all sessions
target_learners: tertiary-level EFL learners at A2 level in an English-medium university preparatory program
target_learning_goals: pragmatic competence
use of pragmatic routines in daily conversation
examples: Treatment groups were taught routines for five weeks on functions such as reacting to news, taking time to think, vague expressions, showing agreement, and dealing with interruptions, with the explicit group also presented meanings and real-life contexts
key_sources: Üstünbaş, Ü. (2017). Language Learners' Feelings about Pragmatics in Action. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 11(2), 155-168. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/novitasroyal

article_title: Examining the Effect of Teacher Guidance on Collaborative Argumentation in Middle Level Classrooms
citation: Hsu, P.-S., Van Dyke, M., & Chen, Y. (2015). Examining the effect of teacher guidance on collaborative argumentation in middle level classrooms. RMLE Online, 38(9). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Examining+the+Effect+of+Teacher+Guidance+on+Collaborative+Argumentation+in+Middle+Level+Classrooms
title: Ten-question argumentative-script teacher guide for whole-class collaborative argumentation
description: An instructional element the authors integrated into teacher guidance in the intervention condition: "Table 2 shows a complete 10-question teacher script for the intervention group." The script sequences questions eliciting position, evidence, counterargument, and rebuttal for both sides of an issue, ending with a compromise question. In the control condition, "the teacher asked only the first and last question," and the teacher used the exact questions in each section.
requirements: A teacher who asks the scripted questions verbatim during whole-class argumentation
An open-ended, authentic or ill-structured issue that requires argumentation
constraints: Designed for students at the beginning stage of developing argumentation skills, for whom the concept of argumentation was new
target_learning_goals: constructing arguments with position, reason, evidence, counterargument, and rebuttal
examples: Script questions included "What might somebody else say to show that your position is wrong?" and "Is there a compromise or creative solution?"
key_sources: Hsu, P.-S., Van Dyke, M., & Chen, Y. (2015). Examining the effect of teacher guidance on collaborative argumentation in middle level classrooms. RMLE Online, 38(9). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1074885

article_title: The Effect of In-Service Training of Computer Science Teachers on Scratch Programming Language Skills Using an Electronic Learning Platform on Programming Skills and the Attitudes towards Teaching Programming
citation: Ahmed Alkaria, Riyadh Alhassan. (2017). The Effect of In-service Training of Computer Science Teachers on Scratch Programming Language Skills Using an Electronic Learning Platform on Programming Skills and the Attitudes towards Teaching Programming. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i11.2608
title: Ted educational platform (ed.ted.com) as the delivery vehicle for remote Scratch teacher training
description: The study used the Ted educational platform at https://ed.ted.com to deliver Scratch training to remotely located teachers. The researchers "selected and presented" suitable videos "to a group of raters to check their suitability for the syllables" before "an account was created in the Ted educational platform". The platform carried multimedia learning content for the experimental group's in-service training.
requirements: Videos vetted by raters for suitability to the curriculum unit and its objectives in the teacher guide
constraints: Used for one educational unit of the third intermediate grade computer curriculum
target_learners: in-service middle school computer science teachers
target_learning_goals: Scratch programming skills
examples: Teachers in Tarif, Rafha and Al Awayleh received lessons remotely without needing to meet the trainers
key_sources: Ahmed Alkaria, Riyadh Alhassan. (2017). The Effect of In-service Training of Computer Science Teachers on Scratch Programming Language Skills Using an Electronic Learning Platform on Programming Skills and the Attitudes towards Teaching Programming. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i11.2608

article_title: Learning from Errors: Effects of Teachers Training on Students' Attitudes towards and Their Individual Use of Errors
citation: Rach, S., Ufer, S., & Heinze, A. (2013). Learning from errors: effects of teachers’ training on students’ attitudes towards and their individual use of errors. PNA, 8(1), 21-30. http://hdl.handle.net/10481/27879
title: Train teachers to establish an error-tolerant classroom culture to improve students' affective experience of errors
description: The article supports professional development in which teachers are informed about the potential use of errors for learning and are encouraged to consider errors as learning opportunities instead of useless interruptions. In the study, teachers in both experimental conditions took part in such a training program, and this produced significant affective gains for students, while additional cognitive-support materials alone did not change students' cognitive-level perceptions or error use.
requirements: Teachers participate in a professional training program covering the potential use of errors for learning and aspects of an error-tolerant and error-positive culture for the mathematics classroom
constraints: The affective support was not sufficient for inducing a change of students' perception of and handling in error situations with respect to the cognitive level
target_learning_goals: Positive attitudes towards errors as learning opportunities
Reduced fear of making errors in mathematics
examples: Teachers of the error-tolerant culture group took part in a five-month researcher-led training; teachers of the second group additionally received materials dealing with strategies to learn from errors
key_sources: Rach, S., Ufer, S., & Heinze, A. (2013). Learning from errors: effects of teachers’ training on students’ attitudes towards and their individual use of errors. PNA, 8(1), 21-30. http://hdl.handle.net/10481/27879

article_title: The Adoption of Tablet and E-Textbooks: First Grade Core Curriculum and School Administration Attitude
citation: Ibtesam Al-Mashaqbeh and Muneera Al Shurman. (2015). The Adoption of Tablet and e-Textbooks: first grade core curriculum and school administration attitude. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.21. http://www.iiste.org
title: Provide teachers with training programs and technical support when introducing tablets and e-textbooks
description: The article concludes that introducing tablets requires more than devices: teachers need training to use the materials and devices, and principals should support them with training programs and technical support. It recommends "having a technical assistant to help students and make teacher concentrate on the curriculum more than on the technical problems", and cites related studies finding that teachers needed more training programs to apply technology in teaching.
requirements: School administration support and a good environment to help teachers and students during the implementation process
constraints: The recommendation arises from reported difficulties (teacher workload, technical problems) in one private school setting, not from a tested comparison of support conditions
target_learners: first grade students and their teachers in elementary schools adopting tablets
target_learning_goals: effective implementation of tablet-based core curriculum instruction
examples: The software company trained teachers to use the tablet items, and the researcher recommended that principals support teachers by providing them with training programs and technical support
key_sources: Ibtesam Al-Mashaqbeh and Muneera Al Shurman. (2015). The Adoption of Tablet and e-Textbooks: first grade core curriculum and school administration attitude. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.21. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1079146

article_title: Analyzing the Efficacy of the Testing Effect Using Kahoot™ on Student Performance
citation: Iwamoto, D. H., Hargis, J., Taitano, E. J., & Vuong, K. (2017). Analyzing the efficacy of the testing effect using Kahoot on student performance. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 18(2). https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr
title: The testing effect (retrieval practice)
description: The testing effect is the phenomenon that "taking an initial test improves performance on subsequent tests." The article reviews evidence that it extends from laboratory settings to real classrooms, including semester-long quizzing with one-to-two-month and five-to-eight-month delays, benefits over re-reading, transfer across quiz/exam formats and applied-versus-conceptual items, and greater benefits with feedback. Roediger and Butler's five points are summarized, including that repeated testing beats a single test and that benefits generalize to different contexts. This study applies the theory via gamified no-stakes quizzes in higher education.
requirements: Some time is required between exposure to material and testing for retrieval practice to be beneficial; active encoding and giving meaning to test items is needed for benefits to appear
constraints: A negative testing effect (poorer recall after subsequent restudy) has been reported for free-recall items, attributed to lack of mnemonic episodic and semantic retrieval
target_learners: learners from middle school through higher education
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and transfer of studied material to subsequent exams
examples: The article cites classroom studies in sixth-grade social studies, eighth-grade science, and college students where quizzed material outperformed re-reading or non-quizzed material on delayed chapter and final exams
key_sources: Iwamoto, D. H., Hargis, J., Taitano, E. J., & Vuong, K. (2017). Analyzing the efficacy of the testing effect using Kahoot on student performance. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 18(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1145220

article_title: The Benefits of Fine Art Integration into Mathematics in Primary School
citation: Brezovnik, A. (2015). The Benefits of Fine Art Integration into Mathematics in Primary School. c e p s Journal, 5(3). https://cepsj.si
title: Effective arts integration requires teacher skill across manifold artistic techniques, not just frequent art lessons
description: The article argues that frequency alone is insufficient: "In order to obtain effective results in fine art, however, the frequent use of fine art lessons alone is not enough; the teacher should develop skills in manifold techniques." It illustrates this with an Appalachian teacher who taught a range of skills including macramé, pottery, drawing, photography, printing, batik, collage and calligraphy. When students experience sufficient diversity in the arts curriculum, differences in their interests, gender differences and differences in artistic performance are revealed.
requirements: The teacher should develop skills in manifold techniques
Sufficient diversity in the arts curriculum and in types of artistic expression
target_learning_goals: creative thinking
engagement with artistic expression
examples: Barone (2001) describes an Appalachian fine art teacher who taught students traditional knot patterns, pottery, fibre processing, work on looms, drawing, photography, printing, paper-making, batik, collage, calligraphy and spraying.
key_sources: Brezovnik, A. (2015). The Benefits of Fine Art Integration into Mathematics in Primary School. c e p s Journal, 5(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1128967

article_title: The Effect of Using Self-Monitoring Strategies in Social Studies Course on Self-Monitoring, Self-Regulation and Academic Achievement
citation: Arslantas, S. & Kurnaz, A. (2017). The effect of using self -monitoring strategies in social studies course on self -monitoring, self -regulation and academic achievement. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 3(2), 452-463. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.327905
title: Equip teachers with the competence to use self-monitoring strategies and inform students of their purpose, or the strategies' benefit is limited
description: Based on the qualitative findings, the article argues that implementing self-monitoring strategies depends on teacher competence and on students understanding why they are used. Teachers stated that "teacher competencies (N=5) are vital in implementing these strategies", and the article concludes it "will be beneficial to equip the teachers with the use of self -monitoring strategies". Students, meanwhile, were not adequately informed about how self-evaluations and techniques contribute to their own development, which the article links to uncertainty about effectiveness.
requirements: Teachers must know which programs, strategies, methods, techniques and instruments are used and must use course-book instruments such as checklists, rubrics, self-evaluation and graphics for their intended purpose
constraints: The article notes that dealing with traditional ways is simpler and does not require a preparation process, so it may be preferred by teachers, and that implementation is difficult within an intensive curriculum
target_learning_goals: self-monitoring skill
academic achievement
examples: Teachers reported that instruments included in course books were often not used for their intended purpose or were regarded as unnecessary
key_sources: Arslantas, S. & Kurnaz, A. (2017). The effect of using self -monitoring strategies in social studies course on self -monitoring, self -regulation and academic achievement. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 3(2), 452-463. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.327905

article_title: The Effectiveness of Drama-Based Instruction in Jordanian EFL Students' Writing Performance
citation: Bataineh, R. F., & Salah, N. A. (2017). The Effectiveness of Drama-Based Instruction in Jordanian EFL Students' Writing Performance. TESOL International Journal, 12(2). https://tiij.org
title: Story dramatization pattern: rewriting a textbook story into dialogue scenes taught through role play over multiple sessions
description: The article's experimental treatment converted the prescribed textbook story The Boy from the Past into a dramatized script and taught it through role play. "The Boy from the Past was rewritten into thirteen scenes in dialogue format and taught through dramatization in ffteen sessions over a period of nine weeks." Students worked in groups to role play the dramatized scenes, answered questions about them, and produced writing tied to each episode's focus (e.g., thesis statement modeling and paragraph production).
requirements: A source story from the students' own textbook
A teacher trained by the researchers to follow set procedures for each session
constraints: Studied with male eighth-grade EFL students in one Jordanian school; the observation was unstructured and had no validity or reliability check
target_learning_goals: Writing performance across thesis statement, unity, completeness and coherence, wording and cohesion, and organization
examples: In the third episode, students in small groups wrote and discussed five questions about the episode, which the teacher elicited onto the board for whole-class discussion.
key_sources: Bataineh, R. F., & Salah, N. A. (2017). The Effectiveness of Drama-Based Instruction in Jordanian EFL Students' Writing Performance. TESOL International Journal, 12(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1247797

article_title: Philosophy for Children: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Stephen Gorard, Nadia Siddiqui and Beng Huat See. (2015). Philosophy for Children: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Ten-stage P4C enquiry session structure from stimulus to review
description: SAPERE's P4C session follows ten named stages: getting set, presentation of stimulus, thinking time, question making, question airing, question choosing, first thoughts, building, last thoughts, and review. Pupils and teacher sit in a circle, pupils generate and vote on the dialogue question, and in the building stage "the rule is to justify opinions with reasons" while the teacher models fallibilism. The stages are a flexible guide and need not all occur in one session.
requirements: A classroom protocol that must be adhered to, with pupils and teacher seated in a circle facing each other
constraints: The stages can be used flexibly as the teacher's expertise grows and do not need to be completed all in one session
target_learners: Primary school pupils across all education age ranges
target_learning_goals: Questioning
Reasoned argumentation
Listening to others' views
examples: Teachers prompt moves such as imagining alternatives and consequences, seeking evidence, quantifying with expressions like 'all', 'some' or 'most', offering examples and counter examples, and questioning assumptions.
key_sources: Stephen Gorard, Nadia Siddiqui and Beng Huat See. (2015). Philosophy for Children: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581147

article_title: The Effect of Schema-vs-Translation-Based Instruction on Persian Medical Students' Learning of General English
citation: Ebrahim Khodadady, Majid Elahi. (2012). The Effect of Schema-Vs-Translation-Based Instruction on Persian Medical Students' Learning of General English. English Language Teaching, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n1p146
title: Teach foreign-language texts in the target language with visual and textual contexts rather than translating them into the learners' mother tongue
description: The article concludes that translation-based instruction "deprives the learners" of the relationships they must discern among schemata, and recommends that teachers "take a more active role by providing appropriate visual and textual contexts for the learners to experience the schemata under instruction". Teaching schemata in English with their meaning, syntactic, semantic and discoursal relationships helped learners understand texts significantly better than mother-tongue teaching in this study.
requirements: Teachers must provide visual and textual contexts in which learners can experience the schemata and their interactions.
Instruction stays within the language of instruction so relationships are consolidated in the target language.
constraints: The article notes TBI has been an indispensable method in non-English environments and that whether communicative approaches produce similar gains remains to be investigated.
target_learners: foreign-language learners of general English in academic contexts
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
structure and vocabulary mastery
examples: The experimental class worked through the first four textbook units entirely in English, with figures used to relate the schema healthy to exercise, nutrition and winter clothing.
key_sources: Ebrahim Khodadady, Majid Elahi. (2012). The Effect of Schema-Vs-Translation-Based Instruction on Persian Medical Students' Learning of General English. English Language Teaching, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n1p146

article_title: The Use of Animation Film in Forming Representations about the Planet Earth and the Solar System
citation: Vereș, S. & Magdaș, I. (2020). The Use of Animation Film in Forming Representations about the Planet Earth and the Solar System. Romanian Review of Geographical Education, 9(1), 38-59. https://doi.org/10.23741/RRGE120183
title: Mediate animated film content through teacher-led discussion and follow-up activities, because children need adult mediation to understand and retain film-presented content
description: A design principle holding that an animated film alone is insufficient for young learners' understanding: the teacher must discuss the film's content, add explanations, and consolidate knowledge with other materials. The article states that "Children need the teacher’s mediation in understanding the contents presented in the animated film, in order to ensure the learning efficiency" and that correct understanding depends on the teacher's expertise in directing understanding, learning, fixing and updating knowledge.
requirements: A teacher who directs the process of understanding, learning, fixing and updating knowledge after viewing
A follow-up learning activity combining the film with other didactic materials
constraints: Stated for primary education and the Solar System topic; the authors note a large amount of information in a short time cannot be learned from one viewing alone
target_learning_goals: forming accurate representations of the Solar System's structure and functioning
improving scientific understanding, knowledge implementation, and reasoning ability
examples: The experimental group reviewed the film, discussed its plot with the teacher, observed a globe and 3D model, and drew the Solar System, while the control group only viewed the film once
key_sources: Vereș, S. & Magdaș, I. (2020). The Use of Animation Film in Forming Representations about the Planet Earth and the Solar System. Romanian Review of Geographical Education, 9(1), 38-59. https://doi.org/10.23741/RRGE120183

article_title: The Impact of Computer Assisted Language Learning (CALL) on Improving Intermediate EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning
citation: Fatemeh Enayati, & Abbas Pourhosein Gilakjani. (2020). The Impact of Computer Assisted Language Learning (CALL) on Improving Intermediate EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning. International Journal of Language Education, 4(1). https://doi.org/10.26858/ijole.v4i2.10560
title: Tell Me More (TMM) language learning software
description: Tell Me More is an asynchronous online self-learning system for language skills that the article used as the experimental treatment. It offers five proficiency levels from beginner to advanced corresponding to A1 to C1, and "TMM seeks to tutor learners by exposing them to over 850 hours of learning content, 4,500 exercises and 37 types of activities" across six workshops (Lesson, Cultural, Vocabulary, Grammar, Oral, Written). It adopts a tutor role, giving meaning, controlling learning, giving feedback, and evaluating learning, with content structured around authentic events.
requirements: Learners need devices (mobile or tablet) on which to install the TMM application, and an introduction/training session on how to use the software for learning
constraints: In the study only 15 to 20 minutes of each 90-minute class session were dedicated to vocabulary teaching, per institute policy
target_learners: Iranian intermediate EFL learners aged 13 to 17 at a language institute
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary learning
listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills
examples: In the study, researchers taught 5 words per session with TMM over 12 sessions; the software presented picture and matching questions and learners advanced after answering correctly
key_sources: Fatemeh Enayati, & Abbas Pourhosein Gilakjani. (2020). The Impact of Computer Assisted Language Learning (CALL) on Improving Intermediate EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning. International Journal of Language Education, 4(1). https://doi.org/10.26858/ijole.v4i2.10560

article_title: Pedagogical Interaction in High School, the Structural and Functional Model of Pedagogical Interaction
citation: Semenova, L. A., Kazantseva, A. I., Sergeyeva, V. V., Raklova, Y. M., & Baiseitova, Z. B. (2016). Pedagogical Interaction in Hugh School, the Structural and Functional Model of Pedagogical Interaction. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(9), 2553-2566.
title: Team teaching (TT) technique with role behaviour
description: The article investigates "a form of practical classes – a social and psychological training that uses the team teaching (TT) technique". "Team teaching is a class that is held by two teachers or a teacher and a student at the same time", whose "main advantage is the addition of diversity and the improvement of effectiveness, since the teachers complement each other". Of the forms shown in Figure 4, "The most effective and efficient form of TT is the second one with role behaviour."
requirements: Two teachers, or a teacher and a student, conducting the class simultaneously
Role behaviour in the most effective form
constraints: Effectiveness ranking of TT forms is the authors' assertion without printed test statistics
target_learning_goals: partnership relationships in teacher-student and student-student systems
intensive interaction and exchange of opinions
examples: Active forms named alongside TT include business games, role-play, round-table discussions, and brainstorms.
key_sources: Semenova, L. A., Kazantseva, A. I., Sergeyeva, V. V., Raklova, Y. M., & Baiseitova, Z. B. (2016). Pedagogical Interaction in Hugh School, the Structural and Functional Model of Pedagogical Interaction. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(9), 2553-2566. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1114604

article_title: The Relation between Teacher Vocabulary Use in Play and Child Vocabulary Outcomes
citation: Ragan H. McLeod, Ann P. Kaiser, and Jessica K. Hardy. (2019). The Relation Between Teacher Vocabulary Use in Play and Child Vocabulary Outcomes. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121418812675
title: Teach vocabulary in play contexts by following the child's lead and using vocabulary supports
description: The article recommends embedding vocabulary instruction in play-based interactions, with teachers using target and sophisticated vocabulary, physical and verbal supports, and conversational turns that follow the child's attentional or communicative lead. It states that the immediate relation between child vocabulary use and teacher inputs when following the child's lead "supports the teaching of vocabulary in play contexts in preschool classrooms." Because play comprises roughly a third of the preschool day and teachers interact minimally during free play, the authors view this as an underused opportunity for children with low-language skills.
requirements: Training and support for teachers to use evidence-based language teaching practices consistently
Providing explicit supports such as vocabulary word lists and demonstrations of meaning-support strategies
constraints: Within-session relations did not extend to end-of-intervention standardized or observational measures, and a higher intervention dosage may be necessary to impact global vocabulary development
target_learners: preschool children with low language skills in Head Start classrooms
young children at risk for language and literacy delays
target_learning_goals: expressive and receptive vocabulary development
examples: In the study, teachers were trained in EMT, coached biweekly, and provided thematic toy sets with approximately 10 target vocabulary words per set for individual play sessions
key_sources: Ragan H. McLeod, Ann P. Kaiser, and Jessica K. Hardy. (2019). The Relation Between Teacher Vocabulary Use in Play and Child Vocabulary Outcomes. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121418812675

article_title: Technology-Supported Global Education: A Mixed Method Study = Teknoloji destekli küresel egitim: Bir karma yöntem çalismasi
citation: Egüz, Ş., Öztürk, C. & Kesten, A. (2019). Technology-supported global education: A mixed method study. Pegem Eğitim ve Öğretim Dergisi, 9(4), 1209-1244. http://dx.doi.org/10.14527/pegegog.2019.040
title: Technology-supported course plans and activities for the 'Our Country and the World' unit
description: A set of 11 lesson plans with five activities, one per unit subject, prepared by the researcher to teach global-education attainments in the 6th-grade 'Our country and the world' unit using communication technologies. The article states "11 lesson plans with five activities were prepared for teaching the attainments related to global education by using communication technologies", evaluated by two field experts and two social studies teachers and pre-applied for four weeks with 21 students. Technologies included newspaper clippings, television, video and news blogs across activities such as Invitation to City, Product Marketing, Newspaper Page Designing, Help Mobilization and Addressing the World.
requirements: Evaluated by field experts and social studies teachers before application
Delivered across 11 sessions of 40 minutes over four weeks
constraints: Applied only to the 'Our country and the world' unit in 6th-grade social studies
target_learning_goals: Global-education attainments: population and economic activity distribution, economic relations, cultural and political relations with other countries, solidarity in disasters, inter-communal interaction
examples: Activities paired each unit topic with specific technologies, e.g. 'Invitation to City' used newspaper clippings, video and news blog
key_sources: Egüz, Ş., Öztürk, C. & Kesten, A. (2019). Technology-supported global education: A mixed method study. Pegem Eğitim ve Öğretim Dergisi, 9(4), 1209-1244. http://dx.doi.org/10.14527/pegegog.2019.040

article_title: Real Experiments versus Phet Simulations for Better High-School Students' Understanding of Electrostatic Charging
citation: Ajredini, F., Izairi, N., Zajkov, O. (2013). Real Experiments versus PhET Simulations for Understanding Electrostatic Charging. European J of Physics Education, 5(1). https://ejpe.phywe.de
title: The teacher should act as the final filter who chooses between real experiments and simulations based on the classroom situation, objectives and concepts to be mastered
description: Because real experiments and computer simulations each contribute different skills, the article assigns the choice between them to the teacher rather than declaring one universally superior.
