The teacher should decide "based on the situation in the classroom, the objectives to be fulfilled and the concepts which should be mastered", acting like a conductor of the orchestra. The article also urges teachers to design activities from experience with current students and to include deeper analysis and explanation of formulas in discussion.
requirements: The teacher must know each approach's distinctive contributions, e.g. simulations save organizational and manual-labour time while real experiments demand designing the set-up and solving practical problems.
constraints: The study's classes lasted only 40 minutes and group sizes (five to six in Real, two in Sim) may have limited involvement and discussion, as the authors state.
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of electrical charging and related electrostatic concepts
examples: The study compared a Real group working with plastic and glass rods with woolen and leather cloth, a Sim group using the PhET simulations Balloons and Static Electricity and John Travoltage, and a traditionally taught control group.
key_sources: Ajredini, F., Izairi, N., Zajkov, O. (2013). Real Experiments versus PhET Simulations for Understanding Electrostatic Charging. European J of Physics Education, 5(1). https://ejpe.phywe.de

article_title: The Effects of Different Pre-Writing Strategies on Iranian EFL Writing Achievement
citation: Lily Mahnam; Dariush Nejadansari. (2012). The Effects of Different Pre-Writing Strategies on Iranian EFL Writing Achievement. International Education Studies, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n1p154
title: Explicitly teach concept mapping, reading relevant texts, and negotiation as pre-writing strategies to enhance advanced EFL students' essay writing
description: The article recommends that writing instructors explicitly teach three pre-writing strategies rather than assigning essays without preparation. It argues that "Students maximize their learning by using concept mapping, reading relevant text, and negotiation of the topic in their essay writing", increasing independence and responsibility. Teachers are advised to familiarize students with these strategies because the activities are easily adopted.
requirements: Students receive instruction in the argumentative essay genre and the strategies before writing tasks
Controversial, familiar topics are used so negotiation and reading activities generate ideas
constraints: The finding is demonstrated for advanced-level EFL students; the article states the instruction "can benefit EFL students at the advanced level of language proficiency"
target_learners: advanced adult EFL learners in university English courses
target_learning_goals: argumentative essay writing achievement
learner independence and responsibility in writing
examples: Over 18 treatment sessions the experimental group alternated concept mapping, reading with skimming/scanning and note taking, and whole-class negotiation with for-and-against columns on the board, writing an essay after each strategy.
key_sources: Lily Mahnam; Dariush Nejadansari. (2012). The Effects of Different Pre-Writing Strategies on Iranian EFL Writing Achievement. International Education Studies, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n1p154

article_title: Automatic Speech Recognition Technology as an Effective Means for Teaching Pronunciation
citation: Amal Khalil Elimat & Ali Farhan AbuSeileek. (2014). Automatic speech recognition technology as an effective means for teaching pronunciation. The JALT Call Journal, 10(1), 21-47. https://jaltcall.org
title: Tell Me More Performance English ASR program
description: The instructional software used by the experimental groups: an ASR-based pronunciation course whose home page offers "three levels (beginners, intermediate, and advanced) and twelve lesson workshops", each containing exercises at word, sentence, and real-life dialogue levels. The student listens to a model, records an attempt, and "the program provides the student with automatic feedback to determine the quality of pronunciation" by comparing attempts to a native speaker. Four workshops (The Menu, Desserts, Organizing a Meal, Setting the Table) were selected for the study after supervisor and teacher review.
requirements: Computers with headsets in a laboratory, student login, and a password-protected setup allowing only target groups to use it at allocated times
constraints: The study used only this program, selected because it suits the level of third-grade students
target_learning_goals: English pronunciation at word, sentence, and real-life dialogue levels
examples: Experimental students logged in, wore headsets, listened to words, sentences, and dialogues, and recorded their voices to hear their own recordings one period a day, two periods a week, for eight weeks
key_sources: Amal Khalil Elimat & Ali Farhan AbuSeileek. (2014). Automatic speech recognition technology as an effective means for teaching pronunciation. The JALT Call Journal, 10(1), 21-47. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1107929

article_title: The Motivation Impact of Open Educational Resources Utilization on Physics Learning Using Quipper School App
citation: Sulisworo, D., Sulistiyo, E. N., & Akhsan, R. N. (2017). The motivation impact of open educational resources utilization on physics learning using Quipper School app. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 18(4), Article 9. https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr
title: Teachers adopting OER-based learning must master online learning strategies, shifting their role from information source to inspiration
description: The article argues that OER adoption makes teacher quality decisive: when students have unlimited access to information, "The teacher's role turned into inspiration when students have already got unlimited access to the information." Teachers' perceived value and motivation toward OER adoption is described as very important for learning success, and teachers with inadequate IT literacy may find this difficult. Teachers therefore need to master online learning strategies with OER to achieve expected competencies.
requirements: Teachers need to master online learning tools and OER-based strategies; teacher perceived value and motivation for OER adoption
constraints: This capability may be difficult for teachers with inadequate IT literacy facing online learning
target_learners: high school students learning through teacher-mediated OER environments
target_learning_goals: sustaining motivation and learning quality under OER-based blended learning
examples: The authors recommend improving teacher quality in mastering online learning tools, naming Quipper School as one alternative to manage good learning.
key_sources: Sulisworo, D., Sulistiyo, E. N., & Akhsan, R. N. (2017). The motivation impact of open educational resources utilization on physics learning using Quipper School app. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 18(4), Article 9. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1161803

article_title: Let's Discuss: Teaching Students about Discussions
citation: Brank, E. and Wylie, L. (2013). Let's discuss: Teaching students about discussions. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Vol. 13, No. 3, August 2013, pp. 23–32. https://josotl.indiana.edu
title: Explicitly teach students about the purpose and practice of discussions before using student-led discussions
description: Before relying on student-led discussions, devote class time to explaining why discussions matter and having students practice leading and questioning. The study's experimental class spent "a full week considering discussions and discussing discussions", reading three articles about discussions and practicing asking questions without designated leaders. This early investment was associated with better early-semester performance and higher course evaluations than a control class that only used discussions.
requirements: Class time must be allocated to a dedicated discussion-about-discussions week without removing other material
Readings on the importance of discussions and suggestions for leading them must be accessible to undergraduates
constraints: The effect was demonstrated with junior and senior level college students; the authors ask whether a younger, less experienced sample would show the same effect
Advantages leveled off by the end of the semester, so the benefit appears greatest early
target_learning_goals: discussion leadership and participation
engagement with course material
critical evaluation of competing viewpoints
examples: In the experimental semester, students read three articles about discussions, completed a homework assignment asking why discussions are positive and what barriers interfere, and all practiced asking questions and leading parts of the discussion rather than designating leaders
key_sources: Brank, E. and Wylie, L. (2013). Let's discuss: Teaching students about discussions. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Vol. 13, No. 3, August 2013, pp. 23–32. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1017045

article_title: The Effect of Collaborative Learning and Self-Assessment on Self-Regulation
citation: Ali Hatami. (2015). The effect of collaborative learning and self-assessment on self-regulation. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2349
title: Teacher-assistance cooperative teaching method (jigsaw plus traditional, mixed-ability triads)
description: The article implements a hybrid teaching method described as "a mixture of traditional schools method and cooperative jigsaw approach". Students were first classified into weak, moderate, and strong levels based on previous scores and teacher judgment, then formed into three-member groups containing one student of each level. Groups chose a sign and name to strengthen relations and received a guide for group activities; jigsaw teaching was used in school and traditional method outside school.
requirements: Students classified into weak, moderate, and strong levels before grouping
Groups of three including one student of each level
A guide for group activities provided to each group
constraints: The method was implemented in geometry instruction for female 11th-grade high-school students over eight 90-minute sessions
target_learning_goals: geometry achievement at low and high cognitive levels
self-regulated learning strategies
examples: Experimental groups were taught geometry for eight 90-minute sessions using this method, with the self-assessment group additionally conducting learners' self-assessment
key_sources: Ali Hatami. (2015). The effect of collaborative learning and self-assessment on self-regulation. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2349

article_title: Management of Teacher Scientific-Methodical Work in Vocational Educational Institutions on the Basis of Project-Target Approach
citation: Elena A. Shakuto, Evgenij M. Dorozhkin and Anastasia A. Kozlova. (2016). Management of Teacher Scientific-Methodical Work in Vocational Educational Institutions on the Basis of Project-Target Approach. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(16), 8834-8845. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Teacher training program for deputy heads and teachers of secondary vocational education institutions
description: Together with the information-methodical center the authors developed and introduced a training program for Deputy Heads and teachers of secondary vocational education institutions. Its goal was methodological and technological training in managing teacher scientific-methodical work to ensure modernization of secondary vocational education content. As printed, "The recommended educational methods are interactive technologies, brainstorming, discussion -seminars, round tables, business games, conferences (Figure 2)", and professional reflection was an obligatory element at the end of each training lesson.
requirements: An obligatory element of professional reflection at the end of each training lesson
constraints: Designed for Deputy Heads, specialists of methodical service and teachers of secondary vocational education institutions
target_learners: Deputy heads and methodical service specialists
teachers of secondary vocational educational institutions
target_learning_goals: managing teacher scientific-methodical work
modernization of the content of secondary vocational education
examples: Figure 2 lists organizational forms separately for scientific-research work and teaching-methodical work, including group consultations, practice-oriented seminars, demonstration lessons, school of a young teacher and scientific-methodical committee meetings
key_sources: Elena A. Shakuto, Evgenij M. Dorozhkin and Anastasia A. Kozlova. (2016). Management of Teacher Scientific-Methodical Work in Vocational Educational Institutions on the Basis of Project-Target Approach. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(16), 8834-8845. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

article_title: The Effect of Coordinated Teaching Method Practices on Some Motor Skills of 6-Year-Old Children
citation: Altinkok, M. (2017). The Effect of Coordinated Teaching Method Practices on Some Motor Skills of 6-Year-Old Children. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 68, 49-61. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2017.68.3
title: 10-week coordination-based Games and Physical Activities program for first graders
description: A physical education program built on the educational method through coordination, delivered to the experimental group "for a total period of 10 weeks comprising five course-hours per week" during Games and Physical Activities lessons. Activities were designed with expert input, performed in activity classes, sports halls, and the school yard, and aimed to develop motor skills while promoting children's activeness and participation.
requirements: Prepared in accordance with the characteristics of motor skills considering expert opinions; children's active participation; delivery in activity classes, sports halls, and the school yard
constraints: Evaluated only in 6-year-old first graders with no attendance problems, with parental permission, in one primary school setting
target_learning_goals: psychomotor development and motor skill improvement
examples: Measurement was carried out by three individuals (a researcher, an assistant, and an interviewer who processed scores), and data collection proceeded through a preliminary study, pre-tests, the program, and post-tests
key_sources: Altinkok, M. (2017). The Effect of Coordinated Teaching Method Practices on Some Motor Skills of 6-Year-Old Children. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 68, 49-61. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2017.68.3

article_title: The Effect of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) on Reading Comprehension in English for Specific Purposes Courses
citation: Fahimeh Farahani. (2018). The Effect of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) on Reading Comprehension in English for Specific Purposes Courses. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 6(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.6n.1p.79
title: Ten-session NLP treatment program for ESP reading
description: The treatment consisted of ten sessions, each presenting one NLP topic: introduction and presuppositions, goal setting with guided fantasy, sensory language across two sessions, metaphor, emotion, belief (flexibility), "There is no Failure; only Feed back", finding the best strategy, and review. Each technique presentation was followed by reading a medical text and answering related questions, with learners applying their diagnosed sensory style. The control group instead received traditional skimming and scanning instruction.
requirements: Ten sessions with one NLP topic each
Medical texts from 'Reading Science and Medicine in English' (Kamyab et al., 2016) followed by comprehension questions
constraints: Implemented with two intact classes of 60 Iranian undergraduate medical-science students
target_learners: Iranian undergraduate EFL learners in medical sciences
target_learning_goals: ESP reading comprehension
examples: Session topics included Goal Setting (Outcome)-Guided Fantasy, Sensory Language (Reid's Test), and Finding the Best Strategy (Flexibility)
key_sources: Fahimeh Farahani. (2018). The Effect of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) on Reading Comprehension in English for Specific Purposes Courses. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 6(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.6n.1p.79

article_title: A Randomized Waitlist Controlled Analysis of Team-Initiated Problem Solving Professional Development and Use
citation: Horner, R. H., Newton, J. S., Todd, A. W., Algozzine, B., Algozzine, K., Cusumano, D., & Preston, A. (2018). A Randomized Waitlist Controlled Analysis of Team-Initiated Problem Solving Professional Development and Use. Behavioral Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/0198742917745638
title: Team-Initiated Problem Solving (TIPS) model for data-based team decision making
description: TIPS is a research-supported problem-solving model that guides school teams through an iterative data-based process. It "guides teams to use data to define precise problem statements" including where, when, who, and behavioral function, plus accompanying goals; teams then select contextually appropriate solutions, build action plans, and gather fidelity and outcome data to monitor implementation and impact, refining plans based on impact analysis. In this study it was taught via a 6-hour workshop plus two coached meetings.
requirements: Professional development workshop plus follow-up technical assistance/coaching from district PBIS coaches
Access to data systems such as SWIS for reporting student behavior
Meeting foundations such as assigned roles and a meeting minute format that guides the agenda
constraints: Studied with elementary school PBIS teams using SWIS; the article calls for testing with middle and high schools, other data systems, academic-focused teams, and district-level teams
target_learners: school PBIS team members (teachers, administrators, related services professionals)
target_learning_goals: data-based team problem solving and decision making for academic and behavior problems
examples: Teams received a 6-hr workshop coupled with two coached meetings covering meeting foundations and the six TIPS problem-solving steps
key_sources: Horner, R. H., Newton, J. S., Todd, A. W., Algozzine, B., Algozzine, K., Cusumano, D., & Preston, A. (2018). A Randomized Waitlist Controlled Analysis of Team-Initiated Problem Solving Professional Development and Use. Behavioral Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/0198742917745638

article_title: The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance
citation: Mandana Eftekhar Paziraie. (2013). The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance. English Language Teaching; Vol. 6, No. 2; 2013. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p71
title: Include the textual metafunction in the EFL writing curriculum
description: Based on the finding that explicit textual-metafunction instruction raised coherence and cohesion ratings, the article recommends that "Textual metafunction should have its place in the writing skill curriculum for English as a Foreign Language (EFL)". It further states that writing teachers can make good use of the textual metafunction during their writing classes, and that students preparing for the IELTS and similar exams can benefit from its use to improve their writing skill.
requirements: Writing teachers need training materials introducing the metafunctions, such as the study's three-chapter pamphlet with exercises
constraints: The supporting evidence comes from one study of sixty adult female intermediate EFL learners at a single institute in West of Tehran
target_learning_goals: coherence and cohesion in English essay writing
examples: The experimental group attended an essay writing class two sessions per week for a ten-week term and was taught to apply the textual metafunction in a standard three-paragraph essay
key_sources: Mandana Eftekhar Paziraie. (2013). The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance. English Language Teaching; Vol. 6, No. 2; 2013. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p71

article_title: Reading in L2 (English) and L1 (Persian): An Investigation into Reverse Transfer of Reading Strategies
citation: Seyed Hassan Talebi. (2012). Reading in L2 (English) and L1 (Persian): An Investigation into Reveres Transfer of Reading Strategies. English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n3p217
title: Teach reading strategies in the L2 to improve strategic reading in both L2 and L1
description: Because languages are in interaction and affect each other, the article recommends that L2 teachers check whether learners are aware of their strategy repertoire in L1 and L2 and, if not, teach the strategies in L2, since this reaches "improvements in strategic learning both in L2 and in L1". The study's results support this: strategy instruction in English improved both English and Persian reading comprehension and strategy questionnaire scores.
requirements: Explicit strategy instruction with modeling and guided group practice
Assessment of reading and strategy use in both languages to verify transfer
constraints: Strategy instruction has shown mixed results in prior research; Cotterall (1990) reported no significant improvement, which the article attributes to strategies being taught only in L2 with no L1 explanation
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and strategic reading in L2 and L1
examples: The experimental group received sixteen 70-minute sessions of CSR-based strategy instruction alongside regular materials, while controls received only regular materials
key_sources: Seyed Hassan Talebi. (2012). Reading in L2 (English) and L1 (Persian): An Investigation into Reveres Transfer of Reading Strategies. English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n3p217

article_title: An Intervention Programme for Promoting More Effective Learning among Foundation Phase Learners in South Africa
citation: Ona Janse van Rensburg. (2015). An intervention Programme for Promoting More Effective Learning among Foundation Phase Learners in South Africa. Journal of Curriculum and Teaching, Vol. 4, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5430/jct.v4n2p110
title: Ten-week multimodal stimulation programme with three one-hour sessions per week
description: The intervention programme is a lesson-level design in which Grade 1 learners participate in a variety of activities specially planned to stimulate the pedagogical factors identified in the literature survey. "The programme was presented over a period of ten (10) weeks at a rate of three (3) one hour sessions per week", held from 9:00-10:00 in the morning. Activities developed skills, knowledge and values and involved learners "both in individual and group capacity", while the rest of the school programme continued as usual for both groups.
requirements: A presenter familiar with the programme's construction and with Foundation Phase teacher education
permission from school authorities and parents
constraints: Presented in an English-medium school in a medium-sized South African city with a multicultural class
target_learning_goals: Stimulation of perceptual, motor, emotional, language and conceptual development for more effective learning
examples: The experimental group took part in the programme while the control group listened to the class teacher reading stories in another classroom
key_sources: Ona Janse van Rensburg. (2015). An intervention Programme for Promoting More Effective Learning among Foundation Phase Learners in South Africa. Journal of Curriculum and Teaching, Vol. 4, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5430/jct.v4n2p110

article_title: Effectiveness of an Intervention Program in Fostering Academic Resilience of Students at Risk of Failure at Secondary School Level
citation: Muhammad Irfan Arif and Munawar S. Mirza. (2017). Effectiveness of an Intervention Program in Fostering Academic Resilience of Students at Risk of Failure at Secondary School Level. Bulletin of Education and Research, 39(1), 251-264. https://ber.journals.pu.edu.pk
title: Teachers can foster resilience in regular classrooms by providing supportive environments that develop protective factors
description: The article concludes that "the teacher can foster the resiliency characteristics among at -risk students by helping them acquirea protective mechanism through providing supportive environment and developing protective factors contributing towards resilience." Teachers do this by providing purposeful activities and opportunities that encourage students to apply their skills, providing explanations, encouraging students to elaborate their responses, appreciating and applauding successes, and providing support during task learning. The study demonstrated this in a three-month intervention with at-risk secondary students.
requirements: Teachers who provide a supportive environment and develop protective factors contributing towards resilience
constraints: Demonstrated at secondary school level only, with the selected protective factors, over a three-month intervention delivered by a researcher rather than a regular teacher
target_learners: Non-resilient at-risk of failure students at secondary school level
target_learning_goals: Academic resilience and protective factors such as self-esteem, self-efficacy and internal locus of control
examples: In the experiment, the researcher spent one hour daily teaching resilience activities to a separate section of non-resilient at-risk students, and treatment-group students reported a more positive classroom-learning environment and obtained significantly higher resilience scores
key_sources: Muhammad Irfan Arif and Munawar S. Mirza. (2017). Effectiveness of an Intervention Program in Fostering Academic Resilience of Students at Risk of Failure at Secondary School Level. Bulletin of Education and Research, 39(1), 251-264. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1210192

article_title: Impact of the Systemic Approach on Literacy Achievement of Jordanian 1st Graders at Mu'tah University Model School
citation: Nail Al-hajaya. (2012). Impact of the Systemic Approach on Literacy Achievement of Jordanian 1st Graders at Mu'tah University Model School. International Education Studies, Vol. 5, No. 1. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n1p100
title: Teach Arabic language as an integrative system rather than as dichotomous, separated disciplines
description: The article argues that segmenting language into modules such as grammar, morphology, and literature distorts the whole picture, since "language in the life use is practiced in integration and wholeness." It advises presenting subsystems "in an integrative combination reflecting a schematic system of language wherein later knowledge is linked with prior knowledge," so learners acquire a wholeness view without artificial separation between reading, writing, and grammar.
requirements: Language subsystems must be taught from their relative position against the whole system
constraints: The article states the common practice of segmenting language into modules is an attempt to make language study easier, and that results are restricted by the psychometric characteristics of the instruments used
target_learning_goals: Integrated reading and writing skills
Meaningful learning of language concepts
examples: The experimental first-grade group was taught literacy through systemic-approach tasks with graphics and illustrations, while the control group followed the traditional Jordanian method
key_sources: Nail Al-hajaya. (2012). Impact of the Systemic Approach on Literacy Achievement of Jordanian 1st Graders at Mu'tah University Model School. International Education Studies, Vol. 5, No. 1. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n1p100

article_title: Joint Book Reading: How Do Blogs Foster Collaborative Comprehension?
citation: Fatemeh Behjat. (2013). Joint Book Reading: How Do Blogs Foster Collaborative Comprehension? i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 3 No. 2, April-June.
title: Teacher's blog with e-books and a comment section for collaborative out-of-class reading
description: The article describes a teacher-built weblog used as the delivery environment for supplementary reading: e-copies of short stories were posted for download, and students interacted asynchronously in a section entitled "leave comments", discussing the main idea of each part of the story and challenging each other's opinions. The teacher scheduled online times and counted comments toward final grades to ensure participation. This element operationalizes joint reading in a virtual environment outside class.
requirements: Students must be online at arranged times and post comments, which the teacher tied to evaluation of final grades
E-book versions of the assigned stories must be downloadable from the blog
constraints: Studied with Iranian EFL university students aged 21-25 majoring in English translation or teaching
target_learning_goals: Foreign language reading comprehension
examples: The experimental group read the same five short stories as the control group but discussed them on the blog's comment section over three months
key_sources: Fatemeh Behjat. (2013). Joint Book Reading: How Do Blogs Foster Collaborative Comprehension? i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 3 No. 2, April-June. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068891

article_title: Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities
citation: Sabirova, E. G., Zakirova, V. G. & Masalimova, A. R. (2016). Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 505-514.
title: Extracurricular program 'Teaching junior pupils to research' with three subprograms
description: During the experiment the authors developed and introduced into school practice a program of extracurricular activity of junior pupils called "Teaching junior pupils to research", intended for extracurricular work in elementary school and institutions of additional education. Its purpose is transformation of the intellectual-creative potentiality of children's personality through elaboration of research skills during self-growth. The program "included three relatively independent programs": lessons directed to formation of research skills; research practice using informational-communication technology as the leading, central subprogram with mini-researches and creative projects; and monitoring of learning and research activity through seminars, conferences and defenses of research works.
requirements: Lessons on formation of research skills start only in the second semester, once children have adapted to school and mastered basic learning skills such as reading, writing and counting
constraints: For 7-8 year olds the program totals 20 hours (1 hour a week, not carried out in the first semester); for 8-10 year olds 66 hours; for 10-11 year olds 36 hours under teacher guidance plus independent extracurricular work
target_learners: junior pupils aged 7-11 in elementary school
target_learning_goals: self-dependent research skills and conception of research teaching as a leading way of learning activity
examples: Eight-year-olds kept a diary of researcher, worked in groups or pairs by request, and first presented mini-research results at specially organized competition defenses where dates were planned according to readiness of their works.
key_sources: Sabirova, E. G., Zakirova, V. G. & Masalimova, A. R. (2016). Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 505-514. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1094583

article_title: On Non-English Majors' Strategy Training in English Reading Comprehension
citation: Xiaoling Yang. (2017). On Non-English Majors' Strategy Training in English Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n10p153
title: Reading classrooms should focus on teaching students how to read strategically and autonomously
description: From the experiment the article concludes that "the main focu s of reading classroom should be on teaching students how to read", so that learners become effective, strategic readers who can deal with their reading independently and autonomously even when the teacher is not there. It recommends that strategy training be taken into account in reading curriculum design.
requirements: Strategy training integrated into regular reading coursework
constraints: Demonstrated in a natural teaching environment with foreign language reading among Chinese non-English majors
target_learning_goals: autonomous strategic reading
reading comprehension
examples: The five-week experiment trained the experimental group in six strategies while the control group received traditional text-focused instruction with the same amount of reading text
key_sources: Xiaoling Yang. (2017). On Non-English Majors' Strategy Training in English Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n10p153

article_title: The Effects of Professional Development Initiatives on EFL Teachers' Degree of Self Efficacy
citation: Mohammad Nabi Karimi. (2011). The Effects of Professional Development Initiatives on EFL Teachers' Degree of Self Efficacy. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 36, 6, May 2011.
title: Teacher Sense of Efficacy Scale (Tschannen-Moran & Woolfolk Hoy, 2001) as the outcome measure
description: The study measured teacher efficacy with the 24-item Teacher Sense of Efficacy Scale, rated on a 9-point continuum from 1 (Nothing) to 9 (A Great Deal), with three 8-item subscales: Efficacy for Instructional Strategies, Efficacy for Classroom Management, and Efficacy for Student Engagement. The article notes it "is becoming a standard instrument in research on teacher efficacy and has had high reliability in previous administrations", with subscale reliabilities of .86 to .90 and full-scale reliabilities of .92 to .95 in previous research.
requirements: Administered as pre-test, immediate post-test, and delayed post-test to both groups
constraints: Prior reliability figures are from previous research, not reported for this sample
target_learning_goals: measuring teachers' efficacy beliefs about engagement, instructional strategies, and classroom management
examples: Used to establish pre-test equivalence (t = .327, p = .745) before the experiment began
key_sources: Mohammad Nabi Karimi. (2011). The Effects of Professional Development Initiatives on EFL Teachers' Degree of Self Efficacy. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 36, 6, May 2011. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ936991

article_title: The Probability Approach to English If-Conditional Sentences
citation: Mei Wu. (2012). The Probability Approach to English If-conditional Sentences. English Language Teaching, 5(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n5p37
title: Teach English conditionals separately from the subjunctive mood
description: The article proposes that "teaching English conditionals separately from the subjunctive mood" simplifies instruction, since teachers otherwise use inconsistent methods—some teach them "side by side, some teachers teach them separately." Separating the two topics allows conditionals to be classified by probability into four basic types rather than by the more complex traditional subjunctive-mood framing.
requirements: Instructors must classify conditionals independently of subjunctive-mood terminology
constraints: Proposed for beginner learners; the article notes the four types are not the only or 'correct' way
target_learning_goals: acquiring the four basic types of conditional sentences
examples: The author's own teaching of freshman English majors applied this separation
key_sources: Mei Wu. (2012). The Probability Approach to English If-conditional Sentences. English Language Teaching, 5(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n5p37

article_title: The Effect of Focused Communication Tasks on Instructed Acquisition of English Past Counterfactual Conditionals
citation: Broszkiewicz, A. (2011). The effect of focused communication tasks on instructed acquisition of English past counterfactual conditionals. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 1(3), 335-363. http://www.ssllt.amu.edu.pl
title: Sequence text-manipulation practice before text-creation activities to move learners from controlled to automatic use of a target structure
description: The article reports Ellis's recommendation that grammar practice proceed from highly-controlled text-manipulation activities, such as paraphrasing or sentence completion, to text-creation activities in which learners produce their own sentences using the target structure. This order, the article states, "helps learners move from controlled to automatic use of the target structure". The study's CPA group followed this procedure during its practice sessions.
requirements: Both activity types must be included, with text-manipulation preceding text-creation
constraints: The article presents this as Ellis's recommendation for output-based grammar activities, not as a finding tested against the alternative order
target_learners: foreign language learners receiving form-focused grammar instruction
target_learning_goals: proceduralisation and automatic use of targeted grammatical structures
examples: The CPA group's practice sessions used completing with the correct form, transformations and translation, followed by story completion as a text-creation task
key_sources: Broszkiewicz, A. (2011). The effect of focused communication tasks on instructed acquisition of English past counterfactual conditionals. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 1(3), 335-363. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1136449

article_title: Using Clickers to Enhance Student Learning in Mathematics
citation: Ye Wang, Chia-Jung Chung & Lihua Yang. (2014). Using Clickers to Enhance Student Learning in Mathematics. International Education Studies, 7(10). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n10p1
title: Support teachers with mentoring and training when integrating clickers, because question quality matters more than the technology
description: The article concludes that taking full advantage of clickers requires proper instruction for teachers on retooling lessons, and that "More important than the technology, is the need to ask the right questions." Poorly structured questions that do not focus on key concepts or reveal misunderstandings can undermine clickers' value. The recommended support route is "mentoring and support from other teachers or professionals."
requirements: Proper instruction for all teachers on how to retool lessons and develop new skills supporting the technology.
constraints: Poorly structured questions or ones that do not focus on key concepts or reveal misunderstandings can undermine the value of clickers.
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students across subjects
target_learning_goals: student engagement, formative assessment, mathematics understanding
examples: The study's teacher redesigned warm-ups and homework into multiple-choice clicker questions and recorded more teachable moments and aha moments in the trial group's journal.
key_sources: Ye Wang, Chia-Jung Chung & Lihua Yang. (2014). Using Clickers to Enhance Student Learning in Mathematics. International Education Studies, 7(10). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n10p1

article_title: Efficacy of Self-Regulated Strategy Development Instruction for Developing Writers with and without Disabilities in Rural Schools: A Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Linda H. Mason, Anne Mong Cramer, Justin D. Garwood, Cheryl Varghese, Jill Hamm, and Allen Murray. (2017). Efficacy of Self-Regulated Strategy Development Instruction for Developing Writers With and Without Disabilities in Rural Schools: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Rural Special Education Quarterly, 36(4), 168–179. https://doi.org/10.1177/8756870517723617
title: Provide rural teachers with team-based professional development plus ongoing virtual support when implementing research-based writing instruction
description: The article recommends that, given factors challenging rural teachers such as geographic location, professional development be organized as school teams attending a central-location workshop with ongoing virtual consultation support. It states that "it is essential that recommendations, such as team-based professional development and ongoing support, are considered," and that providing mechanisms to support teachers in SRSD writing instruction is important. The 1-day workshop plus consultation and five-lesson delivery appeared effective for improving whole-class persuasive writing.
requirements: Professional development provided to school teams including administrative staff
Virtual consultation sessions that review completed lesson steps and student self-regulation use
constraints: Professional development was provided to school teams, which the article notes should be considered when generalizing
target_learners: Grade 5 and 6 students in inclusive rural classrooms
target_learning_goals: Persuasive writing performance for all students through whole-class instruction
examples: Both the professional development provided (1-day workshop plus consultation) and the instructional delivery (five 45-min lessons) appear effective for meeting the goal of improving persuasive writing of all students in inclusive rural classrooms.
key_sources: Linda H. Mason, Anne Mong Cramer, Justin D. Garwood, Cheryl Varghese, Jill Hamm, and Allen Murray. (2017). Efficacy of Self-Regulated Strategy Development Instruction for Developing Writers With and Without Disabilities in Rural Schools: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Rural Special Education Quarterly, 36(4), 168–179. https://doi.org/10.1177/8756870517723617

article_title: Improving Preservice Teachers' Phonemic Awareness, Morphological Awareness and Orthographic Knowledge
citation: McNeill, B. C. (2018). Improving Preservice Teachers' Phonemic Awareness, Morphological Awareness and Orthographic Knowledge. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 43(1). http://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol43/iss1/2
title: Ten-hour metalinguistic coursework module for spelling instruction embedded in a literacy education course
description: A 10-hour instructional module (5 x 2-hour lectures) delivered within a 40-hour literacy education course for first-year preservice teachers, covering phonological awareness (~4 hours), orthographic awareness (~2 hours), morphological awareness (~2 hours), and spelling analysis and selection of appropriate teaching focus (~2 hours). The course "utilised a blended model to support students' learning", with readings, video clips and interactive activities online, and lecture recordings accessible multiple times. The final component had students work in small groups to score and analyse 17 spelling samples from children aged 6-7 years, group children by instructional focus, and report findings with lecturer feedback.
requirements: Lecturer facilitation during group analysis activities, including whole-cohort feedback sessions and circulation among groups
Online course website hosting recordings and spelling samples for review
constraints: The spelling instruction selection measure is not a direct measure of teacher competency in spelling assessment or instruction
target_learners: first-year preservice teachers in a three-year undergraduate teaching degree
target_learning_goals: metalinguistic knowledge for spelling instruction
application of phonemic, morphological and orthographic knowledge to spelling error analysis
examples: Students segmented and blended words into phonemes, role-played drawing children's attention to sounds in shared reading, completed word sorts for orthographic patterns such as final 'tch' versus 'ch', and built word families sharing a free morpheme
key_sources: McNeill, B. C. (2018). Improving Preservice Teachers' Phonemic Awareness, Morphological Awareness and Orthographic Knowledge. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 43(1). http://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol43/iss1/2

article_title: Can Working Memory Strategies Enhance English Vocabulary Learning?
citation: Ibarra Santacruz, D., & Martínez Ortega, D. (2018). Can working memory strategies enhance English vocabulary learning? HOW, 25(2), 29-47. https://doi.org/10.19183/how.25.2.410
title: A ten-task weekly working-memory strategy sequence embedded in EFL lessons
description: The intervention consisted of ten weekly classroom tasks built around the Gathercole and Alloway (2007) strategies plus phonological-loop activities: reducing memory load with scrambled stories, color-coding verbs and nouns, word posters, Socrative and Kahoot quizzes, clustering with graphic organizers, KWL charts, and four listening-based phonological-loop tasks. Each task had printed success criteria. The authors chose these strategies because they "can indeed be incorporated into regular language lessons and do not need major adjustments from the teacher or the classroom setting".
requirements: Strategies are applied one per week over a ten-week period within regular English lessons
constraints: The article does not report which individual strategy contributed most to the effect
target_learning_goals: retention and retrieval of English vocabulary
use of past-tense forms in reading, writing, speaking and listening tasks
examples: Strategy 2 gave students printed verbs in red and nouns in green to match meanings and quiz classmates; Strategy 10 used a bingo game with present and past verb call cards for aural practice
key_sources: Ibarra Santacruz, D., & Martínez Ortega, D. (2018). Can working memory strategies enhance English vocabulary learning? HOW, 25(2), 29-47. https://doi.org/10.19183/how.25.2.410

article_title: Effects of Instruction on Chinese College Students' Thematic Choice in Academic Writing
citation: Wei, J. (2016). Effects of Instruction on Chinese College Students’ Thematic Choice in Academic Writing. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(14). http://www.iiste.org
title: Ten-week instruction in thematic choice for Chinese college students' academic English writing
description: An instructional program of ten sessions (about eight hours total, 50 minutes per session) delivered over 10 consecutive weeks during regular English lessons by the researcher, who was also the students' regular classroom teacher. It was delivered only to the experimental group (CE), while the control group (CC) received regular lessons on planning the writing, structuring paragraphs, writing introductions, writing conclusions, and the writing of one essay. The program targeted thematic choice in academic English writing, aiming to help students choose the right kind of information to place in Theme position.
requirements: Delivered during regular class hours scheduled for English lessons
Participants complete pre- and post-instruction writing tasks for effect assessment
constraints: Delivered only to the experimental group; the study was quasi-experimental because students remained intact in their regular classes due to school policy
target_learning_goals: Making native-speaker-like thematic choices in academic English essays
examples: Ten sessions on thematic choice given to CE group while CC group received ten regular essay-writing sessions over the same period
key_sources: Wei, J. (2016). Effects of Instruction on Chinese College Students’ Thematic Choice in Academic Writing. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(14). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102949

article_title: The Application of a Cloud-Based Student, Teacher, and Parent Platform in English as a Foreign Language Education
citation: Fu-Yuan Chiu. (2014). The Application of a Cloud-Based Student, Teacher, and Parent Platform in English as a Foreign Language Education. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 13(3), 178-187. http://www.tojet.net/
title: Test-Diagnose-Remedy cyclic learning model
description: The CSTPP is organized around a continuous improvement cycle in which students self-test, receive a diagnosis of subject-specific weaknesses mapped to each item in the question pool, and receive targeted remediation through answer explanations and short teaching videos before retesting. As the article states, "The entire learning process involved an uninterrupted cycle of Test, Diagnose, and Remedy, forming a progressive improvement learning process." Stronger students spend less time in the remedy stage and progress at their own pace, while weaker students build confidence by repeatedly addressing weaknesses across cycles.
requirements: a test item pool in which every question corresponds to a subject-specific weakness
remedial materials such as teaching videos targeted to those weaknesses
constraints: the model was studied with junior high school EFL learners over a 3-month period
target_learning_goals: English learning progress customized to individual ability
remediation of specific learning weaknesses
examples: the CSTPP randomly selects 20-23 multiple-choice questions per learning unit and produces diagnostic reports for teachers and parents
key_sources: Fu-Yuan Chiu. (2014). The Application of a Cloud-Based Student, Teacher, and Parent Platform in English as a Foreign Language Education. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 13(3), 178-187. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1034232

article_title: The Web Quest: Its Impact on Developing Teaching Skills of Physical Education Student Teachers
citation: Haythem Abdel Mageed Mohamed & Rasha Nageh Ali Abd El Rheem. (2008). The Web Quest: Its Impact on Developing Teaching Skills of Physical Education Student Teachers. Journal of Research, volume 5, issue 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Web+Quest+Its+Impact+on+Developing+Teaching+Skills+of+Physical+Education+Student+Teachers
title: 70-item Teaching Practice Observation Sheet with three teaching-skill dimensions
description: The study's measurement instrument is a 70-item observation sheet adopted from Azmy & Mohamed (2006), rated on a three-point scale (1=Never; 2=Sometimes; 3= Always). "The teaching practice observation sheet consists of three main dimensions representing the three major teaching skills addressed by the researchers (see Appendix 1); including planning skills (16 items), implementation skills (46 items), and evaluation skills (8 items)." Cronbach alpha coefficients for the three dimensions were between .93 and .98, and inter-rater reliability via the Pearson Correlation Formula on videotaped performances by two lecturers was 0.97.
requirements: Videotaped peer-teaching performances rated by trained external judges, with scores averaged across judges
constraints: Adopted from a previous study in the same faculty context; reliability was estimated on a separate sample of 20 fourth-year PE teacher candidates
target_learning_goals: observable teaching performance in lesson planning, implementation and evaluation
examples: Posttest scores were obtained by videotaping each participant teaching one model PE class in the university sports hall and having three judges rate the videotapes
key_sources: Haythem Abdel Mageed Mohamed & Rasha Nageh Ali Abd El Rheem. (2008). The Web Quest: Its Impact on Developing Teaching Skills of Physical Education Student Teachers. Journal of Research, volume 5, issue 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Web+Quest+Its+Impact+on+Developing+Teaching+Skills+of+Physical+Education+Student+Teachers

article_title: Learning Authentic Leadership in New Zealand: A Learner-Centred Methodology and Evaluation
citation: Maree Roche. (2010). Learning Authentic Leadership In New Zealand: A Learner-Centred Methodology And Evaluation. American Journal of Business Education, Volume 3, Number 3. https://clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE
title: Grint's techne–episteme–phronesis framework: authenticity and wisdom can be learned from experience but not taught
description: The article adopts Grint's (2007) Aristotelian framework distinguishing three leadership development areas with separate outcomes: techne (teachable skills such as emotional intelligence and vision), episteme (the body of research and theory), and phronesis (experience-based wisdom in reading situations and self-reactions). The article argues most leadership courses cover only the first two, and that "leadership development can only be learned though one‟s own life experiences", motivating its learner-centred, experience-based design.
requirements: Learning of phronesis must draw on students' own experiences outside the classroom rather than instructor-led classroom exercises
constraints: The article frames the framework as applying to highly personal areas such as integrity, wisdom and authenticity, which it argues cannot be taught
target_learners: undergraduate business degree students in elective leadership courses
target_learning_goals: authentic leadership development
self-awareness
wisdom (phronesis) from experience
examples: Students reflected on 20 incidents that challenged or developed their authenticity, then wrote a Best Authentic Self narrative with developmental goals
key_sources: Maree Roche. (2010). Learning Authentic Leadership In New Zealand: A Learner-Centred Methodology And Evaluation. American Journal of Business Education, Volume 3, Number 3. https://clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE

article_title: Enhancing Information Systems Auditing Knowledge with Role-Playing Game: An Experimental Investigation
citation: Nitaya Wongpinunwatana. (2013). Enhancing Information Systems Auditing Knowledge with Role-Playing Game: An Experimental Investigation. International Education Studies, 6(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v6n9p72
title: Teaching-methods-activity-fit framework (TMAF)
description: The TMAF combines activity theory with cognitive-fit theory to match teaching methods to the structure of a task. It maps five elements of activity theory — "subject, object, community, tools and division of labour" — against five teaching methods (instructor-led teaching, demonstration, learning by teaching, case study, role-playing game). The framework indicates the role-playing game is the most suitable method for teaching IS audit because it satisfies all five elements, and it grounds the study's research model in which fit level affects perceived knowledgeability, task ability, and enjoyment.
requirements: The task or activity process must be analysable into the five activity-theory elements so teaching methods can be matched to them
constraints: Activity theory is described as "more of a descriptive theory than a predictive theory" and does not address effects of independent on dependent variables, so the framework borrows cognitive-fit theory for prediction
target_learners: graduate accounting students training to become IS auditors
target_learning_goals: understanding and performing information systems control and audit processes
examples: Table 1 of the article scores each teaching method against the five activity-theory elements, with the role-playing game marked Yes on subject, object, community, tools, and division of labour
key_sources: Nitaya Wongpinunwatana. (2013). Enhancing Information Systems Auditing Knowledge with Role-Playing Game: An Experimental Investigation. International Education Studies, 6(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v6n9p72

article_title: The Effect of Incorporating the Extensive Reading Approach into Vocabulary Instruction on Learners' Lexical Depth in an EFL Context
citation: Mohsen Jafarpour. (2014). The Effect of Incorporating the Extensive Reading Approach into Vocabulary Instruction on Learners' Lexical Depth in an EFL Context. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.162
title: Day and Bamford's ten principles defining a successful extensive reading program
description: The article presents Day and Bamford's (2002) ten principles that "define a successful ER program for L2 learners", covering easy and varied materials, learner choice, reading quantity, pleasure and general understanding as purposes, reading as its own reward, faster reading speed, individual silent reading, teacher orientation, and the teacher as a role model of a reader. Teachers are encouraged to use the principles "as a tool to examine their beliefs about reading". The study's treatment operationalised several of these principles.
requirements: A variety of reading material on a wide range of topics must be available
Learners choose what they want to read
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency and volume
Vocabulary development through extensive reading
examples: The study equipped the institution with a library of about 100 graded readers and story books from which students freely chose, matching the learner-choice and easy-materials principles.
key_sources: Mohsen Jafarpour. (2014). The Effect of Incorporating the Extensive Reading Approach into Vocabulary Instruction on Learners' Lexical Depth in an EFL Context. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.162

article_title: Suggestopedia Based Storytelling Teaching Model for Primary Students in Salatiga
citation: Sunardi, Herman J. Waluyo, Astini Suudi, Nugraheni Eko Wardani. (2018). Suggestopedia Based Storytelling Teaching Model for Primary Students in Salatiga. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, Volume 6, Issue 1. https://www.mojet.net
title: Tembang dolanan (Javanese nursery rhymes) as suggestive media and game in the storytelling model
description: Tembang dolanan are Javanese nursery rhymes familiar to students across Java and included in the Bahasa Indonesia national curriculum as 'local poetry' material. The article describes them as simple, playful and humorous songs carrying messages such as "traditions, virtues, politeness, moral lessons, ironies, hygiene, environmental issues, health and religiosity." In the model, tembang dolanan served "as both the suggestive media and the game," stimulating students to move, sing and play roles according to the rhyme lyrics.
requirements: Students' familiarity with tembang dolanan and its inclusion in the national curriculum as local poetry material.
constraints: The article frames the element for primary students in Java; the rhymes are classified as old poems of oral tradition.
target_learners: Primary school students in Java learning Bahasa Indonesia
target_learning_goals: Storytelling, vocabulary learning, and engagement through song and play
examples: In the lessons, tembang dolanan was used to stimulate students to move, sing and play roles according to the lyric of the rhyme.
key_sources: Sunardi, Herman J. Waluyo, Astini Suudi, Nugraheni Eko Wardani. (2018). Suggestopedia Based Storytelling Teaching Model for Primary Students in Salatiga. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, Volume 6, Issue 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1165473

article_title: Research into Learning Process in a Vocational Secondary School in the Context of Sustainable Development
citation: NataÔja van Gejeka. (2013). Research into Learning Process in a Vocational Secondary School in the Context of Sustainable Development. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 15, no. 2. https://doi.org/10.2478/jtes-2013-0012
title: Team project method organisational cycle for integrative collaboration
description: The article describes an organisational process cycle for learners' integrative collaboration within technical study subjects: teams analyse members' cooperation in problem solving, develop an action plan, implement the project, present it, discuss it, and finish with reflection as a critical assessment of the team project and self-evaluation. Teacher participation decreases gradually while each learner's learning autonomy increases as collaborative experiences organise the learning process towards mastery.
requirements: Teams of three to four members formed after a short introductory lecture
A common objective and tasks assigned by the teacher
constraints: Implemented in the study subject Building Constructions at a vocational secondary school
target_learning_goals: integrative collaboration
creative potential
professional skills
examples: The main pedagogical experiment ran one semester with two experimental groups and a control group, using structured observation of 160 minutes at the beginning and four learning hours at the end
key_sources: NataÔja van Gejeka. (2013). Research into Learning Process in a Vocational Secondary School in the Context of Sustainable Development. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 15, no. 2. https://doi.org/10.2478/jtes-2013-0012

article_title: Teaching Community College Students Strategies for Learning Unknown Words as They Read Expository Text
citation: Craigo L., Ehri, L. C., & Hart, M. (2017). Teaching community college students strategies for learning unknown words as they read expository text. Higher Learning Research Communications, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.18870/hlrc.v7i1.350
title: Teach community college students a repertoire of independent word-learning strategies together with elaborated definitions, using instructor modeling, guided practice, and feedback
description: The article recommends that because there are too many words to teach explicitly, students need intentional, strategic, independent word-learning skills built from context cues, morphological analysis, syntax, and elaborated definitions applied during text reading. Instructor modeling with time for student practice and instructor feedback were found to be crucial components for student learning and engagement. In the experiment, all three interventions built on these components and produced large comprehension and word-learning gains over a discussion control on treatment passages.
requirements: Instructor modeling with time for student practice and instructor feedback
A repertoire of strategies including context cues, morphological analysis, and understanding of syntax
Definitions sufficiently elaborate, such as those in glossaries
Naturalistic texts to facilitate transfer when students read on their own
constraints: Effects did not transfer to independent reading of a new passage without prompting
Students may need training to become aware of words whose meanings are unfamiliar
target_learners: community college students in teacher education
post-secondary students reading discipline-specific academic text
target_learning_goals: learning meanings of unknown academic vocabulary words while reading
reading comprehension of discipline-specific expository text
examples: Students in the Strategies group used a chart prompting context, morphology, and syntax questions; the Strategies plus Definitions group compared derived meanings with supplied elaborated definitions; the experimenter modeled, scaffolded, prompted, and corrected errors across three sessions.
key_sources: Craigo L., Ehri, L. C., & Hart, M. (2017). Teaching community college students strategies for learning unknown words as they read expository text. Higher Learning Research Communications, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.18870/hlrc.v7i1.350

article_title: The Impact of Task-Based Instruction Program on Fostering ESL Learners' Speaking Ability: A Cognitive Approach
citation: Mohammad Mohammadipour & Sabariah MD Rashid. (2015). The Impact of Task-Based Instruction Program on Fostering ESL Learners' Speaking Ability: A Cognitive Approach. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.113
title: TED-talk video materials as pre-task authentic input
description: The experimental group's main materials were "some supplementary video files extracted from TED conferences, to which students were exposed before doing the task". Videos were selected according to students' level and the content or spoken genre of each task, using criteria that they be relevant to students' background knowledge and culture, authentic representations of real-life spoken discourse including fillers, hesitation markers, fixed expressions, ellipsis and vague language, and amenable to analysis for raising awareness of spoken discourse features.
requirements: Videos must be relevant to students' background knowledge and culture, authentic, and suitable for close analysis
constraints: Selected from TED talks according to the students' level and the genre tackled by each task
target_learning_goals: awareness of spoken discourse characteristics
speaking sub-skills
examples: Students analysed video tapescripts before tasks to notice turn-taking management, discourse markers, and spoken vocabulary features
key_sources: Mohammad Mohammadipour & Sabariah MD Rashid. (2015). The Impact of Task-Based Instruction Program on Fostering ESL Learners' Speaking Ability: A Cognitive Approach. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.113

article_title: The Effect of Vocabulary Self-Selection Strategy and Input Enhancement Strategy on the Vocabulary Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Golfam Masoudi. (2017). The Effect of Vocabulary Self-Selection Strategy and Input Enhancement Strategy on the Vocabulary Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p32
title: Textual Input Enhancement as attention-directing typographic modification of input
description: Input Enhancement (Sharwood Smith) is an implicit focus-on-form technique that makes target items visually salient in written input. The article defines it: "Using typographical cues such as bolding and italics to draw the reader’s attention to particular information in a text is known as textual enhancement." Its aim is "to change the way input is perceived and processed by language learners". The article notes Sharwood Smith's caveat that attention to an enhanced form does not guarantee learners will internalize it. In the study, texts were highlighted with the words previously chosen by the Vocabulary Self-Selection group.
requirements: Target items visually altered in the text (highlighting)
Learners process meaning-bearing input while attending to enhanced forms
constraints: Sharwood Smith's caveat, quoted in the article: even if learners attend to the enhanced form, "there is no guarantee that they will internalize the form"
target_learning_goals: vocabulary knowledge
noticing of target forms
examples: The Input Enhancement group read the same ten illustrated texts as the other group but could select words only from among the textually highlighted ones
key_sources: Golfam Masoudi. (2017). The Effect of Vocabulary Self-Selection Strategy and Input Enhancement Strategy on the Vocabulary Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p32

article_title: Comparing the Efficacy of Digital Flashcards versus Paper Flashcards to Improve Receptive and Productive L2 Vocabulary
citation: Gilbert Dizon and Daniel Tang. (2017). Comparing the efficacy of digital flashcards versus paper flashcards to improve receptive and productive L2 vocabulary. The EUROCALL Review, Volume 25, No. 1. https://doi.org/10.4995/eurocall.2017.6964
title: Teach vocabulary learning strategies alongside paper flashcards to maximize their effectiveness
description: The article argues that paper flashcards are a much more basic tool than digital flashcard systems, so learners using paper materials should be explicitly taught vocabulary learning strategies to level the playing field. It states that "students ought to be taught VLSs in order to maximize the effectiveness of PFs to retain new vocabulary". In the study, the PF group was taught dropping, association, and oral rehearsal before and during the 12-week treatment, and matched the digital group's gains.
requirements: The VLSs must be taught and modeled before the treatment begins and reviewed to reinforce the studying procedures
constraints: The article states it is unclear how much of an impact the VLSs themselves had, since there was no PF-only comparison group
target_learning_goals: receptive and productive knowledge of high-frequency English vocabulary (NGSL)
examples: The PF group was taught three VLSs adopted from Mizumoto and Takeuchi (2009) and Kornell and Bjork (2007), modeled prior to treatment and reviewed at the start of week two, and made significant RV and PV gains equal to the DF group's.
key_sources: Gilbert Dizon and Daniel Tang. (2017). Comparing the efficacy of digital flashcards versus paper flashcards to improve receptive and productive L2 vocabulary. The EUROCALL Review, Volume 25, No. 1. https://doi.org/10.4995/eurocall.2017.6964

article_title: Evaluating the Impact of Virtual Exchange on Initial Teacher Education: A European Policy Experiment
citation: The EVALUATE Group. (2019). Evaluating the impact of virtual exchange on initial teacher education: a European policy experiment. Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2019.29.9782490057337
title: Student teachers should experience innovative online learning approaches themselves during initial teacher education
description: The report argues that if future teachers are to engage their students in innovative and inclusive approaches to online learning, "they first of all need to experience this type of learning themselves during their own study programmes". Virtual exchange during initial teacher education provides this firsthand experience, preparing student teachers to facilitate similar approaches in their future classrooms.
requirements: Virtual exchange must be integrated into initial teacher education programmes rather than offered only as continuing professional development for in-service teachers.
constraints: The report notes that take-up of virtual exchange initiatives such as eTwinning will remain limited until student teachers experience these online learning approaches during their own training.
target_learners: Student teachers in initial teacher education
target_learning_goals: Digital-pedagogical competence
Intercultural competence
Innovative use of online technologies in teaching
examples: The EVALUATE project organised virtual exchanges involving over 1,000 students across 34 initial teacher training institutions between 2017-18.
key_sources: The EVALUATE Group. (2019). Evaluating the impact of virtual exchange on initial teacher education: a European policy experiment. Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2019.29.9782490057337

article_title: The Formation of Learners' Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine
citation: Igor Korsun. (2017). The Formation of Learnersí Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 117ñ128. https://doi.org/10.1515/jtes-2017-0008
title: Questionnaire measuring the motivational component of learners' cognitive activity
description: The study used a ten-item yes/no questionnaire administered to each learner, with items asking whether the learner can identify a physics concept, knows examples of physics in nature, everyday life, and technique, knows examples of modern research, knows physicists as examples, their sayings and Nobel Prize winners, reads additional literature on physics, and knows a scientific site. Evaluation is by number of "yes" answers: 0ñ3 is a low level, 4ñ7 an average level, and 8ñ10 a high level of the motivational component of learners' cognitive activity.
requirements: Each learner fills in the questionnaire, and items asking for examples require the learner to write them down
target_learners: secondary school learners aged 15ñ17 studying physics
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of the motivational component of learners' cognitive activity in physics
key_sources: Igor Korsun. (2017). The Formation of Learnersí Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 117ñ128. https://doi.org/10.1515/jtes-2017-0008

article_title: Best Management Practice for Understanding Learning in Sustainable Water Resource Management (WRM) for Secondary Science Teachers in Thailand
citation: Chunwadee Chunrasaksakun. (2015). Best management practice for understanding learning in sustainable water resource management (WRM) for secondary science teachers in Thailand. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2521
title: Teacher training should be an integral part of the curriculum development stage
description: The article states that evaluation of teacher perceptions and readiness to adopt and carry out an innovation is crucial to the success of the program, and that "Teacher training programs should be an integral part of the curriculum development stage". The study's own findings support this: trained teachers were able to design learning units from the WRD curriculum framework, and their students achieved significantly higher outcomes than students of untrained teachers.
requirements: Teachers should adjust their thinking and teaching to be aligned with the curriculum and always update their knowledge and skills
constraints: Derived from a specific curriculum innovation (WRD framework) in Thai secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Curriculum implementation competence
Learning unit design
examples: The WRD study trained 28 teachers before curriculum implementation and compared their students' achievement against a control group
key_sources: Chunwadee Chunrasaksakun. (2015). Best management practice for understanding learning in sustainable water resource management (WRM) for secondary science teachers in Thailand. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2521

article_title: Instructional Methods in STEM and English Subjects: A Validation Study
citation: Zendler, A., Klaudt, D., & Seitz, C. (2018). Instructional methods in STEM and English subjects: A validation study. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 4(2), 686-702. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.438378
title: Tentative hierarchical theory of instructional-method effectiveness (fundamental, central, and elementary hypotheses)
description: The article proposes a tentative theory, "understood as a system of hypotheses", organizing propositions about instructional methods, knowledge processes, and school subjects into three levels connected by an "entailment" relation. Fundamental hypotheses state that "Instructional methods differ in their support of knowledge processes in the act of learning" and that "Instructional methods are suitable for different subjects." Central hypotheses name the appropriate methods for computer science and mathematics teaching and for teaching English, and elementary hypotheses state that individual knowledge processes are supported by different instructional methods in each subject.
requirements: The article states the elementary hypotheses could be further detailed only when "comprehensive empirical results are available for learning outcomes from authentic teaching / learning scenarios that compare two or more instructional methods."
constraints: The study was conducted with teachers in the state of Baden-Württemberg; "The results cannot be generalized to other states because of different curricular requirements."
target_learners: secondary school students in computer science, mathematics, and English classrooms
target_learning_goals: supporting the knowledge processes of build, process, apply, transfer, assess, and integrate in the act of learning
key_sources: Zendler, A., Klaudt, D., & Seitz, C. (2018). Instructional methods in STEM and English subjects: A validation study. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 4(2), 686-702. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.438378

article_title: Teacher Effectiveness Enhancement Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Institute for Effective Education. (2016). The Teacher Effectiveness Enhancement Programme: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: The TEEP three-tier pedagogical framework model
description: The TEEP model is a pedagogical framework represented graphically and "broken down into three tiers": a six-phase learning cycle (preparing for learning, agreeing learning outcomes, presenting new information, constructing meaning, demonstrating understanding, and reviewing); five underpinning elements (assessment for learning, thinking for learning, accelerated learning, collaborative learning, and effective use of ICT); and effective teacher and learner behaviours (interactive teaching, classroom management, variety of teaching approaches, and classroom climate). The whole-school training programme is structured around these tiers across five days, and the framework is described as providing "a comprehensive language and framework for understanding how to improve the effectiveness of both teachers and learners in secondary schools".
requirements: All staff in a school receive Level 1 training without exception; the developers report schools where senior leaders do not fully engage struggle to maintain enthusiasm after training
constraints: Neither subject- nor age-specific, but evaluated here only in low-performing secondary schools; delivery varied from school to school depending on existing practices and teacher experience
target_learners: secondary school students in low-performing schools
target_learning_goals: improve teachers' classroom practice
develop characteristics of effective learning in students
raise GCSE attainment
examples: Level 1 training day 1 covers classroom climate and the five underpinning elements; day 2 covers the six-phase learning cycle; day 3 covers effective teacher and learner behaviours; Level 2 adds two days of coaching and mentoring
key_sources: Institute for Effective Education. (2016). The Teacher Effectiveness Enhancement Programme: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581110

article_title: Integrating Mobile Phones into the EFL Foundation Year Classroom in King Abdulaziz University/KSA: Effects on Achievement in General English and Students' Attitudes
citation: Abdulhafeth A. Khrisat & Salameh Saleem Mahmoud. (2013). Integrating Mobile Phones into the EFL Foundation Year Classroom in King Abdulaziz University/KSA: Effects on Achievement in General English and Students' Attitudes. English Language Teaching, 6(8). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p162
title: Ten mobile phone TEFL-oriented features used weekly in the experimental EFL classroom
description: A set of ten mobile-phone features integrated into EFL teaching over seven weeks: the notes feature to collect everyday language, the camera feature to take pictures of texts, the voice memo recorder to record language from media outlets, text messaging for vocabulary reinforcement and circular writing, social networking, phone memory for listening material, installed dictionaries, internet resources, and comprehension checking.
