In the study, students used them "on weekly basis", e.g. to "write any sentence, vocabulary item, proverb, idiom or grammatical structure they come across in or outside the classroom". Materials collected were used by the instructor as pre-activities for reading, writing, speaking or listening.
requirements: Students own or have access to mobile phones with notes, camera, voice recorder, messaging and dictionary features
Instructor training on applying the mobile features in the TEFL classroom, as the experimental instructor received
constraints: Activities were designed to match with the Saudi culture
The features were applied over one seven-week module
target_learners: Foundation-year university EFL students (intermediate level, Arabic L1)
target_learning_goals: General English achievement across the four skills and sub-skills
examples: Experimental-group students messaged daily vocabulary summaries to their teacher and completed a group-based circular writing activity building a five-sentence paragraph across five groups
key_sources: Abdulhafeth A. Khrisat & Salameh Saleem Mahmoud. (2013). Integrating Mobile Phones into the EFL Foundation Year Classroom in King Abdulaziz University/KSA: Effects on Achievement in General English and Students' Attitudes. English Language Teaching, 6(8). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p162

article_title: The Impact of Teaching Communication Strategies on EFL Learners' Willingness to Communicate
citation: Abulfazl Mesgarshahr, Esmaeel Abdollahzadeh. (2014). The impact of teaching communication strategies on EFL learners’ Willingness to Communicate. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2014.4.1.4
title: Teach communication strategies to help learners become more willing to communicate in the classroom
description: Based on the experimental results, the article recommends incorporating communication strategy training into language instruction. It concludes that "teaching CSs helps learners become more willing to communicate in the classroom," and suggests textbooks that incorporate CS teaching into lesson plans might be more effective, with teacher’s guides providing the rationale for strategy training. Teachers should themselves be proficient users and models of CSs, demonstrating strategies such as circumlocuting new words and using appeal-for-help devices. The recommendation is grounded in the measured WTC gains of the trained group.
requirements: Teachers need background knowledge of the rationale for strategy training
teachers should model appropriate strategy use
constraints: Overuse and misuse of some strategies (e.g., repeatedly resorting to one all-purpose verb) should be guarded against, echoing concerns that CSs may foster dependence at the expense of overall communicative competence
evidence comes from pre-intermediate learners and self-report data
target_learners: EFL learners, especially at lower proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: Willingness to communicate
communication strategy use
examples: The experimental group received CS training embedded in class tasks while the control group followed the regular curriculum, and only the trained group’s WTC improved significantly
key_sources: Abulfazl Mesgarshahr, Esmaeel Abdollahzadeh. (2014). The impact of teaching communication strategies on EFL learners’ Willingness to Communicate. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2014.4.1.4

article_title: Engaging Pre-Service Teachers in an Exploration of the Politics of Language
citation: Cheu-jey Lee, Glenda Moss, & Elaine Coughlin. (2010). Engaging Pre-Service Teachers in an Exploration of the Politics of Language. Scholar-Practitioner Quarterly, 5(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Engaging+Pre-Service+Teachers+in+an+Exploration+of+the+Politics+of+Language
title: Teach Standard English critically, as a tool for critiquing language politics, rather than as a superior dialect
description: The authors affirm that instruction of Standard English is crucial for empowering language minority students but argue that teaching it "as if it were superior to other dialects will reproduce rather than reverse linguistic oppression." They propose inviting students, especially language minority students, to examine Standard English closely and to command it as "a tool to critique the politics of the language," avoiding the risk of taking its oppressive ideologies for granted.
requirements: Standard English instruction must include critical examination of its relationship to power and other dialects
constraints: Teaching Standard English as superior reproduces linguistic oppression; the authors take issue only with traditional instruction, not with teaching Standard English itself
target_learners: pre-service teachers preparing to teach them
target_learning_goals: command of Standard English through a critical lens
recognition of the politics embedded in language
examples: The authors propose inviting students to examine how Standard English can position one group in opposition to another, citing Leland and Harste
key_sources: Cheu-jey Lee, Glenda Moss, & Elaine Coughlin. (2010). Engaging Pre-Service Teachers in an Exploration of the Politics of Language. Scholar-Practitioner Quarterly, 5(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ974353

article_title: Technology Facilitated PBL Pedagogy and Its Impact on Nursing Students' Academic Achievement and Critical Thinking Dispositions
citation: Yu, W.-C. W., Lin, C. C., Ho, M.-H., & Wang, J. (2015). Technology facilitated PBL pedagogy and its impact on nursing student's academic achievement and critical thinking dispositions. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075262
title: Integrating technology into PBL to provide time flexibility and asynchronous communication can enhance academic achievement
description: The study demonstrates that combining PBL with a virtual learning environment's communication features (chat rooms, discussion forums, file sharing) allows students to complete PBL steps at their own pace and outside class, addressing time constraints that cause frustration in traditional PBL. The B-PBL group's significantly higher posttest scores support this approach. The authors note that "the flexible nature of technology, allowing for more time and a break between steps" was the key design difference.
requirements: Access to a virtual learning environment with synchronous chat, asynchronous discussion forums, and content posting features
Instructor willingness to allow students to complete PBL steps at their own pace rather than within a single class period
constraints: Tested with undergraduate nursing students in an English for Nursing Purposes course; generalizability to other disciplines not yet established
The study was a quasi-experimental non-randomized design, limiting causal claims
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in course content
English for Nursing Purposes
examples: B-PBL students completed steps 1-4 at their own pace during class, step 5 via e-campus chat room outside class, and step 6 as a collaborative homework reflection
key_sources: Yu, W.-C. W., Lin, C. C., Ho, M.-H., & Wang, J. (2015). Technology facilitated PBL pedagogy and its impact on nursing student's academic achievement and critical thinking dispositions. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057343

article_title: Cognitive Factors That Influence Children's Learning from a Multimedia Science Lesson
citation: Anggoro, F. K., Stein, N. L., & Jee, B. D. (2012). Cognitive factors that influence children's learning from a multimedia science lesson. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 5(1), 93-108. https://www.iejee.com
title: Present text and images simultaneously to support integration of verbal and visual information in multimedia learning
description: The article found that conditions promoting integration of verbal and visual information provide the greatest support to children's learning. When a tutor reads text aloud while images are presented, "temporal contiguity is increased and it may be easier for the student to hold and integrate the visual and verbal components." This principle recommends tutor-read delivery over self-paced reading when the primary challenge is cross-modal integration, as demonstrated by the greater gains in the Tutor-Read condition.
requirements: A tutor or instructor to read text aloud in conjunction with visual presentations
constraints: This could reduce or eliminate the benefits of self-pacing, since the tutor would hold some or all of the control over the pace of reading
Children might have benefitted more from self-reading if the text lacked causal coherence
target_learning_goals: learning molecular properties of states of water from multimedia science instruction
examples: In the Tutor-Read conditions, the experimenter read the text aloud to the child while graphics were presented on the computer screen
key_sources: Anggoro, F. K., Stein, N. L., & Jee, B. D. (2012). Cognitive factors that influence children's learning from a multimedia science lesson. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 5(1), 93-108. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068621

article_title: The Effect of Form versus Meaning-Focused Tasks on the Development of Collocations among Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners
citation: Pishghadam, R., Khodadady, E., & Daliry Rad, N. (2011). The Effect of Form versus Meaning-Focused Tasks on the Development of Collocations among Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 4(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n2p180
title: Teacher-made 40-item multiple-choice collocation test used as pretest and posttest
description: The researchers designed a 40-item multiple-choice collocation achievement test, selected from an initial pool of 50 items, to measure collocation gain scores as both pretest and posttest. Content validity was checked by 'at least six teachers in order to check the adequacy of this test'. Reliability was estimated with Cronbach's alpha, reported as .52 and, elsewhere in the article, .81.
requirements: Content validation by at least six teachers
constraints: Reliability coefficients reported inconsistently within the article (.52 and .81)
target_learning_goals: collocation knowledge measurement
examples: Sample items assess verb-noun and adjective-noun collocations such as 'heavy wind', 'make a right turn', and 'pay a fine'
key_sources: Pishghadam, R., Khodadady, E., & Daliry Rad, N. (2011). The Effect of Form versus Meaning-Focused Tasks on the Development of Collocations among Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 4(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n2p180

article_title: The Acquisition of Phrasal Verbs through Cognitive Linguistic Approach: The Case of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Mohammad Javad Ansari. (2016). The Acquisition of Phrasal Verbs through Cognitive Linguistic Approach: The Case of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.1p.185
title: Teach phrasal verbs by explaining and categorizing particle meanings with visual aids rather than translation alone
description: The article recommends that teachers use the cognitive-linguistic approach to teach phrasal verbs: "the teachers and instructors are recommended to use it so as to teach the PVs." In the treatment, particles were explained and categorized according to their functions, with visual aids and non-prototypical examples, focusing attention on particles and their meanings rather than whole-verb translations.
requirements: Instruction must explain particle meanings and categorize them by function, supported by visual aids
constraints: The author recommends using cognitive linguistics as a complementary aid besides other approaches and methods, not as a new method
target_learning_goals: acquisition of phrasal verbs with orientational particles
examples: In the study, the experimental group received a 25-minute treatment in which particles were explained, categorized by function, illustrated with visual aids, and practiced with one non-prototypical example per particle
key_sources: Mohammad Javad Ansari. (2016). The Acquisition of Phrasal Verbs through Cognitive Linguistic Approach: The Case of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.1p.185

article_title: A Mindful Approach to Teaching Emotional Intelligence to Undergraduate Students Online and in Person
citation: Cotler, J. L., DiTursi, D., Goldstein, I., Yates, J., & DelBelso, D. (2017). A Mindful Approach to Teaching Emotional Intelligence to Undergraduate Students Online and in Person. Information Systems Education Journal, 15(1). http://isedj.org
title: Use team-based learning format to provide a safe environment for developing EI skills
description: The article states that team-based learning in an academic setting provides a safe environment to develop EI skills for individuals who might be less comfortable with extensive peer interaction. All sections in the study used a team-based learning format, and interviews identified team-based learning as a key theme enabling experiential learning opportunities. Students worked with the same group all semester, which one student credited with increased awareness of others.
requirements: Maintaining the same teams throughout the semester
Team-based activities that apply workshop content immediately with peers
constraints: Findings may not be generalizable to non-team-based learning settings
target_learners: undergraduate students including those less comfortable with extensive peer interaction
target_learning_goals: emotional and social intelligence skills including awareness of others and collaboration
examples: One student reported noticing awareness of others more since working with the same group all semester long
key_sources: Cotler, J. L., DiTursi, D., Goldstein, I., Yates, J., & DelBelso, D. (2017). A Mindful Approach to Teaching Emotional Intelligence to Undergraduate Students Online and in Person. Information Systems Education Journal, 15(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1135358

article_title: Animation Based Learning of Electronic Devices
citation: Gero, A., Zoabi, W., & Sabag, N. (2014). Animation Based Learning of Electronic Devices. Advances in Engineering Education, 4(1), Winter 2014. https://journals.gmu.edu/aaa/issue/winter-2014
title: Teacher-presented non-interactive animation with spatially and temporally contiguous verbal explanation is a viable instructional pattern for complex devices.
description: The article describes a lesson pattern in which a non-interactive animation without its own narration is presented to the class by the teacher, who provides verbal explanations in temporal proximity to the animation. The teacher also calls students' attention to key details and specifies the animation's limitations in order to avoid misconceptions.
requirements: Written text must be incorporated in spatial proximity to the animation, and excess items distracting the learner must be avoided.
The teacher's verbal explanations should be given in informal language, using the first and second person.
constraints: The animation is non-interactive and does not include its own narration, requiring the teacher to present it.
target_learning_goals: understanding the structure and principle of operation of complex electronic devices
examples: The lesson dealing with the BJT was based on the use of animation without supplemental material, presented to the class by the teacher.
key_sources: Gero, A., Zoabi, W., & Sabag, N. (2014). Animation Based Learning of Electronic Devices. Advances in Engineering Education, 4(1), Winter 2014. https://journals.gmu.edu/aaa/issue/winter-2014

article_title: Improve Knowledge, Beliefs and Behavior of Undergraduate Female Nursing Students in Al-Alzhar University toward Breast Self-Examination Practice
citation: Abd El-Mohsen, A. S., & Abd El-Maksoud, M. M. (2015). Improve Knowledge, Beliefs and Behavior of Undergraduate Female Nursing Students in Al-Alzhar University toward Breast Self-Examination Practice. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.8. https://www.iiste.org
title: Breast cancer awareness and early detection should be taught in nursing students' undergraduate courses
description: The article recommends integrating breast cancer awareness and early detection content into undergraduate nursing curricula, stating: "this study emphasizes that the need to teach nursing stude nts breast cancer awareness and early detection of breast canc er in their undergraduate courses." This is grounded in the finding that students showed significant knowledge deficiency and poor BSE practice before the educational intervention, and that the training program significantly improved all three outcome domains.
requirements: Educational programs addressing gaps not covered in detail in existing coursework
target_learning_goals: breast cancer awareness
early detection practices
preventive health behaviors
examples: The study implemented a four-session program (two theoretical, two practical reinforcement) at the Health Technical Institute, Al-Alzhar University
key_sources: Abd El-Mohsen, A. S., & Abd El-Maksoud, M. M. (2015). Improve Knowledge, Beliefs and Behavior of Undergraduate Female Nursing Students in Al-Alzhar University toward Breast Self-Examination Practice. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.8. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1082729

article_title: Play and Productivity: Enhancing the Creative Climate at Workplace Meetings with Play Cues
citation: West, Samuel E., Eva Hoff, and Ingegerd Carlsson. (2016). Play and Productivity: Enhancing the Creative Climate at Workplace Meetings with Play Cues. American Journal of Play, 9(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1111974
title: Team climate for innovation: four factors facilitating team innovation
description: West's (1990) theory of team climate for innovation consists of four factors: vision (shared commitment to clearly defined objectives), participative safety (a nonjudgmental climate where members propose ideas without fear of criticism), task orientation (commitment to excellence and continuous improvement of procedures), and support for innovation (organizational expectation and active support for innovative behavior). Reliable measures based on this model have been developed.
requirements: Existing climate measures do not focus on meetings, so meeting-specific measures may be needed
target_learning_goals: team innovation
creative climate
examples: The article's own five-criterion meeting creativity climate measure drew on this model, covering collaboration, openness, engagement, and participation
key_sources: West, Samuel E., Eva Hoff, and Ingegerd Carlsson. (2016). Play and Productivity: Enhancing the Creative Climate at Workplace Meetings with Play Cues. American Journal of Play, 9(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1123863

article_title: Effects of a Teacher Training Programme on Symptoms of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
citation: Froelich, J., Breuer, D., Doepfner, M., & Amonn, F. (2012). Effects of a teacher training programme on symptoms of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. International Journal of Special Education, 27(3), 76-87. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ976560
title: Teacher knowledge, attitudes, and classroom practices influence the behaviour and performance of students with ADHD
description: The article proposes that teachers' knowledge and attitudes about ADHD shape their classroom practices, which in turn affect student outcomes. Teachers tend to hold more negative attitudes towards students with ADHD, may demand less, call on them less frequently, criticise more and praise less, and may thereby negatively affect these students' behaviour and performance. This account motivates teacher training as a point of intervention.
requirements: Teachers must be aware of their own attitudes and practices towards students with ADHD
target_learning_goals: recognise how teacher attitudes and practices affect students with ADHD
key_sources: Froelich, J., Breuer, D., Doepfner, M., & Amonn, F. (2012). Effects of a teacher training programme on symptoms of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. International Journal of Special Education, 27(3), 76-87. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1001061

article_title: Introducing Intertextuality-Aware Instruction as a Novel Approach of Teaching Reading Passages in EFL Context
citation: Khaghaninejad, M. S. (2014). Introducing intertextuality-aware instruction as a novel approach of teaching reading passages in EFL context. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 18(1), 65-83. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075042
title: Teachers should develop professional knowledge of intertextuality to raise learners' consciousness and deepen text meaning
description: The article concludes that "a good language teacher needs to be conscious regarding the role played by intertextuality in different reading passages" to improve comprehension and help learners cope with intertextual challenges. It insists teachers should develop professional expertise in intertextuality tenets so students can access deeper meaning of texts.
requirements: Teacher professional development in intertextuality analysis before classroom implementation
constraints: Grounded in one quasi-experimental study with intermediate Iranian EFL learners
target_learning_goals: teachers' professional knowledge of intertextuality
learners' deeper reading comprehension
examples: The experimental treatment raised learners' consciousness of intertextuality types and reporting ways across ten sessions on selected passages
key_sources: Khaghaninejad, M. S. (2014). Introducing intertextuality-aware instruction as a novel approach of teaching reading passages in EFL context. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 18(1), 65-83. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1047451

article_title: Fostering the Computation Competence of Low Achievers through Cooperative Learning in Inclusive Classrooms: A Longitudinal Study
citation: Moser Opitz, E., Grob, U., Wittich, C., Häsel-Weide, U., & Nührenbörger, M. (2018). Fostering the Computation Competence of Low Achievers Through Cooperative Learning in Inclusive Classrooms: A Longitudinal Study. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 16(1), 19-35.
title: testSTRAT dual-task computation strategy assessment instrument
description: testSTRAT is a researcher-developed test assessing computation strategies through a "dual task" in which students tap regularly on the table at 120 beats per minute while solving computation problems presented on screen. Persistent counters are expected to stop or irregularize tapping or switch to counting strategies. Strategies are categorized as retrieval (answer within 3 sec), decomposition, or counting, with items scored 0 for incorrect, 1 for correct with counting, and 2 for correct by retrieval or decomposition.
requirements: Individual administration in a quiet room with a test administrator timing responses and probing strategy use when processing exceeds 3 seconds or tapping is irregular
constraints: The authors note the test "was possibly not sensitive enough to measure the development of non-counting strategies"
target_learners: Grade-2 students with below-average mathematics achievement
target_learning_goals: Assessment of computation strategy use (counting, decomposition, retrieval)
examples: The test included 13 computation problems at pretest and 19 items at posttest and follow-up, e.g. 8 + 7 and 42 – 39
key_sources: Moser Opitz, E., Grob, U., Wittich, C., Häsel-Weide, U., & Nührenbörger, M. (2018). Fostering the Computation Competence of Low Achievers Through Cooperative Learning in Inclusive Classrooms: A Longitudinal Study. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 16(1), 19-35. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1179942

article_title: Can an Interactive Learning Path on a Tablet PC Counter Misconceptions on the Formation of Clouds and Wind?
citation: Steegen, A.; Hasendonckx, F.; Cock, M. (2018). Can an Interactive Learning Path on A Tablet PC Counter Misconceptions on the Formation of Clouds and Wind? Review of International Geographical Education Online (RIGEO), 8 (1), 53-73. http://www.rigeo.org/vol8no1/Number1Spring/RIGEO-V8-N1-3.pdf
title: Teachers must be aware of student misconceptions before teaching content that targets them
description: The article concludes that the role of the teacher remains important in pointing at and confronting students with possible difficulties or misconceptions within the learning content, and that the first condition is that teachers are aware of these misconceptions before teaching the content. Observing teachers in the study never mentioned the explicit focus on misconceptions as a positive element, and were not conscious of the misconceptions the experiments reinforced.
requirements: Teachers must possess awareness of common student misconceptions before teaching content designed to confront them
constraints: Earlier research in Belgium (Cox, Steegen & De Cock, 2016) already proved a lack of teacher awareness of misconceptions in relation to another topic
target_learning_goals: effective misconception-targeting instruction
conceptual change in earth science topics
examples: Five of six observing teachers completed a survey; none mentioned the strong emphasis on misconceptions and explicit physics references as a positive element
key_sources: Steegen, A.; Hasendonckx, F.; Cock, M. (2018). Can an Interactive Learning Path on A Tablet PC Counter Misconceptions on the Formation of Clouds and Wind? Review of International Geographical Education Online (RIGEO), 8 (1), 53-73. http://www.rigeo.org/vol8no1/Number1Spring/RIGEO-V8-N1-3.pdf

article_title: Using Data to Inform Decisions: How Teachers Use Data to Inform Practice and Improve Student Performance in Mathematics
citation: Cavalluzzo, L., Geraghty, T. M., Steele, J. L., & Alexander, J. K. (2013). Using Data to Inform Decisions: How Teachers Use Data to Inform Practice and Improve Student Performance in Mathematics. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract.
title: TERC's Using Data (UD) professional development program
description: The Using Data program, developed with NSF funding by researchers at TERC and WestEd, provides professional development and technical assistance aimed at helping teachers improve instruction through collaborative analysis of student data and action plans addressing systemic learning problems. As tested, it rolls out over a 2-year period. Data teams of four participating teachers and a data coach work through data analysis using collaborative inquiry, with data coaches typically school-based service providers such as instructional specialists.
requirements: Data teams formed as part of the program consist of four participating teachers and a data coach who leads the team through collaborative inquiry data analysis.
constraints: The program as tested rolls out over a 2-year period, so one-year results capture only early implementation.
target_learners: Elementary teachers of grades 4 and 5 mathematics
target_learning_goals: Teachers' data literacy, data-use knowledge and skills, and use of data to inform mathematics instruction
examples: Sixty schools in a large southeastern urban district were randomized, with 30 treatment schools receiving the UD program and 30 control schools continuing practice as usual.

article_title: Motivating Students through Positive Learning Experiences: A Comparison of Three Learning Designs for Computer Programming Courses

description: The article applies ten criteria of "positive experiences" developed by Jantzen et al. (2011) to analyze students' emotional responses to learning designs: Interactive, Near, Intimate, Authentic, Unique, Involving, Lively, Learning, Understanding, and Interesting. article_title: Unpacking the teaching-research nexus: a phenomenographic analysis of student experiences in a medical university.
citation: Lek M, Stenfors T, Palmgren PJ. (2026). Unpacking the teaching–research nexus: a phenomenographic analysis of student experiences in a medical university. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10653-5
title: The teaching–research nexus as a relational, context-dependent construct experienced by students
description: The article frames the teaching–research nexus as "a relational construct, where students may express understandings ranging from peripheral engagement to more central participation in research processes." The nexus is not a fixed structure but a context-dependent and evolving relationship requiring careful pedagogical design. The article deliberately inverts the usual research–teaching nexus term to focus on students' learning experiences rather than research productivity.
requirements: Pedagogical design that makes research visible and meaningful within the curriculum
constraints: The nexus is context-dependent and shaped by institutional conditions; the relationship is not inherently unidirectional

target_learning_goals: understanding of research
critical thinking
evidence-based decision-making
examples: The study at Karolinska Institutet treated research connection, anchored in Swedish higher education legislation, as equivalent to the teaching–research nexus

article_title: Development and validation of the teachers generative AI professional competence scale.
citation: Aldighrir Wafa Mohammed. (2026). Development and validation of the teachers generative AI professional competence scale. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-65021-6
title: Teachers' Generative AI Pedagogical Judgment, Ethical Leadership, and Professional Agency Scale
description: The Teachers' Generative AI Pedagogical Judgment, Ethical Leadership, and Professional Agency Scale is a 30-item self-report instrument measuring three domains of teachers' professional competence with generative AI. Items 1-10 assess pedagogical judgment, items 11-20 assess ethical leadership, and items 21-30 assess professional agency, all rated on a 5-point Likert scale. The scale was developed through a sequential exploratory mixed-method design involving construct specification, expert review, translation, cognitive pretesting, and psychometric validation with 648 Saudi teachers.
requirements: Respondents must be currently employed classroom teachers with at least minimal familiarity with generative AI tools and recent teaching-related AI use
constraints: The scale was validated with a non-probability web-based sample of teachers in Saudi Arabia, which does not lend itself to claims of statistical representativeness
target_learning_goals: Assessing teachers' professional competence in the responsible use of generative AI

citation: Beres Adam, Ramagiri Lahari, Zhou Jonathan, Prats Michael I, Bahner David. (2026). Transesophageal Echocardiography – Student Early Engagement in Didactic Sonography (TEE-SEEDS). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09600-1
title: TEE-SEEDS simulator-based training protocol
description: A short simulator-based TEE training protocol using the HeartWorks TEE simulator. Students watch an instructional video, then receive 10 minutes of hands-on simulator time covering four standard TEE views: "mid-esophageal four-chamber, mid-esophageal long axis, transgastric short axis, and mid-esophageal bicaval." The session includes faculty demonstration, practice with faculty input, independent view acquisition, and pre/post confidence surveys and knowledge quizzes. The protocol was designed to be brief, addressing curriculum time barriers.

Availability of ultrasound-trained faculty to lead training sessions
constraints: TEE simulators are expensive and not accessible at all schools, limiting generalizability
target_learning_goals: Obtain four standard TEE views
Identify cardiac anatomy on TEE images
Build confidence with TEE and cardiac ultrasound
examples: Second- and fourth-year students received 10 minutes of hands-on simulator time with 5 minutes of practice and 5 minutes of independent view acquisition

citation: Humblet Martien H., Jacobs Esmee M. R., Bagenda Godfrey, Mujumbusi Lazaaro, Lingard Lorelei, Leroy Piet L. J. M., Van Mook Walther N. K. (2026). “Building the boat while sailing” – adapting towards telementoring literacy. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09641-6
title: Telementoring literacy: the adaptive capability of clinicians at both ends of the digital connection to effectively engage with clinical skill training and patient care through telementored interactions
description: The article introduces telementoring literacy as the adaptive capacity of clinicians — at both ends of the digital connection — to effectively engage with clinical skill training and patient care through telementored interactions. It frames this as a layered relationship between capabilities, competencies and skills, refined from existing digital literacy models to emphasize iterative and adaptive development in response to contextual demands, and positions it as extending beyond discrete competencies toward capability and adaptability in variable contexts.
requirements: Requires iterative, reciprocal adaptations between trainees and mentors to navigate the affordances and constraints of the technology-enhanced learning environment.
constraints: The adaptive and situated nature of complex learning remains underacknowledged in existing literacy models, which may complicate expectation management when literacy is positioned as a high-order educational outcome.

target_learning_goals: Adaptive engagement with clinical skill training and patient care through telementored interactions

title: A two-cycle design-based research telementoring program for pediatric POCUS in Uganda using a portable ultrasound device with telementoring software
description: The intervention comprised a two-week in-person POCUS course followed by recurrent, synchronous telementoring sessions using a portable ultrasound device (Philips Lumify™) with telementoring software via tablet (REACTS™). The tablet camera provided a vantage point for the mentor to assess hand and probe handling, and a pointer feature (green dot) allowed the mentor to overlay a pointer on the live ultrasound feed to support instruction and feedback. Twenty telementoring sessions took place (11 in cycle 1 and 9 in cycle 2), with cycle 2 adaptations including fortnightly scheduling, expanded practice beyond tuberculosis, and simplified standard operating procedures.
requirements: A two-week in-person course was considered a necessary basis for continued remote training via telementoring, and a standard operating procedure described setting up the connection and acquiring, saving and reporting POCUS images.
constraints: Due to workload and time constraints, participation narrowed from twenty-four clinicians trained in person to five key users, of whom only two continued into the second cycle.
target_learners: Pediatricians, clinical officers, medical officers and nurses in resource-limited settings
target_learning_goals: Pediatric point-of-care ultrasound competency development (lung and mediastinal POCUS)

title: Three design principles — authentic learning, deliberate practice, and scaffolding complexity — guiding iterative design of telementoring sessions
description: The article's instructional design was guided by three theoretical principles: deliberate practice (effortful, goal-directed skill development and refinement, supported by expert feedback under conditions of high standards and psychological safety), Herrington's principle of authenticity (learning opportunities reflecting real-world settings and tasks reflecting the complexity of real-life practice), and scaffolding complexity within Merrill's first principle of instruction (the gradual increase in task difficulty alongside the progressive reduction of mentor support). These principles shaped a two-cycle iterative design, evaluation and re-design of telementoring sessions following initial in-person POCUS training.
requirements: The intervention has to be grounded in theory and follow iterative cycles of design, implementation, and evaluation, as per the design-based research approach.
constraints: Adaptations were made throughout the project to adhere to the needs of participants within their authentic settings, such as adapting learning tasks to reflect prevalent clinical pathologies.
target_learning_goals: POCUS skill mastery through telementored practice

article_title: Impact of a vertically integrated, symptom-oriented teaching program for hematuria management on clinical competency transfer among urology clerkship students.
citation: Peng Shuang, Wei Yongbao, Dai Caixia, Liang Yuxuan, Huang Li. (2026). BMC Medical Education, 26, Article 1348. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09680-z
title: 10-minute, two-station, four-domain modified OSCE for end-of-rotation competency assessment
description: A feasibility-oriented modification of the traditional multi-station OSCE for competency evaluation. Two stations simulated outpatient initial decision-making/management/communication situations, and responses were mapped to four competency domains (each 0–25 points): history taking and stratification, interpretation of investigations, safe management, communication/follow-up, yielding an OSCE total score of 0-100. It was administered uniformly at the end of the rotation with a total duration of 10 min per student.
requirements: Standardized cases, a unified scoring form, and pre-defined scoring anchors explained before administration to ensure consistent scoring criteria
constraints: Single-rater scoring was used, and the rater was not blinded to group allocation
Formal inter-rater reliability such as the intraclass correlation coefficient and internal consistency were not calculated
target_learning_goals: Competency transfer from knowledge to contextual decision-making and safe behaviors
examples: Station 1 was the outpatient initial decision-making station (5 min), simulating the initial visit for hematuria; station 2 was the management and communication station (5 min), simulating a high-risk hematuria scenario such as clot retention or anticoagulation-related hematuria.

article_title: Help! I Have to Assist My Child With Reading and Spelling: Mothers' Teaching Self-Efficacy and Mother-Child Conflict During Homework.
citation: de Jong Peter F.; Zee Marjolein. (2026). Help! I Have to Assist My Child With Reading and Spelling: Mothers' Teaching Self‐Efficacy and Mother–Child Conflict During Homework. Dyslexia. https://doi.org/10.1002/dys.70048
title: Parents' teaching self-efficacy as a proximal mechanism linking parental and contextual factors to parent–child conflict during homework
description: The article conceptualizes a model in which relatively distal parent and contextual characteristics are linked to a more proximal, situation-specific mechanism—parents' self-efficacy in supporting their child—and, in turn, to parent–child conflict. This ordering is grounded in an integration of Belsky's process model and Bandura's social-cognitive theory, which together suggest that parenting behaviours and family interactions arise from multiple interacting influences that shape parents' self-efficacy beliefs, which in turn guide parents' interactive behaviour. Parents' teaching efficacy is positioned as a proximal mechanism through which these influences may translate into parent–child conflict during homework.
requirements: Homework is assigned by a clinic as part of a formal dyslexia treatment and must be completed approximately four to six times per week
constraints: The cross-sectional design means the directionality implied in the model should be interpreted as theoretically informed
target_learners: Mothers of children with dyslexia receiving clinic-based treatment
target_learning_goals: Supporting children's reading and spelling practice at home
Reducing mother–child conflict during homework
examples: The hypothesized relationships among the variables were presented in a path model (Figure 1)

article_title: Is procrastination among students lower in group work? Evidence from a registered field experiment.
citation: Koppenborg, Markus, Hüffmeier, Joachim, & Klingsieck, Katrin B. (2026). Is procrastination among students lower in group work? Evidence from a registered field experiment. British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70069
title: Team member Effort Expenditure Model (TEEM): indispensability perceptions raise the expectancy component and produce effort gains in group work
description: TEEM explains why group work can increase individual effort and performance relative to individual work. Drawing on expectancy × value theories of motivation, it holds that "group as compared to individual work leads to effort gains, if any of its three components are more pronounced in group as compared to individual work": the expectancy component (behaviour-outcome relationship), the value of the behaviour or its consequences, and the cost/benefit ratio of effort. Perceived indispensability of one's contribution raises the expectancy component. The article extends this account to procrastination, proposing that indispensability activates prosocial motives and norm compliance.
requirements: The own contribution must be perceived as indispensable for the group product, which depends on task structure (conjunctive vs. additive) and relative member ability.
constraints: Indispensability perceptions are less pronounced in additive group work, where weak contributions can be partly compensated by stronger members; effects have not always been found for additive structures.
target_learners: students working on group assignments in higher education
target_learning_goals: individual effort
task performance
reduced procrastination in group work
examples: The experiment operationalized TEEM by informing conjunctive-condition participants that the worst bibliography determined group compensation, and additive-condition participants that the average across three bibliographies determined it, while all were led to perceive low relative ability.
key_sources: Koppenborg, Markus, Hüffmeier, Joachim, & Klingsieck, Katrin B. (2026). Is procrastination among students lower in group work? Evidence from a registered field experiment. British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70069

Two sessions were run, one midway and one in the last week of the cardiovascular module; each had two rounds of 40–50 MCQs aligned to Bloom's levels 1–3, with each team using "a single device to log into the Kahoot! platform" and 60–90 seconds per question for discussion and consensus. Double points, streak bonuses, and certificates for the top three teams added motivational elements, followed by answer explanations.

citation: Waechter Jason, Kusnoor Anita, Eickman Kara, Smith David, Wong Matt, Rogers Suzanne, Lee Chel Hee. (2026). title: TeachingMedicine.com virtual patient platform with automated scoring and individualized feedback
description: A computer-based virtual patient simulation platform on which students complete staged diagnostic cases (introduction, history, physical exam, investigations), building and revising a differential diagnosis of up to five conditions and assigning findings as pertinent positives or negatives. Each case generates "over 125 data points" that drive "individualized automated formative feedback for each completed case", covering Ddx building, DxJ, test ordering, cognitive errors, and final diagnosis. Expert-created algorithmic scorecards for each scenario
Cases spaced every 3–4 weeks throughout pre-clerkship

The platform's owner has a financial interest in the curriculum

description: The article concludes that educators should "specify how and when AI chatbots should be used, promote autonomy and collaboration in student cultures and teach students about the value of cognitive effort to learning". article_title: Supporting comprehension: The advantages of multiple-choice over true-false practice tests.
citation: Hildenbrand Lena; Wiley Jennifer. (2025). Supporting comprehension: The advantages of multiple–choice over true—false practice tests. Memory & Cognition. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-025-01726-9
title: Three-level text representation framework (surface, text-base, situation model) framing comprehension measurement
description: The article adopts the text-comprehension distinction that learning from text requires processing at multiple levels of representation: surface, text-base, and situation-model. As printed, "At the surface level the text is represented in the exact words as they appear. The text-base level then represents the propositional contents of the text. Finally, the situation-model level captures the implicit relations between ideas within a text as well as their connections with prior knowledge." This framework motivates using inference questions rather than memory questions to measure comprehension, since real learning from a text requires constructing a coherent mental model rather than reproducing presented wording.
requirements: Measuring comprehension requires inference questions that prompt learners to verify implicit relations or apply information to novel situations, rather than memory-based reproduction questions.
target_learning_goals: comprehension and situation-model construction from text
examples: The experiments used only inference questions from Griffin et al. texts as practice and final test items, because the focus was comprehension rather than verbatim memory.

description: The article proposes a ten-phase RaT programme for the Faculty of Medicine of Sousse, inspired by the AMEE Guide's three underlying frameworks: Kellogg's Programme Logic Model for programme design, Dundee's three-circle model for educational content, and Kirkpatrick's pyramid for evaluation. The phases run from needs assessment and goal-setting through curriculum development, faculty development, resident training sessions, teaching opportunities, assessment and feedback, curriculum integration, evaluation and continuous improvement, acknowledgement and rewards, to long-term sustainability. The authors state the AMEE guide reported that "the potential benefits of RaT programmes resides in the enhancement of teaching abilities, which leads to greater self-efficacy and teacher identity."

Securing institutional and external funding for sustainability
A leadership succession plan to maintain quality

Patient care outcomes as the ultimate goal "requires currently further research"

target_learning_goals: Teaching ability, self-efficacy and teacher identity, capacity to evaluate and give feedback, interest in education as a career
examples: A prize is proposed for the best resident as teacher at the faculty's annual ceremony, alongside assistants, associate professors and professors

article_title: High-fidelity telesimulation to teach lactation skills to primary care residents, a cluster randomized educational trial.
citation: Hoyt-Austin A, Sadovnikova A, Muñoz S, Donohue LT, Tancredi DJ, Kair LR. (2025). High-fidelity telesimulation to teach lactation skills to primary care residents, a cluster randomized educational trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08118-2
title: High-fidelity telesimulation standardized patient encounter for clinical lactation education
description: A 30-minute videoconference-based standardized patient encounter in which residents complete an unfolding case on maternal breast engorgement with delayed lactogenesis, followed by targeted feedback. "Standardized patients wore a high-fidelity lactation simulation model in case of need for telemedicine examination or questioning by the physician trainees." Standardized patients were lactation consultants trained to give feedback using a validated assessment instrument, and sessions were delivered through LiquidGoldConcept via an institutional license.
requirements: Standardized patients trained in the case and in providing targeted clinical lactation feedback using a validated formative and summative assessment instrument
An institutional license for the telesimulation platform and asynchronous pre-work completed before the encounter
constraints: The study version was delivered during the COVID-19 pandemic with both arms receiving education via videoconferencing
target_learning_goals: clinical lactation skills including obtaining a breastfeeding history, breast examination, assisting with infant latch, and managing common breastfeeding concerns
examples: Intervention groups self-scheduled the 30-minute encounter (20 minutes with the standardized patient plus 10 minutes of oral feedback) asynchronously within Canvas during a 4-week well newborn rotation

article_title: The relation between teaching-related self-efficacy and general job-related well-being - a cross-sectional study among young physicians.
citation: Kiver Benjamin, Berberat Pascal O., Gartmeier Martin. (2025). The relation between teaching-related self-efficacy and general job-related well-being – a cross-sectional study among young physicians. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://journals.publisso.de/en/journals/jme/volume42/zma001777
title: Teaching-related self-efficacy as a domain-specific self-efficacy construct
description: The article applies Bandura's self-efficacy concept, an individual's confidence in their own resources for coping with challenges, to the teaching domain. It defines teaching-related self-efficacy as "the assessment of one's own abilities to design didactic measures that best support students in achieving specific learning goals". The article treats it as domain- or task-specific, distinct from global self-efficacy, and measures it with an adapted Pfitzner scale (Cronbach's alpha 0.75). It serves as the central explanatory variable linked to job-related well-being components.
requirements: Measured with validated self-report scales; the article's scale required adaptation of items after Pfitzner et al. and showed a Cronbach's alpha of 0.75
constraints: Hypotheses were formulated only after data collection, rendering the analyses exploratory; the study is cross-sectional and cannot draw causal conclusions
target_learners: young physicians with teaching duties at university hospitals
target_learning_goals: didactic competence for designing courses that support student learning
examples: The study surveyed 293 physicians using an adapted teacher self-efficacy scale alongside well-being measures during mandatory lecturer training at TUM University Hospital
key_sources: Kiver Benjamin, Berberat Pascal O., Gartmeier Martin. (2025). The relation between teaching-related self-efficacy and general job-related well-being – a cross-sectional study among young physicians. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://journals.publisso.de/en/journals/jme/volume42/zma001777

article_title: Characteristic competencies for effective teachers in healthcare education.
citation: Iahn-Aun Marina; Aun Marcelo Vivolo; Pereira Welbert Oliveira. (2025). Characteristic competencies for effective teachers in healthcare education. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12539862/
title: Teacher knowledge spans academic content, general pedagogical, and pedagogical content knowledge, providing credibility and security
description: The review treats teacher knowledge as a foundational competence involving theoretical and technical knowledge plus professional and academic experience, which provides "credibility to the classes" and security during teaching. It reports a three-way division from the literature: academic content knowledge (factual knowledge of a topic), general pedagogical knowledge (implementing general teaching skills), and pedagogical content knowledge (based on theoretical knowledge and practical experience). Minor knowledge gaps can be compensated by other competencies, but lack of mastery of subject or methodology is noticed by students and harms engagement and learning.
requirements: Teachers must thoroughly understand their subject and its underlying scientific principles; without this knowledge teaching is impossible, per the review
constraints: Small knowledge gaps are common in dynamic classrooms and can be complemented by other well-developed competencies
target_learning_goals: credible, accurate subject teaching that supports student engagement
key_sources: Iahn-Aun Marina; Aun Marcelo Vivolo; Pereira Welbert Oliveira. (2025). Characteristic competencies for effective teachers in healthcare education. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12539862/

article_title: Characteristic competencies for effective teachers in healthcare education.
citation: Iahn-Aun Marina; Aun Marcelo Vivolo; Pereira Welbert Oliveira. (2025). Characteristic competencies for effective teachers in healthcare education. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12539862/
title: Integrate self-reflection into continuous teacher development so teachers become autonomous learners who adapt teaching to student needs
description: The review describes self-reflection as educators' ability to think critically and constantly about their classes, activities and students' outcomes, recognized as essential for professional behavior in health education. Teachers who practice constant self-reflection "evolve faster and enhance their teaching skills". Integrating reflection into teacher training lets teachers assess pedagogical performance, understand strengths and limitations, and become autonomous learners with greater ability to identify and correct issues affecting teaching performance.
requirements: Reflection should be embedded in continuous professional development; exchanging experiences with other teachers facilitates reflection
target_learners: healthcare teachers in training and practicing faculty
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of teaching performance and adaptation to student needs
key_sources: Iahn-Aun Marina; Aun Marcelo Vivolo; Pereira Welbert Oliveira. (2025). Characteristic competencies for effective teachers in healthcare education. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12539862/

article_title: Moderated mediation of technostress, TPACK, and growth mindset on competency in interdisciplinary teaching among STEM lecturers.
citation: Su Wenhao, Fadzil Hidayah Mohd, Rauf Rose Amnah Abd. (2025). Moderated mediation of technostress, TPACK, and growth mindset on competency in interdisciplinary teaching among STEM lecturers. Scientific Reports 15, 37633. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-21476-7
title: Integrated moderated mediation framework combining TPACK, the Iceberg Competency Model, and Implicit Theories to explain CIT under technostress
description: The article integrates three models into one framework for how STEM lecturers develop competency in interdisciplinary teaching under technostress. TPACK "captures measurable instructional capacity, the Iceberg model highlights the layered nature of competence, and Implicit Theories explain how individual beliefs modulate the development process." Technostress is interpreted as arising from perceived TPACK misalignments, while growth mindset acts as a psychological buffer linking cognitive dispositions to observable instructional competencies. The framework was empirically validated via PLS-SEM with 405 lecturers.
requirements: Measurement of technostress, TPACK, CIT, and growth mindset as latent constructs, operationalized with validated scales
constraints: The Iceberg model is applied as a conceptual scaffold only, not as a direct operational basis for measurement
The TPACK framework has limited explanatory scope for stress-specific processes
target_learning_goals: Competency in interdisciplinary teaching
Integration of technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge
examples: The framework was tested with a cross-sectional survey of 405 Chinese STEM lecturers using PLS-SEM, explaining 58.0% of CIT variance.
key_sources: Su Wenhao, Fadzil Hidayah Mohd, Rauf Rose Amnah Abd. (2025). Moderated mediation of technostress, TPACK, and growth mindset on competency in interdisciplinary teaching among STEM lecturers. Scientific Reports 15, 37633. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-21476-7

article_title: Entrustment of student supervision to GP trainees - a qualitative interview study of factors influencing entrustment decisions.
citation: Gehrke-Beck Sabine, Holzhausen Ylva. (2025). Entrustment of student supervision to GP trainees - a qualitative interview study of factors influencing entrustment decisions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07870-9
title: Schematic entrustment model of factors influencing GPs' decisions to entrust GP trainees with student supervision
description: The article presents a schematic model (Fig. 1) integrating the factors found in the interviews into an entrustment model for teaching, "which is based on the clinical entrustment models" of Gin and colleagues and Holzhausen and colleagues. It organizes trainee factors (enjoyment of teaching, teaching skills, familiarity with the practice environment, knowledge), GP factors, the GP-trainee relationship, task characteristics, context factors, and perceived risks as inputs to the GP's entrustment decision. The article argues the concept of entrustment applies to delegation of teaching responsibilities in general practice.
requirements: Applying the model requires weighing trainee capability, GP needs, task and context factors as reported by the GP making the entrustment decision
constraints: Derived from a single qualitative study of student supervision in German general practice; the authors state findings are limited to teaching tasks related to supervision of students in that setting
Reliability, integrity and humility, important in clinical entrustment, were not explicitly mentioned by respondents
target_learners: GP trainees (postgraduate medical trainees) in general practice settings
target_learning_goals: Supervision of medical students as a teaching professional activity
Explicit entrustment decisions about teaching responsibilities
examples: Figure 1 integrates the factors found in the interviews into a schematic entrustment model based on clinical entrustment models

citation: Lazarides, R., Frenkel, J., Petković, U., Göllner, R., & Hellwich, O. (2025). 'No words'—Machine‐learning classified nonverbal immediacy and its role in connecting teacher self‐efficacy with perceived teaching and student interest. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(Suppl. 1), S15–S31. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12732
title: Teacher education and training should include a focus on nonverbal immediacy because it fosters student perceptions of enthusiastic teaching and subsequent interest
description: The article recommends that teacher preparation attend to teachers' nonverbal communication: 'nonverbal communication in terms of body language, facial expressions and physical proximity foster student perceptions of enthusiastic teaching behaviours and subsequent student interest'. On this basis it states that 'teacher education and training that includes a focus on NVI might benefit both teaching and learning', highlighting instructional strategies that let teachers express enthusiasm and interact closely with students.
requirements: Teachers need opportunities to learn instructional strategies that allow them to express enthusiasm and interact closely with students
constraints: The article notes fostering teachers' NVI could potentially also shape their TSESE, which it leaves open for future research
The supporting evidence is limited to mathematics lessons on quadratic equations with 50 teachers

examples: In the study, teachers higher in TSESE displayed higher machine-learning assessed NVI, which related to students' ratings of enthusiastic teaching and, in Model 2, to post-lesson interest

article_title: Predictive validity of admission tests and educational attainment on preclinical academic performance - a multisite study.
citation: Jaehn M, Hissbach J, Frickhoeffer M, Weppert D, Zimmerhofer A, Hampe W, Kadmon M, Becker N. (2025). Predictive validity of admission tests and educational attainment on preclinical academic performance – a multisite study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07974-2
title: Test-criterion content match hypothesis
description: The article invokes the test-criterion content match hypothesis, attributed to Sackett et al., to explain why certain admission subtests predict academic performance better than others. It holds that predictors correlate more strongly with outcomes when their content closely matches the criterion's content: "subtests covering a substantial amount of medical or scientific content and containing elements of both crystallized and fluid intelligence" showed the strongest associations with preclinical performance. The study uses this framework to interpret its subtest-level correlation patterns and to guide future combination of TMS and HAM-Nat subtests.
requirements: Subtest-level validity analyses that distinguish content-rich from content-poor subtests within an admission test
constraints: The article applies the hypothesis to preclinical academic performance in undergraduate medical entry; it does not test it against clinical-year or postgraduate outcomes
target_learners: undergraduate medical school applicants and students
target_learning_goals: selection of applicants likely to succeed academically in preclinical medical training
examples: The study's subtest analyses found the HAM-Nat knowledge test and the TMS reasoning and text-comprehension subtests (BMS, QFP, TC, DT) most strongly associated with PCGPA and M1

citation: Tseng Yi-Ling, Wu Hua-Shan, Huang Pei-Yu, Hsaio Pei-Shan, Tseng Hui-Chen. (2025). Effects of a Situated Simulation Teaching Strategy on Knowledge of Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy among Surgical Nurses in Taiwan. Advances in Skin & Wound Care. https://doi.org/10.1097/ASW.0000000000000293
title: Researcher-developed 10-item NPWT knowledge evaluation scale for surgical nurses
description: A self-administered, semistructured two-part questionnaire developed by the researchers after literature review and consultation with three wound experts. The knowledge part contains 10 items covering "NPWT indications and effects, operation process of NPWT devices, patient assessment and care, and anomaly response", rated on a 3-point Likert-type scale with total scores from 10 to 30. The scale's content validity index was 0.83.
requirements: Administered as a self-administered questionnaire completed within 5 to 7 minutes
constraints: The article reports Cronbach α of .76 and test-retest reliability of .67, which it characterizes against benchmarks of .8–.9 for good internal consistency and .5–.75 for moderate reliability
target_learning_goals: assessment of NPWT-related care knowledge
examples: The same questionnaire was used for immediate pretest and posttest administration around the simulation intervention.

title: Ten-day sequenced micro-learning content framework for PIVC placement
description: The intervention's educational content followed a day-by-day framework (Table 1) progressing from "PIVC basics" and catheter selection, through placement protocols for different ages, vein selection and localisation, asepsis and patient safety, to "Post-intubation care assessment and complication prevention programme". Each day carried one or two focused topics delivered as short messages, embodying fragmented, spaced delivery aligned with nurses' workflow patterns.
requirements: Content must be mapped to clinical guidelines and national standards; the study revised items against three Chinese national standards and guidelines
constraints: Framework was designed for PIVC placement education in Chinese hospital settings
target_learners: Clinical nurses in emergency, medical and surgical wards
target_learning_goals: PIVC placement knowledge
aseptic technique and patient safety
complication prevention
examples: Day 1 covered PIVC basics and catheter selection strategies; days 7–8 covered asepsis and patient safety during tube insertion

article_title: Using Hologram-Based Augmented Reality in Anatomy Learning: The TEACHANATOMY Randomized Trial.
citation: Zingg L, Häusler M, Hein J, Jecklin S, Kottner S, Gascho D, Cavalcanti N, Voinov P, Götschi T, Carrillo F, Lagler F, Fürnstahl P, Farshad M. (2025). Using Hologram-Based Augmented Reality in Anatomy Learning: The TEACHANATOMY Randomized Trial. Academic Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/ACM.0000000000006012
title: TEACHANATOMY hologram-based AR learning application for cranial nerve anatomy on HoloLens 2
description: An interactive hologram-based AR learning application built for the Microsoft HoloLens 2, digitizing a cadaveric head specimen via photogrammetry (approximately 300 images processed in RealityCapture) and imported into Unity 3D. Cranial nerves were segmented with textures for interactive selection, providing access to detailed educational information about each nerve's route and function. The application incorporated adaptive learning technology using an Anki-based algorithm and gamification elements including multiple-choice questions with 3 attempts. Routes of cranial nerves were projected onto the dissected head specimen, with structures highlighted and color coded.
requirements: Microsoft HoloLens 2 headset
Calibration of headsets for each user to ensure optimal functionality and comfort
Holograms placed at a distance of at least 70 cm from the user to minimize vergence-accommodation conflict
constraints: Initially tailored for cranial nerves, though the methodology can be adapted to other anatomical structures such as bones and muscles
Average cost of a HoloLens 2 ranging from 4,000 to 5,000 euros (4,155 to 5,193 USD)
target_learners: First- and second-year medical students with no prior anatomy education
target_learning_goals: Learning the anatomy of the cranial nerves, including their routes, functions, and typology
examples: In the TEACHANATOMY randomized trial, AR group participants completed 3 learning blocks of approximately 20 minutes on cranial nerve anatomy, followed by an adaptive repetition block, then scored significantly higher on knowledge tests than the TL group.

title: TENTS-based observational measurement protocol with trained, blinded medical student observers
description: The study measured safety behaviors in real operating rooms using the validated Teamwork Evaluation of Non-Technical Skills (TENTS) instrument, chosen over the TeamSTEPPS Team Performance Observation Tool for its focused evaluation of nontechnical teamwork dimensions. Seventeen medical student volunteers conducted real-time observations on a 0-3 scale; per the article, "The students received 1.5 hours of instruction on TeamSTEPPS patient safety behaviors and were trained to apply the validated TENTS instrument consistently." Students were blinded to surgeons' treatment status during postintervention observations and provided written justifications for extreme scores.
requirements: Observer training (1.5 hours of instruction plus facility tours and a practical demonstration of the TENTS scoring process) and blinding of observers to treatment status
constraints: The authors acknowledge the TENTS instrument and scoring could be imperfect
target_learners: surgeons observed during real surgical cases
target_learning_goals: nontechnical teamwork behaviors including communication, leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support
examples: 101 baseline observations and 24 postintervention observations per group were recorded on paper forms during real surgical procedures

title: Two-stage simulation-based telenursing training program for undergraduate nursing students
description: A structured training program embedded in an undergraduate nursing degree, delivered in two stages: lecturer-led instruction covering "diverse nursing practices, ethical aspects of telehealth, clinical skills including communications skills", followed by simulation practice in which students "conducted virtual patient assessments and physical examinations". examples: Students practiced treating patients using telenursing tools and communication skills learned in stage 1, then completed pre and post questionnaires

article_title: The impact of perinatal mental health training on knowledge and practice of primary care physicians: a systems strengthening initiative in Telangana, India.

description: The TEAM tool is a validated questionnaire for evaluating teamwork in medical emergencies, used here to measure acquisition and retention of non-technical skills across the three simulation moments. Question twelve scores the team's global non-technical performance on a 0–10 scale. The authors chose it for its prior validation, Portuguese translation, easy application, and free availability.

constraints: Assesses team-level performance as a whole rather than individual residents

examples: Used to compare means across M0, M1, and M2 in a cohort of 85 residents in 16 interprofessional teams.

title: Teach students effective study strategies to promote goal achievement in less time and counteract negative affect
description: The article concludes that because better strategies let students reach goals in less time and reduce negative affect associated with long, unfocused study hours, instruction should target study strategies. It states these findings "underscore the need to teach students good study strategies not only to promote goal achievement in less time but also to counteract negative affect and stress", and notes meta-analytic evidence that self-regulated learning training improves planning and monitoring.
requirements: Training programs addressing planning, monitoring, concentration and procrastination, as meta-analytic evidence indicates such programs can improve students' study strategies
constraints: Evidence base is correlational self-report data from university students; the article calls for experimental studies and replication in other samples such as school children
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use
daily goal achievement
reduction of negative affect and study load
examples: The study assessed daily planning, monitoring, concentration and procrastination alongside goal achievement over 30 days in students' natural study environment

article_title: Assessing the impact of critical care training on pharmacy students in Egypt: a pre-post study.
citation: Moustafa HAM, Hamid AE, Hassoub G, Kassem AB. (2024). Assessing the impact of critical care training on pharmacy students in Egypt: a pre-post study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06427-6
title: Ten-day critical care experiential training course for pharmacy students
description: A condensed 10-day critical care training course delivered in waves of six or seven trainees at an 80-bed Egyptian hospital, designed by a clinical pharmacist and supervised by an academic. Each day combined a one-hour lecture with five hours of experiential learning: "participating in ward and critical care rounds with a multidisciplinary team, exploring case-based scenarios, interpreting lab results, dosing, mitigating medication errors and drug interactions". Trainees progressed from observing to performing supervised tasks, and completed daily pre/post knowledge tests plus self-efficacy, self-esteem, and satisfaction questionnaires.
requirements: Professional clinical pharmacy preceptors specializing in critical care plus an academic supervisor
Daily pre- and post-tests and validated questionnaires (knowledge Scale-CVI 0.82, Cronbach's alpha 0.73)
constraints: Delivered as an elective in a small private non-academic hospital; small groups of six or seven trainees per wave
target_learning_goals: critical care knowledge across eleven topics
self-efficacy and self-esteem for critical care practice
communication and consultation skills
examples: 72 students from four Egyptian universities completed the course in 8 waves over 3 months, with daily pre- and post-tests on each day's topic
key_sources: Moustafa HAM, Hamid AE, Hassoub G, Kassem AB. (2024). Assessing the impact of critical care training on pharmacy students in Egypt: a pre-post study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06427-6

article_title: Feasibility of focused cardiac ultrasound training for non-cardiologists in a resource-limited setting using a handheld ultrasound machine.
citation: Acheampong Benjamin MD, Starnes Joseph R MD, Parra David MD, Soslow Jonathan H MD, Awuku Yaw A MD, Aliyu Muktar H MD. (2022). Feasibility of focused cardiac ultrasound training for non-cardiologists in a resource-limited setting using a handheld ultrasound machine. Cardiovascular Journal of Africa. https://doi.org/10.5830/CVJA-2022-057
title: Ten-week multimodal focused echocardiography training pattern combining didactic, proctored and independent phases
description: A training sequence based on American Society of Echocardiography recommendations in which trainees first complete didactic lectures and observation, then a 10-week practical phase of "a minimum of 20 individual scans per trainee with interpretations", moving from six weeks of proctored scanning to three further proctored weeks and finally one week of independent imaging and interpretation. Feedback was immediate during proctored scans.
requirements: Didactic component covering ultrasound principles, cardiac anatomy and physiology, machine orientation and scanning windows
Proctored image acquisition with immediate feedback from an experienced echocardiographer
Progression to independent imaging and interpretation before evaluation
constraints: Evaluated only with two residents at a single teaching hospital
Focused on qualitative assessment of LV and RV structure and function and pericardial effusion; colour flow, doppler and valvular assessment were not included in the evaluation phase
target_learners: internal medicine residents and other non-echocardiographer clinicians in resource-limited settings
target_learning_goals: acquiring limited echocardiographic windows
qualitative interpretation of ventricular structure and function
detecting pericardial effusion
examples: Two residents each performed 50 echocardiograms and independently interpreted 20 randomly selected studies at three predetermined timepoints
key_sources: Acheampong Benjamin MD, Starnes Joseph R MD, Parra David MD, Soslow Jonathan H MD, Awuku Yaw A MD, Aliyu Muktar H MD. (2022). Feasibility of focused cardiac ultrasound training for non-cardiologists in a resource-limited setting using a handheld ultrasound machine. Cardiovascular Journal of Africa. https://doi.org/10.5830/CVJA-2022-057

article_title: Test-enhanced learning in Neuroanesthesia for the First Year anesthetic residents: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Raksakietisak M, Lertsiripatarajit V, Aroonpruksakul N, Plailaharn N, Raksamani K. (2024). Test-enhanced learning in Neuroanesthesia for the First Year anesthetic residents: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education 24:905. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05887-0
title: Test-enhanced learning at the postgraduate medical level should be designed with attention to test format and feedback, since unfeedbacked context-free MCQs may not enhance learning
description: The article proposes that when TEL fails to show effects in postgraduate trainees, designers should reconsider two design factors: test format and post-test feedback. It reports that "there is an advantage of SAQ over MCQ and a benefit of context-rich MCQs (which require the application of knowledge) over context-free MCQs", and that the TEL effect is "marginally better when feedback is provided after the test". The study itself used context-free MCQs without feedback or score disclosure.
requirements: Test formats of the intervention and assessment should be considered, since the article states the effects of TEL are stronger when the formats of the intervention and assessment tests are identical
constraints: The recommendation derives from the authors' interpretation of prior literature and their null trial, not from a tested manipulation of format or feedback in this study
target_learning_goals: retention and retrieval of complex medical knowledge such as neuroanesthesia
examples: In this study the intervention used ten-question MCQs with four answer choices, and participants were not shown their scores or given feedback on their responses.
key_sources: Raksakietisak M, Lertsiripatarajit V, Aroonpruksakul N, Plailaharn N, Raksamani K. (2024). Test-enhanced learning in Neuroanesthesia for the First Year anesthetic residents: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education 24:905. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05887-0

article_title: Prevalence of Dunning-Kruger effect in first semester medical students: a correlational study of self-assessment and actual academic performance.
citation: Knof Harald, Berndt Markus, Shiozawa Thomas. (2024). Prevalence of Dunning-Kruger effect in first semester medical students: a correlational study of self-assessment and actual academic performance. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11515314/
title: Teach self-assessment skills explicitly at the beginning of medical studies, since realistic self-assessment is a major difficulty for beginning students and low performers' calibration is unlikely to improve by itself
description: The article concludes that "Realistic self-assessment is a major difficulty for students at the beginning of their studies" and that "adequate calibration among low performers is unlikely to happen by itself". It therefore recommends that further research address "how self-assessment skills can be taught at the beginning of medical studies to counteract these findings". Because first-year students are at the start of their learning curve, the authors argue possible interventions to improve self-assessment can be most effective at this stage.
requirements: Interventions must be designed to develop metacognitive skills, which the article says are essential for realistic self-assessment and must first be developed in the setting of university teaching
constraints: The article frames this as a direction for further research rather than a tested intervention; it did not itself test any teaching strategy for self-assessment
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment
self-directed learning
professional self-regulation
examples: The authors assessed self-assessment ability across three semester cohorts as a foundation for developing strategies to improve self-assessment, and call for research on teaching these skills at the start of medical studies
key_sources: Knof Harald, Berndt Markus, Shiozawa Thomas. (2024). Prevalence of Dunning-Kruger effect in first semester medical students: a correlational study of self-assessment and actual academic performance. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11515314/

citation: Ott Thomas, Demare Tim, Möhrke Julia, Silber Saskia, Schwab Johannes, Reuter Lukas, Westhphal Ruben, Schmidtmann Irene, Dietz Sven-Oliver, Pirlich Nina, Ziebart Alexander, Engelhard Kristin.
