BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05714-6
title: Ten-minute stand-alone instructional video on humeral intraosseous access
description: A ten-minute instructional video on humeral intraosseous access for adult emergency patients, produced by the authors: "A ten-minute instructional video about humeral intraosseous access was produced by the authors according to the current literature and the manufacturer's instructions." Participants watched it individually on an iPad in a quiet room, and the same device and skill trainer appeared in the video and the test. It served as the intervention in both randomised trials and proved effective as a stand-alone tool without didactic embedding.
requirements: Viewing device (an iPad was used) and a quiet room for individual viewing
Identical equipment and skill trainer in video and test to support transfer
constraints: The video targets humeral intraosseous access specifically; tibial access is the more common emergency site
Effectiveness was evaluated only in a simulation laboratory
target_learning_goals: performing humeral intraosseous access correctly, including anatomical access point and angle of insertion
examples: Participants individually watched this video on an iPad in a quiet room during the mandatory training, followed by a videotaped performance test

citation: Ott Thomas, Demare Tim, Möhrke Julia, Silber Saskia, Schwab Johannes, Reuter Lukas, Westhphal Ruben, Schmidtmann Irene, Dietz Sven-Oliver, Pirlich Nina, Ziebart Alexander, Engelhard Kristin. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05714-6
title: Weighted 15-item checklist score (0–20) for assessing humeral intraosseous access performance
description: A performance checklist developed by the authors because "there are no validated checklists for assessing humeral IOA"; they adapted an already validated tibial IOA score through five rounds of focus group sessions. "The resulting checklist consisted of 15 weighted items quantifying the performance of humeral IOA", with item weights of 1 to 3 assigned by clinical relevance, yielding a score from 0 (worst) to 20 (best). Two blinded raters evaluated videotaped tests and agreed on one score per videotape.
requirements: Videotaped test performance for scoring
Two raters blinded to group assignment and time point
constraints: The authors state they did not perform a statistical validation of the adapted score and that weighted items may influence the score disproportionally; further validation is worthwhile
target_learning_goals: assessing procedural performance of humeral intraosseous access
examples: The score served as the primary outcome in both trials, with blinded raters watching each videotape simultaneously and agreeing on one score per videotape

article_title: Does clinical experience influence the effects of team simulation training in stroke thrombolysis? A prospective cohort study.
citation: Ajmi Soffien, Kurz Martin, Lindner Thomas Werner, Dalen Ingvild, Ersdal Hege Langli. (2024). Does clinical experience influence the effects of team simulation training in stroke thrombolysis? A prospective cohort study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-086413
title: Use team simulation training for stroke thrombolysis as a tool for both onboarding and continuous learning, not only for novices
description: The article recommends team simulation training for stroke thrombolysis for registrars at all experience levels, since simulation attendance was followed by similar DNT improvements for experienced and inexperienced registrars. It states that "Team simulation training for stroke thrombolysis can be a useful tool both for purposes of onboarding and continuous learning", echoing Gaba's framing of simulation as a tool for lifelong education. The programme used weekly in situ team simulation sessions focused on procedural adherence and team leadership skills.
requirements: A team simulation design that, per the European Stroke Organisation standards, matches the level of the learner and the educational goal
constraints: Single-centre context; findings influenced by local onboarding procedures and simulation design features that might be unique to the programme
target_learners: neurology registrars, both inexperienced and experienced
target_learning_goals: procedural adherence in acute stroke thrombolysis
team leadership and team coordination skills
examples: Weekly team simulation training sessions with briefs, summaries and closed-loop communication were part of a QI project introduced in February 2017
key_sources: Ajmi Soffien, Kurz Martin, Lindner Thomas Werner, Dalen Ingvild, Ersdal Hege Langli. (2024). Does clinical experience influence the effects of team simulation training in stroke thrombolysis? A prospective cohort study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-086413

article_title: The Effect of the Team Members Teaching Design vs. Regular Lectures method on the Self-efficacy of the Multiple sclerosis Patients in Iran. Randomised Controlled Trial.
citation: Dehghani Ali, Fakhravari Fariba, Hojat Mohsen. (2024). The Effect of the Team Members Teaching Design vs. Regular Lectures method on the Self-efficacy of the Multiple sclerosis Patients in Iran. Randomised Controlled Trial. Investigacion y Educacion en Enfermeria. https://doi.org/10.17533/udea.iee.v42n2e13
title: Team Members Teaching Design: a team-teaching approach in which each member studies a different part of the subject and every learner also teaches
description: TMTD is one of the team and cooperative teaching methods, resting on two hypotheses: "each member of the team studies a different part of the subject" and "each learner can teach her team members, so each member acts as both a teacher and a learner." The article implements it by dividing patients into teams, redistributing members with identical content across expert groups for discussion, then returning each member to their original team to teach their topic. It is used here to deliver self-care education to MS patients in small groups, which the authors say "can lead to the creation of an active learning environment for all learners."
requirements: Small teams with content divided into equal volumes distributed to patients before the session
Structured stages: same-content discussion groups followed by teaching within original teams, with a researcher summarizing and answering questions
target_learners: Adult patients with multiple sclerosis (ages 18-60) in this study
target_learning_goals: Self-care knowledge and skills for controlling disease complications, including diet, pain and fatigue management, urinary disorders, stress coping, and exercise
examples: Patients were divided into four teams; after discussing shared content for 10 minutes, members returned to their original teams and for 10-15 minutes each presented their content to their teammates.
key_sources: Dehghani Ali, Fakhravari Fariba, Hojat Mohsen. (2024). The Effect of the Team Members Teaching Design vs. Regular Lectures method on the Self-efficacy of the Multiple sclerosis Patients in Iran. Randomised Controlled Trial. article_title: Teachers recruit mentalizing regions to represent learners' beliefs.
citation: Vélez, N., Chen, A. M., Burke, T., Cushman, F. A., & Gershman, S. J. (2023). Teachers recruit mentalizing regions to represent learners’ beliefs. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2215015120
title: Teaching as utility maximization balancing informational value to the learner against communicative costs and teacher preferences
description: The article frames teaching as a cooperative-communication utility-maximization process in which teachers select examples by weighing three values: the informational value to the learner (maximizing the learner's posterior belief in the target concept, equivalent to minimizing surprisal), the movement cost to the teacher, and the teacher's idiosyncratic preferences for examples along the target's contours. The utility function combines these with free weighting coefficients, and examples are selected probabilistically via a softmax. Learner beliefs are computed under either pedagogical (recursive) or literal (single-step) assumptions. In this study the literal-learner version best explained teachers' choices.
requirements: A representation of the learner's beliefs over candidate concepts, updated as examples are provided, so the informational value of each candidate example can be computed
constraints: In this task, teachers did not engage in computationally costly recursive mentalizing; the best-fitting model assumed a learner who interprets examples literally
The article notes it remains an open question why teachers opted for these shortcuts
target_learning_goals: selecting examples that efficiently communicate a target concept to a learner
examples: The model was fit to 28 fMRI participants' choices in a generalized rectangle-game teaching task with 40 multiple-choice questions, and used to derive parametric fMRI regressors of learners' posterior belief and belief update
key_sources: Vélez, N., Chen, A. M., Burke, T., Cushman, F. A., & Gershman, S. J. (2023). Teachers recruit mentalizing regions to represent learners’ beliefs. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2215015120

article_title: Examining SEB skills' incremental validity over personality traits in predicting academic achievement.
citation: Yoon Hee Jun, Roberts Brent W., Sewell Madison N., Napolitano Christopher M., Soto Christopher J., Murano Dana, Casillas Alex. (2024). Examining SEB skills' incremental validity over personality traits in predicting academic achievement. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0296484
title: Frame classroom social-emotional instruction as building demonstrable skills rather than changing personality traits
description: Because SEB skills are capacities that can be exercised when situations call for them, the article argues instruction should target skill performance rather than trait change: "Asking teachers to teach how to perform SEB skills and students to demonstrate that they learned how to perform those skills is far more consistent with educational policy than asking teachers to change their students' personality traits." Skills can be organized into the short, scaffolded modules typical of curricula, whereas trait change does not fit that structure.
requirements: Curricula structured within semesters or shorter scaffolded modules, into which skill instruction can be organized
constraints: The article presents this as an argument from the skills conceptualization, not as a tested intervention result
target_learning_goals: Developing social, emotional, and behavioral skills such as self-regulation and leadership
Improving academic performance through SEB skill interventions
examples: The article notes individuals can exhibit self-regulation and leadership skills only when situations call for it, and suggests practitioners use the BESSI to examine effects of SEB skill interventions designed to improve academic performance
key_sources: Yoon Hee Jun, Roberts Brent W., Sewell Madison N., Napolitano Christopher M., Soto Christopher J., Murano Dana, Casillas Alex. (2024). Examining SEB skills' incremental validity over personality traits in predicting academic achievement. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0296484

article_title: The co-development and evaluation of an e-learning course on spinal cord injury physical activity counselling: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Hoekstra F, Gainforth HL, Broeksteeg R, Corras S, Collins D, Eleftheriadou E, Gaudet S, Giroux EE, Kuipers LS, McCallum S, Ma JK, de Passillé E, Rakiecki D, Rockall S, van den Berg-Emons R, van Vilsteren A, Williamson M, Wilroy J, Martin Ginis KA. (2024). The co-development and evaluation of an e-learning course on spinal cord injury physical activity counselling: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05141-7
title: Technology-enhanced learning (TEL) evaluation framework for developing and evaluating e-learning resources
description: The TEL evaluation framework, developed in the context of medical education and built on the CIPP evaluation model and the Kirkpatrick model, guides both development and evaluation activities for e-learning resources. "The TEL-framework outlines seven areas of evaluation activities: conduct needs analysis and environmental scan; document processes, decisions, and final product, test usability, document key events during implementation and final product, assess participant experience and satisfaction, and assess learning outcomes, and estimate cost, reusability, and sustainability." The article used it to structure the co-development and RCT evaluation of the SCI counselling course, alongside CRe-DEPTH reporting.
requirements: Engagement of potential end-users early and throughout the development process
Systematic evaluation of usability, learning outcomes, and user experience prior to large-scale implementation
constraints: The authors note they did not use the related ETELM-LP questionnaire itself, instead using shorter modified items informed by it
target_learning_goals: Effective physical activity counselling of clients with SCI
examples: The article's reporting is structured by the seven TEL evaluation activities, from needs analysis through learning outcomes assessment

article_title: Rolling the DICE (Design, Interpret, Compute, Estimate): Interactive Learning of Biostatistics With Simulations.
citation: de Azevedo Cardoso Taiane, Waleed Muhammad, Ogut Eren, Marques da Cruz Manuel, Thiesmeier Robert, Orsini Nicola. (2024). Rolling the DICE (Design, Interpret, Compute, Estimate): Interactive Learning of Biostatistics With Simulations. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/52679
title: Teach statistics in conjunction with epidemiology through simulations rather than isolated lectures with given data sets
description: The article argues that statistics in the health sciences is often taught in isolation through standard lectures followed by computer exercises with given data sets, which can lead to a disconnect between statistical and epidemiological methods and insufficient awareness of concepts such as sampling variability. It proposes teaching methods that deliver statistical concepts in conjunction with epidemiology, using simulations to explore the major steps of a scientific investigation. The authors state that "teaching methods that deliver statistical concepts in conjunction with epidemiology for students in the health sciences are crucial for educational development."
requirements: Simulation-based activities built on a causal framework (the article uses the approach of Fox et al) implementable in statistical software
constraints: The statements expressed in this paper are based on the experiences and opinions of the authors
target_learners: Students in the health sciences, including public health and epidemiology
target_learning_goals: Sampling variability, error probabilities, statistical model construction, and study design reasoning
examples: DICE asks students to design, generate, analyze, interpret, and communicate their own simulated investigation instead of analyzing a supplied data set
key_sources: de Azevedo Cardoso Taiane, Waleed Muhammad, Ogut Eren, Marques da Cruz Manuel, Thiesmeier Robert, Orsini Nicola. (2024). Rolling the DICE (Design, Interpret, Compute, Estimate): Interactive Learning of Biostatistics With Simulations. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/52679

article_title: Game-based learning to improve diagnostic accuracy: a pilot randomized-controlled trial.
citation: Morgan Daniel J., Scherer Laura, Pineles Lisa, Baghdadi Jon, Magder Larry, Thom Kerri, Koch Christina, Wilkins Nick, LeGrand Mike, Stevens Deborah, Walker Renee, Shirrell Beth, Harris Anthony D., Korenstein Deborah. (2024). Game-based learning to improve diagnostic accuracy: a pilot randomized-controlled trial. Diagnosis. https://doi.org/10.1515/dx-2023-0133
title: TestingWisely online diagnostic-reasoning game
description: A publicly available online game (https://bird.testingwisely.com/) developed iteratively with clinician feedback to train estimation of post-test probability. The article describes that it "requires users to estimate probability of diagnosis based on 10 simplified case presentations", takes 5 minutes or less per game, and delivers "immediate feedback on each question ... using natural frequency methods with a score, tips, and comparisons to other users". It was the core of the 45-minute GBL intervention in the pilot RCT.
requirements: Users complete a short tutorial, watch a 4-minute video explaining natural frequencies, and play the game tutorial and two games
constraints: The game's timed gestalt-estimation format was experienced as stressful for some participants
target_learning_goals: estimating probability of disease before and after diagnostic test results
Bayesian updating of diagnostic probability
examples: In the pilot RCT, participants played the game tutorial and two games as the GBL intervention

article_title: A novel step-by-step training program for transanal endoscopic surgery.
citation: Popa Călin, Schlanger Diana, Prunoiu Virgiliu Mihail, Puia Ion Cosmin, Zaharie Florin. (2023). A novel step-by-step training program for transanal endoscopic surgery. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04296-z
title: Low-cost tubular simulation platforms for transanal endoscopic surgery training (5, 7.5 and 10 cm, TEO/TAMIS compatible)
description: Three detachable tubular systems of 5, 7.5 and 10 cm diameter, fixed on a stable support and compatible with either a TEO or a TAMIS platform, designed to mimic the curvatures and diameters of a distended rectum. The 5 cm and 7.5 cm systems serve synthetic exercises and the 10 cm system holds a prepared swine stomach for biological exercises. The platforms were "built using usual household materials", at "an approximate cost of building a platform was 60 euros", which the authors present as making the model feasible for low-income settings.
requirements: A TEO (Karl Storz) or gel-point TAMIS (Applied Medical) platform plus ordinary laparoscopic instruments (grasping and non-traumatic forceps, scissors, needle-holder)
constraints: The 5 cm diameter tubular system is used only for synthetic material exercises, since it permits only a limited range of motion
target_learning_goals: tissue manipulation
cutting and dissection
suturing in a narrow transanal workspace
examples: The swine stomach was prepared with closure of the cardia to keep insufflation, with the TEO or TAMIS platform fixed at the antro-piloric region
key_sources: Popa Călin, Schlanger Diana, Prunoiu Virgiliu Mihail, Puia Ion Cosmin, Zaharie Florin. (2023). A novel step-by-step training program for transanal endoscopic surgery. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04296-z

article_title: A novel step-by-step training program for transanal endoscopic surgery.
citation: Popa Călin, Schlanger Diana, Prunoiu Virgiliu Mihail, Puia Ion Cosmin, Zaharie Florin. (2023). A novel step-by-step training program for transanal endoscopic surgery. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04296-z
title: Step-by-step simulation training sequence from basic synthetic exercises to biological-material exercises
description: A structured progression of seven timed exercises moving from basic synthetic-material tasks (Teddy bears, Matches, Beans for tissue manipulation; Circles for cutting and dissection; Glove finger for suturing) to biological-material tasks on swine stomach (dissection and excision; suturing) that more accurately replicate intraoperative conditions. Each exercise has defined completion requirements assuring quality of execution, and the program "consists of standardized exercises with targeted training of essential skills". Supervision with feedback during and after each round is built into the delivery.
requirements: Each exercise explained and demonstrated by a trainer before the start; supervised hands-on activity with cues, practical tips and feedback during and after each round
constraints: The program trains basic skills only; it does not go as far as teaching TaTME, serving as a base before more advanced techniques
target_learners: surgeons in training focused on colorectal surgery
specialist surgeons new to transanal endoscopic surgery
target_learning_goals: basic skills for transanal endoscopic surgery: tissue manipulation, cutting, dissection and suturing
examples: Round 2 of the dissection exercise increased difficulty by positioning the lesion in a more lateral position

article_title: Simulation in healthcare during COVID-19: An experience with residents in Anaesthesiology.
citation: Laurens L.M., Bañeras J., Biarnés A., Nuñez S. (2023). Simulation in healthcare during COVID-19: An experience with residents in Anaesthesiology. Revista Española De Anestesiologia Y Reanimacion. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.redare.2021.08.001
title: Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM) scale for assessing non-technical skills in critical situations
description: The Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM) scale, described in the article as "a globally validated scale for assessing TNTS in critical situations" with a Spanish version. It has 11 items in three sections — leadership, teamwork and task management — each scored 0 to 4, plus a 1-to-10 global rating, completed by all participant roles after each scenario.
requirements: Completed by all participants, including residents, moderators, external observers and peers, at the end of each scenario
constraints: Participants did not describe the role they played, so assessment differences by role could not be analysed
target_learners: Assessors of team performance: residents, moderators, external observers and peers
target_learning_goals: Measuring leadership, teamwork and task management of teams in critical situations
examples: In this study 130 TEAM forms were completed across the two days, of which 12 were discarded for incomplete data, leaving 118 valid questionnaires

article_title: Test-enhanced learning improves learner attendance during a laparoscopic box trainer simulation program.
citation: Lowe B, Ng J, Jordan S, Waynforth D, Angstetra D, Brazil V. (2022). Test‐enhanced learning improves learner attendance during a laparoscopic box trainer simulation program. Australian and New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajo.13528
title: Test-enhanced learning: regular, well-defined assessments of performance throughout the training phase of learning
description: Test-enhanced learning (TEL) is described as a pedagogic approach that "uses regular, well-defined assessments of performance throughout the training phase of learning". Testing is considered to support learning by encouraging retrieval of information or skills and fostering effortful and deliberate practice, while providing opportunities for direct, specific supervisor feedback against clearly benchmarked goals. The article positions TEL as an element of mastery learning that, unlike mastery learning, does not require predetermined pass criteria but focuses on learning at every point along the learning curve.
requirements: Regular assessments during the training phase
Benchmarked goals and specific feedback from a supervisor
constraints: The article notes there is currently limited experience with the use of TEL in complex procedural work
target_learners: Medical students and surgical trainees in simulation programs
target_learning_goals: Complex procedural skills such as laparoscopy
examples: The study applied TEL by formally testing and timing TEL-group students weekly against competent, advanced and elite time targets.
key_sources: Lowe B, Ng J, Jordan S, Waynforth D, Angstetra D, Brazil V. (2022). Test‐enhanced learning improves learner attendance during a laparoscopic box trainer simulation program. Australian and New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajo.13528

article_title: Test-enhanced learning improves learner attendance during a laparoscopic box trainer simulation program.
citation: Lowe B, Ng J, Jordan S, Waynforth D, Angstetra D, Brazil V. (2022). Test‐enhanced learning improves learner attendance during a laparoscopic box trainer simulation program. Australian and New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajo.13528
title: Ten-week laparoscopic box trainer simulation program with graded time targets
description: A structured laparoscopic simulation curriculum delivered on standard box trainers over ten weekly one-hour weekend sessions facilitated by two to four surgical supervisors. Students received "a laparoscopic program with ten exercises to complete; videos of the exercises to perform; and timed targets to achieve, with competent, advanced and elite levels identified", and were encouraged to reach competent times with mastery before progressing. Peer pair allocations were maintained within groups for the program duration.
requirements: Weekly face-to-face sessions with surgical supervisor instruction
Timed targets and exercise videos for each of the ten exercises
constraints: The article reports attendance declined in the mid portion of the program in both groups
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students with no prior laparoscopic experience
target_learning_goals: Basic laparoscopic psychomotor skills
examples: Table 1 prints graded time targets, for example thread transfer competent 60 s, advanced 45 s, elite 25 s.
key_sources: Lowe B, Ng J, Jordan S, Waynforth D, Angstetra D, Brazil V. (2022). Test‐enhanced learning improves learner attendance during a laparoscopic box trainer simulation program. Australian and New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajo.13528

article_title: BMAT's predictive validity for medical school performance: A retrospective cohort study.
citation: Davies DJ, Sam AH, Murphy KG, Khan SA, Choe R, Cleland J. (2022). BMAT's predictive validity for medical school performance: A retrospective cohort study. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14819
title: Test companies have an ethical responsibility to support independent research on the psychometric properties of admissions tests funded from applicant fees
description: The authors argue that because admissions tests are high-stakes and funded from applicant fees, test providers should actively enable independent evaluation of their tools. They state: "We believe test companies have the ethical responsibility to encourage and support independent research examining the psychometric properties of their tools, particularly where the tool is funded from applicant fees." They contrast companies that have managed this successfully (UCAT, MCAT) with BMAT, where no independent research was commissioned despite calls for it more than a decade earlier.
requirements: A mechanism for independent researchers to access test data and commission validity studies.
constraints: The article notes evidence for any new admissions test cannot exist at launch and must be accumulated over time.
target_learners: medical school applicants and admissions decision-makers
target_learning_goals: fair, evidence-based selection of applicants to medical school
examples: The authors note that despite calls for more rigorous independent BMAT research published more than 10 years earlier, no more studies or technical reports were published by the test company and no independent research was commissioned, while many more medical schools adopted the test.
key_sources: Davies DJ, Sam AH, Murphy KG, Khan SA, Choe R, Cleland J. (2022). BMAT's predictive validity for medical school performance: A retrospective cohort study. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14819

article_title: Change in pre- and in-service early childhood educators' knowledge, self-efficacy, and intentions following an e-learning course in physical activity and sedentary behaviour: a pilot study.
citation: Bruijns BA, Vanderloo LM, Johnson AM, Adamo KB, Burke SM, Carson V, Heydon R, Irwin JD, Naylor P-J, Timmons BW, Tucker P. (2022). Change in pre- and in-service early childhood educators’ knowledge, self-efficacy, and intentions following an e-learning course in physical activity and sedentary behaviour: a pilot study. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-022-12591-5
title: TEACH e-Learning course in physical activity and sedentary behaviour for early childhood educators
description: The TEACH e-Learning course is a ~5 h online professional learning course for pre- and in-service early childhood educators, with expert-developed content generated via a Delphi process. The article states "the course comprised four modules developed for ECEs", covering introductory movement-behaviour content, the childcare environment and outdoor/risky play, practical strategies to promote physical activity and minimize sedentary time, and ECE-focused professional learning with resources and a video library. It was pilot tested with a pre-post survey design.
requirements: Delivered as an online e-Learning course completed within two weeks in the pilot; content developed via a Delphi expert process
constraints: The article notes the course was not designed for a specific program or intervention but to provide general training in these areas
target_learners: pre-service early childhood educators in post-secondary programs
in-service early childhood educators practicing in childcare
target_learning_goals: knowledge of physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and movement guidelines for early childhood
self-efficacy to promote physical activity and minimize sedentary behaviour
behavioural intention and perceived behavioural control for childcare movement practices
examples: In the pilot, pre-service ECEs from three Canadian colleges and in-service ECEs recruited via social media completed the course and pre- and post-course online surveys
key_sources: Bruijns BA, Vanderloo LM, Johnson AM, Adamo KB, Burke SM, Carson V, Heydon R, Irwin JD, Naylor P-J, Timmons BW, Tucker P. (2022). Change in pre- and in-service early childhood educators’ knowledge, self-efficacy, and intentions following an e-learning course in physical activity and sedentary behaviour: a pilot study. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-022-12591-5

article_title: Effects of using a cognitive aid on content and feasibility of debriefings of simulated emergencies.
citation: Freytag J, Stroben F, Hautz WE, Penders D, Kämmer JE. (2021). Effects of using a cognitive aid on content and feasibility of debriefings of simulated emergencies. GMS J Med Educ 38(5):Doc95. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001491.shtml
title: TeamTAG — a cognitive aid listing six CRM principles with behavioural anchors for structuring teamwork debriefings
description: TeamTAG (TEAMwork Techniques Analysis Grid) is a debriefing guideline developed by the working group that, in the article's words, "uses behavioural anchors to support observations and provides a structure for debriefing". It "lists six CRM principles, each with associated observable behaviours", selected to match the simulation scenario, participants' skill level, facilitators' experience, and observability. In the study it was used alongside the GAS structure in the intervention condition, with facilitators instructed to address all six principles during the first five debriefings.
requirements: Used together with the GAS debriefing structure by a trained facilitator; intervention facilitators received an introduction to TeamTAG and training in the CRM concept
constraints: Principles were selected to match the specific simulation scenario, participants' skill level, facilitators' experience, and observability of the principles during the simulation
target_learners: Medical students in their tenth semester or beyond in simulated emergency training
target_learning_goals: Teamwork and non-technical skills based on Crisis Resource Management principles
examples: In the trial, intervention debriefings followed the GAS structure with TeamTAG, and facilitators were instructed to address all six CRM principles during the first five debriefings
key_sources: Freytag J, Stroben F, Hautz WE, Penders D, Kämmer JE. (2021). Effects of using a cognitive aid on content and feasibility of debriefings of simulated emergencies. GMS J Med Educ 38(5):Doc95. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001491.shtml

article_title: Evaluating bowel enterotomy closures in simulated deep body cavities using the reversing half-hitch alternating post and square knots: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Sykes EA, Lemke M, Potter D, Li T, Mir ZM, Sheahan G, Wu V, Zevin B. (2021). Evaluating bowel enterotomy closures in simulated deep body cavities using the reversing half-hitch alternating post and square knots: a randomized controlled trial. Canadian Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1503/cjs.016719
title: Teach both RHAP and square knots to novice learners so they can select knot type by available working space
description: The article recommends that novices learn both knot constructions during proficiency-based knot-tying curricula. Teaching RHAP alongside the square knot lets trainees "appropriately select their knot type according to the available working space, and to minimize failure rates of their knots," since square knots lose security in confined spaces while RHAP performance is preserved at depth.
requirements: Proficiency-based training with structured feedback and validated checklist scoring before clinical application
constraints: Evidence limited to novice learners; generalizability to residents and experienced surgeons not established
Simulated environment only; transfer to the operating room was not confirmed in this study
Results based on braided 2–0 silk; may not generalize to monofilament sutures
target_learners: undergraduate students new to surgical knot tying (novice learners)
target_learning_goals: surgical knot tying
small bowel enterotomy repair
examples: After 20 randomized novices trained to defined proficiency, deep-cavity repairs with RHAP knots were faster (16 v. 21 min) and more secure (105 v. 35 mm Hg burst pressure) than square-knot repairs.
key_sources: Sykes EA, Lemke M, Potter D, Li T, Mir ZM, Sheahan G, Wu V, Zevin B. (2021). Evaluating bowel enterotomy closures in simulated deep body cavities using the reversing half-hitch alternating post and square knots: a randomized controlled trial. Canadian Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1503/cjs.016719

article_title: Development of a volumetric pancreas segmentation CT dataset for AI applications through trained technologists: a study during the COVID 19 containment phase.
citation: Suman Garima, Panda Ananya, Korfiatis Panagiotis, Edwards Marie E., Garg Sushil, Blezek Daniel J., Chari Suresh T., Goenka Ajit H. (2020). Development of a volumetric pancreas segmentation CT dataset for AI applications through trained technologists: a study during the COVID 19 containment phase. Abdominal Radiology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00261-020-02741-x
title: Volumetric pancreas segmentation CT dataset built by trained technologists with radiologist ground-truth correction
description: The project produced a labeled CT dataset for AI applications: 347 contrast-enhanced portal venous phase CTs (≤3-mm slices) randomly selected from reports describing a normal pancreas, de-identified and converted to NIfTI format. Technologists segmented "an initial batch of 188 CT studies" and a second batch of 159 using freehand tools; two radiologists reviewed all cases and redid inaccurate segmentations with an AI-assisted module in 3D Slicer to serve as ground truth.
requirements: Radiologist review and correction of technologist segmentations to establish ground truth
De-identification of DICOM data and storage in a secure offline shared folder
constraints: The number and composition of CT scans were based on ready availability of a curated dataset rather than statistical considerations
Only scans with an unremarkable pancreas in the original report were included
target_learners: Trained technologists performing the annotation work
target_learning_goals: Development of volumetric pancreas segmentation skill sufficient for dataset labeling
examples: Corrected segmentations covered 71 of 188 first-batch cases and 77 of 159 second-batch cases; technologists' performance was quantified against ground truth via DSC, JC, FP and FN rates
key_sources: Suman Garima, Panda Ananya, Korfiatis Panagiotis, Edwards Marie E., Garg Sushil, Blezek Daniel J., Chari Suresh T., Goenka Ajit H. (2020). Development of a volumetric pancreas segmentation CT dataset for AI applications through trained technologists: a study during the COVID 19 containment phase. Abdominal Radiology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00261-020-02741-x

article_title: Simulation training for emergency skills: effects on ICU fellows' performance and supervision levels.
citation: Zante Bjoern, Schefold Joerg C. (2020). Simulation training for emergency skills: effects on ICU fellows’ performance and supervision levels. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02419-4
title: Ten Cate's five supervision levels for entrustable professional activities as an assessment framework for procedural skill training outcomes
description: The study operationalizes skill performance and trust using Ten Cate's five supervision levels for entrustable professional activities, ranging from "Observation but not execution, even with direct supervision" through "execution with direct, proactive supervision", "execution with reactive supervision, i.e., on request and quickly available", and "supervision at a distance and/or post hoc" to "supervision provided by the trainee to colleagues". Fellows self-assess expected supervision levels and consultants assess required supervision levels before and after training, making entrustment the outcome measure of training effectiveness.
requirements: Both fellow self-assessment and consultant external assessment of supervision levels for each skill, before and after training
constraints: The authors describe supervision levels as a somewhat subjective determination; external assessment was based on consultant consensus without assessed inter-rater reliability
target_learning_goals: Entrustment and readiness for unsupervised performance of emergency procedural skills
examples: Consultants re-assessed supervision levels for each skill of each individual fellow after skill training to determine future required supervision levels for daily ICU work
key_sources: Zante Bjoern, Schefold Joerg C. (2020). Simulation training for emergency skills: effects on ICU fellows’ performance and supervision levels. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02419-4

article_title: The Influence of Teachers on Motivation and Academic Stress and Their Effect on the Learning Strategies of University Students.
citation: Trigueros R., Padilla A., Aguilar-Parra J.M., Lirola M.J., García-Luengo A.V., Rocamora-Pérez P., López-Liria R. (2020). The Influence of Teachers on Motivation and Academic Stress and Their Effect on the Learning Strategies of University Students. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17239089
title: Support student autonomy rather than exercising psychological control to reduce academic stress
description: Because the SEM showed teacher psychological control positively predicted academic stress and autonomy support negatively predicted it, the article concludes teachers should adopt an autonomy-supportive style: "by promoting personal initiative, self-regulation, self-concept, and by offering relevant objectives and the use of minimum contingencies, the teacher will encourage support for student autonomy". It further recommends implementing "educational programmes that enrich the class dynamics that take place at university, so that students feel more motivated and can channel academic stress in a more positive way".
requirements: Teachers must offer relevant objectives, use minimum contingencies, and promote student initiative and self-regulation
constraints: The study is cross-sectional SEM based on self-reported questionnaires with non-probabilistic sampling, so causal and population-generalisable claims are limited
target_learning_goals: reducing academic stress
fostering self-determined motivation
examples: The study measured perceived autonomy support with the short Teacher as Social Context Questionnaire and psychological control with a 7-item scale, both single-factor student-report scales
key_sources: Trigueros R., Padilla A., Aguilar-Parra J.M., Lirola M.J., García-Luengo A.V., Rocamora-Pérez P., López-Liria R. (2020). The Influence of Teachers on Motivation and Academic Stress and Their Effect on the Learning Strategies of University Students. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17239089

article_title: Longitudinal team training programme in a Norwegian surgical ward: a qualitative study of nurses' and physicians' experiences with teamwork skills.
citation: Ballangrud R, Aase K, Vifladt A. (2020). Longitudinal team training programme in a Norwegian surgical ward: a qualitative study of nurses' and physicians' experiences with teamwork skills. BMJ Open 10(7): e035432. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-035432
title: TeamSTEPPS three-phase model of change for implementing team training in clinical settings
description: TeamSTEPPS is a publicly released, evidence-based team training programme based on teamwork theory and change theory, developed by the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality with the Department of Defense. It organises implementation into a recommended "model of change" with three phases: (1) assessment and planning, (2) training and implementation, and (3) sustainment. The programme aims to optimise five teamwork principles — team structure, communication, leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support — and in this study was implemented over 12 months on a surgical ward with monthly tool rollouts.
requirements: Trained instructors: the four ward healthcare professionals responsible for training completed the TeamSTEPPS V.2.0 Master Training Course and were certified as instructors.
A change team with members from all ward professions and an action plan based on identified patient safety issues.
constraints: Most TeamSTEPPS studies are carried out in the USA without longitudinal follow-up, and ward team structure differs from ICU settings, restricting possibilities for interprofessional reflections.
target_learners: Healthcare professionals: physicians, registered nurses and certified nursing assistants in hospital wards
target_learning_goals: Teamwork skills: communication, leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support
Patient safety behaviour and communication in daily clinical practice
examples: One day of interprofessional team training in a simulation centre for all 41 ward professionals (6 hours classroom training and 2 hours high-fidelity simulation), followed by monthly implementation of one tool and refresher courses after four and eleven months.
key_sources: Ballangrud R, Aase K, Vifladt A. (2020). Longitudinal team training programme in a Norwegian surgical ward: a qualitative study of nurses' and physicians' experiences with teamwork skills. BMJ Open 10(7): e035432. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-035432

article_title: Training in endocrine surgery.
citation: Gimm Oliver, Barczyński Marcin, Mihai Radu, Raffaelli Marco. (2019). Training in endocrine surgery. Langenbeck's Archives of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00423-019-01828-4
title: Telementoring via video-conferencing for introducing new endocrine surgical techniques
description: Telementoring is a video-conferencing arrangement in which an experienced remote surgeon guides a surgeon-learner through a new procedure in real time. The review describes its use for posterior retroperitoneoscopic adrenalectomy across institutions and continents, reporting that "In our experience, telementoring was convenient and effective in helping with the execution of a new surgical technique." Reported cases proceeded uneventfully with short operative times and uncomplicated discharge, including a Melbourne introduction mentored by an overseas surgeon with more than 200 PRA procedures.
requirements: Careful preparation of cross-institutional telementoring issues
A surgeon-learner with the skills and experience to complete the procedure using alternative techniques in case of complications or technical failure
constraints: The review reports transmission loss occurred once in the Yale–MD Anderson cases, though it was re-established within seconds and not disruptive
target_learners: established surgeons learning a new operative technique
surgeon-learners in locations without highly experienced surgeon-mentors
target_learning_goals: acquiring competence in a new operative technique (e.g., posterior retroperitoneoscopic adrenalectomy) under remote expert guidance
examples: Two consecutive PRAs at Yale New Haven Hospital telementored from MD Anderson; eight laparoscopic telementored adrenalectomies performed between sites 430 km apart with outcomes comparable to standard laparoscopic adrenalectomy
key_sources: Gimm Oliver, Barczyński Marcin, Mihai Radu, Raffaelli Marco. (2019). Training in endocrine surgery. Langenbeck's Archives of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00423-019-01828-4

article_title: A Randomized Trial of Instructor-Led Training Versus Video Lesson in Training Health Care Providers in Proper Donning and Doffing of Personal Protective Equipment.
citation: Christensen L, Rasmussen CS, Benfield T, Franc JM. (2020). A Randomized Trial of Instructor-Led Training Versus Video Lesson in Training Health Care Providers in Proper Donning and Doffing of Personal Protective Equipment. Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness. https://doi.org/10.1017/dmp.2020.56
title: Test training videos for completeness, accuracy, and clarity before use, and revise them when errors or unclear actions are found
description: The article found that unedited visibility problems in training videos caused real errors: participants complained it was "hard to see how to take off the gloves," and one participant watched the doffing video 6 times without noticing an action that "was not properly shown." The authors responded by adding two unedited supplementary videos and conclude that videos should be tested, feedback invited, and revisions made when errors are found.
requirements: Videos must be tested with real trainees before use in training, with feedback invited and revisions made when errors or unclear actions are found.
constraints: Editing videos to keep them short made some actions hard to see; the authors note the rapid revision gave the video group feedback similar to personal feedback in live training, though they consider it did not impact results.
target_learners: health care providers training in PPE procedures
target_learning_goals: correct donning and doffing of personal protective equipment
examples: Two additional unedited videos demonstrating glove removal more slowly were added after Day-1 participants reported the action was hard to see; a participant missed an untying step not properly shown in the doffing video.
key_sources: Christensen L, Rasmussen CS, Benfield T, Franc JM. (2020). A Randomized Trial of Instructor-Led Training Versus Video Lesson in Training Health Care Providers in Proper Donning and Doffing of Personal Protective Equipment. Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness. https://doi.org/10.1017/dmp.2020.56

article_title: Does Telemedical Support of First Responders Improve Guideline Adherence in an Offshore Emergency Scenario? A Simulator-Based Prospective Study.
citation: Landgraf P, Spies C, Lawatscheck R, Luz M, Wernecke K-D, Schröder T. (2019). Does Telemedical Support of First Responders Improve Guideline Adherence in an Offshore Emergency Scenario? A Simulator-Based Prospective Study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-027563
title: Telemedical support set-up: corpuls-3 monitoring unit plus Frontline Communicator link to a remote physician
description: The intervention combined a "telemedically enabled vital data monitoring unit (corpuls-3 with corpuls.web" and a "communication device (Frontline Communicator" connecting teams wirelessly to a remote emergency physician in Berlin who followed a checklist. The remote physician could view one-way video and advise teams on items such as glove use and locating the blood pressure cuff and stethoscope. Five anaesthesiologists with prehospital emergency expertise served as remote physicians.
requirements: A telemedically enabled monitoring unit and a two-way audio/one-way video communication device connected to a remote physician with a checklist
constraints: Neither participants nor remote physicians were experienced in telemedicine in this study
target_learning_goals: guideline-adherent primary survey of a trauma patient
correct collection of vital signs and patient history
examples: Supported teams surveyed noninvasive blood pressure, blood oxygen saturation and ECG via corpuls-3 while a remote physician in Berlin followed the scenario by video
key_sources: Landgraf P, Spies C, Lawatscheck R, Luz M, Wernecke K-D, Schröder T. (2019). Does Telemedical Support of First Responders Improve Guideline Adherence in an Offshore Emergency Scenario? A Simulator-Based Prospective Study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-027563

article_title: Quantifying the medical student learning curve for ECG rhythm strip interpretation using deliberate practice.
citation: Waechter Jason, Reading David, Lee Chel Hee, Walker Mathieu. (2019). Quantifying the medical student learning curve for ECG rhythm strip interpretation using deliberate practice. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc40. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001248.shtml
title: Freely accessible online ECG rhythm strip practice platform with automated multi-component feedback and optional instructor email
description: The online platform at teachingmedicine.com delivered rhythm strip practice cases for 14 ACLS-level diagnoses in three discrete modules, each case requiring 8 characterization questions and 2 diagnosis questions. It recorded accuracy against expert consensus and time on task, and provided "Four types of immediate feedback": correctness marking, a side-by-side criteria table for errors, an explanatory case discussion, and instructor email response within 24 hours. Motivation features displayed evolving performance and peer comparisons.
requirements: Feedback depends on instructor availability for the email component; the article reports about 1 email question per 360 cases practiced.
constraints: The practice library contained only 42 unique cases, so students practicing more than 42 cases repeated cases; the authors judge the library too small for targeting 80% or greater accuracy.
target_learning_goals: ECG rhythm strip diagnosis of 14 ACLS-level rhythms
examples: 314 students completed 18,466 practice cases with feedback delivered for every case; exam cases were drawn separately for the Calgary paper exam.
key_sources: Waechter Jason, Reading David, Lee Chel Hee, Walker Mathieu. (2019). Quantifying the medical student learning curve for ECG rhythm strip interpretation using deliberate practice. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc40. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001248.shtml

article_title: Resident performance in basic perioperative transesophageal echocardiography: Comparing 3 teaching methods in a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Weber U, Zapletal B, Base E, Hambrusch M, Ristl R, Mora B, Schaller B. (2019). Resident performance in basic perioperative transesophageal echocardiography: Comparing 3 teaching methods in a randomized controlled trial. Medicine 98(36):e17072. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000017072
title: Web-based TEE simulator and CAE Vimedix mannequin simulator as TEE training tools
description: Two simulation artifacts anchored the training interventions. The e-learning group used a freely accessible online TEE simulator developed by the Perioperative Interactive Education group at Toronto General Hospital, which "allows viewing standard TEE image planes and has a steerable 3D heart model." The simulation and examination groups used the CAE Vimedix mannequin-based TEE simulator, on which residents demonstrated the 11 basic views within a 10-minute limit, scored 0–10 per view on imaging angle, clarity, and visualization of three anatomic structures.
requirements: Residents in the e-learning group were limited to 1 hour with the online simulator per study session and no additional studying
Practical examinations were standardized on the simulation mannequin for all groups
constraints: The study evaluated knowledge and demonstration of normal images only, not abnormal-image interpretation or machine operation
target_learners: Anesthesia and intensive care residents with no prior echocardiography training
target_learning_goals: Acquire the 11 basic perioperative TEE views, including echo-anatomy knowledge and psychomotor probe-handling skills
examples: Residents completed 2 individual 1-hour training sessions via the online simulator, one-on-one with the mannequin, or one-on-one in the operating theatre
key_sources: Weber U, Zapletal B, Base E, Hambrusch M, Ristl R, Mora B, Schaller B. (2019). Resident performance in basic perioperative transesophageal echocardiography: Comparing 3 teaching methods in a randomized controlled trial. Medicine 98(36):e17072. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000017072

article_title: School performance is age appropriate with support services in very preterm children at 11 years of age.
citation: Nyman A, Korhonen T, Lehtonen L, Haataja L, on behalf of the PIPARI Study Group. (2019). School performance is age appropriate with support services in very preterm children at 11 years of age. Acta Paediatrica. https://doi.org/10.1111/apa.14763
title: Assess very preterm children's educational outcomes with teacher ratings of daily classroom and academic functioning alongside cognitive test scores
description: The article argues teachers are key informants on daily adaptive functioning because cognitive scores alone miss functional educational outcomes. The authors state: "At school age, teachers are key informants when gathering data on these aspects of the daily adaptive functioning of very preterm born children." Their questionnaire rated academic skills and classroom functioning against Finnish National Core Curriculum criteria, plus support services received.
requirements: A teacher who teaches all or a majority of subjects, consulting other teachers if needed, comparing the pupil to age-appropriate curriculum criteria
constraints: The authors note some special education teachers may have had lower expectations, which could have contributed to the lack of group differences in teacher ratings
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of academic and classroom functioning
examples: Teachers rated reading, reading comprehension, spelling, text production, mathematics, social skills, group work, independent work, persistency and concentration in three categories dichotomised to average-or-above vs mild-or-severe problems
key_sources: Nyman A, Korhonen T, Lehtonen L, Haataja L, on behalf of the PIPARI Study Group. (2019). School performance is age appropriate with support services in very preterm children at 11 years of age. Acta Paediatrica. https://doi.org/10.1111/apa.14763

article_title: The teaching order of using direct laryngoscopy first may improve the learning outcome of endotracheal incubation: A preliminary, randomized controlled trial.
citation: Gu Minglu MM, Lian Ming MM, Gong Chao MM, Chen Lianhua MD, PhD, LI Shitong MD, PhD, Lu. Min. (2019). The teaching order of using direct laryngoscopy first may improve the learning outcome of endotracheal incubation: A preliminary, randomized controlled trial. Medicine 98(21): e15624. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000015624
title: Teach endotracheal intubation with direct laryngoscopy before video laryngoscopy
description: The article recommends sequencing ETI training so that trainees practice direct laryngoscopy first and video laryngoscopy second. Its trial found that "if trainees first learn to perform ETI using DL, then the subsequent learning of VL will be improved," while starting with VL gave no subsequent benefit for learning DL. The recommendation rests on shorter second-series intubation times and fewer CUSUM attempts in the DL-first group.
requirements: Trainees with no prior ETI experience; a supervised setting with an attending anesthesiologist present; a formal ETI course with simulator-based practice before live intubations
constraints: Conducted at only 1 teaching institution; results may not generalize because staff training techniques might differ; the study did not test whether mixed sequences (e.g., 10 VL attempts + 10 DL attempts) improve a designated technique; results are offered as reference criteria only, not authoritative criteria
target_learners: Medical students and new trainees with no endotracheal intubation experience in anesthesiology rotations
target_learning_goals: Performing endotracheal intubation with direct and video laryngoscopy, reducing intubation time and failure rate
examples: In the trial, the DL-first group's second-series mean intubation time was significantly shorter (P = .006) and its trainees crossed the 20% acceptable failure rate line in a mean of 18 attempts, versus more than 20 for the VL-first group
key_sources: Gu Minglu MM, Lian Ming MM, Gong Chao MM, Chen Lianhua MD, PhD, LI Shitong MD, PhD, Lu. Min. (2019). The teaching order of using direct laryngoscopy first may improve the learning outcome of endotracheal incubation: A preliminary, randomized controlled trial. Medicine 98(21): e15624. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000015624

article_title: Females show more sustained performance during test-taking than males.
citation: Balart, P. & Oosterveen, M. (2019). Females show more sustained performance during test-taking than males. Nature Communications, 10, 3798. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-11691-y
title: Use test length as a tool for reducing gender gaps in test scores, extending time framed as rewarding sustained performance rather than compensating for weakness
description: The article proposes that test design can reduce gender gaps: "our findings point to test length as a tool for reducing the gender gaps in test scores", with longer tests shrinking the math gap and shorter tests expected to shrink the reading gap. It also suggests reframing time extensions, such as the Oxford change, as rewarding a skill in which female students perform relatively better rather than compensating for a female weakness. The recommendation rests on the study 2 association and the study 1 sustaining-performance finding.
requirements: Tests must have a time limit for sustained performance to be relevant, since without one there is no reason a test should measure sustained performance
constraints: Study 2 does not exploit exogenous variation in test length, making a causal interpretation challenging
No changes in test length can be made without considering potential consequences for test validity
target_learning_goals: fair and valid assessment of math, science, and reading achievement
reducing gender gaps in test scores and STEM-related outcomes
examples: Study 2 regressed the standardized math gender gap on the number of questions across 203 timed tests, finding females on par with males at 125 questions
The article reframes the Oxford University time-extension policy as rewarding sustained performance rather than compensating for time-pressure weakness
key_sources: Balart, P. & Oosterveen, M. (2019). Females show more sustained performance during test-taking than males. Nature Communications, 10, 3798. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-11691-y

article_title: Technology-Based Interventions, Assessments, and Solutions for Safe Driving Training for Adolescents: Rapid Review.
citation: Emre Sezgin, Simon Lin. (2019). Technology-Based Interventions, Assessments, and Solutions for Safe Driving Training for Adolescents: Rapid Review. JMIR mHealth and uHealth. https://doi.org/10.2196/11942
title: Three-category taxonomy of technology-based approaches to teen driving safety: in-vehicle technologies, smartphones, and gamification
description: This rapid review organizes the literature on technology-based teen driving safety into three categories: "(1) in-vehicle technologies (using built-in tracking devices in the car and an installed black box), (2) smartphones (using apps and the sensors of a smartphone), and (3) gamification (an extension of smartphones used to increase compliance and sustainability of safe driving)". The taxonomy structures the review's synthesis of 16 studies, its Table 2 grouping, and its assessment of evidence maturity, with in-vehicle technology having the most evidence and gamification the least. It also underpins the review's recommendations for future intervention development.
requirements: Studies must test the driving behavior of teens with technology-based intervention methods, published in peer-reviewed journals between January 2000 and March 2018, to map onto the taxonomy.
constraints: The review did not break findings down by method categorization or teens' learning progress level, and did not address regional or national policies and regulations for transportation and driving.
target_learners: adolescent and young novice drivers (approximately 16-24 years old)
target_learning_goals: safe driving behavior and injury prevention
reduction of risky driving events
examples: The review's Table 2 groups the 16 included studies under the headings In-vehicle technologies, Smartphone, and Gamification with smartphone.
key_sources: Emre Sezgin, Simon Lin. (2019). Technology-Based Interventions, Assessments, and Solutions for Safe Driving Training for Adolescents: Rapid Review. JMIR mHealth and uHealth. https://doi.org/10.2196/11942

article_title: Rating the quality of teamwork-a comparison of novice and expert ratings using the Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM) in simulated emergencies.
citation: Freytag Julia, Stroben Fabian, Hautz Wolf E., Schauber Stefan K., Kämmer Juliane E. (2019). Rating the quality of teamwork—a comparison of novice and expert ratings using the Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM) in simulated emergencies. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-019-0591-9
title: Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM), German translation
description: TEAM is an observational instrument of 11 items measuring teamwork behaviour of medical teams in critical situations, with 3 subscales (leadership, teamwork, task management), items rated 0–4, a sum score of 0–44, and a global rating scale of 1–10. The authors translated it into German using TRAPD methodology and validated it in a simulation study, concluding it "is a reliable and valid tool to assess teamwork performance that closes a gap in measuring teamwork behaviour in German-speaking countries."
requirements: Raters receive rater training including an introduction to TEAM, information about common rating errors, and frame-of-reference training with videotaped examples
constraints: TEAM scores should not be compared across different cases, per the authors
Suitability for situations other than CPR and performance benchmarks require further research
target_learners: final-year medical students in emergency simulation
target_learning_goals: assessing teamwork, leadership and task management in emergency care
examples: Used by 6 novice and 6 expert raters to independently rate 7 teams rotating through 6 simulated emergency cases
key_sources: Freytag Julia, Stroben Fabian, Hautz Wolf E., Schauber Stefan K., Kämmer Juliane E. (2019). Rating the quality of teamwork—a comparison of novice and expert ratings using the Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM) in simulated emergencies. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-019-0591-9

article_title: Teacher Knowledge for Active-Learning Instruction: Expert-Novice Comparison Reveals Differences.
citation: Auerbach A. J., Higgins M., Brickman P., Andrews T. C. (2018). Teacher Knowledge for Active-Learning Instruction: Expert–Novice Comparison Reveals Differences. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-07-0149
title: Teacher noticing as a construct for studying knowledge for active-learning instruction in undergraduate STEM
description: Teacher noticing treats classrooms as complex social environments where teachers cannot attend to everything; it is knowledge in action used to reason about what teachers see and make instructional decisions in real time. The article applies this K–12 construct to undergraduate active learning for the first time, arguing active-learning instructors must recognize and respond to student thinking in real time, and operationalizes it with a video-based lesson-analysis survey comparing experts and novices.
requirements: Requires rich knowledge built through experience to notice and reason efficiently
Requires stimuli such as videos of authentic lessons and evaluative writing prompts to elicit noticing
constraints: The article notes teacher noticing had not previously been used as a theoretical construct for active-learning instruction in undergraduate STEM
target_learners: Undergraduate STEM instructors, especially those teaching large (50+ student) courses
target_learning_goals: Knowledge for effective active-learning instruction, including attending to student thinking
examples: Participants watched three videos of authentic active-learning lessons of no more than 5 minutes and responded to prompts about what was effective and what needed improvement
key_sources: Auerbach A. J., Higgins M., Brickman P., Andrews T. C. (2018). Teacher Knowledge for Active-Learning Instruction: Expert–Novice Comparison Reveals Differences. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-07-0149

article_title: Self-perceived competence in early diagnosis of cervical cancer among recently graduated physicians from Lima, Peru.
citation: Zafra-Tanaka JH, Hurtado-Villanueva ME, Saenz-Naranjo MdP, Taype-Rondan A. (2018). Self-perceived competence in early diagnosis of cervical cancer among recently graduated physicians from Lima, Peru. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0203778
title: Teach medical students first-level-of-care screening procedures such as VIA and VILI, not only hospital-centered procedures
description: The authors recommend that Peruvian medical education extend beyond hospital-based procedures to the screening tests graduates will actually perform in first-level care, since the survey found lower self-perceived competence for VIA and VILI than for PAP. They write that "efforts should be made to teach Peruvian medical students competencies in not only hospital procedures, but also in those that they will perform as physicians at the first level of care, such as VIA and VILI."
requirements: Medical curricula currently centered on the hospital environment, where PAP and colposcopy dominate
constraints: Recommendation grounded in self-perceived rather than objectively measured competence
target_learners: recently graduated physicians performing rural social service (SERUMS) in Peru
target_learning_goals: competence in performing VIA and VILI cervical cancer screening at the first level of care
examples: The survey found only 60.5% and 58.1% of graduates felt adequately competent for VIA and VILI respectively, versus 86.2% for PAP
key_sources: Zafra-Tanaka JH, Hurtado-Villanueva ME, Saenz-Naranjo MdP, Taype-Rondan A. (2018). Self-perceived competence in early diagnosis of cervical cancer among recently graduated physicians from Lima, Peru. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0203778

article_title: Helping Babies Breathe, Second Edition: A Model for Strengthening Educational Programs to Increase Global Newborn Survival.
citation: Kamath-Rayne BD, Thukral A, Visick MK, Schoen E, Amick E, Deorari A, Cain CJ, Keenan WJ, Singhal N, Little GA, Niermeyer S. (2018). Helping Babies Breathe, Second Edition: A Model for Strengthening Educational Programs to Increase Global Newborn Survival. Global Health: Science and Practice. https://doi.org/10.9745/GHSP-D-18-00147
title: Ten essential action points for national dissemination and implementation of Helping Babies Survive programs
description: An Utstein-style stakeholder meeting formulated 10 essential action points for national dissemination and implementation of the Helping Babies Survive and Helping Mothers Survive programs. The points span establishing a maternal-newborn-child health alliance, forming a working group for advocacy and planning, nation-to-facility training plans, simultaneous provision of adapted materials and equipment, supporting local champions, and setting up "local systems for frequent, brief refresher training, debriefing, and audits."
requirements: Country-level alliance with public, private, and nongovernmental partners; a functional working group; a financial plan to implement and sustain the program
constraints: Achieving impact at the population level requires integration of the curriculum into the regional health system
target_learners: Birth attendants, facilitators, and national health leaders in resource-limited settings
target_learning_goals: Sustained nationwide coverage of high-quality neonatal resuscitation training
examples: The action points include collecting and reporting local data on a standardized set of indicators and developing looped reporting and feedback to and from all levels of the health system
key_sources: Kamath-Rayne BD, Thukral A, Visick MK, Schoen E, Amick E, Deorari A, Cain CJ, Keenan WJ, Singhal N, Little GA, Niermeyer S. (2018). Helping Babies Breathe, Second Edition: A Model for Strengthening Educational Programs to Increase Global Newborn Survival. article_title: Enhancing communication skills for telehealth: development and implementation of a Teach-Back intervention for a national maternal and child health helpline in Australia.
citation: Morony Suzanne, Weir Kristie, Duncan Gregory, Biggs Janice, Nutbeam Don, Mccaffery Kirsten J. (2018). Enhancing communication skills for telehealth: development and implementation of a Teach-Back intervention for a national maternal and child health helpline in Australia. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-2956-6
title: Two-hour Teach-Back training workshop with video, handouts and telephone-simulating role play
description: A single 2-h group workshop for 7–8 nurses, run by two facilitators with a collaborative rather than didactic approach. It comprised two modules (introduction to Teach-Back; Teach-Back in practice), a short video of a distracted caller to illustrate a universal precautions approach, two double-sided handouts of strategies and phrases, and role play with nurses' backs to each other to simulate the telephone environment, swapping roles and partners. Nurses "enjoyed the practical application of skill during role play".
requirements: Small-group face-to-face format; facilitators experienced in call centre operations and Teach-Back training; evidence-based materials adapted to the workplace
constraints: Not all calls are amenable to Teach-Back; nurses were told to use professional judgement; one nurse felt the training had too much theory and not enough role playing
target_learning_goals: knowledge, skills and beliefs for using Teach-Back in telephone consultations
examples: Group 2 completed two role-plays with different partners; nurses identified call scenarios suitable for Teach-Back and phrasings that felt natural
key_sources: Morony Suzanne, Weir Kristie, Duncan Gregory, Biggs Janice, Nutbeam Don, Mccaffery Kirsten J. (2018). BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-2956-6

article_title: Conveying practical clinical skills with the help of teaching associates-a randomised trial with focus on the long term learning retention.
citation: Hoefer, S. H., Sterz, J., Bender, B., Stefanescu, M.-C., Theis, M., Walcher, F., Sader, R., Ruesseler, M. (2017). Conveying practical clinical skills with the help of teaching associates—a randomised trial with focus on the long term learning retention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0892-5
title: Teaching associates as trained simulation-patient instructors providing concurrent visuohaptic multimodal feedback
description: Teaching associates are advanced students trained to act as simulation patients and use their own bodies to teach examination techniques, giving immediate feedback so students practice until they get it right. In this trial the feedback was defined as concurrent visuohaptic multimodal feedback, an augmented feedback provided by the TA during the exercise, with feedback information transferred by speech also strongly perceived in a visual and haptic manner. The authors align the method with the guidance hypothesis.
requirements: TAs receive a training session (240 min) covering giving feedback and performing the examination, plus a training manual with a detailed description of all items
students practice on the TA's body during the exercise period so feedback can be concurrent
constraints: The article situates the method especially in gynecology, urology, and proctology, and notes studies of TAs in other contexts are rare
target_learning_goals: complex practical clinical examination skills such as the structured head and skull examination
examples: In the trial, two TAs led the examination exercise for the intervention group within the 210-minute cranio-maxillofacial surgery module, replacing one-on-one peer practice under instructor supervision
key_sources: Hoefer, S. H., Sterz, J., Bender, B., Stefanescu, M.-C., Theis, M., Walcher, F., Sader, R., Ruesseler, M. (2017). Conveying practical clinical skills with the help of teaching associates—a randomised trial with focus on the long term learning retention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0892-5

article_title: Repeated testing improves achievement in a blended learning approach for risk competence training of medical students: results of a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Spreckelsen C., Juenger J. (2017). Repeated testing improves achievement in a blended learning approach for risk competence training of medical students: results of a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1016-y
title: Test-enhanced learning: retrieval during testing increases retention, explained by total-time and retrieval hypotheses
description: Test-enhanced learning is defined in the article as "increased retention of knowledge or skills that is produced by the act of retrieval during testing". The article presents two explanatory factors: the total-time hypothesis (enhanced exposure to learning content) and the retrieval hypothesis (cognitive effort stimulated by recalling knowledge to solve the test). Instructional designs implement it via repeated testing and feedback supporting self-regulation, and repeated testing can be further improved by spaced learning with increasing intervals between test repetitions.
requirements: Tests that require learners to actively retrieve knowledge or skills, ideally with feedback and spaced repetition of tests
constraints: The article notes laboratory-setting evidence and flags, citing Cantillon, that test-enhanced learning needs evaluation as a curriculum-wide strategy to avoid skewing learning study behaviour
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of knowledge and skills
risk estimation and communication competence
examples: The study operationalized test-enhanced learning as a sequence of six short weekly online tests with immediate electronic feedback, delivered via Moodle with 6-day availability windows enabling spaced learning
key_sources: Spreckelsen C., Juenger J. (2017). Repeated testing improves achievement in a blended learning approach for risk competence training of medical students: results of a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1016-y

article_title: Peer-assisted learning: time for nomenclature clarification.
citation: Olaussen Alexander, Reddy Priya, Irvine Susan, Williams Brett. (2016). Peer-assisted learning: time for nomenclature clarification. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.3402/meo.v21.30974
title: Ten Cate and Durning's three-component framework: education distance, group size, and formality
description: The review reports that Ten Cate and Durning "distinguish PAL programmes based on three believed core components: 1) education distance, 2) group size, and 3) formality". The present authors endorse education distance as the key factor separating peers from near-peers and group size as practically important, but note there is limited evidence on the impact of formality on PAL outcomes and that formality is difficult to include in nomenclature given its wide variation across institutions.
requirements: Distinguishing PAL programmes by education distance, group size, and formality
constraints: The article states there is limited evidence around the impact formality has on PAL outcomes, and formality varies vastly amongst education institutions
target_learners: healthcare students in peer-assisted learning programmes
target_learning_goals: classifying PAL programmes by structural dimensions
