article_title: Simulation training for emergency teams to manage acute ischemic stroke by telemedicine.
citation: Richard Sébastien PhD, Mione Gioia MD, Varoqui Claude MD, Vezain Arnaud, Brunner Arielle MD, Bracard Serge PhD, Debouverie Marc PhD, Braun Marc PhD, Peralta. Luis Pinet. (2016). Simulation training for emergency teams to manage acute ischemic stroke by telemedicine. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000003924
title: Telestroke spoke-team simulation training module (Virtuall)
description: A standardized medical simulation training module in which 1 or 2 physicians and 2 nurses per session manage a simulated acute stroke patient with a manikin (SimMan, Laerdal Medical) while the rest of the team observes via video and audio transmission. The scenario includes an 85-year-old patient with left hemiplegia, NIHSS score 16, imaging results, and a collegial rt-PA decision with the hub. The article states "The simulation was followed by a debriefing with the neurologist and the expert physician for simulation training," and every learning goal was broached with corrections and advice. It was delivered to 225 learners from 6 spoke emergency teams between February 2013 and May 2015.
requirements: At least 1 neurologist from the hub, a physician and a nurse experienced in medical simulation training, and a technician supervise each session.
Material for catheterization, blood withdrawal, dummy rt-PA, antihypertensive drugs, syringe pumps, dose-calculation tables, and NIHSS tables must be available.
constraints: Examination of motor functions was not possible with the manikin, so a video of an anonymized patient was used.
Application of the scenario could be improved by including the weighing equipment and a simulation of the telestroke software.
target_learning_goals: examine stroke patients and report cases concisely to the expert center
prepare patients and administer intravenous rt-PA treatment
understand telestroke procedures and rt-PA indications
examples: 225 learners from 6 emergency teams in the Virtuall telestroke system received the module in sixteen sessions from February 2013 to May 2015.
key_sources: Richard Sébastien PhD, Mione Gioia MD, Varoqui Claude MD, Vezain Arnaud, Brunner Arielle MD, Bracard Serge PhD, Debouverie Marc PhD, Braun Marc PhD, Peralta. Luis Pinet. (2016). Simulation training for emergency teams to manage acute ischemic stroke by telemedicine. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000003924

article_title: Text messaging versus email for emergency medicine residents' knowledge retention: a pilot comparison in the United States.
citation: Hoonpongsimanont W, Kulkarni M, Tomas-Domingo P, Anderson C, McCormack D, Tu K, Chakravarthy B, Lotfipour S. (2016). Text messaging versus email for emergency medicine residents' knowledge retention: a pilot comparison in the United States. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2016.13.36
title: Text-message and email delivery intervention for EM resident knowledge retention
description: A delivery-method intervention in which researchers created EM educational material from the board-review textbook "Emergency Medicine: A Focused Review of the Core Curriculum" and delivered it via the Celly group text messaging system twice daily (100 messages over two months) to the text group, while the email group received one mid-period email with the exact same material. Outcomes were measured with a 40-question pre- and post-intervention exam from the Physician's Evaluation and Educational Review VII and VIII.
requirements: Residents needed to possess a mobile phone and be familiar with text messaging
constraints: The text messaging system had a maximum character restriction, requiring symbols and abbreviations
target_learners: PGY 1 to PGY 3 & 4 emergency medicine residents
target_learning_goals: Retention of emergency medicine core content for ABEM board preparation
examples: Fifty-eight residents at three US EM residency programs were randomized within PGY to text or email delivery in 2014

article_title: Students' perception and experience of intimate area examination and sexual history taking during undergraduate clinical skills training: A study from two Saudi medical colleges.
citation: Abdulghani Hamza Mohammad et al. (2016). Students’ perception and experience of intimate area examination and sexual history taking during undergraduate clinical skills training: A study from two Saudi medical colleges. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000004400
title: Balance sensitive clinical-skills training with patients' religious, sociocultural, and ethical values by providing positive teacher support and supervision
description: The article holds that acquiring intimate-area examination and sexual-history-taking competence requires balancing student learning needs with religious and socioethical principles governing patient interactions. It concludes teachers must 'provide the necessary support to the students during their IAE and SHT clinical skills training' and develop novel techniques without compromising the Kingdom's religious, sociocultural, and ethical beliefs.
requirements: Supervision and proper training must be present; the article reports lack of supervision and lack of proper training as significant student-reported barriers.
constraints: In this cultural setting, religious teachings discourage opposite-sex examination of private parts, and patient refusal rates were high (54.7% for IAEs, 35.5% for SHT).
target_learning_goals: clinical skills training for sensitive examinations and sexual history taking
examples: Students reported lack of supervision (39.8% male, 39.5% female) and lack of proper training as barriers to IAE learning.
key_sources: Abdulghani Hamza Mohammad et al. (2016). Students’ perception and experience of intimate area examination and sexual history taking during undergraduate clinical skills training: A study from two Saudi medical colleges. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000004400

article_title: Technology in postgraduate medical education: a dynamic influence on learning?
citation: Bullock A, Webb K. (2015). Technology in postgraduate medical education: a dynamic influence on learning? Postgraduate Medical Journal 91(1081):646-650. https://doi.org/10.1136/postgradmedj-2014-132809
title: Mapping uses of technology for learning onto Kolb's learning cycle and Eraut's intentions of informal learning
description: The article maps three technology uses onto learning theory: simulations offer concrete experience and active experimentation, social media may support reflective observation, and apps offer access to knowledge assisting abstract conceptualisation in Kolb's cycle. It likewise relates them to Eraut's "three intentions of informal learning: implicit, reactive and deliberative", matching point-of-care apps to reactive learning and simulation to deliberative learning (table 1).
requirements: Educational uses of technology must be relatable to stages of the learning cycle or to intentions of informal learning for the mapping to apply
constraints: The article notes that m-learning, simulation and social media are umbrella terms encompassing a range of different learning purposes and may be associated with different underlying education theories
target_learning_goals: workplace learning
reflection on practice
clinical decision-making
examples: Table 1 links m-learning to abstract conceptualisation and reactive learning, simulation to concrete experience, active experimentation and deliberative learning, and social media to reflective observation and implicit, reactive and deliberative learning
key_sources: Bullock A, Webb K. (2015). Technology in postgraduate medical education: a dynamic influence on learning? Postgraduate Medical Journal 91(1081):646-650. https://doi.org/10.1136/postgradmedj-2014-132809

article_title: Improving confidence and competence of healthcare professionals in end-of-life care: an evaluation of the 'Transforming End of Life Care' course at an acute hospital trust.

title: Transforming End of Life Care (TEoLC): a free 2-day multiprofessional course for non-specialist palliative care providers
description: The TEoLC course is a free, 2-day course run by an inner-city tertiary hospital since 2012 for "multiprofessional, non-specialist palliative care staff working in local hospitals and the community". It covers last days of life, the AMBER care bundle, Fast Track discharge, symptom management, advance care planning, difficult conversations, spiritual and cultural aspects, and family support. Teaching uses lectures, case-based group work, interactive workshops and Q&A sessions, taught by palliative care nurses, consultants, social workers and a chaplain.

constraints: Content is dynamic, responding to participants' needs, and was developed from national and local policy imperatives and staff's informally expressed needs

examples: 236 staff completed the course across 10 training sessions between May 2012 and April 2014

article_title: Association between physical activity and teacher-reported academic performance among fifth-graders in Shanghai: a quantile regression.
citation: Zhang Yunting, Zhang Donglan, Jiang Yanrui, Sun Wanqi, Wang Yan, Chen Wenjuan, Li Shenghui, Shi Lu, Shen Xiaoming, Zhang Jun, Jiang Fan. (2015). title: Teacher-reported Academic Performance Scores questionnaire based on Oliviero Bruni's Teacher school achievement form
description: The outcome instrument is a teacher-reported academic performance scores (APS) questionnaire "developed based on the Oliviero Bruni's Teacher school achievement form", composed of six items covering reading ability, reading comprehension, mathematics, executive ability, interest and attention. Components such as listening and speaking, reading, writing, and mathematical calculation and reasoning were rated by head teachers on 5-point scales and summed. article_title: A randomised controlled trial of extended immersion in multi-method continuing simulation to prepare senior medical students for practice as junior doctors.
citation: Rogers Gary D, McConnell Harry W, Jones de Rooy Nicole, Ellem Fiona, Lombard Marise. (2014). A randomised controlled trial of extended immersion in multi-method continuing simulation to prepare senior medical students for practice as junior doctors. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-90
title: Tension-to-learn: revealed knowledge gaps in safe simulation as intrinsic motivation
description: The article takes as its theoretical underpinning the work of Burns and Gentry, inspired by Loewenstein's curiosity gap: a tension to learn is created when students appreciate a manageable gap between their current knowledge or skill and the state they aspire to achieve. Extended simulated patient care, where the consequences of skill and knowledge gaps can be demonstrated safely, is expected to generate a powerful tension to learn, motivating engagement with the associated just-in-time workshops. CLEIMS draws on the experiential pedagogical tradition of Dewey, Rogers, Knowles and Kolb.
requirements: Students must be invested in becoming competent practitioners so that a revealed deficiency in a valued quality acts as a motivator
constraints: The article presents this as a theoretical rationale; it was not directly tested as a mechanism in the trial
target_learners: medical students preparing for the junior doctor role
target_learning_goals: motivating engagement with just-in-time workshops and seminars
examples: The authors suggest the more complex Year 4 multi-patient simulations generated greater tension to learn than the simpler Year 3 experience
key_sources: Rogers Gary D, McConnell Harry W, Jones de Rooy Nicole, Ellem Fiona, Lombard Marise. (2014). A randomised controlled trial of extended immersion in multi-method continuing simulation to prepare senior medical students for practice as junior doctors. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-90

article_title: How to learn effectively in medical school: test yourself, learn actively, and repeat in intervals.
citation: Augustin Marc. (2014). How to Learn Effectively in Medical School: Test Yourself, Learn Actively, and Repeat in Intervals. The Yale Journal of Biology and Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4031794/
title: When learning factual knowledge, students should test themselves, actively recall information, and retest at expanding time intervals
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that whenever students learn factual knowledge, they "should test themselves while learning, actively recall information, and retest the facts at expanding time intervals" to make learning most effective. The author states these strategies help students learn the most in the least amount of time and assure optimal long-term retention of factual knowledge.
requirements: Learning content must be factual knowledge that can be freely recalled and retested at successive intervals
constraints: The author emphasizes that learning how to learn is not a standard part of the medical curriculum, and providing time to teach it is difficult because time is scarce in the medical curriculum
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of factual knowledge
Efficient learning under time constraints
examples: The article's example of applying the principle is recalling the five main adverse effects of beta-blockers by writing them down rather than rereading, then retesting at expanding intervals
key_sources: Augustin Marc. (2014). How to Learn Effectively in Medical School: Test Yourself, Learn Actively, and Repeat in Intervals. The Yale Journal of Biology and Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4031794/

article_title: Acceptance of technology-enhanced learning for a theoretical radiological science course: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Nkenke Emeka, Vairaktaris Elefterios, Bauersachs Anne, Eitner Stephan, Budach Alexander, Knipfer Christoph, Stelzle Florian. (2012). Acceptance of technology-enhanced learning for a theoretical radiological science course: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-18
title: Offer technology-enhanced learning as a flexible complement that reduces the need for face-to-face lectures without impairing exam results, rather than as a replacement for traditional teaching
description: The article concludes that technology-enhanced learning "has the potential to reduce the need for face-to-face lectures" while examination results remain unimpaired, but that it "cannot replace traditional education". It recommends letting each student combine e-learning modules and face-to-face lectures at their best convenience, since learners adapt e-learning use to their own circumstances and will not use all e-learning resources all the time. Face-to-face contact retains a place because learning is a social process and students consider lectures the basis of their education.
requirements: Face-to-face lectures remain available so students can back up e-learning with direct teacher contact
E-mail reminders and an introductory platform-familiarization session support uptake of the online modules
constraints: Students indicate they consider traditional teaching the basis of their education, so TEL cannot completely replace face-to-face lectures
The TEL group was significantly less confident in passing the exam even though results did not differ
target_learners: university students in theoretical health-science courses
target_learning_goals: theoretical radiological science knowledge assessed by multiple-choice examination
examples: In the trial, TEL students attended a mean of 2.5 of 8 lectures yet scored 18.3 ± 1.3 on the exam versus 18.6 ± 1.2 in the traditional group
key_sources: Nkenke Emeka, Vairaktaris Elefterios, Bauersachs Anne, Eitner Stephan, Budach Alexander, Knipfer Christoph, Stelzle Florian. (2012). Acceptance of technology-enhanced learning for a theoretical radiological science course: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-18

article_title: Assessing basic life support skills without an instructor: is it possible?
citation: Mpotos Nicolas, De Wever Bram, Valcke Martin A, Monsieurs Koenraad G. (2012). Assessing basic life support skills without an instructor: is it possible? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-58
title: Testing effect on skills learning via retrieval and elaboration of procedural knowledge
description: The article invokes the testing effect: adding a test as a final activity in a BLS course "seems to have a stronger long-term learning impact as compared to spending an equal amount of time practising the same skills". It attributes this to continuous retrieval processes and elaboration during retrieval, extending the account to procedural knowledge.
requirements: Future studies should investigate the intrinsic testing effect and the extrinsic learning effect of formative testing, informing the participant about performance and guiding towards further skills improvement and mastery
constraints: The article notes these theoretical assumptions were developed for declarative knowledge acquisition and only fit skills learning by extension
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of psychomotor skills such as BLS
examples: The authors propose incorporating automated skills testing as formative assessment in an adaptive learning cycle with repetitive testing
key_sources: Mpotos Nicolas, De Wever Bram, Valcke Martin A, Monsieurs Koenraad G. (2012). Assessing basic life support skills without an instructor: is it possible? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-58

article_title: The impact of a team-based intervention on the lifestyle risk factor management practices of community nurses: outcomes of the community nursing SNAP trial.
citation: Chan Bibiana C, Jayasinghe Upali W, Christl Bettina, Laws Rachel A, Orr Neil, Williams Anna, Partington Kate, Harris Mark F. (2013). The impact of a team-based intervention on the lifestyle risk factor management practices of community nurses: outcomes of the community nursing SNAP trial. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6963-13-54
title: Team-based SNAP intervention for community nurses
description: A multi-component service-level intervention to build generalist community health nurses' capacity for brief lifestyle (SNAP) assessment and intervention. It comprised a one-day training program with "role-plays with simulated clients (actors), group discussions and activities", integration of standard assessment tools and prompts into routine initial visits, a local service referral directory, and support resources such as written action plans, guides, tape measures and pedometers. A seconded site nurse supported local implementation.
requirements: One-day group training focused on the 5As model, motivational interviewing and goal setting
Standard assessment tools embedded in routine initial client visits
A local referral directory and implementation resources for nurses and clients
constraints: Referral component was limited by lack of local services, long waiting lists and transport difficulties
Time pressures from an acute-care-focused model of care threaten sustainability
target_learners: Generalist community health nurses in community health services
target_learning_goals: Brief lifestyle risk factor assessment and intervention skills
Motivational interviewing and goal setting
Confidence and self-efficacy in preventive care
examples: In the Community Nursing SNAP trial, four NSW community health services were randomly allocated to early or late intervention, with 129 nurses surveyed at baseline, 6 and 12 months.
key_sources: Chan Bibiana C, Jayasinghe Upali W, Christl Bettina, Laws Rachel A, Orr Neil, Williams Anna, Partington Kate, Harris Mark F. (2013). The impact of a team-based intervention on the lifestyle risk factor management practices of community nurses: outcomes of the community nursing SNAP trial. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6963-13-54

article_title: Teaching about health care disparities in the clinical setting.
citation: Glick SB, Fernandez L, Irby DM, Harleman E, Fernandez A. (2010). Teaching About Health Care Disparities in the Clinical Setting. J Gen Intern Med 25(Suppl 2):95–101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-009-1203-6
title: The TEST model (diagnose the learner, teach rapidly, provide feedback) as a framework for teaching health care disparities in time-limited clinical settings
description: The Time-Effective Strategies for Teaching (TEST) model is an established clinical-teaching model the authors adapt to disparities education. It structures teaching in three steps: "diagnose the learner's instructional need, then teach rapidly to that need and provide feedback." The paper argues it is "straightforward, easy to use," applicable in both inpatient and outpatient settings, and responsive to time-limited environments, and illustrates each component with clinical case scenarios.
requirements: A clinical teacher willing to address observed behaviors that may contribute to disparities, and a brief diagnostic step (probes or two-minute observation) before teaching
constraints: The authors present no empirical evaluation; the model's suitability for disparities teaching is argued, not tested
Intended for teaching within routine, time-limited clinical encounters rather than dedicated curricula
target_learners: Clinical teams in inpatient and outpatient settings
target_learning_goals: Recognizing and responding to provider behaviors and system circumstances that contribute to health care disparities
examples: Four case scenarios: interpreter use for limited English proficiency, knee replacement refusal, mistaken assumption of substance abuse, and failure to diagnose low health literacy
key_sources: Glick SB, Fernandez L, Irby DM, Harleman E, Fernandez A. (2010). Teaching About Health Care Disparities in the Clinical Setting. J Gen Intern Med 25(Suppl 2):95–101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-009-1203-6

article_title: Standards of resuscitation during inter-hospital transportation: the effects of structured team briefing or guideline review - a randomised, controlled simulation study of two micro-interventions.
citation: Høyer Christian B, Christensen Erika F, Eika Berit. (2011). Standards of resuscitation during inter-hospital transportation: the effects of structured team briefing or guideline review - A randomised, controlled simulation study of two micro-interventions. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/1757-7241-19-15
title: Checklist-based structured team briefing for inter-hospital transfer
description: A checklist developed by the authors reflecting the headlines in the resuscitation algorithm, used to structure a face-to-face briefing between the junior physician and the ambulance crew before a simulated transfer. Each item was followed by five task-allocation possibilities, from "1) ambulance crew only" to "5) physician only", with the optimum allocation marked based on the qualifications and competencies of physicians and crew. Physicians used a mean of about 206 seconds (approximately 3 1/4 minutes) to conduct the briefing.
requirements: Physicians must be instructed to use the time they feel necessary to read the checklist and brief the crew
Task allocation must reflect the actual qualifications and competencies of team members
constraints: The authors' data do not allow extrapolation of briefing time consumption to real clinical life
target_learners: junior physicians (graduated within 5 years) managing inter-hospital transfers
target_learning_goals: team leadership
task delegation
resource coordination during resuscitation
examples: In the simulation study, physicians in the team briefing group (n = 17) briefed the ambulance crew using the checklist before the simulated cardiac arrest scenario
key_sources: Høyer Christian B, Christensen Erika F, Eika Berit. (2011). Standards of resuscitation during inter-hospital transportation: the effects of structured team briefing or guideline review - A randomised, controlled simulation study of two micro-interventions. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/1757-7241-19-15

article_title: Teacher-made models: the answer for medical skills training in developing countries?
citation: Tran Trung Q, Scherpbier Albert, Van Dalen Jan, Wright Pamela E. (2012). Teacher-made models: the answer for medical skills training in developing countries? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-98
title: Teacher-made IV injection part-task trainer developed by skills-lab teachers at UMP Ho Chi Minh City
description: A hand-made part-task trainer for intravenous injection developed by teachers of the Skills Lab at the University of Medicine and Pharmacy, Ho Chi Minh City. It is "a hand-made silicone bandage which has one vein, a thin protection under the vein and a blood container", wrapped around a simulated patient's forearm, and cost 5 USD compared to 300–400 USD for a commercial IV model. It was tested and improved over time and used to train and assess IV injection skills.
requirements: Locally available materials and teacher involvement in design and production through a unit for learning material research and development
constraints: The study authors cannot be sure results on this teacher-made model apply to other teacher-made models
target_learning_goals: Intravenous injection technical skill and communication with the patient during the procedure
examples: Used in a randomized pretest-posttest study with three groups of nursing students at UMP HCMC, with students of the same course acting as simulated patients
key_sources: Tran Trung Q, Scherpbier Albert, Van Dalen Jan, Wright Pamela E. (2012). Teacher-made models: the answer for medical skills training in developing countries? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-98

article_title: Teacher-made models: the answer for medical skills training in developing countries?
citation: Tran Trung Q, Scherpbier Albert, Van Dalen Jan, Wright Pamela E. (2012). Teacher-made models: the answer for medical skills training in developing countries? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-98
title: Involve teachers in designing and producing locally made skills-training models as a sustainable, low-cost alternative to commercial simulators in resource-limited settings
description: The article recommends that medical schools in limited-resource settings make their own training models from locally available resources, with teachers involved in design and production. It concludes that "The TM appears to be an effective and appropriate alternative to CM for training on basic IV skills" at considerably lower cost, addressing the unsustainability of expensive commercial simulators whose capital and maintenance costs may exceed local budgets.
requirements: A unit or mechanism to motivate and support teachers to design and produce learning materials using locally available resources
constraints: Effectiveness was demonstrated for basic IV injection skills; generalization to other teacher-made models was not investigated
target_learners: Undergraduate medical and nursing students in developing countries
target_learning_goals: Basic clinical procedural skills such as intravenous injection
examples: UMP HCMC established a unit for learning material research and development whose staff motivate and support teachers to produce models; the IV model cost 5 USD versus 300–400 USD commercial
key_sources: Tran Trung Q, Scherpbier Albert, Van Dalen Jan, Wright Pamela E. (2012). Teacher-made models: the answer for medical skills training in developing countries? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-98

article_title: On the need to enhance physical insight via mathematical skills
citation: Sergio Rojas. (2007). Physical intuition and mathematical reasoning: On the need to enhance physical insight via mathematical skills. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.0059
title: Teach mathematical computation skills such as rotational inertia explicitly alongside conceptual understanding
description: The article argues that dismissing computations of moments of inertia, center of mass, and fields as distracting mathematics undermines reasoning in non-intuitive topics like rotational dynamics. It endorses the view that "students must be taught both concepts and problem solving skills explicitly if we want students to be proﬁcient at both." Practice should include proper physical interpretation of quantitative results.
requirements: Students need conceptual knowledge before carrying out experiments, per the article's statement that experiments presuppose having found I mathematically
constraints: The article notes intuition cannot serve as a good guide for computing I, so practice rather than intuition-building is required
target_learners: undergraduate students in calculus-based introductory physics courses
target_learning_goals: rotational dynamics
computing moments of inertia
connecting mathematical computation to physical insight
examples: The article proposes that honor students given enough training in computing rotational inertia of composite and simple objects would have answered more of the seven questions correctly
key_sources: Sergio Rojas. (2007). Physical intuition and mathematical reasoning: On the need to enhance physical insight via mathematical skills. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.0059

article_title: Relativity without tears
citation: Silagadze, Z. K. (2007). Relativity without tears. https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.0929
title: Shift the teaching focus from length contraction and time dilation to space-time structure and symmetries
description: The article argues that instructors should bear in mind the conventionality of the name theory of relativity and shift the pedagogical emphasis away from the familiar paradoxical effects. It states: "it should be instructive to bear in mind the conventionality of the name a nd the shift of focus from the length contraction and time dilation (whic h are rather obvious eﬀects in Minkowski's four-dimensional geometric f ormulation) to space-time structure and symmetries." In this framing, the essence of the theory is the independence of the laws of nature from the observer's point of view, not the relativity of space and time.
requirements: Familiarity with the Minkowski four-dimensional geometric formulation, in which length contraction and time dilation are obvious effects
target_learning_goals: understand special relativity through symmetries and space-time structure rather than paradoxical effects
examples: The article's own development follows this shift: after the one-postulate derivation it introduces the Erlangen program and Cayley-Klein geometries, treating Minkowski space-time as a coset space of the Poincaré group
key_sources: Silagadze, Z. K. (2007). Relativity without tears. https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.0929

article_title: Ettore Majorana's Inaugural Lecture on Theoretical Physics (Naples, Italy; Jan.13, 1938)
citation: Bruno Preziosi and Erasmo Recami. (2007). Ettore Majorana's Inaugural Lecture on Theoretical Physics (Neaples, Italy; Jan.13, 1938) with comments by the editors. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.0941
title: Teach the mathematical tools of quantum mechanics as physicists would, without worrying about excessive formal rigour
description: In his inaugural-lecture notes Majorana states that the mathematical tools essential to quantum mechanics should be exposed "not as mathematicians but rather as physicists would do", with the explicit criterion of not worrying about excessive formal rigour, which is often impossible to achieve. The aim is to discuss as clearly as possible the effective way physicists have actually used those tools for over a decade. This use, which has never led to difficulty or ambiguity, is what constitutes the essential source of their certainty.
requirements: The tools should be presented before the theory proper, so they are already familiar when students must use them
constraints: Formal rigour is not always easy and often totally impossible to achieve, so the exposition deliberately foregoes it
target_learners: university students beginning the study of atomic physics
target_learning_goals: understanding and applying the mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics
examples: Majorana planned to open his Naples theoretical physics course with an ample and clear discussion of the essential mathematical tools before deriving the theory from experimental data
key_sources: Bruno Preziosi and Erasmo Recami. (2007). Ettore Majorana's Inaugural Lecture on Theoretical Physics (Neaples, Italy; Jan.13, 1938) with comments by the editors. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.0941

article_title: The theory of relativity and the Pythagorean theorem
citation: L. B. Okun. (2008). The theory of relativity and the Pythagorean theorem. https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.2379
title: Teach modern physics from an advanced standpoint based on symmetry principles rather than from historical development
description: The paper recommends presenting relativity, in Felix Klein's phrase, "from an advanced standpoint": the modern standpoint based on symmetry principles and the theory of relativity avoids terminological confusion and paradoxes that a historical route produces. Teaching should cut the 'umbilical cord' to the preceding 'mother theory' of Maxwell's field theory plus Newton's mechanics, of which relativistic mass was the cord.
requirements: Instructors must themselves command the symmetry-based, c = 1 formulation of relativity, including the invariant-mass relation m2 = e2 − p2
constraints: The author states it is unacceptable to present the dependence of mass on velocity as an experimental fact, calling it a mere interpretational 'factoid'
target_learners: physics teachers and popularizers of science
target_learning_goals: understanding the theory of relativity
correct use of the concepts of mass, energy and momentum
examples: The paper presents the main formulas of relativity using mostly the Pythagorean theorem, with mass as one cathetus, momentum as the other, and energy as the hypotenuse
key_sources: L. B. Okun. (2008). The theory of relativity and the Pythagorean theorem. https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.2379

article_title: From Classical to Quantum Mechanics through Optics
citation: Jaume Masoliver, Ana Ros. (2009). From Classical to Quantum Mechanics through Optics. https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.3258
title: Teach quantum mechanics through the optics route rather than as an axiomatic system detached from classical mechanics
description: The paper argues that presenting quantum mechanics as a brand-new axiomatic development overlooks its intimate relation with classical mechanics, especially the Hamiltonian formulation. It instead reconstructs, for teaching purposes, the historical-pedagogical passage in which the Hamiltonian analogy leads to the eikonal correspondence, Schrödinger's phase hypothesis, the de Broglie wavelength, and finally the Schrödinger equation. As the paper puts it, "There is, therefore, a passage going from classical mechanics to quantum mechanics through optics, a path taken by Schr¨ odinger one century after Hamilton."
requirements: Learners need prior command of the Hamiltonian and Hamilton-Jacobi formulations of classical mechanics and of geometrical optics (wave equation, eikonal, Fermat's principle) for the route to be followable.
constraints: The correspondence between classical and wave mechanics is not biunivocal and demands conjectures; the derivations presented are approximations in the small-wavelength limit unless supplemented by the equivalence argument the paper cites.
target_learners: advanced undergraduate and graduate physics students
target_learning_goals: understand the conceptual origins of the Schrödinger equation
connect quantum mechanics with classical Hamiltonian mechanics and optics
examples: The paper follows Schrödinger's original idea step by step: Hamilton's analogy, the eikonal identification, the phase hypothesis S = K·phase, the stationary and generalized Schrödinger equations, and Schrödinger's wave-packet construction for the harmonic oscillator.
key_sources: Jaume Masoliver, Ana Ros. (2009). From Classical to Quantum Mechanics through Optics. https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.3258
